HC frees Ghaziabad woman from father's custody to join Muslim husband
Chauhan said she was 26 years old, had completed her BA and had married Akbar Khan.
The Allahabad high court on Tuesday allowed a 26-year-old Ghaziabad woman to leave her father’s custody and live with her Muslim husband, holding that an adult is entitled to choose her life partner and live according to her own wishes.
Justice Sandeep Jain passed the order on a habeas corpus petition, filed in September 2025, in connection with Sonika Chauhan, who was produced before the court on Tuesday in compliance with its September 8 order. She was brought to the court by a sub-inspector and a woman constable from Indirapuram police station.
During her interaction with the court, Chauhan said she was 26 years old, had completed her BA and had married Akbar Khan. She said she wanted to live with him and alleged that her father had confined her at home because he disapproved of her marriage.
Khan also appeared before the court and expressed his willingness to live with Chauhan.
Her father, Lakshman Singh Chauhan, however, alleged that his daughter had been blackmailed by Khan and was acting under his pressure.
After interacting with all the parties, the court held that a person who has attained age of majority has the fundamental right to choose a life partner and live according to her own wishes.
Such a choice, it said, is personal to the individual and cannot be dictated or controlled by the wishes of parents or other family members.
The court accordingly held that Chauhan was at liberty to live with Khan and directed the police to provide adequate security to the couple. It also directed the family members not to interfere in their matrimonial life.

Imagine a customer walking into a premium lifestyle store to buy a vase, but leaving with a dinner set, tableware, candles, and a few other pieces of décor for their living room. A few months later, the same customer is back, looking for a housewarming gift for family and friends. This is the loyalty that brands yearn for. Give more reasons for the customers to return and get a larger share of their wallet as well as their mind space. It’s never about one vase. This is exactly where the next leg of growth lies for the premium and mass-premium lifestyle market – not by abandoning what they are known for, but by finding more ways to bring the same customer back into their world. While some are simply moving from kitchenware into décor and gifting or from clothing into home and occasionwear, others are seeing an opportunity in new channels to reach those customers. The catch, however, is that every new avenue, be it physical retail, marketplaces, or quick commerce, comes with its own set of challenges. And there’s no channel that can be sacrificed. More stores mean more fixed costs More categories mean more inventory and operational complexity Wider distribution can bring reach but reduce control over the brand experience More discounting can move volume while making it harder to justify the premium tag The question, then, is not whether these brands can find new avenues for growth, but which of them can deliver growth without stretching their economics or diluting the brand. The Bar For Premium Is Rising From mass-premium homeware to more design-led and aspirational propositions, brands are carving out different positions to woo a crowded market. But the underlying challenge is: how do you give customers more reasons to buy? For Nestasia, the answer lies in making premium design accessible to a broader set of Indian consumers while expanding the occasions and categories around the brand. Cofounder Aditi Murarka Agrawal says the brand sees room to grow both its customer base and category presence. The mass-premium opportunity is therefore less about making premium products cheaper and more about widening the addressable consumer base without stripping away the attributes that justify the premium. Nestasia’s positioning sits around this balance of design, quality and accessibility, particularly for middle- and upper-middle-income consumers who may be trading up selectively rather than buying luxury across the board. “We see substantial room for deeper penetration. We already operate across D2C and marketplaces and have our exclusive brand outlets (EBOs). Meanwhile, trade and other offline channels remain relatively untapped opportunities that we are exploring to reach newer customer cohorts,” Agrawal said. Then, the customer is also changing. Products that once were bought purely for utility are increasingly being evaluated for how they look and what they say about the home. Kitchen tools, cookware, storage and dining products are becoming part of a broader design vocabulary. “The Indian consumer has become far more discerning. There is much greater exposure to international brands, and with that comes a sharper understanding of design, material and longevity. People are buying fewer things, but they want those things to mean something and to last,” said Rashi Sethia, the CEO of Nicobar, a modern Indian lifestyle and fashion brand. This shift changes the growth equation for premium brands. If consumers are becoming more deliberate about individual purchases, brands cannot rely on simply increasing product launches or pushing volume. They need to create more occasions in which the same consumer sees the brand as relevant, while retaining the design, material and craftsmanship cues that support the original purchase. While this creates an opportunity, it also raises the bar for many. Meanwhile, Kushal Bhagia, the founder and partner at All In Capital, sees repeat behaviour, full-price sell-through, contribution margins, customer acquisition costs and lifetime value as the more meaningful measures of demand. “For a premium consumer brand, I would want to see improving contribution margins, disciplined customer acquisition, healthy inventory turns and a credible path to EBITDA profitability. Growth can create value, but only if the economics improve as the business scales,” Bhagia added. The Cost Of Staying Premium Finding more customers is only one side of the equation, but serving them without diluting what made the brand attractive in the first place is another. For ellementry, a premium handcrafted homeware brand, expansion has meant moving beyond kitchenware and tableware into décor, furniture, soft furnishings and gifting. But founder Ayush Baid sees a clear limit to category expansion. “Our filter is fairly simple: does the category let us use the same design philosophy and manufacturing strengths such as our artisans, our materials, our craftsmanship, or does it require us to build an entirely new competency from scratch?” he said. This matters because premium positioning can make some conventional growth tactics counterproductive. A case in point is heavy discounting, which may accelerate sales but can also teach customers to wait for promotions. Similarly, wider distribution may create reach but can compress the experience through which a design-led brand communicates its value. The same tension is emerging with quick commerce. For ellementry, platforms such as Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart have created new impulse and gifting-led buying occasions that were not meaningful to the brand a few years ago. But the channel also changes the nature of discovery: a premium product can suddenly compete alongside convenience-led purchases and price-led promotions. Nicobar’s approach is similarly selective. Its expansion into gifting, eveningwear, menswear and home is being framed not as a way to increase the product count, but as an attempt to accompany the same customer across more occasions. “So, as we look at new categories and new markets, the first question is never: ‘How big is this opportunity?’ but ‘Does this feel genuinely right for Nicobar?’” CEO Sethia said. Physical retail creates another version of the same trade-off. A store can help a consumer experience materials, craftsmanship and the full product universe, but it also creates rent, staffing and inventory costs. The Next Growth Engine If premium brands cannot simply sell more of the same product to the same customer, the next phase of growth will depend on creating more reasons to buy. That need for growth becomes clearer when the scale of some of these businesses is put into perspective. Nestasia reported ₹115 Cr in revenue in FY25 but posted a ₹7.7 Cr loss, while Nicobar reported ₹174.8 Cr in revenue in FY25 and a ₹13.6 Cr profit. Aditya Birla Group-acquired Jaypore reported ₹93.5 Cr revenue in FY25, with a loss of ₹55.9 Cr. These are meaningful businesses, but they are still some distance from the scale of India's larger consumer franchises. Therefore, the next phase is less about proving demand for premium lifestyle products and more about finding the levers that can take a ₹100–200 Cr brand to its next stage of scale. Nestasia is eyeing adjacent categories and new channels; the company sees an opportunity in moving towards more elevated homes, better dining experiences and design-led kitchen spaces. For ellementry, the opportunity extends beyond India. According to cofounder Baid, the brand is seeing demand for Indian design and craftsmanship internationally, while digital channels are making premium products more accessible to consumers. “The key to making these opportunities commercially viable will be balancing design and craftsmanship with operational efficiency, consistent quality, and the right distribution strategy,” he said. Geography could become an equally important growth lever. The next affluent customer may not necessarily emerge from a traditional metro city. Consumers in smaller cities are increasingly exposed to global brands and design trends, while physical access to premium labels remains more limited. Nicobar sees physical expansion outside the metros as an inevitable part of the growth strategy. But the economics have to catch up with the aspiration: sensible retail costs, adequate demand and supply chains capable of maintaining quality. All in all, the broader opportunity for these brands lies not in India’s rising affluent population but in the premium that their customers can willfully cough up repeatedly. A larger category portfolio can increase wallet share, but only if the categories reinforce the brand. More stores can create discovery, but only if they eventually generate attractive returns. New channels can widen reach, but not if they train consumers to expect discounts. The brands that crack this equation well won’t just sell one vase but a reason to keep coming back. SPOTLIGHT | The Indian Puja Box Wants To Modernise Everyday Rituals Founded in 2021 by Maithili and Giresh Vasudev Kulkarni, the D2C startup offers curated puja kits and devotional products aimed at making everyday Hindu rituals more convenient and organised, building around the idea of a ‘masala dibba’ for puja essentials. Its flagship Puja Boxes bring together essentials such as agarbatti, dhoop, Gangajal, kumkum, haldi, chandan and ghee/oil wicks, packaged in premium wooden boxes priced upwards of ₹2,000. The brand sells primarily through its D2C website and also caters to gifting and bulk orders. The brand is tapping the shift towards convenience-led religious consumption, packaging traditionally fragmented puja essentials into curated, ready-to-use kits. By 2024, the startup was profitable and clocking ₹5.5 Lakh in average monthly revenue. The Deep Dive ECOMMERCE BUZZ RentoMojo’s Bumper Market Debut: The furniture and appliance rental company closed its maiden trading session 32.24% above the IPO issue price at ₹534.25 on the NSE, giving the furniture and appliance rental startup a market capitalisation of ₹5,548.8 Cr. Practo’s Leadership Reset: The healthtech startup has appointed former COO Jagnoor Singh as CEO, while cofounder Shashank ND will become the managing director and executive chairman as Practo prepares for a proposed public listing and Shashank shifts focus to his new venture ‘Cent’. Rebel Foods Narrows Losses: The foodtech unicorn cut its FY26 net loss by 16.3% to ₹281.8 Cr, while its revenue jumped 20.7% to ₹1,951.6 Cr. Its international revenue jumped 38.8% YoY to ₹283.81 Cr, while revenue from India grew 18%. UPI Gets Its First MDR Framework: NPCI has introduced a 0.4% MDR on P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300, which is set to take effect on October 15. P2P payments and small merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month will remain exempt. The Operator Question With online customer acquisition getting expensive, how can a premium lifestyle brand use physical stores to attract new buyers without overspending? Share a practical playbook for choosing the location, store size and budget. We reached out to Rashi Sethia, the CEO of premium lifestyle brand Nicobar, to understand the playbook here. Here’s what she divulged: Turn Stores Into Brand Experiences: Nicobar sees its stores as more than points of sale. They are spaces where customers can experience the brand, its design and products, making physical retail an important way to acquire new customers. Let Digital Demand Guide Expansion: The brand uses online demand to identify cities and neighbourhoods where it already has customers but no physical presence. It also looks at locations where its target consumers already spend time, including areas around cafés, restaurants and other lifestyle spaces. Test Before Going All In: Nicobar does not believe bigger stores are necessarily better. Right-sized stores, pop-ups, exhibitions and dedicated gifting spaces can help the brand tell its story while testing demand before committing to a larger physical footprint. The focus is on keeping fixed costs such as rentals disciplined while investing in store design, product selection and frontline staff.

Imagine walking into a neighbourhood medical store with a prescription in hand. The pharmacist checks the medicine, packs it and hands it over. But what happens when there is no prescription? According to a nationwide survey, for a large number of consumers, the answer is that the medicine may still be sold. The finding comes as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed installing CCTV cameras at medical stores to make prescription-medicine sales traceable.
The survey, conducted by LocalCircles, saw about 1.06 lakh responses from consumers across 327 districts of India. Of the total respondents, 63% were men and 37% women. Besides, 52% of them were from tier-1 districts, 29% from tier-2 districts and 29% from tier-3, 4 and 5 districts.
The survey found that 64% of consumers said their chemist never or rarely asked for a doctor’s prescription before selling medicines in the past 12 months. Only 15% said their chemist mostly or always refused to sell medicines without a prescription. The survey also found that only 31% of consumers were able to get assistance from a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 13% said they were assisted by someone who was not a qualified pharmacist.
The findings come as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has floated a draft notification proposing mandatory CCTV surveillance at every medical store that dispenses drugs sold on a doctor’s prescription. Under the proposal, the supply, other than by wholesale, of any drug sold on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner would have to take place under a CCTV surveillance system installed and maintained at the premises.
The proposal also comes against the backdrop of intensified enforcement in multiple States against chemists selling prescription medicines without valid prescriptions, operating without registered pharmacists and failing to provide proper bills.
Neighbourhood chemist remains the main source
The survey found that the neighbourhood chemist remains the primary source of medicines for most consumers. The question on how respondents had primarily purchased medicines in the previous 12 months received 16,822 responses. This revealed that 86% of the respondents primarily depended on local chemists, followed by 14% on ePharmacy apps.
Who is actually behind the counter?
The survey then looked at whether consumers were receiving assistance from qualified pharmacists when they needed help with medicine or disease-related queries. The question received 19,409 responses. 31% of the consumers said they were able to get assistance from a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always. 27% of them said they never or very rarely received such assistance.
Home delivery is not free of the prescription gap
The survey also examined prescription checks when medicines were delivered to consumers’ homes. The question received 15,473 responses. 41% of consumers surveyed said a prescription was never or rarely asked for during home delivery.
A missing bill can mean a missing trail
Consumers were also asked whether they received proper bills when buying medicines from local chemists. Of the 20,573 respondents, 26% said they were not provided a GST bill. “A bill is not merely a tax document. It carries the batch number, expiry date and identity of the seller and provides a record if a medicine turns out to be expired, defective or counterfeit,” it said.
The survey also sought to establish whether consumers had purchased medicines that later turned out to be counterfeit or ineffective. The question received 18,457 responses. 15% of consumers said they had bought medicines that were later found to be fake or counterfeit.

Watch: Six-year-old girl from China sets new Rubik's Cube world record
A young girl has broken the women's world record for the 3x3x3 Rubik's Cube twice in three days at the World Cube Association.
At age six, Lian Yunzhi has become the only female cuber in the world to have an average time under 4.5 seconds. She first broke the record with an average of 4.52 seconds and then 4.27 seconds at competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, China.
The young competitor from Sichuan Province has mastered more than 1,300 Rubik's Cube solving algorithms after vigorous training that involved spending two to three hours a day on the cube over the past year.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Gautam Adani and family have returned to the top of the M3M Hurun India Rich List 2026, surpassing Mukesh Ambani and family. According to the report released on September 23, Adani’s wealth increased 13% to ₹9.23 lakh crore, while Ambani’s wealth fell 10% to ₹8.63 lakh crore.
The latest edition tracks 1,810 individuals with a minimum wealth of ₹1,000 crore. Their combined wealth grew 12.8% year-on-year to ₹187.5 lakh crore, equivalent to $1.96 trillion. India now has 391 dollar billionaires, including 27 new additions during the year.
Adani leads, while new names enter top ranks
Adani’s wealth exceeds Ambani’s by ₹59,400 crore, placing him at the top of the rankings. LN Mittal and family of ArcelorMittal moved into third position after their wealth surged 93% to ₹3.39 lakh crore. The report linked the rise to stronger steel prices and protection measures in Europe’s steel sector.
Anil Agarwal and family of Vedanta Resources climbed to ninth position after an 87% increase in wealth to ₹2.08 lakh crore. Samir Mehta and family of Torrent Pharmaceuticals entered the top 10 with wealth of ₹1.89 lakh crore following a 52% rise.
AI becomes a new wealth creation engine
Artificial intelligence featured as a separate sector in the Hurun list for the first time, with 19 individuals collectively holding wealth of ₹3.07 lakh crore. Fifteen of these were new entrants.
Among the emerging AI entrepreneurs were Tanay Kothari and Sahaj Garg of Wispr Flow, each with wealth of ₹4,200 crore. The list also included founders linked to companies such as CTRL S Datacentres, Yotta, Sarvam AI and Emergent AI.
The report noted that AI’s 15 new entrants contributed ₹1.82 lakh crore in wealth, making it the largest wealth contributor among sectors generating new names.
Mumbai continued to lead as the city with the highest number of wealthy individuals at 465, followed by New Delhi and Bengaluru. The list included 131 women, with Roshni Nadar Malhotra and family remaining India’s richest woman at ₹2.79 lakh crore.

భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య ఉద్యమ సమయంలో RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక ఫోటో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారమవుతుంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నప్పటి ఫోటో.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ ఫోటో రెండు వేర్వేరు సందర్భాల్లో తీసిన ఫోటోలను జోడించి ఎడిట్ చేసి సృష్టించబడింది. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ ఫోటోలో RSS కార్యకర్తలు నిలబడి ఉన్న భాగాన్ని రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దానికి సంబంధించిన అసలు ఫోటో (ఆర్కైవ్) లభించింది. ఈ ఫోటోను ‘డెక్కన్ క్రానికల్’ వార్తా సంస్థ తమ వెబ్సైట్లో 2016లో ప్రచురించిన ఒక కథనానికి ప్రతీకాత్మక చిత్రంగా ఉపయోగించింది. ఈ ఫోటోలో బ్రిటన్ రాణి లేరు.
ఇక వైరల్ ఫొటోలో బ్రిటన్ రాణి ఉన్న భాగాన్ని రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దానికి సంబంధించిన అసలు ఫోటో ‘Getty Images’ వెబ్సైట్తో పాటు ‘History Ville‘ అనే ఎక్స్ (X) ఖాతాలో లభించింది. ఆ వివరాల ప్రకారం, 1956లో ఎలిజబెత్-II రాణి నైజీరియా పర్యటనలో నైజీరియా సైనిక దళాలను తనిఖీ చేస్తున్నప్పుడు ఈ ఫోటో తీయబడింది. దీన్ని బట్టి, సంబంధం లేని పై రెండు ఫోటోలను ఎడిట్ చేసి, RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నట్లుగా తప్పుడు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
చివరిగా, RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నట్లుగా చూపుతున్న ఈ ఫోటో ఎడిట్ చేయబడినది.

A nine-second long video clip is has gone viral on social media, showing a man assaulting a puffed rice vendor. In the video, the man is seen overturning the box hanging from the snack seller’s neck and pouring all the food items onto the vendor’s face before they scatter onto the street. As this purported attack unfolds, the vendor stares at the man helplessly.
The video was posted by X user Alka Maurya on September 16 and has garnered more than 2,85,000 views and shared over 1,500 times till publication time. The caption of the post, translated from Hindi, reads: “(He) must be feeling so proud after doing something like this.” (Archive)
कितना गर्व महसूस कर रहा होगा ऐसे करके हैं ना …… pic.twitter.com/F6upi4I2ZD
— Alka Maurya (@MauryaAlka76391) September 16, 2026
Apart from Maurya, film actor Kamaal R Khan posted the same video with the caption: “How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now.” (Archive)
How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now. pic.twitter.com/o2T2AJzGoj
— KRK (@kamaalrkhan) September 17, 2026
Other social media users circulated the viral clip with similar captions, condemning the man seen purportedly attacking the vendor.
As a billboard visible in the video reads ‘Welcome to Patna Junction’, the Patna police was tagged in the comment section of certain posts, requesting them to take stringent action against the man who allegedly assaulted the vendor.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the viral video clip, we ran reverse image search on several relevant keyframes. It led us to a video posted by content creator Sonu Paswan on Instagram. With 1,79,000 followers, he posts scripted videos highlighting the helpless condition of the working class people in India. Paswan has a social media presence on Facebook and YouTube as well. And according to his social media bios, he is from Darbhanga, Bihar.
In all of his videos, accessible on his Facebook page, Paswan himself can be seen playing different “poor characters” being harassed and attacked by others as he helplessly accepts his fate.
On September 18, Friday, Paswan posted a video on his Instagram page, where he clarified that he enacts emotional scenes on poverty as ‘content’ on his social media platforms. He clarifies that the viral clip does not depict a real attack on him, but is in fact a prepared skit. “I want to tell you that in the video you are seeing, the vendor is me and the man who is attacking me is part of my team. I want to let you know that we, as a team, make emotional videos on poverty. I request you to take this video purely as entertainment, and not believe that this is real,” he said.
The caption of this video reads, translated from Hindi, “Because we make emotional videos on the poor…You all give me so much love…but you guys have taken this clip to heart.
I know I have hurt you guys with this video. Please delete the video from your channel…I request you not to share this video any further.”
View this post on Instagram
After the clip started going viral and attracted significant backlash, on September 17, most of his videos on YouTube and all of his previous videos on Instagram had to be deleted. In the aforementioned video, Paswan urges audiences to not share the viral clip and excerbate his situation even further. “I request you to not share the clip on your personal profiles, please do this much for your brothers,” he said. He shared the same clarification on his YouTube page.
Moreover, Paswan posted videos of the guy who is acting as the attacker in the video, also clarifying the viral clip is indeed a skit, on his Instagram and YouTube pages. “The video you guys are watching and getting emotional and taking to heart is just our content…its not real…please stop roasting this video. Because of you [sharing the viral clip as real] all my efforts have gone to waste, all my videos, over 300 videos…I have had to delete them all. I request you to keep supporting and loving us,” he states in the video.
View this post on Instagram
Given that their skit went viral, misleadingly as a real incident, the content creators said they received backlash and trolling, compelling them to remove their previous videos. At present, Paswan’s Instagram page only features the two clarification videos and his YouTube page features the same. However, his Facebook still displayed his earlier content. The description of his Facebook page, translated from Hindi, also reads: “I make emotional videos on poverty.”
True to the description, Paswan’s Facebook page contains videos similar in theme to the viral video. In these videos, visibly destitute people or poor vendors are seen being humiliated or suffering at the hands of others, while accepting their fate.
Paswan can be identified acting in all of these videos, and a visual match can be established, indicating that he was indeed the person seen in the viral video. Thus, it can be concluded that a scripted video made by a content creator has gone viral, leading netizens to falsely believe that it depicts a real incident of attack on a puffed rice vendor.

England fast bowler Wood retires from internationals
- Published
England fast bowler Mark Wood has announced his retirement from international cricket with immediate effect.
The 36-year-old, who is one of the fastest bowlers to ever play for England, has been blighted by injuries throughout his career.
The Durham paceman only returned to action in the first Ashes Test in Perth in November after 15 months out with an elbow injury followed by knee surgery.
However, he bowled just 11 overs before suffering swelling in the same left knee and subsequently flew home for treatment. He has not played for England since.
"Although this may not come as a surprise given the past year, it just feels like a natural time at the end of my contract," Wood said in a statement on social media.
"I've always tried to be resilient and come back from injury to prove people wrong and show everyone what I can do. Unfortunately, this time I lost the battle.
"On medical advice, Test cricket and 50-over cricket are not possible, so the England dream has slowly been ground out of me over the last year.
"Playing for England has been the greatest honour I could have ever wished for and a dream come true."
Wood added that he hopes to continue playing cricket in some capacity.
Wood took 119 wickets in 38 Tests after making his debut in 2015, and that summer he helped win back the Ashes on home soil.
However, he has suffered a string of ankle, knee and elbow injuries during his career.
In a bid to limit the stress on his body, he lengthened his run-up in 2018, and that did allow him to play key roles in some of England's biggest successes in recent years.
The altered run-up did not impact his pace and he was part of the team that lifted the 2019 50-over World Cup, where he took 18 wickets.
He was also in the squad that won the T20 World Cup in 2022, but missed the end stages of the tournament with a calf problem.
In white-ball cricket, Wood retires as England's sixth-highest wicket-taker in men's T20s with 54 from 38 matches, and he took 80 scalps in 70 one-day internationals.
Wood played a key role in helping England come from 2-0 down in the 2023 Ashes, with his return to the team - and blistering spells of bowling - helping them level the series.
"It's been a privilege to watch the latter part of a great career," said Rob Key, managing director of England men's cricket.
"To have been a point of difference in Ashes series wins, two World Cup wins, and to have thrilled crowds every time he got the ball in his hand is something very few players achieve. He can look back with enormous pride on a career very well spent."
'One of the most thrilling sights in the game'
Anyone who has ever played cricket at any level will have tried to bowl fast. The dream is to be able to hurtle the ball down at irresistible speed: batters flinching, stumps flying.
Mark Wood lived that dream. Few who have played for England, or any country, know what it is like to bowl with Wood's speed.
The sight of Wood flying in, bowling himself off his feet - literally, on many occasions - was one of the most thrilling in the game. He captured the imagination of supporters not only with his raw pace, but his personality. Wood engaged with supporters and never took himself too seriously. It seemed he always remembered that cricket is supposed to be fun.
Naturally, there will be the nagging doubt of what might have been had his career not been so badly hit by injuries. The human body is not designed to bowl fast and the rigours of the job hit Wood worse than most.
But, when the stars aligned, it was electrifying. A demolition of West Indies in St Lucia in 2019, complete with a remodelled, longer run-up, showed what Wood would be capable of in the latter part of his career.
He was one of the few England players to emerge with credit from the awful Ashes tour of 2021-22 and his entrance to the return series in 2023 was unforgettable.
Held back until the third Test, when England were already 2-0 down, Wood bowled at the speed of light at Headingley. In one of the great Ashes spells, Wood knocked over Usman Khawaja with a 95mph thunderbolt.
At the end of the Test, in a nail-biting run chase, Wood was at the crease with Chris Woakes to see England over the line. Woakes was another held back until the third Test and, without these great friends performing the way they did that summer, England would have been soundly beaten.
Wood has been a multi-format performer for England. He was in the XI on the unforgettable day at Lord's when the World Cup was won in 2019, coming out to bat with Ben Stokes despite carrying an injury. Wood was also in the squad when England lifted the T20 World Cup in 2022.
He is one of a handful of England players to have won both World Cups and the Ashes, having been part of the last England team to regain the urn in 2015. With Wood gone, the only remaining England player in Test cricket to have tasted Ashes glory is Joe Root.
There was no last hurrah in Australia. A long recovery from elbow and knee injuries did not produce the pace England were craving down under. Wood could only play in the first Test in Perth and said last month he was "ashamed" at what happened.
His retirement confirms the end of an era in English pace bowling. First Stuart Broad, then James Anderson, followed by Woakes and Wood into retirement. Throw in the all-round talent of Stokes, and England have lost 1,871 Test wickets in less than three years.

Sri Lanka court convicts 15 over deadly 2019 Easter bombings
COLOMBO, Sri Lanka — A Sri Lankan court found 15 men guilty on Tuesday of involvement in the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, which killed more than 260 people and wounded about 500.
The April 21 attacks targeted three churches and three hotels across the island nation during Easter services and celebrations. The Islamic State group-inspired bombings, among the deadliest in Sri Lanka's history, killed 42 foreigners and devastated communities across the country.
In 2021, authorities filed 23,270 charges against 24 suspects accused of planning or inspiring the attacks. The charges included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and firearms and explosives offenses under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
None of those believed to have directly participated in the attacks are alive.
Sri Lanka has not carried out executions since 1976, meaning death sentences typically result in life imprisonment.
Two Sri Lanka-based Islamic militant groups were accused of carrying out the bombings.
Sri Lanka's Catholic Church has claimed, without providing evidence, that those identified so far as perpetrators are not the masterminds behind the bombings, and that there was a bigger conspiracy behind the attacks.
In July, a former police chief and a former senior defense ministry official were also sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks.

- Rockstar has installed a giant "Welcome to Vice City" sign on Miami's Kaseya Center.
- Miami-Dade County is reportedly receiving $975,000 for the marketing agreement.
- GTA 6 launches November 19, with Rockstar's marketing campaign receiving an aggressive push.
Rockstar Games has apparently decided that advertising GTA 6 on billboards simply isn’t dramatic enough. The studio has now put up a giant “Welcome to Vice City” sign on top of Miami on top of Miami’s Kaseya Center, and the whole stunt is costing a reported $975,000. Yes, almost a million dollars to essentially tell Miami that Vice City has arrived.
The massive pink-and-white sign was installed on the roof of the Kaseya Center on September 22, with a helicopter lifting the letters into position before workers secured them to the central area. The venue fits accurately because it is home to the Miami Heat and sits in downtown Miami, making the promotion highly visible from the air.
According to the agreement reports, Miami-Dade County is set to receive $975,000 from Rockstar for this aggressive GTA 6 marketing promotion. Earlier county discussions also reportedly explored other GTA 6-themed ideas, including temporarily branding parts of Miami International Airport as “Vice City Airport.” However, the Miami Sheriff turned down this GTA 6 campaign as it promoted violence against law enforcement officers.
It seems like Rockstar is physically placing the game’s fictional version of Miami into the real city’s skyline. The campaign is also arriving as Take-Two’s CEO talks about pushing GTA 6 marketing to the next level.
Meanwhile, the Miami deal has not been completely free of controversy. Some Miami-Dade officials questioned whether public property should be used to promote a game centered around criminal activity and violence.
However, the connection between Vice City and Miami goes beyond the latest marketing push. For years, the real city has embraced references to the franchise as GTA-themed souvenirs, and fan-created art has become a part of Miami’s pop culture. For Rockstar, the message is pretty straightforward. GTA 6 is coming to Vice City, and Vice City is coming to Miami first.

Steven Sessegnon exclusive: The twin brother of Fulham's Ryan rebuilding at AFC Wimbledon after 'tough' period at Wigan
Steven Sessegnon discusses his 'tough' time at Wigan, returning to his roots to join AFC Wimbledon in the summer, the moment he faced his twin brother Ryan for the first time and more; watch Cambridge vs AFC Wimbledon live on Sky Sports+ on Saturday; kick-off 3pm
Tuesday 22 September 2026 14:20, UK
Steven and Ryan Sessegnon walked out at Craven Cottage side by side, each holding their daughters, last month.
The twins had made their way through Fulham's academy together and played in the first team together on a handful of occasions - but that night, they played against one another for the first time ever.
It was a special moment; a full-circle moment.

In any of the previous three seasons, a game like this would have been a perfect chance for a family reunion, as Steven had been living in Manchester for three years while playing for Wigan.
But now he's back home. And not just 'home' in terms of being back in south-west London. Properly back home.
He points ahead as he speaks to Sky Sports on a terrace at the Dons' training ground in New Malden. "We used to play academy games literally across this grass."
He points to the left. "I spent time at Coombe Boys School, which is five minutes up the road."
Fulham's Motspur Park training ground is six minutes' drive away. There, his nephew Kayden is part of the U18 squad.
"It's really wholesome to be back," says Sessegnon. "It helps massively being around family.
"I get to see my older brothers, my nieces, my nephews and I see my brother [Ryan] a few times a week.
"We play at two different levels, so there isn't too much to speak about as if we were in the same league, but we catch up on life, being dads, being providers, being men in our families and what the future looks like."
Sessegnon's return home has come at an important point in his career.
In his first season at Wigan in 2023/24, he played 29 games in all competitions. In his second, he suffered calf and knee injuries, before not playing again from January 4 2025.
At the start of his third, Gary Caldwell, who had replaced Ryan Lowe in February 2025, placed him on the transfer list.
"Things happen fast in football," Sessegnon says. "When I was put on the transfer list, I was told I wasn't going to play and I didn't go on the pre-season trip - but I ended up starting the first game of the season through injuries or lack of availability, and I thought I did well.
"It's fair game, it's part of it. The manager came in, the club wanted to go in a different direction. As long as everyone can come out of it happy and people can move onto clubs they know they can do well at, there's no problem with it."
A move away did not materialise so, on the few occasions Caldwell did select him, he was deployed at centre-back, where he had never played before.
"It was tough. Very, very tough. I felt like I could contribute to a team, but didn't really have the trust or belief behind me to do it.
"But as much as I could say I didn't have the proper backing to be in my own position, I was still given a chance to play football. It was down to me and it just never happened.
"There was no issue with anyone else apart from myself. I learned a lot there, a lot I can take with me for the rest of my career. It was a learning curve.
"The biggest thing was professionalism. Even in the worst stages of when I wasn't playing and I was told I wasn't going to be a part of it, I could still carry myself and be the best possible person.
"I felt I owed it to myself to show people I was still a very good trainer, a very good player and I think that helped me stick around longer than they probably wanted me to."
Sessegnon was released by the Latics in the summer and joined AFC Wimbledon on a two-year contract, with the option for a further 12 months, on June 25.
"I was preparing to go on holiday with my family and I got a call. As soon as they said Wimbledon, local, I said 'let's get it sorted'," he recalls.
"But it was also about the position I would play, how the gaffer [Johnnie Jackson] set it out. It wasn't complicated. I knew I could come in and, if I could get minutes, I would show my ability."
Sessegnon's first Dons appearance came on August 8 against Newport in the Carabao Cup, almost six months after his last competitive game for Wigan. He looks in genuine disbelief when he hears that.
His full league debut came on September 7, in a 2-0 Sky Bet League One win over Bromley. He has had to bide his time, but he understands why.
"It's like injuries, you have a bit of anxiousness about getting going again, but I had the pre-season and here at Wimbledon, they looked after me very well. The gaffer has looked after me very well and communicated very well with me.
"In my head I wanted to start and play as many games as I could, but coming off the bench a few times has probably benefitted me to get to grips with football again.
"It's probably the simplest football I've played in my career, but the most effective. We're able to create chances, I'm able to get the ball high up the pitch.
"It's not overthought, and I think it brings the best out of the whole squad and definitely myself. I've enjoyed it so far and it takes the pressure off the whole squad; we know we can create chances, we just have to be solid."
The Dons have certainly been solid, with five clean sheets from seven games so far - the joint-most in the Sky Bet EFL.
They are four points behind leaders Bradford going into Saturday's trip to Cambridge - which is live on Sky Sports+ - despite having only scored five goals so far.
That said, they are still among the bookmakers' favourites to be relegated this season.
But now, back on home soil, Sessegnon has the chance to help AFC Wimbledon defy the odds again, just around the corner from where it all began.

Jesse Baird was “petrified” of Beau Lamarre-Condon because he was an armed police officer who could make a false allegation that would ruin his career, a court has heard.
Lamarre-Condon has been accused of fatally shooting Sydney couple Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, with a police service weapon at Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
The 31-year-old pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Lamarre-Condon developed an “obsession and infatuation” with Baird, which manifested in compulsive actions during their brief relationship, the prosecution alleged.
By the time Baird decided he wanted to end things in November 2023, the behaviour had escalated.
Corey-Dean Thorpe, who had previously been in a years-long relationship with the 26-year-old and remained close friends, began sobbing in the witness box as he told the trial how Baird felt.
“He was petrified,” Thorpe told the New South Wales supreme court.
“I’d never heard him so scared in his voice before.
“He just kept repeating, ‘he has a gun’.”
Baird told Thorpe he was “extremely scared” of Lamarre-Condon because he had a gun and was a member of the police force, the court heard.
Asked by crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC if the 26-year-old had said he was scared to go to the police because Lamarre-Condon was a police officer, Thorpe agreed.
Baird was also worried Lamarre-Condon would make a false allegation against him that would “ruin his career”, Thorpe said.
 Because he was a television presenter on children’s show Totally Wild and an AFL umpire, he needed a certification to work with children, the court heard.
During their relationship, Baird told Thorpe that Lamarre-Condon would go through his phone when he was asleep, find other men Baird had been talking to, and block their numbers before deleting their chats.
Damon Wilson, another man Baird was casually seeing, had to cancel their meeting in November 2023 because the TV presenter was in Melbourne for work, he told the court.
A week later, Wilson was added to Lamarre-Condon’s close friends list on Instagram. The police officer posted a photo of a bouquet to his close friends story, captioned “when he’s in Melbourne but still sends you these” with a heart-eyes emoji.
Wilson messaged Baird, who confirmed he was not in a relationship with Lamarre-Condon. Wilson said to Baird in a message: “I was a little confused why he added me to his close friends as soon as we met then starting posting photos of you guys … you getting him flowers. Glad we are on the same page”.
A week later Wilson received a protracted message from Lamarre-Condon warning him about Baird’s supposed “gaslighting”.
“He literally destroyed me,” Lamarre-Condon said in messages read to the court.
“It took me so long to recover from all the manipulation.
“He has tried to make me look like the bad guy.”
Around this time, Baird sent messages to Thorpe asking for advice on how to break up with Lamarre-Condon.
Baird told Thorpe he was worried about what would happen when he ended things “because of the gun and because the accused had stalked and controlled him”, the prosecutor alleged.
On 3 February 2024, months after the break-up, one of Baird’s best friends, Matthew Edwards, asked if he had heard from Lamarre-Condon.
Edwards said Baird had replied: “No, thank fuck, I’m so done with him”.
“Once I move house, this will be the last piece of me that Beau knows.”
Baird confirmed his new relationship with Davies to Edwards soon after during their last phone call together.
“He was almost falling in love with him,” Edwards told the court.
“I’d never seen Jesse as happy with Luke as what I’d seen him ever. There was something about Luke that just lit Jesse up: they were the real deal.”
Lamarre-Condon’s defence team has claimed the police officer was acting in self-defence when he disguised himself as an Uber Eats driver and entered Baird’s home on 19 February.
Defence lawyer John Stratton SC argued a struggle had ensued which led to the shots that killed Davies and Baird.
The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

LeBron the star as Angola aims to cash in on E1 racing
- Published
It is difficult to imagine an electric powerboat racing series capturing the attention of an Angolan audience for whom football and basketball is king, but the presence of NBA royalty LeBron James certainly helped.
The 41-year-old was among the A-listers in Luanda as the E1 World Championship rolled into southern Africa for the first time at the weekend, having made its debut on the continent last year in Lagos, Nigeria.
"It's not a short trip, but he [LeBron] is here because he believes in what we're doing," E1 chief executive Jamie Copas told BBC Sport Africa in the Angolan capital.
"You can't underestimate the value of it. They [the celebrity owners] come with huge followings."
James, like fellow sport stars Rafa Nadal, Tom Brady, Didier Drogba and Virat Kohli and actor Will Smith, is an E1 team owner after buying into the series.
Similar to Formula E on land, it aims to blend sport with strong messaging around sustainability and green technology.
James said Angola had made his first trip to the country "super welcoming" after visiting the National Museum of Slavery.
"Obviously there is a lot of history here," the new signing for the Philadelphia 76ers told local media.
"A lot of history that not only is here in the country but also [crosses] over to America."
Angola's men are reigning African basketball champions, securing a record-extending 12th continental title on home soil last year, and unsurprisingly spectators of the E1 racing at the Clube Naval de Luanda clamoured for a glimpse of one of basketball's biggest icons.
Journalist Omar Prata, covering the race for the Jornal de Angola, admitted that E1 was not on his radar until Hollywood star Smith, whose Westbrook Racing team is sponsored by Visit Angola, announced in March that a deal had been agreed to race in Luanda for the next three years.
"I see the potential it could bring to project the city at a time when the government is trying to work on tourism," Prata said.
"And of course it means a lot to have LeBron James here. Angolans have seen him on television, they try to emulate him on the street courts, they have his posters."
Boosting Angola long-term
The star power of E1's owners is helping to bring eyeballs to what is a traditionally niche sport where powerboat pilots skim and bounce around tight courses at speeds close to 100kmph.
Yet, on a calendar that features traditional celebrity haunts like Miami, Monaco and Lake Como, Luanda's name seems an outlier.
Among those taking in the action from the fanzone was local resident Edson Cabeta.
"It is the first time I have seen anything like this," he said.
"Today it is foreigners doing this; tomorrow, perhaps we could have an Angolan team."
The aspiration is that hosting an E1 race will help Angola boost visitor numbers, with minister for tourism Marcio de Jesus Lopes Daniel saying enhanced foreign awareness of the country is the "first step" in a long-term plan.
"Our ambition is not simply to make Angola famous," Daniel told the BBC.
"It is to make Angola more desirable to visit, invest in and do business in."
Angola has not been afraid to speculate to accumulate in the past, bringing Lionel Messi's Argentina side to Luanda for a football friendly last November to celebrate 50 years of the nation's independence.
Daniel said it would be "premature" to assess the economic impact of this weekend's race in Luanda.
"An event of this scale generates demand across several sectors and it creates opportunities," he added.
"We want to turn the international attention generated by E1 into future trips, stays, private investment and jobs. That is the real return we are looking for."
Sustainability challenges
Beyond the spectacle and waterfront backdrops, E1 aims to transcend motorsport.
Sustainability has been one cornerstone, and marine conservation efforts around the race in Angola included mangrove restoration.
Putting sustainability front and centre inevitably invites scrutiny - particularly when races have taken place in Saudi Arabia, the United States, Nigeria and now Angola, all major oil-producing nations.
"The world's on a journey," Copas said.
"We're welcomed in places that do have a lot of fossil-fuel infrastructure.
"Each one of those markets is conscious of it and wants to be doing more from a green point of view. If we can help, why wouldn't we?"
Copas told BBC Sport Africa that E1 would only consider air freight as a last resort for transporting its teams and that they aim to showcase their technology on each stop, persuading people that electric charging is a viable alternative to diesel even on water.
But as the global series expanded to 10 teams and seven races in 2025, its own emissions rose from 1,672 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in its first season to 4,049 tonnes in its second, according to E1's own annual sustainability report.
"We need to travel to meet new people, to tell our stories, which we would hope would be of greater benefit than the carbon footprint that we have," Copas explained.
"We work really hard to offset our carbon and to make sure every stage of our logistics journey is done in the most sustainable way.
"It would be crazy for us to say we're not going to travel and we're not going to race, because then we can't do the job that we're here to do."
There is an acknowledgement within E1 that the work is unfinished and that more active reductions are needed.
'Continuing the story'
E1 was due to return to Lagos in October, but Nigeria's race was cancelled earlier this month, perhaps showing how the series is still working to establish itself.
It means its longer-term impact in Africa will take time to judge, but the effect of its celebrity owners was obvious around the paddock in Luanda.
After visiting his pilots, Will Smith stopped for selfies and handshakes with fans, telling the crowd it was "great to be here".
On the water, however, there was no fairytale result as Westbrook Racing's hopes of victory were ended by a mechanical fault, with Team Brady taking the inaugural Luanda title.
Smith could have used the help of Kianda, the mermaid-like Angolan water spirit traditionally regarded as a protector of fishermen.
It will take one of her miraculous interventions if electric powerboat racing is to usurp football or basketball in Angolan affections, but Copas hopes E1 can leave a different legacy.
"I think it's for us to help tell Angola stories, and for Angola to help tell ours.
"We will be back next year, we will be back the year after. It's not just about what we're doing in the few days we're here.
"We'd love to see the journey they're on develop even more, and us playing a part in that."

The first shuttle talks between the United States and Iran for months raised hopes on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) that the adversaries could make some progress towards ending the West Asia war, although neither side spelled out any change in their positions.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, the first such contacts since an interim ceasefire agreement collapsed in July.
"Steve and Jared had a very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran, merely mediators. Let's see what happens with that," U.S. President Donald Trump said. "They've been mediated for a while, but I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal. It's what we're hearing from everybody."
Earlier, Mr. Trump had told the UN General Assembly in a speech that he had to decide whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate" the country. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian was due to address the gathering on Wednesday (September 23, 2026).
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran had engaged with the United States through a Qatari mediator in New York and conveyed conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and a halt to U.S. "acts of aggression".
Some Iranian state media had earlier reported that Mr. Araghchi and Mr. Witkoff had met, but Iranian officials clarified to Reuters that this was not face-to-face. Mr. Araghchi met the Prime Minister of Qatar, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who has been one of the main mediators at previous talks.
Oil prices hold at two-week low
The diplomatic opening helped keep oil prices near two-week lows, with Brent crude now holding just below the $100-a-barrel threshold it had shot through this month, after Houthi fighters in Yemen launched a major offensive and fired into Saudi Arabia.
The war, launched by Mr. Trump in February alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury", has lasted nearly seven months, killing thousands of people, disrupting global energy supplies and spreading to other countries in the region — first to Lebanon and more recently to Yemen.
Mr. Trump repeated previous assertions that the war could end around the time of November's U.S. midterm elections, though he has not explained why.
Since diplomacy broke off in July, the sides have repeatedly exchanged fire, although Mr. Trump has held back from a full-blown resumption of strikes after receiving advice from his military commanders that munitions were running low.
An interim agreement reached in June and signed by Mr. Trump and Mr. Pezeshkian would have given Iran its main demands — lifting financial sanctions and unfreezing assets in return for talks on limiting its nuclear programme.
But that deal unravelled within weeks over shipping rules in the Strait of Hormuz, conduit for a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas before the war. Iran wants to exert greater control of the strait and collect fees from ships that use it, which Washington rejects.
Despite near-daily attacks on tankers, traffic through the strait has gradually increased in recent weeks. Oil producers have paid shipping companies fees worth as much as a quarter of a cargo's value to switch off transponders, navigate the route and transfer crude to other vessels beyond the strait.
Exports from the United Arab Emirates have already recovered to pre-war levels, and Saudi Arabia has sold 60 million barrels of Gulf oil for both this month and next, to be delivered beyond the strait off the coast of Oman, a big increase from August.
Even so, disruption continues to squeeze global energy markets. About a third of Gulf oil is estimated to be missing from global supplies. Shortages have particularly hit refined products such as diesel, causing inflation, pushing up interest rates and hurting Mr. Trump's Republicans ahead of the elections.
The risk of further disruption has increased since the Iran-backed Houthis advanced in Yemen this month, threatening traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, an alternative export route used by Saudi Arabia.
Washington, for its part, has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, deepening Iran's economic crisis. Iranian officials say they are willing to endure the blockade to achieve their goals, and will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until it is lifted.

King Charles has referred a landmark slavery reparations petition from Jamaica to a high-level UK appeals court for legal advice, Jamaica’s culture minister announced in parliament on Tuesday.
Referring to the move as a “really big deal”, Olivia Grange told Jamaica’s MPs the monarch had confirmed that their legal questions have been passed on to the London-based privy council – the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.
The petition seeks guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences.
“Indeed we went fearless and boldly into this chapter when we petitioned the king on Monday, September 7, 2026 – one day after the 245th anniversary of the commemoration of the Zong massacre, an event that captures the barbarity of chattel enslavement,” Grange said in parliament.
“The king could have ignored us. The king could have delayed responding to us. The king could have made a decision not to refer the questions to the privy council, or he could make a decision to refer the questions,” she said, before adding “King Charles has referred the petition filed on the 7th of September, 2026, on behalf of the people of Jamaica to the Judicial Committee of the privy council.”
Jamaica had activated a rarely used mechanism in the Judicial Committee Act 1833, which allows the king to refer questions of “legal or constitutional nature” to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts, according to the country’s legal counsels.
The minister said that taking the matter to the International Court of Justice, was not an option for Jamaica.
“The United Kingdom has placed specific reservations on the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ which prevent the Court from adjudicating on disputes between the United Kingdom and the government of any other country which is or has been a Member of the Commonwealth”.
A privy council opinion would not compel the UK government to pay reparations, but Jamaican officials believe it could shape negotiations and legal options and set a precedent for other Commonwealth nations seeking reparations.
Earlier this month, Grange led a Jamaican delegation to London to officially lodge the petition. While in the UK, the group, lawyers and members of the country’s national council on reparation met diaspora communities, MPs, church leaders and cultural institutions – among them the British Museum, from which Jamaica is seeking the return of artefacts taken during colonial rule.
Tuesday’s announcement follows the Caricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place in Barbados last week. Officials at the conference said that Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal.
Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options.
Speaking at the conference, Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the CRC, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today.
He said: “When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?”
Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”.
Grange told parliament that the country is “awaiting directions from the Judicial Committee of the privy council as to the next steps to be taken in the case. And the attorney general is preparing to deal with the case”.

PHOTOS: The precarious life of fisherfolk
He works from 2 a.m. to 7 a.m. every day. In pitch darkness, he carries baskets of fish on his head from boats in Kasimedu harbor to the auction house, navigating slimy and damp pathways littered with fish scales and wet with seawater. It's a third of a mile each way. He makes the trip 40 or 50 times during his shift for the daily auction, which begins at 4 a.m.
Pavadairayan, who is 60 years old and goes by one name, is one of hundreds of workers known as basket men. It's a tough job. Each basket weighs about 35 pounds. Their bosses don't trust them: "If supervisors think that fish are missing, they can dock your pay and fine you several thousands of rupees. Basket men have few rights," he says.
They earn about $5 a day.
Despite the hardships, Pavadairayan says he loves the job because the rest of the day is his own. He spends his mornings sleeping and lounging.
"Many other basket men go out and do other odd jobs," he says. "But I always refuse. This money is enough for me. Sleeping with a full belly under open skies, a salt sea breeze fanning your face: that's what I call heaven."
A smuggler's story
Pavadairayan is one of around 30,000 people who are part of the bustling scene at the Kasimedu harbor in the southern Indian city of Chennai. In addition to basket men, there are fishermen, auctioneers, fish hawkers and wholesalers, transport workers, ice suppliers. The harbor itself is overcrowded, built for fewer than 600 boats and now estimated to be serving over 1,000.
They have stories to tell about their labors and their lives. Their experiences testify to the struggles they face — and to their undying love for the sea.
Nandu Kumar, who is 65, says he used to be a smuggler.
Dressed in a grey shirt and a checkered lungi (a traditional garment men wear, made of light cotton and wrapped around the waist), Kumar is seated on an overturned boat on the harbor's sandy shores. In the pale light of early dawn, he looks vulnerable, almost fragile, with a wispy white beard and contemplative eyes.
He's always worked as a fisherman. But in the early '80s, desperate to make a living, he says he'd help smuggle in imported alcohol and cigarettes on his boat. This was the time when India imposed steep customs duties and limits on consumer-goods imports. Smuggling was profitable until 1991, when economic reforms began taking effect.
So Kumar gave up on his illegal cargo and went back to battling the sea for fish.
Years later, in December 2010, tragedy struck., Kumar says. His daughter's husband, who drank heavily, toppled off his boat and drowned. "This fishing life — it's harshest on the body," Kumar says. "Your shoulders ache all the time. Sometimes, alcohol is the only way you can cope and forget the pain."
His daughter struggled to come to terms with her loss. Months later, she took her life, ingesting the pesticide she had bought to weed the garden.
After his daughter's death, Kumar took in her infant daughter and son — and soon realized that spending weeks at sea was no longer practical. Fishing was a gamble. A group of ten fishermen would go out to sea for three weeks or months in a boat, and sometimes, come back empty-handed. Kumar needed a steady income to care for his grandchildren. "With the support of my two sons, I decided to start selling fish," he says.
Today, he runs a shop at the harbor and does brisk business.
A risky business
Members of fishing communities in Kasimedu are well aware of the risky nature of the business, says Bhagat Singh, a researcher, social worker and member of the Coastal People Rights Movement, a grassroots campaign led by fishing and indigenous communities to protect their traditional marine livelihoods against corporate displacement and unregulated development.
Singh's own father was a fisherman, and he knows the community well. ""It's feast or famine. That is the rhythm of life at the harbor. For workers and fishermen here, earning a living is hard enough. One bad season, one poor catch, or one spell of illness can be enough to push a family into dire poverty. There are no safety nets. Worse, they have little access to government support and their labor remains largely invisible, " he says.
On an average, the fisherman at Kasimedu earn around $200 a month, he says — if they have good catches. The precariousness of the job is a reason why the younger generation seeks out more reliable employment. But that need for independence that is so inherent to their personalities eventually surfaces, he says. "Many of my friends are not happy in corporate jobs or in related industries. Eventually, they do find their way back fishing again, and many make this career change mid-life."
Nizamuddin, 25, belongs to the younger generation of fishermen. He's also the only man in the entire harbor wearing a wet suit. When he's not out fishing, he helps repair nets, dock boats and haul fish from the hold to pass onto the basket men.
The power of the sea
He is aware that young people his age are conspicuously absent from Kasimedu, but he's always embraced his job. "It's a hard life but I wasn't very good at studying," he says. "This is the only work I know and it has helped my family survive." He's put two older brothers through school and college. They now have good jobs, he says, but he's never regretted his own career choice.
The fisherman-turned-fish vendor Kumar knows all too well that the seas hold power over those who've worked there. "It's like your mother's lap. You may travel far and wide, and don't need it anymore, but you will return for the warmth and comfort it gives you," he says.
Every now and then, in the early hours of the morning, Kumar sits in the stillness to watch the fishermen return with their catch and feels a pang of longing. "Life on a boat is hard, but it is also exhilarating," he says. "There are moments when you never know what will happen next. I quite miss that."
