Presidents Cup 2026: Can Europe inspire new 'Miracle at Medinah' and shock International Team victory over Team USA?
Team USA have won the last 10 editions of the Presidents Cup; Geoff Ogilvy captains the International Team as they look for a first victory on American soil; Ryan Fox revealed how the Internationals plan to take inspiration from Team Europe this week at Medinah, live on Sky Sports Golf
Wednesday 23 September 2026 06:37, UK
If the International Team are going to end Team USA’s Presidents Cup dominance this week, live on Sky Sports, they may require their own 'Miracle at Medinah' to do it.
Fourteen years on from Team Europe producing a historic final-day comeback to claim Ryder Cup glory at the same venue, Geoff Ogilvy sees his side head in as heavy underdogs to avoid an 11th consecutive Presidents Cup defeat.
The United States have won every edition since 2005 and only been beaten once in the event's history, before seven of the 24 players involved in this year's contest were even born, with all logic pointing to that run continuing in Illinois.
Nothing less than victory will be acceptable for Team USA, 12 months on from a humbling home Ryder Cup loss where only a singles fightback prevented a heavier defeat, with Brandt Snedeker aware of the expectation to deliver.
"It's the elephant in the room you have to address," Snedeker said. "Just because these last (Presidents Cup) teams have been successful, doesn't mean we're going to be successful.
"We have to reset the bar for our team, tell them we have a standard to play to and we're 0-0. These 12 guys have accomplished nothing and we're going to hammer that into them."
Team USA undoubtedly have the stronger line-up based on world rankings and PGA Tour success, with the International Team having four rookies and just three players from the world's top 30 in their eclectic line-up.
Ogilvy is ready to embrace the tough challenge ahead, but the Ryder Cup has shown - where Team Europe are typically underdogs but have won nine of the last 12 editions - that being the favourite 'on paper' doesn't necessarily bring victory.
"These team events are so compelling of what Europe has done," Brandel Chamblee told Golf Channel. "Europe have shown that a cohesion of a team can overcome a huge talent gap.
"Almost every time it [the Ryder Cup] is played, you [Europe] are the underdogs and just thrash the United States. Many people will think a massive victory for the United States is a foregone conclusion and they're a massive favourite, but sport loves an underdog."
Team USA needed a final-day comeback to win in 2019 and overcame being swept in a foursomes session during the 2024 edition, but Ogilvy - who was part of the course redesign at Medinah - believes the gap between the two teams is tightening.
"Clearly winning something for the first time - the first time in a very long time - it's probably more difficult than if you're winning all the time," Ogilvy admitted. "But we're getting closer all the time."
Can Europe inspire Internationals to historic win?
Seven different nationalities represent the International Team, comprising of players outside of the United States and Europe, all playing under a black and gold 'shield' introduced by Ernie Els in 2019 to unite the team.
Nico Echavarria (Cognizant Classic) and Tom Kim (Genesis Scottish Open) are both winners on the PGA Tour this season, while Adam Scott and Ryan Fox arrived in Chicago after strong performances on the DP World Tour at the BMW PGA Championship.
"I think we can learn a lot from [Europe], just not being intimidated by it [playing Team USA]" said Fox, the reigning Champion Golfer of the Year, at Wentworth. "I feel like we know a lot of the European players really well and if these guys can do it, we can do it, too.
"We can definitely emulate them and take a little bit out of how they get together as a team. I think the European Team has done a really good job of that over probably the last decade, maybe even longer, just having one collective goal.
"I feel like we're getting pretty close to that as an International Team - certainly feels like that this year. I think that's the way we win: have that collective goal, all buy into it, and it will be an exciting week for us."
Team Europe are the current holders of both the Ryder Cup and Solheim Cup, following wins in New York and the Netherlands respectively, with Masters champion Rory McIlroy also hoping to see the Presidents Cup also leave American hands this week.
"All we need now is the Internationals to do it (win) - that would be great," McIlroy said at Wentworth.
McIlroy's wish is unlikely, but far from impossible. Expect four days of passion and excitement, regardless of whether this is the week the Internationals end their losing streak.
Who will win the Presidents Cup? Watch the United States take on the International Team exclusively live on Sky Sports, with all four days live from Thursday on Sky Sports Golf. Get Sky Sports or stream golf and more with no contract.

A top Ukrainian drone commander said on Tuesday that his forces have used uncrewed aerial vehicles to knock out 300 ships in Russia's "shadow fleet" over 11 weeks.
Maj. Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, said as drone crews reached this tally after they attacked and "burned" 21 tankers over the last three days.
The strikes have been part of a Ukrainian campaign from early July targeting the hundreds-strong fleet of merchant tankers assessed to be carrying sanctioned Russian gas and oil.
While many of these vessels access Russia from the Baltic, the Ukrainian effort has focused on the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. The campaign has been dubbed Operation MoLoChKa, or an acronym that translates into "Moscow will fall through Crimea."
Brovdi said on his Telegram channel that the uncrewed Systems Forces had disabled 166 ships in the Black Sea and another 134 in the Sea of Azov.
"The Sea of Azov, along with the Kerch Strait, is closed and will remain so. In the northern and northeastern Black Sea, it is 'maybe we'll slip through' mode," his statement said.
He's been one of the top commanders to champion a strategy of using mid- and long-range drones to enact a siege of sorts on Crimea, the peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014.
The region is a key logistical hub for Russia's forces on the southern front, and Ukrainian commanders like Brovdi have likened it to a lynchpin of the war as a whole. The past few months have seen them hammering roads, bridges, energy facilities, and transport vessels in a bid to choke the peninsula with resource shortages.
Notably, Operation MoLoChKa has relied on aerial drones, as counter-jamming, artificial intelligence, and flight technology have progressed to the point where Ukraine can use them to more consistently hit Russia's rear.
Previously, Kyiv had relied on surface and underwater drones to battle Russia's navy, driving back its Black Sea Fleet from Ukraine's coast.
Brovdi's statement on Telegram included over two dozen clips that appear to have been shot from drones speeding overhead toward large vessels on open water.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has embarked on a broader, long-range drone attack campaign aimed at Russia's oil and gas industries, hoping to sap the Kremlin's ability to pay for and supply its war effort.
On Tuesday, Ukraine's armed forces said they had knocked out 45% of Russia's oil refining capacity.

Fleming on England discipline, Stokes, late arrival and coaching styles
- Published
Stephen Fleming has given his first interviews since becoming England's Test coach.
The New Zealander, who replaces his close friend Brendon McCullum, spoke at length - covering Bazball, Ben Stokes' departure, England's discipline problems, his own coaching style and more.
Here's what he had to say...
Fleming on Carse and England's discipline problems
England have been dogged by off-field issues in recent times. Harry Brook was involved in an altercation with a nightclub bouncer last year, Ben Duckett was videoed apparently drunk in Australia, Stokes and Gus Atkinson broke a team curfew and Brydon Carse was investigated by police after an incident in Derby.
Fleming said: "It's been disappointing, because I understand what people are working towards. These events can derail a lot of things and divert attention from what really matters.
"When I look at epitomising an international cricketer and what they should stand for, it's Joe [Root].
"When he sits in an interview and openly expresses his disappointment, or uses "hacked off", I know there's work to be done.
"Also, the belonging, identity, what are we doing here together and how we can be the best version of ourselves. A lot of that work has begun.
"That's one of the key things for me to develop and my work with Joe has begun."
On Carse, specifically, Fleming said the bowler is available for selection but added: "There are standards. We pick on runs and wickets primarily, but I think it's foolish not to also say there are standards that need to be set."
On his relationship with McCullum
Fleming has a long-standing relationship with McCullum as a former team-mate, friend and business partner. He replaces his fellow Black Cap, whose tenure as Test coach began with stunning highs before turning sour with the Ashes defeat and his sacking this summer.
"He was heart-sore it had worked out that way, but he was incredibly positive about the experience and opportunity.
"He's been unwavering on that. His belief about where these teams can go is strong, and that was a major part when I was talking to him about doing the role.
"I love his confidence and aggressive nature. I'm more measured.
"Somewhere in between we've got a beautiful working relationship with a huge amount of respect.
"I have so much respect for what Ben Stokes and Brendon did for this English side. They changed the landscape of cricket and that's a really powerful thing."
On what went wrong with Bazball
McCullum's side beat New Zealand and South Africa in their first summer before a memorable win in Pakistan. They were unable to win any of their five-Test series against India and Australia, however.
"I was in awe of what that team were doing and how they were doing it.
"The last 12 months, the evolution – teams caught up, there was talent lost, a lot of reasons. That's now my opportunity.
"There was a thousand wickets lost – [James] Anderson, [Stuart] Broad, then [Chris] Woakes.
"When you do something special and you start doing it differently, everybody else takes a bit of time, then they catch up.
"The pressure then goes on to evolution and that can create some challenges. That's my take on it.
"The Ashes wasn't what they wanted and that is what this team is measured on.
"All I can think about is now my opportunity to pick it up, and maybe add my style, which is looking at personality, a little bit more measured."
On Stokes
Stokes, who announced his shock retirement in June, played under Fleming at Chennai Super Kings in the Indian Premier League. Fleming revealed the pair spoke at Durham earlier this week.
Fleming said: "He'd just come off another monster bowling spell.
"He was in a great space, really happy, enjoying his time with Durham.
"He's got a good winter planned with the family and is very much at peace with his decision. When a player makes that decision to retire, I respect that decision 100%.
"To try to turn that around and question that is wrong. I know how much goes into that type of decision, and I respect that."
Fleming on his wait to arrive
Fleming was named England coach on 30 July but did not take charge of the recent series win over Pakistan, instead following from home.
Fleming said: "There were commitments and family commitments I had that I just wasn't in a position to break. That's more about me as a person, than dropping everything and coming over here.
"I watched and connected with Joe and the team straight away once it was approved – I've got a stress fracture in my left ear from phone calls.
"Watching remotely, I won't say it was an advantage, but watching them operate with eyes wide open as to what was expected, the opportunity, the challenges, and there was also another part – introducing Joe back into captaincy, and Marcus Trescothick the opportunity to do the head coach's role.
"That's part of why I love the game, bringing people forward, developing people, leadership, and they did brilliantly.
"It gave me an opportunity to catch my breath, and then start pretty fresh with a clear mind about what's ahead."
Fleming on his own coaching style
Though Fleming has extensive experience in franchise cricket, he has never coached a red-ball side. He was New Zealand captain for 80 of his 111 Tests, however.
On the playing style he wants, Fleming said: "If people were watching a team, I'd love people to say they are well-planned, there's a discipline and a really strong basic structure to what we're doing, but there's also a bit of flair.
"That's not necessarily me and the way I played, but it's what I loved about this English side when they started playing like this.
"It's taking the best of that and adding that planning aspect, so if supporters could look at us and say 'yeah, they are disciplined, well-planned and competitive'. That's a good start.
"The greatest thing for a team to do is to be able to play conditions and situations.
"One thing this team has earned is the ability to be positive. One of the other aspects is winning the tough moments and making sure we don't just play entertaining cricket and win moments, but win games."
On the Ashes and the World Test Championship
Fleming's first series in charge is against South Africa in December. After two Tests in Bangladesh and a one-off anniversary Test in Melbourne in the winter, attention will then turn to next summer's Ashes. Fleming rejected the idea English cricket is too obsessed by beating Australia.
"No, because I have an obsession with it as well," he said. "New Zealand has an obsession with it, we love it.
"We want to beat Aussie. We're heavily linked to England performances. We have a deep desire to beat Australia in everything, as the little cousin.
"We are linked, and I'm incredibly excited about being part of it. You don't think you're ever going to get that opportunity.
"To have that opportunity and be part of it, I can't wait. I want to be my best self and have a team that represents itself in the best possible way. I've got a vision of that and it's aspirational. It will be brilliant."
On the World Test Championship, an event England are yet to reach the final of, he said: "England could do much better than that.
"And even attitude just around the over rate, I think, comes down to identity and style of play.
"And if that's one of the pinnacle trophies in world cricket, why would we not be trying to get it along with every other marquee event that comes our way?"

Ukraine is ready to sign a landmark drone defence agreement with the United States as Washington looks to tap Kyiv's battlefield experience in countering low-cost, mass-produced unmanned systems, CBS News reported on Tuesday (local time).
According to the report, citing sources, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is prepared to sign the agreement on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week.
However, the report said the deal could instead be finalised at a later date when the US is ready to sign.
Ukraine's battlefield-tested drone technology has particularly gained attention amid the recent war involving Iran.
During the early days of the conflict, Iran used Shahed-type one-way attack drones against American military installations across West Asia. Russia has used the same family of drones extensively against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Earlier in March this year, Ukraine dispatched specialised military and drone-expert teams to West Asia following a formal request from the United States.
In a video address, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had “the greatest experience in the world in countering attack drones”, referring to expertise developed through years of Russian drone attacks.
Ukraine has also said that the US and 10 other countries across the Middle East and Europe have sought its assistance in dealing with the growing drone threat.
One of the biggest lessons from the Ukraine war has been the growing mismatch between the cost of an attacking drone and the weapon used to destroy it.
Iranian-style attack drones can cost tens of thousands of dollars, while interceptor missiles deployed by sophisticated Western air-defence systems can cost hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars.
That creates a difficult economic equation when large numbers of relatively inexpensive drones are launched simultaneously.
NPR national security correspondent Greg Myre highlighted this problem in an earlier podcast with his publication, noting that US ships and military bases have air-defence systems designed largely to counter expensive missiles with expensive interceptors.
Myre said Ukraine "has pioneered a range of smaller, cheaper interceptor drones", with some costing as little as $1,000.
Russia's invasion has forced Ukraine to rapidly adapt its military technology and tactics, Myre said.
Years of repeated Russian drone attacks have given Ukrainian forces extensive operational experience in identifying, tracking and intercepting unmanned systems.
That experience has also created a feedback loop between Ukraine's military and its domestic defence industry, with systems tested in combat, rapidly modified and returned to the battlefield, according to Myre.
This battlefield-driven innovation is now attracting interest from countries facing similar threats.
For the US, Ukraine's experience offers a way to address a problem that has become increasingly important for American forces: how to defend bases, ships and troops in West Asia against large numbers of relatively cheap drones without exhausting expensive air-defence interceptors.
Low-cost drones are also increasingly being used by state and non-state actors, including the Houthis and Hamas, against US allies, making counter-drone technology an important component of modern air defence.
Ukraine has also sought to expand its defence partnerships beyond the US.
According to the Kyiv Post, Kyiv has signed comprehensive 10-year defence and security agreements with Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar.
The agreements come as West Asian countries face growing drone threats following the US-Israel-Iran conflict and a series of attacks and retaliatory strikes involving unmanned systems.
As Myre observed, the dynamic between Washington and Kyiv has shifted: “Ukraine needs American air-defence capabilities, while the US has a growing interest in Ukraine's experience with inexpensive drone interceptors.”

For years, cybersecurity practitioners have tracked different types of malware and detected potential infections using digital fingerprints to identify different hacking tools and follow their use over time. As attackers are increasingly incorporating agentic AI components into their hacking tools, researchers from Cisco Talos shared an open-source framework on Monday that they hope will be used widely to classify and analyze AI-integrated malware. They also have proof that it's already working.
They're calling the framework Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network, or CAIRN, named after the stacks of stones that hikers set up on trails to mark the path or emphasize something about a certain spot. As malware authors expand their use of AI services, Cisco Talos researchers have used CAIRN to identify a hacking tool with fully autonomous command-and-control infrastructure. Dubbed CLOSEDQUORUM, the malware plotted its moves within a target system by polling up to four large language models (LLMs) about what it should do and taking its directives from that hive mind.
“The core idea is that AI integration has these vestiges, like fingerprints, that are left behind,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos who led development of CAIRN. “That gives us a signal that we can use to track these samples, classify them, and look at what's happening. What are attackers trying? What kind of emergent behaviors are we seeing? That's a valuable resource to the defensive community as these things become more mainstream.”
In July 2025, the Ukrainian cybersecurity response unit CERT-UA warned about a phishing campaign it had detected using malware known as “LAMEHUG.” The implant communicated with an LLM called Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct through a Hugging Face API to get commands. “At the time I was like, ‘Wow, this is amazing. There’s gonna be this big boom of AI-enabled malware and the landscape is totally going to change,’” Fetterman says.
A year later, though, when he went to do a retrospective this summer of malware integrating AI, Fetterman was shocked that he could still only find a few documented examples. “There really wasn't a lot there. I think I came up with maybe nine different named malware families,” and some of those were proofs of concept created for research, he says. “It just wasn't what I was expecting, and I think I also had a hard time believing that that was the reality of where we were. So I wanted to start digging into that.”
The result is CAIRN, which is designed to flag AI-integration characteristics and attributes from metadata, and use this to classify and tag malware samples with, essentially, a unique ID. The system then analyzes each artifact in the context of everything in the CAIRN library and groups them by various traits to illustrate potential trends and connections. Fetterman says that after working on and using CAIRN for the past few months, he has discovered about 20 additional examples of AI-integrated malware.
“So while I do think this is still largely experimental for attackers, the landscape is a lot more complex and diverse than has been publicly reported,” he says. “There's a lot going on out there, and it does provide a valuable early signal to what's going to happen.”
The CLOSEDQUORUM hacking tool that CAIRN identified is Windows malware that checks with DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Google Gemini to develop a consensus on what its next steps should be. Even if one AI service is unavailable, the malware still polls the others, creating enough redundancy that the system is totally closed and has no mechanism for human input. Cisco Talos researchers saw some links between the malware and cybercriminal forums about credit card fraud going back to 2025, and it is designed to steal login credentials and cryptocurrency. The researchers could not confirm who developed the malware, though, or whether it has actually been used in real-world attacks.
“Initially, everyone saw AI as a productivity tool, right?” says Matt Olney, senior director of threat intelligence at Cisco Talos, referring to both legitimate work and malicious hacking. “Now what we're seeing is that it's becoming operationalized. So for attackers, it's allowing them to run more campaigns, hit more spaces, handle more and different computers, because they have this very intelligent box in the backend that can ask questions and give responses.”

Some people sharing the quote claimed Trump was specifically referring to the deaths of 18 service members during the conflict. He was in fact referring to the conflict itself.
A rumor circulated online in September 2026 that U.S. President Donald Trump had called the Iran war, initiated by the United States and Israel in February 2026, "small potatoes."
Users shared the claim on social media and Reddit. Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., shared the purported quote and added, "Tell that to the families of the 18 troops we've lost, the hundreds of wounded servicemembers, and the Americans suffering every single day from record high prices."
The quote was correctly attributed to Trump.
Trump made the statement during a news conference in the Oval Office on Sept. 4, during which he signed executive orders related to the cattle industry.
The news conference was available to view on the White House's official YouTube channel. The comment in question begins around the 25-minute mark after a reporter referred to Vice President J.D. Vance's statement that he did not consider the conflict in Iran a war and asked, "Can you explain to the American people if this is not a war, what exactly is it?"
Trump responded (emphasis ours):
A lot of people don't call it a war. I call it a military conflict. Because it's small potatoes for us. It's not a big thing. We did Venezuela and we did this. In Venezuela we lost nobody, in this we lost 18 people. And in Vietnam we lost 100,000 people, and in other conflicts you lost tens of thousands of people.
Trump continued by elaborating on some of the military operations the United States has enacted since the start of the conflict. He said, "It's a military conflict, but it's very intermittent. I could see somebody not calling it a war."
Asked directly by the same reporter whether he considered the deaths of 18 service members to also be "small potatoes," Trump said he'd met their families and had gotten "very friendly" with some and again mentioned the number of deceased from past conflicts to compare the size of the numbers.
The White House press office told Snopes via email:
President Trump cares deeply about our men and women in uniform, which is why he approved a historic pay increase for our military servicemembers and restored a focus on our warfighters at the Pentagon. Every loss of life within our armed forces is a tragedy and one loss too many, and the President honors and remembers the sacrifice of every hero who has fallen in the line of duty. The President was recognizing the importance of ensuring that Iran, a country that for 47 years has chanted "Death to America" and killed our troops overseas, can never possess a nuclear weapon.
Media outlets widely reported Trump's quote, including CNN, The Associated Press and USA Today.
Some social media posts called out Trump's comment and claimed he specifically called the number of deceased service members "small potatoes." In truth, he made the comment about the conflict itself, not specifically the number of service members killed.

At Area Hospital, Bhadrachalam, in Telangana’s Bhadradri Kothagudem district, a single specialist has helped bring specialised eye surgery to patients from remote tribal areas and even neighbouring States.
The Ophthalmology Unit of the hospital has completed 400 cataract surgeries since its dedicated ophthalmic operation theatre was established in December 2023. Patients have travelled to Bhadrachalam not only from Bhadradri Kothagudem district but also from Warangal, Karimnagar, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Odisha.
The unit currently performs around 20 cataract surgeries a month and has increased its surgical schedule from one to two days a week. The achievement is significant given the geographical challenges of the agency area and the limited availability of specialist manpower.
The ophthalmic operation theatre, the first-of-its-kind in the entire district, was established in December 2023, even before a similar facility was established at Government General Hospital (GGH), Kothagudem. It was set up with financial support from former District Collector Anudeep Durishetty on the initiative of District Coordinator of Health Services (DCHS) Dr. G. Ravi Babu.
The facility subsequently received continued support from successive District Collectors Jitesh V. Patil and Ankit, and ITDA Project Officer B. Rahul. “Their support included intraocular lenses, surgical consumables and other requirements, enabling the unit to provide cataract surgery services consistently,” said Dr. Ravi Babu.
The hospital performs modern phacoemulsification cataract surgeries. The 400 procedures have been completed without major complications. The unit is also among the best-performing ophthalmology units under the Telangana Vaidya Vidhana Parishad (TVVP), despite functioning with a single ophthalmologist appointed on a contract basis.
“For a hospital located in a remote tribal region, the ability to provide specialised surgical care without patients having to travel to major urban centres represents a significant healthcare service. The hospital has been able to sustain the service through a combination of administrative support, dedicated infrastructure, essential surgical consumables and specialist medical and support staff,” added Dr. Ravi Babu.
He appreciated ophthalmologist Dr. Santosh as well as the entire ophthalmology nursing, operation theatre and support teams for their sustained commitment. According to Dr. Ravi Babu, the ophthalmic operation theatre was established using district funds and, so far, has not received State funds.

A disturbing video of a man assaulting a Bhelpuri vendor is going viral on social media (here, here, and here). The video shows the man approaching the vendor, eating Bhelpuri from his basket, spitting on him, and assaulting him. The video is being shared with claims that it shows a real incident in Patna, with users demanding action against the man. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a real incident of a man assaulting a Bhelpuri vendor in Patna.
Fact: The video is scripted and does not show a real incident in Patna. The men seen in the video clarified that it was made for entertainment and that both are part of the same team. Several other videos on their social media accounts also show them acting together in different situations. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a YouTube channel named Sonu Paswan. The man seen allegedly assaulting the vendor in the viral video posted a clarification video (archived) on the channel, stating that the video was made for entertainment purposes and does not depict a real incident. He said he regularly makes such emotional videos and appealed to viewers not to share the video with false claims. He also urged viewers to stop mocking or roasting his work.
We also found a clarification video (archived) by the vendor on the same channel. He stated that he creates emotional videos centred around poverty and that the man seen assaulting him in the video is also a member of their team. He clarified that the video does not depict a real incident.
We also found several other videos on Sonu Paswan’s Facebook account, in which both men seen in the viral video appear together, acting in different situations.
To sum up, this viral video of a man assaulting a Bhelpuri vendor in Patna is scripted, not a real incident.

Medicines for brittle bones and breakages are grabbing the attention of the pharma industry, which has been incentivized by a long-awaited regulatory change.
Osteoporosis, a condition affecting older adults that causes bones to become thin and fragile, used to be a top priority for pharmaceutical companies. Eli Lilly, Merck, Novartis, and GSK each had their own treatment designed to stop bones from weakening. But the cumbersome requirements for taking the drugs, as well as a series of safety concerns, stifled their use. Many patients who are eligible for osteoporosis therapies don’t take any of the drugs available today.
Several companies hope to fill that void. Eli Lilly is recruiting scientists to work on osteoporosis therapies, according to Bloomberg. Other pharmaceutical companies are rumored to be following suit. Venture capitalists, having taken notice, are now making bone health one of their priorities.

Hockey coaches didn't submit training plan before Matthew Mayich collapsed in workout: Arizona university
Lawyer says Hamilton-born St. Louis draft pick in stable, critical condition, family 'praying for a miracle'
Hockey coaches at Arizona State University (ASU) didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before an outdoor workout last month that saw NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapse, leaving him in hospital in critical condition.
James Rund, the university official leading the review, wrote that the Hamilton-born 21-year-old collapsed just before 8:30 a.m. during the Aug. 20 training session at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus.
The report, which calls for a "a blue-ribbon advisory panel," said the temperature was about 30 C, and the student athletes were involved in "calisthenics, bodyweight exercises such as pushups and planks, and running."
The hockey coaches asked permission for Timothy Zeisel, who was there for the workout and had "spoken with the ASU Hockey team in the 2025-26 season about topics of leadership and teamwork," to speak to the team. However, the coaches didn't "submit a plan of training activities for review by ASU’s strength and conditioning coaches" before training began.
Near the end of the workout, "Matthew appeared to struggle, and then in rapid succession stumbled, dropped the medicine ball and fell to the ground. He attempted to get up and resume running but fell to his knees," wrote Rund, ASU's senior vice-president of educational outreach and student services.
Mayich in stable, critical condition, lawyer says
The Mayich family's lawyer, Rob Carey, said on Tuesday that "Matthew is in stable but critical condition still. The family is still praying for a miracle, but nothing has significantly changed. But even if that happens, we will never have the young man who came to Arizona last month, a hockey star and (by all accounts) a wonderful person."
In an interview last week from Phoenix, Ariz., with CBC News, Mayich's father, John Mayich, said "we know Matthew's a fighter and we're hoping he pulls through this."
Before the workout, Matthew was "perfectly healthy," said his mother, Christina.
Carey said that "when Matthew went down, there was no plan and no preparation, so he was treated in a way that hurt his chances rather than helped them."
"A month later, nobody's been named, nobody's been suspended, nobody's been fired for violating the very policies ASU published today, and the university wants to appoint a committee."
He added that "a committee isn't going to tell us why grown men with a rulebook in their hands let this happen to a young man at his first real workout in the desert. That's what an investigation is for, and it's why we're going to ask the county attorney to do one."
Carey said in early September that based on his own investigation, he believes Mayich endured a "military-style, brutal, gruelling workout" with no breaks and no water for over an hour.
"You have an elite NHL-drafted athlete showing up on the first coach-led workout, the very first day the team could organize formally, and he left the field with no chance of recovery," Carey said. "Obviously there's something wrong."
Rund said ASU would "be undertaking a comprehensive review of its practices to identify and implement best practices regarding the planning, conduct and monitoring of athletic activities. and the response to emergencies that arise during athletic activities."
In early September, a spokesperson for the ASU Police Department said they were investigating what happened to Mayich, which is a "standard procedure" for an incident of this severity.
The report said ASU would have a panel of experts provide best practice recommendations for:
- Planning and approval of outdoor athletic activities, including strength and conditioning activities, practices and competitions.
- Staffing, monitoring and conduct of outdoor athletic activities, including adjustments to address changed conditions or adverse reactions.
- Preparation for and response to adverse events or reactions occurring during outdoor athletic activities.
- Use of outside consultants in the planning and delivery of strength and conditioning, and practice activities.
Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020. He was selected in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft by the St. Louis Blues.
Doug Armstrong, the Blues' president of hockey operations, said in a news release in late August, "The entire Blues organization is keeping Matthew Mayich close to our hearts as we pray for his comfort and recovery while he continues to undergo medical treatment in Arizona."
The organization also extends its "deepest support" to his family, friends and teammates during this difficult time, Armstrong said.
'A tremendous hockey player'
During his six seasons with the Huskies and one as a member of the Hamilton Jr. Bulldogs, Mayich established "himself as a tremendous hockey player and, more importantly, an outstanding person both on and off the ice," the Hamilton Steel Hockey Club, formerly the Huskies, said.
The statement was sent to CBC Hamilton on behalf of the organization, former Huskies president Mike Spadafora and former Huskies head coach Chris Travale. Spadafora is currently the councillor for Hamilton's Ward 14 and running for re-election in the Oct. 26 municipal vote.
"Without fail, whenever [Mayich] is asked, he comes back every year to speak and skate with a new crop of young kids," Travale said. "His message is always about so much more than hockey — it’s about relationships, friendships, and the experiences you have along the hockey journey."
Mayich's father said Matthew "didn't care if he was at a small rink in Hamilton or a big rink in St. Louis with a lot of people — he just loves the game."
The incident has made waves in the sports world, prompting the Professional Hockey Players’ Association to speak up about the lack of protections for young athletes.
"When athletes feel pressure to remain silent about an injury, illness, exhaustion or concern because they fear the consequences of speaking up, the system has failed them," said PHPA executive director Brian Ramsay in a statement on Sept. 10 that doesn't directly name Mayich.
"Athletes should never have to choose between their health and their careers. Period."

Iran’s president faces stark choice in UN speech after Trump threatens ‘annihilation’
Trump told the UN he has two choices on how to deal with Iran - and Masoud Pezeshkian faces a similar dilemma. Gergana Krasteva reports

Iran's president Masoud Pezeshkian has arrived in New York ahead of his speech at the UN General Assembly Wednesday, amid renewed hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough to the Middle East war.
At the annual high-level gathering at the UN headquarters, the Iranian politician will get the chance to defend his country’s position on the global stage.
But his speech comes just hours after US president Donald Trump renewed his threats against Iran in his speech to the assembly in New York.
Trump said he faces two choices on how to deal with the Iranian regime, one of which was “annihilation”. The Iranian delegation walked out when he made the remarks Tuesday.
Pezeshkian faces a similar choice in terms of what tone to strike in the speech, either pushing for further diplomacy or bowing to Iranian hardliners at home who want a more aggressive stance.
Below we look at what we know about Iran’s reformer president and the deadlock both sides hope to break.
Who is Masoud Pezeshkian?
The 71-year-old has served as the president of Iran since 2024, leading the country through two major conflicts - first the 12-day war with Israel in 2025 and through the US-Israeli conflict that began in February.
Before entering politics, he worked as a heart surgeon, leading him to become president of the prestigious Tabriz University of Medical Sciences in the 1990s. His work eventually lead him to becoming Health Minister, putting him under a spotlight.
A member of the reformist faction, Pezeshkian was elected by over 16 million people on a campaign to moderate Iran’s conservative outlook, including loosening strictures about female dress.
The politician was the only moderate reformist among the six candidates at the time, and went as far as criticising the country’s morality police.
He had pledged to stop street confrontations over the mandatory hijab, particularly after the death of Mahsa Jina Amini while in police custody, which sparked the Woman, Life, Freedom mass demonstrations.
Before the US war, Pezeshkian had promised to improve Iran’s relationship with the West. He had hoped to revive the agreement with the US over his country’s nuclear programme in exchange for lifting international sanctions against it.
But after the assassination of Ali Khamenei in February 2026, he was heavily sidelined from military decisions.
Throughout the war he has welcomed talks with the US, remarking: “If we do not negotiate, what else are we to do?”
Away from politics, Pezeshkian suffered a personal tragedy in 1994 when his wife died and their youngest son were killed in a car crash. He has never remarried, and has raised his daughter and two other sons alone.
What do we know about his UN speech?
Pezeshkian is expected to use his speech to drive forward Iran’s agenda and point the finger at the US and Israel for starting the war in the Middle East, and for alleged war crimes in Minab, where a suspected US strike hit a school, killing more than 121 children along with 26 teachers.
Before departing from Tehran, the president said he would defend Iran’s positions and speak about the suffering of its people, alleged war crimes by its adversaries and the erosion of trust in negotiations, Iran International reported, according to state news agency IRNA.
“We have been at the negotiating table several times and signed an agreement. They [enemies] acted against the negotiations and understandings reached. The world has seen and continues to see that they have easily violated those understandings,” Pezeshkian said.
However, he has already faced backlash at home for even attending the event, given the ongoing conflict and the US strikes on nuclear facilities last year.
A former senior Revolutionary Guards said he should have stayed in Tehran - and used that as the opportunity to protest US aggression, Iran International reported.
Hossein Kanani-Moghadam, a former commander in Iran's Revolutionary Guards, said the General Assembly could still give Pezeshkian a useful diplomatic platform, but added: “If I were Pezeshkian, I would not go to New York.”
Given that he is attending however, hardliners in Tehran called on Pezeshkian to not show any signs of weakness and to criticise other countries in the region that have provided support for the US, Iran Insight reports.
Why was his entourage denied visas?
Even before the Iranian delegation landed in New York, the US took a hostile stance and denied visas to the media team joining the president.
Pezeshkian said the measure shows that the US is concerned about its actions being brought to the world’s attention.
“They are trying to prevent the voice of the Iranian people from being heard and have blocked the presence of Iran’s media delegation,” he said. “However, many international media outlets are present, and if we manage our message effectively, we will be able to make the voice of the Iranian people heard.”
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqae also complained earlier about the US decision, saying the administration is “seeking to hide the truth” by barring Iranian journalists.
“When an administration slams its doors shut - even on American journalists it happens to dislike - and bars foreign reporters, including the Iranian president’s media team, whose voices it would rather silence, it is not managing access; it is trying to hide the truth and further its misinformation campaign by trampling on the right of access to information,” he said in a post on X.
“A nation that once took pride in tearing down the Iron Curtain now finds itself standing behind one of its own.”
US authorities have not yet commented on the matter.
Could there be a breakthrough?
A senior Iranian official earlier told Reuters that the delegation in New York has full authority to revive diplomacy with the US, even though Pezeshkian has not had a central role in the negotiations process.
They said that the government has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the US begins easing military pressure and lifts its blockade on ports.
In the past, Iranian officials have been reluctant to meet with US officials, but that may change as pressure is piling on from the energy market. Brent crude continues to hover around $100 (£74) per barrel, up from about the $70 (£52) range in the weeks before the start of the war.
Trump meanwhile has said he is still in “deciding mode” about the next steps in the conflict. However, he has not ruled out meeting with his Iranian counterpart during his trip.

HHS unveils new initiatives on animal testing
HHS laid out its latest strategies to speed the shift away from using animals in medical testing. Beginning next February, research methods other than animal testing can be used when “appropriate” for determining the safety of drugs and biologics, according to a final FDA rule issued yesterday. At the same time, the NIH unveiled several initiatives designed to encourage the use of non-animal approaches such as cell-based assays, organs-on-a-chip, and computer models.
STAT’s Ed Silverman wrote about the new policies and spoke with advocates on both sides of the long-running debate. Read more.
700,000
That’s how many seniors have started taking GLP-1s since July, when Medicare began covering the drugs, Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks told CNBC on Monday.
Medicare is technically prohibited from paying for weight loss drugs, but the Trump administration circumvented the law by making the drugs available through a demonstration program, sort of like an experimental pilot. But as John Wilkerson reported over the summer, this theoretically temporary program may prove difficult to actually end.
Drugmakers look to bolster brittle bones again
Osteoporosis used to be a top priority for pharmaceutical companies. Big players like Eli Lilly, Merck, and Novartis each had their own treatments designed to stop bones from weakening. But a lot of eligible patients don’t take the existing medications, likely due to a long list of side effects, along with the simple fact that they can be annoying to take. Patients are often required to stay upright for 30 minutes and avoid eating for up to an hour.
But late last year, drug developers were handed a fresh incentive to address those concerns: The FDA said in December that it would allow companies to use a new clinical endpoint that could shave years off of development timelines. And several companies already seem to be jumping at the chance. Read more from STAT’s Allison DeAngelis.
A private equity-owned hospital chain goes nonprofit
It’s unheard of: Quorum Health, a private equity-owned hospital system, is in the process of converting to a nonprofit organization. While individual institutions have made the change before, Quorum will transition all 11 of its hospitals, most of which serve rural areas.
There are concrete benefits to the nonprofit structure, including tax advantages, discounted drugs, and the ability to apply for grants. But some are concerned that the deal is structured to benefit Quorum’s current investors to the detriment of the hospitals and their patients. “The question is, are the creditors taking enough of a discount to leave a hospital company that is viable?” said Jim Baker, executive director of the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, a nonprofit watchdog group. Read more from STAT’s Tara Bannow on the high stakes transition.
The state of youth gender-affirming care
Last Friday, the Justice Department announced that it had reached settlement deals with NYU Langone and the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center over the provision of gender-affirming care to young people. Both hospitals agreed to stop providing puberty blockers, hormones, and rare surgical procedures to minors. At least six institutions have made such deals, though none have admitted to or been convicted of any wrongdoing. For the Trump administration, ending the services is the point, as health officials have repeatedly asserted their desire to stop what they call “sex-rejecting procedures.”
The chilling effect of the government’s dogged offensive against transgender health care has been swift. Dozens of hospitals have stopped providing care, even if they haven’t directly been targeted by legal action. NYU Langone said in a statement that the settlement protects patients from the threat of extensive government subpoenas that had been directed at the institution. The AP has more on the agreements.
How to support mentally ill pregnant people
A decade before she began pursuing pregnancy, Meg LeDuc had a harrowing break with reality. She stopped taking her antipsychotic medication, leading to multiple overdoses, including twice within two weeks. Even with years of stability separating her from that experience, LeDuc worried that, if she became a mother, she would be a danger to her own child.
She and her husband were cautious, seeking prenatal counseling on the safety of her medication regimen in pregnancy and her potential for relapse. But as LeDuc notes in a new First Opinion essay, this sort of care remains out of reach for many women with serious mental illness, 20% of whom are uninsured.
“People experiencing such devastating delusions deserve humane, quality care. With such care, we are capable of leading rich, fulfilling lives,” she writes. “And even being good parents.” Read more about the limits of reproductive psychiatry.

One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls.
Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child.
Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk.
South Africa is reeling after the discovery of nine women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year.
Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.”
Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet.
The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him.
Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according to News24.
Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct.
“Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.”
When Sibiya appeared before the Madlanga Commission in February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation.
Sibiya also denied that he had received a gift of 20 impalas from Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift.
Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering, declined to comment on the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.

Cyclist who dressed as man to avoid Taliban wins silver medal
- Published
A female cyclist from Afghanistan who previously disguised herself as a man when chasing a career in the sport has won a silver medal at the Asian Games.
Fariba Hashimi fled her country after the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
She says she trained in disguise out of necessity before then in an effort to avoid being attacked, in a country where women's rights are heavily restricted.
She earned her medal in the women's road race near Nagoya in Japan on Tuesday.
The 23-year-old's achievement follows her seventh-place finish in the women's individual time trial on Sunday.
Describing her medal as "something special", Hashimi hopes it can inspire other women in Afghanistan to follow their dreams.
"I was born inside a country where the women who dream are getting attacked, and I'm really happy that I have fought against that," she said.
"I hope that the next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear."
Hashimi followed her sister Yulduz, also an international cyclist, into the sport at the age of 15, despite danger in their home province of Faryab.
"I always dressed as a man to go to training, wearing two or three different masks so people would not recognise or attack me," Hashimi previously told Reuters., external
Hashimi said she would have to avoid stones being thrown at her whilst riding her bike.
Hashimi now lives and trains in Italy thanks to help from the Italian former world champion Alessandra Cappellotto.
Looking back at life in Afghanistan, Hashimi said the Taliban "took away our freedom".
"This silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women, and I'm really happy," she said.
"I'm not alone, I know that behind me millions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me."
Hashimi and her sister competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics and are now setting their sights on the 2028 Los Angeles Games.
"I never want to give up," Hashimi said, "and hopefully we can see [what can happen] again in Los Angeles."

Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.
On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.
Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.
I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.
As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.
The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.
Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.
So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.
For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.
Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.
In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.
“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”
The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.
India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.
For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.
In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.
A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)
“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.
Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.

That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”

As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.
Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. Italy has selected Paolo Strippoli’s The Spiral (L’Estranea) as its candidate for the Best International Feature Film at the 99th Academy Awards.
The drama, which world premiered in Competition at this year’s Venice Film Festival, stars Jasmine Trinca as a woman who arrives at her daughter’s apartment during a storm to confess a lie that will undermine the family’s foundation and their relationship as it comes out in the open.
Trinca is joined in the cast by Romana Maggiora Vergano, Adriano Giannini, Valeria Bruni Tedeschi.
It is Strippoli’s fourth film after award-winning The Holy Boy (2025), Flowing (2022) and A Classic Horror Story (2021).
Watch on Deadline
The film is lead produced by Marina Marzotto and Mattia Oddone at Rome-based Propaganda with Rai Cinema, in coproduction with France’s Paris-based Kazak Productions, Belgium’s Tarantula and Italy’s Bari-based Dinamo Film.
01 Distribution will release the film in Italy on October 18. Le Pacte is handling international sales.
The Spiral was a selected from a shortlist of 21 potential candidates which also included another two Venice 2026 Competition titles, Nanni Moretti’s It Will Happen Tonight and Marco Bechis’ Back To Buenos Aires, as well as Orizzonti title The House of the Monkey which won Best Screenplay and Riccardo Scamarcio, Best Actor.
The selection committee was overseen by Italian cinema guild Anica and gathered Giorgio Carlo Brugnoni, Cristina Comencini, Federica Lucisano, Francesco Melzi D’Eril and Nick Vivarelli, who voted on the choice.
In a note explaining their selection, they said it had been driven by the fact that The Spiral is “a new genre film, by a young director who has recently begun his career and has been appreciated by audiences and national and international critics.”
Italy last won the Best International Feature Film Oscar in 2014 with The Great Beauty by Paolo Sorrentino.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
- Published
"What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give."
"For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"
Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.
The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive last Sunday. Her battered body, partly burned, found later in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.
Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death.
"How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish.
"There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."
Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.
The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one.
His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni.
The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge.
"We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining.
"I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her.
"No family should have to deal with what we are faced with."
Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July.
Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women.
Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.
Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked.
Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis.
South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that during the last quarter – between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered.
The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder.
Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events.
And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster.
Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis.
It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit.
This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further.
Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime.
"Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide.
"Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman."
Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa.
It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue.
"It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking."
Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done.
President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls."
Lebogang Ramofoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity.
"The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time in memorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994.
"What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed.
"This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on - that cycle has not been broken."
In Kempton Park, a district of Ekurhuleni where five of the nine recent bodies were found, Lumka Maqhubela is part of the Girl2Woman Foundation group which has held protests to raise awareness of the crimes.
"We are grieved, we are scared," she says. "If the police cannot protect us any more the government should step in and do something.
"It's clear that we are not safe, we cannot be told by the police to be more vigilant. They should be doing more to make our communities safe – what else are we expected to do? We are not safe anywhere, not in our homes, not in the streets, it needs to stop."
"I feel uncomfortable," says Thulisile Sibande, 32. "When I go to a shop, I have to look around. I'm shocked and scared. So scared, it's a trauma."
Thembi Mabena, 60, tells the BBC she lived in the same neighbourhood as Dineo Motapane.
"She was laughing every day, with everybody," she remembers. "Now I'm worried.
"I know many children, girls, who tell me they are afraid to go to the shop alone. There is no safety, even for me too. I am old, but there is no safety."
"In South Africa," says Lerato Mzizi, 20, simply, "women are not safe any more."

In September 2026, social media users shared a video of an unusual animal encounter. The clip showed a rhino and a much smaller muntjac deer appearing to play together and butt heads in the snow.
"A tiny 13 kg Chinese muntjac deer playfully challenged a 1.7-ton rhino named Maruśka at the Wrocław Zoo in Poland," one Reddit post (archived) captioned the video.
Since January 2026, the clip has appeared in posts on X, Threads, Facebook and YouTube. Overlaid text in a YouTube video described (archived) the encounter as "David vs. Goliath," while some social media users wondered if the footage was generated using artificial-intelligence tools. For example, one Reddit user wrote (archived): "Saw this on another reddit post and many people were saying it's AI, but I'm really not sure it is."
However, the video was real. It showed Maruśka, a female Indian rhinoceros, and Tata (Polish for "Dad"), a male Chinese muntjac, a small deer species.
The footage originated from Zoo Wrocław in Poland. Managers of the zoo's official Facebook and Instagram pages posted the clip on Jan. 8, 2026. In the caption (translated from Polish), the zoo framed the scene as a humorous confidence mismatch and said the muntjac's bravado was driven by mating-season hormones:
Looks like someone forgot to look in the mirror this morning
Respect to Maruśka for her angelic patience!
Where does this bravado come from in the male Chinese muntjac?
It's nature calling! His partner is in heat, and testosterone is surging in the bachelor. He needs to burn off energy and show who's boss - even if his sparring partner weighs 1.7 tons. Who would have thought there was such a warrior in such a small body?
The clip was widely covered by national and local Polish news media outlets that cited the zoo as the source.
After the video went viral online, Zoo Wrocław published a follow-up article on Jan. 12, 2026, crediting the clip to employee Kamil Guzik, a foreman in the zoo's carnivorous mammals section.
Wrocław.pl — an online news portal in Wrocław, the city where the video was captured — spoke with Maciej Okupnik, a hooved-animal keeper at Zoo Wrocław, who explained why the two species shared a space.
The website quoted Okupnik as saying muntjacs and rhinos can live in proximity to one another both at the zoo and in the wild. He said muntjacs are territorial and mark areas with scent glands near their eyes, while rhinos typically tolerate other animals in their territory because "they're not afraid of anyone." He reportedly described the encounter as theatrical and said similar standoffs had occurred before but this was the first time staff had filmed one.
TVN24, a Polish news media channel, said Okupnik emphasized that the male muntjac's behavior was driven by a mix of territorial instinct and hormones because his partner was "in heat." He said the animal's priority was to defend his space and impress the female, not to challenge the rhino, and that Maruśka was not aggressive toward him in day-to-day interactions. Okupnik added that the rhino appeared to treat the lunges as an invitation to play, with no signs of real aggression. At one point, Maruśka snorted as if to signal she had enough and simply walked away.
Snopes has fact-checked several rhino-related rumors before. For example, in June 2025, we examined a claim that the northern white rhinoceros was extinct after the last such rhino died.
