The iPhone Duo hides several firsts and oddities: horizontal rear cameras, vertical UI elements, top-mounted volume buttons, Apple Pencil support, titanium construction, Smart Take, a circular status bar, unusual USB-C placement, and no Action button or Pro camera controls.
Apple launched many devices at its recent Surprise and Shine event, but there was no doubting the star of the show. It was the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, and the device that many are expecting to do for foldables what the iPhone did for smartphones almost two decades ago. Small wonder then that the past few days have seen everyone and their grandmother discussing the iPhone Duo.
Debates have been raging over its animations, its crease, its cameras, its apps, and of course, its price. Some are hailing it as the coolest thing since sliced bread, while others insist it is a spawn of Satan in smartphone shape. But in all this debate and discussion, some important aspects and features of the Duo have either escaped attention or have not been adequately covered.
Here are ten things you might have missed about Apple’s first foldable.
Table of Contents
The first iPhone with horizontally arranged cameras on the back…selfie cameras on the corners
iPhones have been coming with multiple cameras (two or three) on their backs for a while now. However, they have always been arranged vertically, one below the other, or in the case of some Pro devices, with two cameras one below the other and the third one placed between them but slightly to the side, forming a triangle of sorts. The iPhone Duo thus becomes the first iPhone to have cameras placed next to each other horizontally, in what some would term a very Pixel-like style. The selfie cameras also get new locations – moving to the right corner of the external display and close to the right corner of the internal display (when opened), where it actually lies under the display. Regular iPhone users are sure to notice a change in perspective.
The dock, navigation, and even the Dynamic Island just got radically right, and utterly vertical
The cameras on the iPhone Duo might have gone horizontal, but some elements of the UI have gone vertical! While everyone has been focusing on the crease in the middle of the iPhone Duo and its visibility (it’s not easy to spot, by all accounts). Apple moved many iOS elements to the right side and gave them a vertical orientation. Lock screen controls, navigation buttons, the home screen dock, and even the Dynamic Island are on the right side of the iPhone Duo, and what’s more, are arranged vertically.
The Dynamic Island even slides open vertically to show information and updates. Evidently, this was done because of the width of the iPhone Duo (it is also the widest iPhone ever), which would have made it difficult to reach these elements. They have therefore been placed on the same side as the display unlock/power button, which is also a fingerprint scanner. This is pretty right-wing in UI terms, literally.
Volume buttons on the top
The iPhone Duo comes with a rather different volume button placement from other foldables. While it is conventional for most foldables and indeed, most ‘normal’ phones, to have volume buttons on the right or left side, the iPhone Duo actually has volume buttons on the top, aligned slightly towards the right. This is a volume button placement we have seen on the newer iPad minis but not on any other iPhones or iPads. It is a rather odd location in our opinion, and if opened and rotated clockwise, it would place the buttons on the lower part of the right side, and on the top of the left side if rotated anti-clockwise.
Camera Control? Present! Action button? Er…
While the iPhone Duo comes with a Camera Control button like other recent iPhones, it, rather surprisingly, does not have an Action button, which is generally seen on the left side of most iPhones and can be customized to carry out a number of tasks. It used to toggle Silent mode on and off, before being changed to an action button. Clearly, it was either not good enough to make the cut for the Duo or perhaps there simply was not enough space for it.
Apple Pencil support exists, but only for the Type-C one
The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone to come with Apple Pencil support. What’s more, it supports the Apple Pencil on both its internal as well as external display. But there is a catch – it only supports the basic Apple Pencil (USB-C). This means that while one can scribble and sketch easily, there’s no pressure sensitivity and no support for double taps. One will also need a Type-C cable to charge it, as it cannot charge magnetically. Given the price and potential of the device, it would have been good to have Apple Pencil Pro support on it.
Only new iPhone with Titanium
Remember how Titanium was the coolest thing in premium phones a few years ago. Well, while it still remains a very premium material, it has largely disappeared from the smartphone scene, with even Apple seemingly moving on to other materials, with only the iPhone Air using Titanium last year. This time around, it is the iPhone Duo that carries the Titanium legacy forward. While the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max use “forged aluminum” and ceramic glass, the iPhone Duo comes with a main chassis made with grade 5 Titanium, and 3D-printed titanium is also used for the hinge cover.
The only iPhone camera with Smart Take
Although its cameras might not seem as formidable as those on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the iPhone Duo has a slice of camera magic up its sleeve that no other iPhone has. This is Smart Take, which, with some AI magic, automatically works out when you are perfectly placed for a photograph and takes it without you needing to hit a capture button or prompt the device in any manner. It is supposed to work very well with individual and group selfies, and uses the rear cameras while showing you a preview on the cover display. While the feature is designed mainly for the fold form factor, it would be great to see it on “normal” iPhones too, although one might not be able to see previews!
A Type-C port placed under the cover display
In another case of rather unusual placement, the Type-C port of the iPhone Duo is actually placed on the base of the cover display or the upper panel. In many foldables, the charging port is placed on the lower panel, so that the phone can be opened without moving the charging cable. That is clearly not going to be possible on the iPhone Duo.
The status bar is closed…and is now a circle
The move to a foldable form factor has led to a redesign of some UI elements on the iPhone Duo. Perhaps the most surprising of these is the status bar. Until now seen in the top right corner, and displaying signal strength, Wi-Fi, and battery, it has now been changed to a circle, with the battery life and signal strength being on the circumference and Wi-Fi being at the center. It is not really as intuitive as its predecessor, but we guess users will get the hang of it.
No Pro controls in the camera
The iPhone Duo comes with two 48-megapixel cameras on the back – a new Fusion Main camera, and the same ultrawide that is on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. But while these pack in a lot of features such as three photographic styles, smart focus tracking, next-generation portraits, macro photography and more, the iPhone Duo’s camera app does not come with the Pro Controls seen on the 18 Pro and Pro Max, which let users play around with shutter speed, white balance, and aperture. This l is a bit of a pity, especially given the vast viewfinder the open Duo can serve up. But well, to be fair, this was never meant to be a camera phone.

President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to discuss artificial intelligence when they meet in Washington this week, as Washington and Beijing explore ways to manage the technology's national security risks despite their broader rivalry.
But one China technology policy analyst says the comparison many draw with nuclear arms control has its limits.
"AI isn't like nuclear weapons, and where we are with AI is also not like nuclear weapons," said Antonia Hmaidi, the head of the science, technology, and innovation program at the Mercator Institute for China Studies, at a media briefing on Friday.
"With nuclear weapons, it is relatively simple to verify, at least broad claims that the other side makes. It's very, very difficult to hide huge numbers of nuclear weapons somewhere. With AI, this is not the case," she said.
AI is expected to be one of the biggest agenda items when Trump and Xi meet at the White House on Thursday, alongside trade and export controls.
On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US had proposed a new US-China AI dialogue and a notification mechanism for AI-related incidents that rise to the level of national security.
Trump and Xi's meeting also comes as the debate over AI safety has intensified. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently called for AI companies to slow the pace of frontier AI development.
Trump has pushed back against slowing AI development, arguing the US should maintain its lead over China even as some researchers warn that increasingly powerful AI systems could pose catastrophic risks.
But verification is one of the biggest obstacles to meaningful AI agreements, Hmaidi said.
"How do you verify a claim that, if Xi were to say, 'Our labs are stopping to develop AI for biotechnology, for bioweapons'? How would you even verify that? And the other way around, of course," she said.
Hmaidi said those challenges extend beyond formal agreements. and questioned proposals for an AI equivalent of the Cold War "red line" between Washington and Moscow, asking how governments would even know when to use such a mechanism.
"But even there, how would you even decide when to call the red line?" she said.
Another challenge is that AI is still evolving rapidly, making it difficult for governments to agree on what exactly they would be limiting.
"We don't know where this will take us. Will it take us to AGI, as some are claiming in the US? Will it take us to a stalled situation where progress will stop? We don't know," Hmaidi said, referring to artificial general intelligence, or AI that can perform a broad range of intellectual tasks at or above the human level.
That uncertainty makes both countries unlikely to agree to limits on AI development," she added.
Even if Trump and Xi announce AI initiatives, Hmaidi said they are more likely to involve technical exchanges or broad principles than binding commitments.
She pointed to proposals requiring humans to make the final decision on nuclear weapons use as an example of an agreement that would be politically straightforward but "not in any way binding" and "not even verifiable in any way."
"I would be surprised if there were anything verifiable, or any AI announcement that would actually increase safety in a real way," she said.

England host Spain on Saturday in their Nations League opener and, while the competition doesn't offer a direct qualification route, it does provide a secondary route for teams who don't qualify automatically.
Despite being co-hosts of Euro 2028, Thomas Tuchel's men are not guaranteed a spot in the tournament - with all hosts having to earn their place.
But, assuming England will qualify for the tournament, who do you think will be in the side for the opener in the summer of 2028?

As many as 71% of consumers surveyed in Mumbai said chemists never or rarely refused to sell medicines without a doctor’s prescription, compared with 64% nationally, according to a LocalCircles survey published on September 18, 2026. The findings come as the Centre has proposed mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores selling prescription drugs, and the Maharashtra FDA has intensified enforcement against retailers.
The Mumbai survey by LocalCircles, which received more than 20,000 responses across its questions, also found that only 28% of respondents said they were assisted by a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 21% said they were assisted by someone who was not a qualified pharmacist.
On prescription checks, 36% of 3,697 Mumbai respondents said chemists never refused to give them medicines without a prescription and another 35% said they did so very rarely. Only 9% said chemists refused such sales most of the time and 5% said they always did so.
The gap was also visible in home deliveries. Of 3,122 respondents, 18% said their chemist never demanded a doctor’s prescription during ordering or delivery and 40% said this happened very rarely. Only 23% said a prescription was sought most of the time or always.
The survey showed that neighbourhood chemists remain the main source of medicines in Mumbai. Of 3,012 respondents, 57% said they visited or sent someone to a local chemist, while 26% ordered from their chemist through phone calls or WhatsApp for home delivery. Only 17% primarily used e-pharmacy apps.
The national survey, published a day earlier on September 17, 2026, showed similar, though somewhat lower, levels of reported non-compliance. Across India, 64% of consumers surveyed said their chemist never or rarely insisted on a doctor’s prescription, while only 15% said chemists did so most of the time or always. Only 31% said they were assisted by a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 13% said the person assisting them was not qualified.
The nationwide survey received more than 106,000 responses from consumers across 327 districts. It also found that 41% said chemists never or rarely sought prescriptions during home delivery, compared with 58% in Mumbai.
The findings come as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has floated draft amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, proposing mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores supplying medicines sold on a registered medical practitioner’s prescription.
The draft, issued through Gazette notification G.S.R. 791(E) dated September 8, proposes inserting a new sub-rule after Rule 65(2). It states that retail supply of prescription medicines should take place under CCTV surveillance installed and maintained at the premises. The proposal is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs and curbing sales without valid prescriptions. The government has invited objections and suggestions before finalising the amendment.
The proposed rule comes amid a sharper enforcement drive by the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration. Between June and August 2026, the FDA inspected 2,902 drug establishments, including 2,295 sales establishments and 607 manufacturing units, and initiated action against 880 licensees.
Of these, 677 licences were suspended, and 203 were cancelled, with 740 of the 880 actions involving retailers and wholesalers. During the same three-month period, the FDA conducted 104 search-and-seizure operations, seized illegal drugs and cosmetics worth Rs 11.41 crore, registered 20 FIRs and made 21 arrests.
FDA inspectors flagged several of the same issues reflected in the consumer survey, including the sale of medicines without registered pharmacist supervision, dispensing prescription medicines without valid prescriptions, incomplete Schedule H1 records and sales without proper invoices. Other violations included expired medicines being kept in sale stock and inadequate temperature controls for products such as insulin and vaccines.
The Mumbai survey also found billing gaps. While 76% said they generally received a printed GST invoice and 3% received a manually prepared GST bill, 20% effectively did not receive a proper GST bill.
LocalCircles said the Mumbai findings would be shared with the Maharashtra FDA, Union Health Ministry and CDSCO, and called for stricter verification of registered pharmacists, prescription checks for phone and WhatsApp deliveries and better documentation of medicine sales.

Mumbai-based fintech Easy Platform Services, which owns and operates digital lending startup Zype, turned profitable in FY26, posting a consolidated profit after tax (PAT) of ₹5.3 Cr against a loss of ₹12.9 Cr in FY25. The startup’s consolidated total income jumped 66.6% to ₹176.6 Cr during the year from ₹106 Cr in FY25, according to ratings agency ICRA. Easy Platform continued to remain profitable in the first quarter of the ongoing fiscal year. It provisionally posted a PAT of ₹6.1 Cr on a total income of ₹66 Cr in Q1 FY27. The financial figures were disclosed in ICRA’s rationale for assigning a provisional A-(SO) rating to pass-through certificates (PTCs) worth ₹8.07 Cr issued by Nebula Trust 2026, a special-purpose trust set up for the securitisation transaction. The instruments are backed by a pool of personal loan receivables originated by Easy Platform’s NBFC subsidiary, Respo Financial Capital. Easy Platform’s total managed assets increased 63.5% to ₹621.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹379.9 Cr in the previous fiscal year. They rose another 28.5% to a provisional ₹798.4 Cr in Q1 FY27. Easy Platform also witnessed an improvement in asset quality. Its gross stage 3 ratio declined to 2.2% in FY26 from 3% in FY25 and fell further to 1.7% in Q1 FY27. Stage 3 assets largely comprise credit-impaired loans that are overdue for more than 90 days. Meanwhile, capital-to-risk weighted assets ratio (CRAR) increased to 33.3% in FY26 from 24.7% in FY25. The ratio moderated to 23.6% in Q1 FY27 but remained above the regulatory requirement of 15%. Founded in 2019 by Yogi Sardana and the late Ajay Relan, Easy Platform operates digital lending platform Zype, which offers unsecured personal loans to salaried individuals across Tier I, II, and III cities. Easy Platform is also the parent company of Respo, in which it owns a 100% stake. The RBI-registered NBFC primarily offers unsecured personal loans through Zype, which supports customer acquisition, underwriting, loan servicing, and collections. Respo received its NBFC licence from the RBI in June 2023. It also operates as an IRDAI-registered corporate agent and earns commission income from the distribution of insurance products. Zype raised ₹90 Cr (about $10.3 Mn) in its Series B funding in August 2025 in a round led by Japanese VC firm UNLEASH Capital Partners, with existing investor Xponentia Capital also participating. The fundraise took Zype's total equity capital raised since inception to about $28 Mn. As of June 30, 2026, Xponentia Opportunities Fund I and Xponentia Opportunities Fund II cumulatively held an 85.5% stake in Easy Platform. UNLEASH Capital held a 4.7% stake, while Sadana owned 3.7%. Zype competes with consumer lending platforms such as Fibe, KreditBee, and Navi.

Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
- Published
The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis.
The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it.
Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650.
It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti.
Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building.
In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money".

Police cordoned off a section of the street and removed people from the entrance to the building, including members of the media, striking some protesters with batons.
A representative of tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas shouted at the police through a megaphone: "Think for 10 seconds about Maricarmen, who could be your own grandmother."
"There is a police deployment as if this were a military operation," said Beatriz Duro, Maricarmen's lawyer. "This is the fourth time [they've tried to evict her] but the first time they've come right to the door of the property. It's completely disproportionate."
In June, the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called for the pensioner's eviction to be halted and for her to be offered affordable alternative accommodation. The local government said she had declined its offer of a place in an elderly care home.
The central government said Urbagestión had refused its repeated attempts to negotiate Maricarmen's situation. The BBC has attempted to contact the company.
The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead.

A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes.
In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year.
The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed".
However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Since President Donald Trump returned to office, he has moved aggressively to leave his mark. Many of his most visible legacy projects are not pieces of legislation, though. They’re part of a campaign to reshape Washington, DC, itself.
The psychology behind Trump’s obsession with DC renovations
Trump is trying to future-proof his legacy.
Last year, Trump knocked down the East Wing of the White House to make way for his massive new ballroom. He tried renovating the Reflecting Pool, which did not turn out well. He regilded four large statues near the National Mall, paved the White House Rose Garden, and drenched the Oval Office in gold and golden appliqués.
Other Trump plans are still in the works: He’s proposed building a 250-foot triumphal arch in a traffic circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, just across the Potomac River. He now says the arch would double as a “military complex,” housing drones, snipers, and ammunition.
And, of course, there’s the ongoing fight over the Kennedy Center, which Trump has threatened could be “ripped down” if he doesn’t get his name on the building in some capacity (he already tried once, and was ordered by a court to remove it).
It’s all a lot to keep track of. Luckily, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with New York magazine’s Ben Terris, who recently spent time with Trump touring the ballroom construction site. Terris explains what ties all the disparate projects together and what they reveal about the Trump’s effort to reshape the nation’s capital — and his own legacy.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
What is up with Trump’s obsession with physical landmarks?
Before I even talked to him, I did a lot of reporting about why he seems to be so obsessed with all this stuff. And it’s really like a legacy for him. He’s trying to build something that will last beyond his time here, both his time here in the White House and probably his time here on Earth. He wants to actually have physical monuments to himself.
Somebody who’s close to him told me that the president doesn’t care that much about legislation. He doesn’t care that much about the kind of nuts and bolts of being a president. He cares a lot about buildings and prizes. If he has buildings and prizes, then he feels like his legacy will go on forever. That’s why he wants the Nobel Prize. That’s why he’s building an arch for himself in Washington. It’s really about a legacy that will withstand the test of time in his mind.
Which is to say, he doesn’t really realize that the right legislation could get him more prizes.
Most presidents try to be very successful presidents and have other people build monuments for you. He’s trying to honor himself, basically. It’s something I asked him about actually when I sat down with him in the Oval Office. There was a viral moment a few months ago from Senator Jon Ossoff, the senator from Georgia who may run for president. And he said at a rally that the president is building monuments to himself because he knows that nobody will do it when he’s gone.
I asked the president this because I thought maybe he’d take a shot at Jon Ossoff or deny it, but I was very surprised. He just said, “Yeah, that’s true. Nobody will do it when I’m gone. When I’m gone, nobody will do it.”
It feels kind of self-aware, surprisingly, of Donald Trump to not take a shot at Jon Ossoff, but to just agree with him and say, “Yeah, that’s exactly my motivation.”
Part of me though — okay, here’s a guy who recognizes that when he’s gone, history may not necessarily look fondly upon him. But also there was a part of me that thought that that’s not actually what he was saying.
What he was maybe saying is, “I’m the only person in the world capable of building something as beautiful and important as these monuments. I alone can fix it. I alone can build it.” Nobody else has the ability to do this the way that he has. So on the one hand, possibly self-aware that he won’t be recognized the way he wants to be. On the other hand, maybe it’s just a kind of egomaniac talking about how he’s incredible at things and nobody else can do it. I think it’s all kind of tied up in that he’s not the most introspective person I’ve ever talked to, let’s put it that way.
But even the least introspective person in the world, when he gets to be 80 years old, might start thinking about what’s left of him after he’s gone.
Tell me about the tour President Trump gave you.
I thought I was going to get 20 minutes with him in the Oval Office. I ended up getting 45 minutes in the Oval Office and then almost a 45-minute tour of the White House grounds.
He showed me the Rose Garden, where they put statues and they turned it into a kind of paved-over terrace that looks like Mar-a-Lago. He showed me the Presidential Walk of Fame, where they have all the pictures of the presidents and then the autopen for Joe Biden, and a room called the Palm Room where he put down a new marble floor that he was very proud of.
The helipad was still being constructed. He walked me over there and introduced me to the construction workers as they were building this helipad. And then he took me to the ballroom itself and showed me this behemoth building.
“Legislation can be rolled back, executive orders can be reversed. This is something that he feels like can last forever.”
There’s steel rising 70 feet in the air. It’s the size of one-and-a-half football fields. He was bragging about how there’s more steel there than in the Washington Commander stadium that’s being built. It’s this enormous thing that you can’t really see anywhere in Washington unless you go up the Washington Monument and look at it from afar. And I was just in the middle of this thing and I couldn’t really believe how huge it was.
He wanted to show me this is where the entrance is going to be, [where] the chandeliers will be. He told me he could picture it all already because this is, quote, “What I do.”
He’ll gaze out the window in the morning first thing in the morning from the residence to see the work. He’ll look out the window at night to see the work. He is monitoring this very closely.
One thing that the ballroom especially shares with the Kennedy Center is that it feels like this administration is doing its darnedest to outmaneuver the courts, to get around any legal questions concerning the work. Did that come up at all while he was giving you this tour?
When I was getting the tour, the Supreme Court had not yet ruled that they could keep going. There was a kind of pause on their ruling where they were allowed to keep doing construction while the Supreme Court figured out how they were going to rule on it. And so clearly they were racing against the Supreme Court to get as much done as possible. They really wanted to become like a fait accompli. They wanted it to look like the whole thing was done. It was beyond going back.
I was asking the president, “Are you worried that the Supreme Court is going to rule that you can’t keep doing construction unless you get permission from Congress?” Congress does have the right to decide what happens to federal buildings, so it would make sense that they would be able to make a decision on this. And he said he wasn’t worried about it at all. He said, “the Supreme Court’s going to make the right decision. The people want this.”
He’s like, “If I needed to get Congress’s approval, I could do it, but it’s not going to happen.” And he ended up being right. He doesn’t need Congress’s approval. The Supreme Court’s letting him do it.
But Congress may get shaken up in about a month and a half. Is that on his radar?
Yes, and certainly Democrats are aware. I talked to a bunch of Democrats for this story mostly about what happens next. Are they going to start investigating the ballroom? Are they going to start looking at subpoenaing donors and looking at the contracts and figuring out if there’s a pay-to-play scheme, if there was illegal construction happening? And Democrats are champing at the bit for that.
They’re calling it a target-rich environment. They’re ready to get subpoena power. And they’re also talking about in 2028, what do we do if we get the White House ourselves? Will we tear this down?
[Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez] says she wants to turn it into a soup kitchen. There are all sorts of ideas for it. I asked the president about that too. I said, “Are you worried that Democrats will get the White House in 2028 and they come and they tear down this ballroom right after you built it?” And he basically said, “I’d like to see them try.”
He said, “We’re building this ballroom with nuclear concrete.” That’s what he called it, nuclear concrete, concrete that can withstand a nuclear blast. He’s like, “If it can withstand a nuclear blast, I’d like to see Democrats try to take it down.”
He told me somebody could go to the ballroom with a jackhammer and spend two days straight jackhammering one column and it wouldn’t even leave a mark. And so he’s basically daring them to try to tear it down because he’s building something that he feels like can withstand a nuclear blast so it can withstand Democrats.
At the end of the day, all of this is just about his legacy. That’s what you learned by hanging out with him and talking to him about it. Do you think by spreading his efforts across DC, he’s ensuring that at least something stands and that his legacy is ultimately secured?
He definitely thinks that these buildings can withstand more than anything else. Legislation can be rolled back, executive orders can be reversed. This is something that he feels like can last forever.
I do think there’s a world in which Democrats tear down some of the stuff. The arch is a good example. I mean, the ballroom is hard to tear down, right? First of all, it’s super expensive. It’s huge. It also has to be replaced with something. You can’t just tear it down and then leave a hole in the ground. You have to then build another ballroom, which would be kind of a crazy thing to do and take all this time and then become another story about how Democrats are spending all their time building a ballroom.
Is it possible? Sure. It just seems a little bit harder to imagine, but the arch, you could see that thing getting dynamited on some Fourth of July and then just leaving it as a traffic circle. So I could see a world in which maybe some of these things get destroyed in a kind of, I don’t know, epic fashion. Why not?
It feels like he might be onto something, which is that it would be very controversial to just tear something down for the sake of it out of spite.
Absolutely.
There’s also two years left in his term. Do you get the sense that this is slowing down or ramping up?
It’s hard to say. I have a hard time believing it’s going to end, especially if he becomes a lame-duck president and there’s even fewer things he can do legislatively.
Why not just keep building things and putting your name on things because there’s nothing else to do with your time?
He said that in the first term, the reason he didn’t do a lot of this stuff is because he was too under siege, that it was a difficult time to build a ballroom because of the Russian investigations or the impeachment trials and stuff like that.
Maybe he gets tied up in all that same kind of stuff if Democrats take charge, but I also feel like he’ll have an easier time just trying to ignore subpoenas. It’s going to be a really messy time. And so maybe he’ll just hole himself off into a room somewhere designing more buildings, because what else is he going to do?

One horse refused to jump, another tested positive for tick fever and a third never got its blood work done leaving it unable to travel for competition.
India’s hopes in the eventing team in the equestrian competition ended with one day to go after Arjan Nagra was disqualified following his horse Cooley Goodwood’s refusal to attempt two obstacles in the jumping event of the competition. Two other Indian riders – Fouad Mirza on Camouflage 38 and Ashish Limaye on Willy Be Dunn managed to complete the jumping competition.
The eventing competition consists of three events – dressage, jumping followed by cross country. Although each country is allowed four riders, only the top three scores are considered for the team competition.
The Indian trio successfully completed the dressage event. However, following Nagra and his horse’s disqualification, the Indian team were left with only two riders forcing their disqualification as well.
Although India had planned to send four riders, only three riders were finally sent because the horse of the fourth - Bolivar Gio Granno of Ahaan Kumar – tested positive for tick fever and was not allowed to travel to Japan.
Although the ad hoc committee currently running Equestrian Federation of India had also appointed a reserve player – Pradeep Jhangam, it is learned that his horse didn’t get its blood work (which is how a horse is tested for fitness and infection and thus declared fit to travel) would be unable to travel to Japan as well.
At the eventing team events in Tokyo, India was one of only two teams out of eight teams to not feature four riders (China was the other one).
It is also learned that although India didn’t send a fourth rider or a reserve rider, some 50 lakh rupees had already been spent towards the transportation of eight horses although only seven were actually sent.
India have had a history of success in the team event winning medals at three consecutive Asian Games between 1998 and 2006. However they have only medalled once (in 2018) since then.

A review of available evidence has linked exposure to air pollutants with an increased risk of death by suicide or suicidal thoughts, with particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10 and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) posing the greatest risks.
The findings, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, underscore the need to consider environmental exposures as potentially modifiable risk factors in suicide prevention strategies, researchers said.
The team from Queen's University Belfast in the UK analysed results from 29 studies that looked at the effects of air pollution exposure on suicide and suicidal thoughts.
The interplay of individual, biological, and contextual factors means that suicide prevention is really a public health issue, they said.
However, while the effect of environmental exposures on mental health outcomes, such as depression or anxiety, has been extensively studied, the potential role of environmental factors on the risk of suicide is less well understood, the researchers said.
"This meta-analysis shows statistically significant positive associations between short-term exposure to PM2.5 and PM10, long-term exposure to PM2.5 and NO2, and risk of death by suicide, attempted suicide and suicide ideation," the authors wrote.
Positive links might exist for other air pollutants, including sulphur dioxide and ozone, and noise pollution, the team added.
"The results highlight the importance of considering environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors in suicide prevention," they said.
The researchers explained that air pollutants and water polluted with arsenic, lead, lithium or nitrate, have been linked to neurological effects, including chronic inflammation and nerve damage, which can impair brain function and influence mood and stress resilience.
Further, traffic and other environmental noise and light pollution has been suggested in studies to increase stress levels through a disruption of the body clock, they said.
Ben Mullins, professor at Curtin University's school of population health in Australia, said the study has undertaken one of the first meta-analyses exploring the link between air pollution and suicide.
"It is well known that many air pollutants, specifically many metals, may cause wide-ranging neurological effects, including depression, anxiety, etc. Therefore, a link between air pollutant exposure and mental health disorders, including suicide, is not unexpected," Mullins, not involved with the study, said.
"However, the effect sizes in the included studies were relatively small, and the authors did not adequately address confounding factors or other explanatory variables," Mullins said.
The professor added, "For example, other studies have found stronger links between weather and climate extremes and suicide. These extremes are however, in turn, often associated with air pollution events." "More work to decouple these effects, as well as socio-economic or other confounders, is needed in order to better understand this important issue, including causation mechanisms and potential mitigation," Mullins said.

Italy plans to propose a ban on burqas and niqabs in schools, among other restrictions, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said at an event of the youth wing of her Brothers of Italy party on 20 September. The decision, once enforced, would potentially put Italy back in the spotlight of Europe’s long-running debate over face-covering veils, religious expression and integration. Meloni’s government will also propose a limit on the number of foreign students per classroom. PM Meloni announced the the proposed restrictions at a gathering of the youth wing of her nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy (FdI) party, adding that they would also make Italian language lessons compulsory for parents of foreign students having “serious difficulties integrating into the school system”. “For us, anyone who comes to Italy and wants to build their future here must learn our language, understand our culture, and respect our rules,” Meloni said to a standing ovation at the Gioventu Nazionale national festival in Rome. “It is the only serious way to welcome them,” she said. The proposal also seeks to require the parents of foreign students who are having serious difficulties integrating at school to learn Italian. The ruling center-right coalition is grappling with the rapid rise of Roberto Vannacci’s National Future movement, which some polls now show as the second-strongest right-wing political group after Brothers of Italy, ahead of a general election expected next year. Meloni’s government last week moved to scrap a road tax, in a step widely seen as appeasing voters who have grown increasingly frustrated with spiraling energy prices. Brothers of Italy is a national-conservative and right-wing populist political party in Italy led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. The proposal has specifically referred to burqas and niqabs, but not hijabs. Burqas are full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including the eyes. Niqabs are similar, but the eyes are visible. A hijab covers the hair and neck but leaves the face uncovered. “You must go to school with your face uncovered,” Meloni said, arguing that no one in Italy should be able to decide that a young woman must hide her face in the name of tradition. Italy already has a 1975 law restricting the wearing of clothing that makes identification difficult in public places. Italy has never had a nationwide law specifically banning burqas or niqabs in schools. A 2008 ruling later clarified that full-face coverings may be worn for religious or cultural reasons if the face is revealed when identity verification is required. However, the anti-immigrant League party, which is part of Meloni’s ruling coalition, submitted a bill earlier this year that would ban helmets or garments, except in specific circumstances such as sporting events or places of worship. The proposed school ban comes as Italy joins a wider European debate over how far governments can regulate face-covering clothing. Europe has no single rule on burqas and niqabs. Countries have taken different approaches, from blanket public-space bans to restrictions in schools, hospitals and public transport. The proposed measure still needs to go through the legislative process before it becomes a law. Once approved by the government, the changes would need parliamentary approval within 60 days to pass into law. Here is how other countries in Europe have bans on Hijabs, Niqabs: France: In 2011, France became the first European country to introduce a nationwide ban on clothing that conceals the face in public spaces. Violations can lead to a fine and, in some cases, a civic education course. Belgium: In 2011, Belgium enforced a nationwide ban on wearing any clothing or veils that completely or partially conceal the face in public spaces. Violations can result in fines and prison sentences of up to seven days. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2017 that Belgium's ban on face veils does not violate the European Convention on Human Rights. Bulgaria: In Bulgaria full-face veils have been banned in public spaces since 2016, with wearing them restricted to private homes and places of worship. Austria: In 2017, a nationwide ban on full-face coverings took effect in Austria, too. Later the ban covered schools. From September 2026, girls up to the age of 14 are prohibited from wearing Islamic headscarves that cover the head at school. Denmark: It also introduced a nationwide ban on face-covering clothing in public places in 2018, including garments such as the burqa and niqab. Netherlands: In the Netherlands, a 2019 law restricts face coverings in places such as schools, hospitals, government buildings, and public transport, rather than imposing a blanket public-space ban. Switzerland: A national ban on face coverings in public spaces was enacted in 2023 after voters approved the measure in a national referendum. Portugal banned face coverings in public spaces, with exemptions including health, professional, artistic and religious settings in August 2026. So, France, Belgium and Denmark prohibit face coverings broadly in public, while the Netherlands limits them to specific settings. Meloni’s proposed move is more narrowly focused on schools, somewhat similar to what exists in Austria. Meloni is also pushing an electoral law that would provide a seat bonus to give election winners a more stable parliament and increase her chance of gaining a majority in next year’s election. The lower house approved the electoral-reform bill legislation last week and it will now go to the upper house. The premier has repeatedly ruled out an alliance with Vannacci, who opposes sending aid to Ukraine and favors restricting abortion and toughening immigration. Earlier this month, Meloni’s government became the longest-lasting since Italy became a republic in 1946. Italy's next general election is scheduled to occur no later than 22 December 2027, though discussions within political circles have raised the possibility of an earlier vote in spring or autumn 2027 In the 2022 Italian general election, the centre-right coalition led by Giorgia Meloni's Brothers of Italy (FdI) won an absolute majority of seats in the Italian Parliament. Four dead after powerful Typhoon Dujuan lashes Japan
- Published
Four people have died in Japan after Typhoon Dujuan battered Tokyo and surrounding prefectures with torrential rains and destructive winds, local reports said.
The storm cut power for 50,000 people and caused the suspension of hundreds of flights. Most evacuation orders were lifted on Tueday as the storm pulled away from Japan's eastern coast.
At the height of the storm on Monday, authorities warned of an "imminent threat to life" and urged 1.9 million people to move to shelters.
The fatalities were from landslides in Kanagawa and Chiba prefectures. Six others were reported missing, public broadcaster NHK reported.
Dujuan had sustained winds of 130km/h (80.8mph) and gusts of 194 km/h.
The typhoon is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", which has warmed the ocean, fuelling the formation of storms.
Authorities had advised the public to pay attention to weather information.
Dujuan, which is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year, hit in the midst of a five-day holiday and forced the cancellation of several events.
Concerts scheduled for Monday at the Rock in Japan music festival were cancelled, while the Tokyo Game Show, a video game convention, also cancelled Monday's programme.
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi offered her condolences in a post on X to those who lost thier lives in the typhoon, before saying she would be continuing with her scheduled trip the United States as planned.
"With a sense of urgency, I instructed Chief Cabinet Secretary Takehara and Minister Hosono to respond with utmost preparedness," she wrote, before saying she had boarded a flight to the US.
She will be speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, and will meet with US President Donald Trump.
The Yokosuka City Fire Department told the BBC that a woman in Kanagawa prefecture, aged in her 60s, was believed to have been buried alive after a landslide swept the house she lived in.
Following a search by rescue crews, she was found inside the home and pronounced dead, NHK reported.
Separately, Sodegaura City Fire Department in Chiba prefecture told the BBC a man in his 50s was rescued after getting trapped while working to clear debris at a landslide site.
The department said the worker fell into a bamboo thicket, along with some heavy machinery. He was then taken to hospital before his death was confirmed, according to local reports. Police are investigating the details of the incident.
Some research suggests that Japan has become more exposed to destructive storms, but climate change is not thought to be increasing the number of these storms globally, and could even make them less common in some regions.
As temperatures rise, typhoons that do form are likely to become more intense on average, however.
Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds.
And because a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, these storms could also bring heavier rainfall.
This year, El Niño - the natural weather phenomenon bringing warmer water to parts of the tropical Pacific - is another factor.
El Niño doesn't have a clear effect on the total number of typhoons, but it can affect where typhoons form, their strength and which countries they hit.
Some El Niño events may expose Japan to stronger typhoons, for example.
The typhoon is continuing to travel along the country's Pacific coast, heading north. The extent of the damage today may not be known until Tuesday.
Additional reporting by Chie Kobayashi and Mark Poynting, climate reporter

Walmart-backed PhonePe has received in-principle approval from the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE) for two payment licences, taking the IPO-bound fintech major closer to launching its first locally regulated payments operation outside India. The approvals cover Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes (RPSCS) and Stored Value Facilities (SVF). While the RPSCS licence covers regulated retail payment services, the SVF licence permits the issuance and operation of stored-value products such as digital wallets. However, the in-principle approvals do not allow PhonePe to immediately begin commercial operations. The fintech major will have to fulfil the remaining regulatory requirements and secure final approval from the CBUAE. Following the final nod, PhonePe plans to collaborate with regional banks, licensed payment service providers, and local technology vendors in the UAE. It will also explore opportunities to support Aani and Jaywan, the country’s domestic payment networks, using its technology platform. The development would mark PhonePe’s first international foray involving domestic business operations. The fintech major already enables Indian travellers in the UAE to scan local QR codes and make UPI payments at NEOPAY and Network International terminals through its partnership with NPCI International Payments. PhonePe has been laying the groundwork for overseas expansion for some time. In September 2025, it incorporated PhonePe International Holdings Ltd in Abu Dhabi with a share capital of AED 20,000. In its UDRHP, PhonePe said its UPI payment service was available to Indian users in Singapore, the UAE, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bhutan, France, Qatar, and Mauritius through the infrastructure provided by NPCI International Payments. However, this cross-border facility is different from the domestic operations that PhonePe plans to launch in the UAE after receiving the final regulatory approvals. The development comes days after PhonePe’s monetisation prospects in India received a boost from the reintroduction of MDR on certain UPI merchant transactions. PhonePe remains India’s largest UPI app by transaction volume. It processed around 11.25 Bn transactions worth ₹14.26 Lakh Cr in August, translating into a volume market share of 45.9%. However, its share slipped marginally from 46.1% in July. Despite its market leadership, the fintech major’s net loss widened 62% YoY to ₹2,792 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,727.4 Cr in the previous fiscal year. The increase was driven by higher employee and marketing expenses, ESOP costs, and one-time write-offs. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr from ₹7,105 Cr in FY25. Including other income of ₹467.4 Cr, total revenue increased 10% YoY to ₹8,387.9 Cr. PhonePe paused its IPO plans in March amid geopolitical tensions in West Asia and volatility in global equity markets. However, the fintech major is now looking to revive the listing process following greater clarity on the UPI MDR framework. Sources told Inc42 last week that PhonePe is targeting a public listing between February and March 2027. “They have an almost 45% share of merchant payments. With greater clarity on the MDR regime, PhonePe is now looking to revise its IPO plans and could target a listing between February and March 2027,” the sources said.

The Wales captains looking to conquer England
- Published
You might argue that for Welsh rugby to lose one Wales captain to an English club was unfortunate but two on the same day was just careless.
That is what happened in December 2025 when flanker Jac Morgan and hooker Dewi Lake announced they were leaving Ospreys for Gloucester for the 2026-27 season.
A two-for-one deal for the English club, who are investing in the Welsh duo to help turn their fortunes around.
Now the pair are preparing to make their Prem debuts against Exeter this Saturday.
Lake has been unveiled as the new Gloucester captain with Morgan as one of his deputies, demonstrating the favourable impression the pair have already made.
BBC Sport Wales caught up with them at their new Kingsholm home to talk about their early Gloucester experiences, leaving Ospreys and Welsh rugby politics behind and forgetting they are speaking Welsh in their new English environment.

Home from home as Welsh influence continues
The duo have been almost inseparable since meeting a decade ago and were chosen as co-captains for the 2023 World Cup by former Wales coach Warren Gatland.
Lake is 27 and Morgan 26, with only eight months separating them.
Where one is, the other is never far behind, with Lake and Morgan having developed an almost telepathic understanding. They do not quite finish each other's sentences. But it is not far off.
The pair say they did not speak to each other about signing for Gloucester but fate has ensured they stay together in the next chapter of their rugby story.
"I am incredibly happy we got to land at the same club together," said Lake.
"We have come up together and spent 10 years day in, day out.
"He's an incredible friend off the field, but on the field also an incredible leader and player.
"Even the first day at Gloucester, we texted each other and said we'll meet at half past seven in the car park because neither of us wanted to go in on our own.
"To be able to get to see him day in day out and still spend time with him is incredible. I feel the bond we've created is really strong."
Lake described Gloucester as not too dissimilar to life in Wales, helped by a strong Welsh contingent of Max Llewellyn, Freddie Thomas, Josh Hathaway and Deian Gwynne who are already at Kingsholm.
Morgan agreed, saying: "It's been like a home from home. It's great to have a couple of fellow Welshmen here."
Not just fellow Welshmen but Welsh speakers, with Gwynne and Llewellyn comfortably conversing in their native language.
"A lot of us are speaking Welsh to each other when we're in the building," said Morgan.
"So it's been great to be able to do that. It's hard sometimes when you know someone can speak Welsh, it's hard to speak English to them!"
Lake added: "Jac and I rarely speak English to each other.
"We've got to catch ourselves and stop ourselves sometimes when other people are involved in conversations as well.
"In our first week we caught ourselves talking Welsh to each other at the breakfast table.
"We apologised and were forgetting we're not in Wales anymore, but we still speak Welsh to each other where we can."
No milk challenge as Gloucester welcome new boys
The duo are grateful the infamous Gloucester "milk challenge" initiation stopped before they joined.
New players used to have to finish eight pints of milk within a time limit of about 20 minutes without being sick.
The penalty for being sick or not finishing the challenge in time was having their head shaved.
"It's gone, thankfully," said Lake.
"Jac and I spent the full summer on ChatGPT with pictures of ourselves bald just to start preparing ourselves."
It has been replaced by a more physical "shed challenge" that includes running up and down steps with sandbags and flipping tyres.
"Being here at Gloucester has been class so far," said Lake.
"The boys and coaches have been welcoming, it feels like a place where I'm able to get better, learn a lot and test my game in a new league.
"I wanted to challenge myself and be uncomfortable, if you like, in a new environment.
"That's the reason why I decided to make the move and I'm sure Jac feels the same."
Morgan says Gloucester being a traditional rugby city and community was a draw.
"A lot of people have been stopping us in the street and saying welcome to Gloucester," said Morgan.
"You can see how much this club means for the city and you sense the history.
"A lot of the boys mentioned 'the Shed' [Kingsholm stand], so it'll hopefully be a great experience to be able to play in front of the home crowd.
"We want to get a few more wins this year, do better than last year and see where it goes."
Morgan has also drawn on previous Welsh legends at Gloucester with Tomos Williams, James Hook and Richard Hibbard having previously played at Kingsholm.
"There's a lot of Welsh who have played here in the past and they're part of the history," said Morgan.
"There's a photo of Hibs [Hibbard] up in the corridors there, so it's good being able to see that.
"You speak to a lot of the past players about their experiences and Gloucester loved having them at the club."
Lake and Morgan join a sizeable Welsh contingent in English club rugby this season alongside the likes of Aaron Wainwright, Dafydd Jenkins, Rhys Carre, Nicky Smith, Tomas Francis, Tomos Williams and Louis Rees-Zammit.
'Ospreys gave us everything in rugby'
Despite the excitement of their new life, Morgan and Lake are sad to leave Ospreys behind.
"We're both thankful of everything the Ospreys have given us over the last few years and the bonds we created with players and coaches," said Morgan.
"Probably the hardest part was leaving the people and you've got best mates back at home.
"We're still in contact with everybody but the lack of day-to-day contact is probably one of the hardest things to leave."
That passion includes paying to watch their old side.
"We still come in Mondays and the first thing we talk about is the Ospreys score on the weekend," said Lake.
"We both paid £5 the other night to watch them play against Coventry in a pre-season game.
"So the love for the club and people is still there with both of us and will not go away.
"It was a tough decision to leave, it was always going to be. Ospreys did everything for us, gave us an opportunity and platform and the chance to represent our country."
One thing they do not miss is the Welsh rugby politics, with Lake and Morgan signing for Gloucester at a time of uncertainty over whether Ospreys would survive beyond last season.
"The off-the-field stuff going on in background was tough to deal with sometimes," said Lake.
"It's nice to get away from it sometimes. It's one less thing to think about when you're playing here. It's easier for us to be here and not think of it.
"Over the last year or two, it's kind of dictated a lot that's gone on at the Ospreys, in terms of stuff we've had to do away from training and representing that region.
"It'll never be something we don't think about because we've still got friends there that will be affected by what is going on.
"We will try and catch up with the boys back home and still worry about them."
Since Morgan and Lake announced their Gloucester move, Ospreys have been given a stay of execution for at least two seasons.
But one of Ospreys or Scarlets are set to disappear by 2028 with a professional side in the west being cut by the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU).
"We don't have to deal with it but we still love the club and want Ospreys to be safe," said Lake.
"That's something we speak of and think about often."

Wales moving in right direction with World Cup looming
Lake and Morgan are set to return to Wales for the Nations Championship in November.
A victory in the summer against Fiji was followed by away defeats against Argentina and South Africa, with home games against Japan, New Zealand and Australia to follow in the autumn.
Reflecting on the summer campaign, Lake said: "It was a mixed bag. The Argentina game was probably the most disappointing.
"We had enough talent in our tank to beat that team but we didn't make them work too hard and we let ourselves down.
"I still think it's a positive summer in terms of where we've been, compared to where we are now.
"We can see the the growth and the fact we're talking about we should have beaten Argentina.
"We wouldn't have been saying that two years ago."
A World Cup in Australia is on the horizon in a year's time but firstly the new life in Gloucester awaits. One Lake and Morgan will enjoy together.

Abortion is on the ballot again as post-Roe policies continue to evolve
MAPLEWOOD, Mo. — After Missouri voters added abortion protections to the state constitution in 2024, Kelly McCoomb decided to keep her yard sign supporting the measure in the basement of her suburban St. Louis home.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Abortion access is important to McCoomb. She wants her daughter to grow up in a state where the option is available if needed, and the sign was a keepsake from the day Missourians voted to reverse the state's near-total ban.
McCoomb also couldn't shake the feeling that she'd need to display the sign in her yard again soon.
"I have little faith in our Missouri government," McCoomb said, sitting on her front porch.
Sure enough, just two years later, the state's Republican-dominated legislature is asking Missouri voters to overturn the abortion protections they recently supported. The conflicting measures even have the same title: Amendment 3.
But while a "yes" vote in 2024 supported adding protections to the state constitution, a "no" vote in 2026 would keep them. McCoomb covered the "YES" on her yard sign with a "NO" made from black duct tape before placing the sign back in her yard.
Voters will weigh in on abortion in Missouri, and three other states, in the November general election. Missouri is also one of two states voting on it for the second time since 2024. Nevada will vote again, too.
The spate of referenda comes after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned federal abortion protections with its 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization – leaving each state to make its own abortion policy. The result has been a patchwork of state rules with varying degrees of bans or limitations, and even a series of "shield laws" in states where abortion remains legal that aim to protect providers from prosecution in states where it's not.
"I just think there's a constitutional crisis that's coming," said Kristi Hamrick, vice president of media and policy for the anti-abortion organization Students for Life Action.
"Can you have 50 state standards on whether or not a human being is a human being? Can you have 50 state standards on whether human beings have legal protection?" Hamrick said.
Advocacy groups work to clarify abortion rules
That patchwork of abortion protections is the reason Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom introduced the 2024 ballot measure to enshrine the state's law allowing abortions up to 24 weeks after conception into the state constitution, said Denise Lopez, president of the coalition.
The measure received strong support two years ago from 64% of voters. Nevada law requires two majority votes to enshrine constitutional amendments, so voters will need to support the expanded protection again in November for it to be enacted.
The Nevada ballot measure wouldn't change the state's existing law allowing abortions up to 24 weeks after conception. But the proposal would make it more difficult to overturn abortion access, requiring voter approval of any new ban in two elections.
Lopez said Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom has been campaigning to ensure voters are still mobilized.
"Folks care about it," she said. "They're seeing what's happening at the national level, and they want to make sure that whatever's happening in our neighboring states, like Idaho and Utah, doesn't happen here in Nevada."
Idaho, where a ballot measure establishing abortion rights recently qualified to go before voters in November, has one of the strictest abortion bans in the country. Voters will decide whether state statute should allow abortion through fetal viability, the point when a fetus can survive after birth, which is generally considered to be around 24 weeks.
In Utah, abortion is allowed up to 18 weeks while legal challenges to the state's ban continue.
In Virginia, where abortion is already allowed through two trimesters of pregnancy, until 28 weeks, voters will decide whether to amend their state constitution to codify those rights.
Missouri is the only state voting this year on removing abortion protections already on the books. The measure would repeal the 2024 amendment that guaranteed abortion access through fetal viability in the state and replace it with a ban on abortions with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies and pregnancies resulting from rape or incest. Abortions for rape and incest would have to occur before 12 weeks of pregnancy.
Missouri was the first state to ban abortion after the Dobbs decision in 2022. At that time, abortions had already mostly ceased in the state after three decades of state regulations targeting the practice, including a 72-hour waiting period, minimum dimensions for procedure rooms and hallways in clinics that provide abortions, and a mandate that the clinicians have admitting privileges at nearby hospitals, among others. Only 150 abortions were performed in Missouri in 2021, down from 5,772 in 2011, state records show.
Despite Missouri voters backing the abortion amendment in 2024, it took nearly two years for medication abortions to resume in the state.
A second vote on abortion in Missouri causes confusion
Margot Riphagen-Dunn, CEO of St. Louis-based Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, said the whiplash of a second statewide vote on abortion mirrors the confusion that patients have experienced about whether abortion is available in the state.
"Chaos is kind of the point here," Riphagen-Dunn said, "and it is absolutely a tactic that gets in the way of being able to provide."
The confusion has presented problems for abortion opponents in the state as well.
"I think it's unfortunate," said Reagan Barklage, who is a vice president of Students for Life of America and the treasurer of the Missouri Students for Life Ballot Committee. "People need to be very clear on what they're voting for."
Barklage said she has had to correct anti-abortion voters while out canvassing to remind them that they are voting "yes" on Amendment 3 this year even though they voted "no" on Amendment 3 last time.
"It is crazy that it ended up being even the same number. I do not think that was intentional, but we've got to deal with what we've got," Barklage said, adding, "I hope the pro-choicers kept their yard signs from last time."
In Maplewood, Missouri, McCoomb said she was happy that her repurposed sign supporting abortion access had been noticed.
"I hope lots of people see and remember to revote," McCoomb said.

What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
- Published
The UN has just called for the predominant world map to be replaced with one that more accurately reflects the true size of continents like Africa.
The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy on the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger.
It adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own.
There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks.
Mercator map
The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.
Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University London College explained.
"He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."
To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.
His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.
The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.
But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.
For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.
"Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.
Equal Earth map
The Equal Earth map aims to address this problem with the Mercator projection.
It was developed by a team of cartographers in 2018 to present the size and shape of landmasses more accurately.
As a result, the Equal Earth map was initially adopted by 54 members of the African Union, before being adopted by the UN.
But to do this, it sacrifices the straight lines that made the Mercator projection perfect for navigating with - and it cannot be used for measuring the true distance between different places.
"You can preserve area, or you can preserve shape, or you can preserve distance and direction, but not everything at once perfectly, because otherwise you'd be back to a sphere," Cheshire said.
Peters map
The Peters world map was designed by German historian Arno Peters in the early 1970s. The rectangular map is based on the projection first described by Scottish cartographer James Gall in 1855.
The projection sacrifices accuracy of shape in favour of accuracy of scale. So, polar regions are squished, while the bits near the equator are stretched.
This fixes the Greenland-Africa size issue, allowing those who use it to get a sense of the comparative size of different landmasses, all while preserving straight lines of longitude and latitude.
However, the map severely distorts the shapes of Earth's landmasses, making them all look slightly off.
The straight lines on the Peters map do not represent true constant compass bearings and so are useless for navigation.
