Why is Monaco staging a sprint race? F1 Q&A
- Published
Formula 1 has a rare Saturday race this weekend for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
Kimi Antonelli goes into round 15 of the season with an imposing 81-point lead in the drivers' championship over Mercedes team-mate George Russell.
BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the event in Baku.
What are your thoughts on having a sprint race next year at Monaco? I was very surprised to see that on the calendar, given that the race has so little chance of overtaking - Graham
- F1 to have 10 sprint races in 2027, including Monaco 
  - Published6 days ago
Formula 1 announced the 2027 calendar last week, with the number of sprint events increased from six to 10, and one of them Monaco.
This has proved controversial with some fans.
Why pick the worst track on the calendar for overtaking to have two races in one weekend, some have wondered. What's the point of having two boring races; isn't one enough?
The thinking behind it, though, is less about the races than about qualifying, and how making Monaco a sprint could mix up the weekend.
Monaco qualifying is renowned as one of the highlights of the season. In that case, surely two great qualifying sessions is better than one?
It was also pointed out by F1 that it gives the chance of two different grid orders and therefore more variability.
There is another factor to consider, too.
Monaco is one of the most demanding tracks on the calendar, and it is renowned as somewhere drivers have to build up to the limit progressively so they can become confident with knowing how the car will behave when they get there.
Get that wrong, push too hard too soon, and the chances of an accident are considerably higher.
So asking the drivers to go straight into a qualifying after a single practice session is a really difficult challenge.
It is likely to mean more mistakes, more action, more drama, and therefore more entertainment.
The same goes for grand prix qualifying.
Yes, by then the drivers will have done a sprint race. But there are always changes made to the cars for qualifying, so again the drivers will be going in blind to some degree.
Yes, the sprint is likely to be a procession. How could it be anything else? But it adds an extra degree of jeopardy to the whole weekend.
Do you think F1 might consider the F2 approach for the virtual safety car, where drivers cannot pit under a VSC but can pit under a full safety car? As a regular viewer of both series, I think this works well in F2 and is another way to solve the jeopardy a short VSC period brings to a race. - Caroline
The VSC was discussed at the so-called FIA sporting advisory committee last week, but sources say no consensus emerged there as to potential changes.
It was also on the agenda for the F1 Commission meeting on Monday but there were no significant developments.
Lando Norris, who lost victory in Madrid by the VSC timing, said after the race that the drivers had previously discussed with the FIA the idea that the VSC should be out for a minimum of a lap so this sort of thing could not happen.
But every potential 'solution' comes with consequences. In that case, F1 might end up with a full lap of VSC just to recover a bit of debris.
The VSC was introduced so that relatively small-scale incidents could be dealt with without the lengthy disruption of a full safety car.
It's accepted that the safety car affords possibilities to gain and lose out, so why should the VSC not do the same? The argument is that, generally, these even out over the season, although the Norris case in Madrid had particularly dramatic consequences.
Antonelli benefited from this one, for example, but has lost out in other scenarios this year. For example, when the VSC gifted Lewis Hamilton the lead in Barcelona, even if that was rendered moot by Antonelli's subsequent retirement.
Why did Mercedes put George Russell on a two-stop strategy in the Spanish Grand Prix when the race has the longest pit lane of the season? George was the only driver out of the top 15 finishers on a two-stop and did this decision cost him a podium finish? - Richard
Mercedes were a bit stuck when the virtual safety car was deployed on lap 14 in Madrid.
The team had split the drivers' tyre strategies - Kimi Antonelli took the conventional strategy and started on the mediums, Russell had gone for the hards.
With overtaking so difficult in Madrid, it was always likely that one option would turn out to be sub-optimal. The timing of the VSC was very unfortunate for those who started on hard tyres because it coincided with the pit-stop window for those on mediums.
Mercedes had two choices - stay out, or pit and change tyre compound, as drivers are obligated to use two compounds during a dry grand prix.
Charles Leclerc, who also started on hards and was running immediately ahead of Russell, stayed out. Mercedes pitted in the hope of trying to beat Leclerc.
Whichever tyre Russell chose was unlikely to make it to the end, so Mercedes knew at that point they would almost certainly have to stop again.
The hard tyre was comfortably the best race tyre in Madrid, and on his mediums Russell did not have the pace to narrow the gap to Leclerc to less than it takes to do a pit stop. So there was nothing to lose by pitting again.
Team boss Toto Wolff said: "He said the tyres were not in a great shape, the mediums. We didn't think they would go to the end. (We thought) the better opportunity was not to hang out and wait for a red, but to change the tyres and get on with it."
Russell said: "Maybe I could have stayed out with Leclerc but I would have still finished behind him. Maybe I could have not pitted on to the hard again but everything I would have done would have brought us to the same position."

During the Madrid race, Max Verstappen was told to hand the place back to Lewis Hamilton. Which he did. However, what would happen if Lewis had fallen maybe two or three cars further back. Does Max still have to hand back the place (and lose places to other cars) or would he just have to take a penalty? - Wayne
The scenario you paint actually happened in Madrid. Verstappen also got ahead of Antonelli on the first lap, so when Red Bull told him to let Hamilton by, he also had to let the Mercedes past.
Shortly after that happened, the message "no further action" was displayed on the timing screens and television coverage over the incident.
That was because Verstappen had given the place back by then. Otherwise, he would have been penalised.
So, yes, if a driver is adjudged to have committed an offence that requires giving the place back, they must do so regardless of whether there are at that point other cars between them.
There are two examples of this from Fernando Alonso's career.
In the 2005 Japanese Grand Prix, he passed Christian Klien's Red Bull by cutting the chicane, let him by again on the straight and then passed him into Turn One.
But race director Charlie Whiting did not notice that Alonso had let Klien back past, and after some discussions with the Renault team, he demanded Alonso cede the position.
That was two laps later, by which time Alonso was seven seconds up the road.
At Silverstone in 2010, Alonso, now at Ferrari, was forced off the track by Robert Kubica when trying an overtaking move at Vale, and ended up passing the Renault driver off the track.
Because he had been forced off, Ferrari decided not to give up the position. But Whiting told them they had to, after discussions with the team.
Problem was, at exactly that point, Kubica pulled into the pits to retire, so Alonso could not give the place back - and he was given a drive-through penalty.
Before he could serve it, there was then a safety-car period which closed up the field. Penalties could not be served under a safety car, so the two situations combined dropped Alonso right to the back of the field. He ended up finishing 14th, which was a costly blow to his title hopes.

Record prize fund for 2028 European Championships
- Published
The European Athletics Championships in 2028 will offer a record prize fund worth about £3m when they are staged in Silesia, Poland.
Prize money will be awarded to athletes finishing in the top eight across all 50 events.
Gold medal winners will earn 30,000 euros (£25,720), while silver and bronze medallists will receive 15,000 euros (£12,860) and 10,000 euros (£8,573) respectively.
Athletes finishing fourth to eighth across the 50 disciplines will receive awards of 5,000, 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 euros respectively.
European Athletics has restructured the way in which prize money is awarded, ensuring athletes finishing in the top eight in every discipline receive financial recognition.
The prize fund on offer at the last championships, held in Birmingham in August of this year, did not involve a standard payout for every medal position.
Instead, a total pot of 500,000 euros (£428,000) was split equally between the top 10 performances across 10 categories - five for men and five for women - determined by the World Athletics scoring tables.
Great Britain and Northern Ireland won 19 medals in Birmingham, including nine golds.
But none of those gold medal performances earned one of the 50,000 euro 'Gold Crown' bonuses awarded by the organisers.
The significant increase in money for the European Championships reflects how elite athletes' on-track earning potential is growing.
World Athletics recently provided what it described as "the richest prize pot in the history of the sport", with $10m (£7.4m) put up for its new three-day Ultimate Championship event in Budapest.
Each individual event winner received $150,000 (£110,000).

Roberto Mancini returns as Italy head coach but can the Azzurri recover from lowest ebb with a youth-inspired revolution?
Roberto Mancini is back as Italy head coach after a second spell; the former Man City boss won Euro 2020 with the Azzurri, who have not qualified for the last three World Cups; With exclusive insight from Gianluigi Donnarumma, Sky Sports' Sam Blitz analyses the road back for Italy...
Wednesday 23 September 2026 07:36, UK
This year, Italian football fell to its lowest ebb. In Europe, no Italian club made it past the quarter-finals - while Atalanta were the only Serie A side to reach the Champions League last 16. But that was nothing compared to the national team.
Italy did not qualify for the third World Cup in a row. An unthinkable prospect given they have won the competition four times.
The first two failures to qualify were masked over by the Euro 2020 triumph at Wembley. That at least gave the nation hope.
- Italy fixtures: Who do they play in the Nations League?
- Crisis! Italy fail to qualify for third straight World Cup
The third World Cup failure was one last straw. A 48-team World Cup did not include Italy. It brought about the resignations of not just head coach Gennaro Gattuso, but also Italian FA president Gabriele Gravina and Gianluigi Buffon as the team's head of delegation.
"It's a sensitive subject that affects me a lot, because not qualifying for three World Cups in a row is tough, and Italy certainly doesn't deserve that," Italy captain Gianluigi Donnarumma tells Sky Sports.
Now Italy have gone back to the future. Roberto Mancini, the manager who won the Euros five years ago, is back at the helm.
"We have to work. The only way forward is to work," adds Donnarumma. "There has now been a change of coach, the return of Mr Mancini - and the objective is to work and try to take Italy back to where it deserves to be.
"I know it's not easy for the fans, but especially for us, because only we know how much it means to us to play in a competition like the World Cup.
"So we'll give everything to bring Italy back to where it deserves to be. We have a great responsibility because history says that Italy should always be there. History has taught us that. So we have to bring Italy back to where it belongs."
Yes, Italy belongs at the top table. But it has been far off the level for some time. The latest World Cup disaster was the latest in a long line of slippery slopes since they reached the top of the world in 2006.
Twenty years later, that penalty shoot-out win over France is still Italy's last appearance in a World Cup knockout game. They have just won just one World Cup match since then - the 2-1 victory over England in Brazil 2014.
Yes, there was the successful European Championships campaign of 2012 that saw Italy reach the final. But since those days, Italy have not been the same. And there are multiple reasons for it.
Italy have not been able to replicate the world-class talent they once possessed. The World Cup-winning side of 20 years ago had the likes of Fabio Cannavaro, Alessandro Nesta, Gattuso and Alessandro Del Piero.
Six years later in 2012, that generation still lived on through Buffon, Daniele De Rossi, and Andrea Pirlo. But since the retirement of stalwarts Giorgio Chiellini and Leandro Bonucci, the next generation of Italian football has been lost.
According to the CIES Football Observatory, between 2020 and 2025, Italy produced just 413 football exports. It ranked 24th in the world, behind the United States, Japan and Russia.
The other four nations in Europe's big five leagues all managed over 1,000 players in the same category. Italy's players - young or old - are just not as fancied by Europe's elite.
The lack of quality coming from the Italian ranks could also be seen in the national team. Between June 2025 and February 2026, only one capped player for the national team was under the age of 24 - Inter's young forward Pio Esposito. England managed a dozen in the same period.
In 2025, Italy also gave 1.9 per cent of their Serie A minutes to eligible players under the age of 21. That was the second-lowest out of the top 50 leagues in world football. Only the United Arab Emirates Pro League managed fewer.
It also contributed to a weaker Serie A last season. Veteran players Kevin De Bruyne, Luka Modric and Jamie Vardy were among the high-profile signings. And there was a similar lack of creativity amongst the managers too.
The likes of Antonio Conte, Max Allegri, Gattuso, Luciano Spalletti and Maurizio Sarri have all been passed around the top Italian clubs without much variation. Even this summer, Sarri moved to Atalanta, while Allegri joined Juventus.
Cesc Fabregas' Como revolution - resulting in their Champions League qualification earlier this year - is exactly what can happen when tactical ideas emerge from outside that never-ending cycle. Ruben Amorim has also turned up at AC Milan and played some eye-catching football with the Rossoneri.
But there are some signs that times could be changing for Italy. Mancini's first Italy squad back contained a few positive surprises. A 34-player roster included nine uncapped players - and 11 players under the age of 23.
That includes Borussia Dortmund's 18-year-old striker Samuele Inacio, Chelsea-bound defender Honest Ahanor, now at Crystal Palace. Brentford's Michael Kayode is among the new 'young revolution'.
As well as Inacio and highly-rated Inter forward Esposito - who has five goals in nine Italy caps - there is also FC Nurnberg's Ali Zoma who has 20 goals in 36 appearances in the German second division. Midfielder Issa Doumbia is also a key player at Sporting CP this season.
There's a new generation of young Italian stars.
"There will certainly be some established players. We're getting older, but we're still young, and there will also be some very young players joining the team," says Donnarumma.
"So it will be a mixture, and we need to help these young players integrate well. They can give us a great deal of help.
"They're certainly talented players who need to play and gain experience, but I'm sure Italy will return to where it belongs."
Italy have a very tricky Nations League group, with Belgium, Turkey and France competing in a very competitive Group A.
But a nation who has been lingering in the dark for so long needs just one spark.

I was close to joining Liverpool in 2016 - Mbappe
- Published
Kylian Mbappe has revealed how "close" he came to joining Liverpool in 2016, saying he went against the advice of his mother who "fell in love" with Anfield.
The France and Real Madrid striker said the Reds tried to sign him at 18, while he was playing for Monaco in Ligue 1.
Former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp said the club laid on a private jet and food for Mbappe and his family in an attempt to sign him, before he eventually joined Paris St-Germain.
Speaking to the Athletic, Mbappe said his mum was a "big fan" of Klopp and wanted her son to move to Merseyside.
"I was close to [joining] Liverpool. The favourite destination for my mum was Liverpool. She wanted me to go there," he said.
"I didn't listen because I wanted to play in my city, Paris. I didn't want to leave my country before I was someone.
"But yes, my mum was always saying, 'Liverpool - you're going to be there, playing at Anfield, it's going to be insane for you'."
Mbappe, now 27, said his mother went out to Liverpool for the "first step" of the negotiation.
"She went to the city, the stadium, she met the people. She was like, 'it's a wonderful club, everybody's so kind, it's a family club, a big club', said Mbappe.
"She went to Anfield and fell in love with it. She watched a few games alone, to feel the atmosphere, because she wanted to imagine me in this stadium."
Klopp, who spoke about the possible move on Magenta TV as a pundit at the 2026 World Cup, explained how a flight was taken from Blackpool to Nice in France, where "the entire Mbappe family boarded a private jet with five rooms or something".
"We really went all out. Then we flew around in a circle, talked with the family, ate good food," Klopp said.
He said they had not wanted to be seen having talks - but the meeting proved fruitless.
"We flew in a circle. It was fantastic. And then he went to Paris," Klopp added.
"It's a funny story," said Mbappe.
"But in the end, I took the decision to go to PSG because for me, born and raised in Paris, there was no better feeling than to show I could be a star in my hometown."
Mbappe later joined PSG on loan, in a deal including an option for the move to become permanent for 180m euros (£165.7m). He went on to spend seven years in Paris, becoming the club's record scorer before leaving for Real Madrid in 2024.

A study by Chennai-based diabetologists has attempted to find out how India has managed to reduce the prices of new and expensive diabetes drugs and what lessons this could possibly hold for other low- and middle-income countries (LMIC). The study, ‘Making Modern Diabetes Medications Affordable and Accessible: Lessons from India for Other Countries’, was led by V. Mohan, chairman, Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, Chennai, and was published in the journal Diabetes Care.
What did the study find?
Of the 589 million adults in the world with diabetes, 80% live in LMICs, the study noted. Modern diabetes therapies such as GLP-1 receptor agonists as well as SGLT2i (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors) improve cardiovascular and renal outcomes, while analogue insulins help reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia. However, affordability remains a barrier: diabetes requires lifelong care and management of complications.
India’s ability to maintain low medication prices is closely linked to its role as a major pharmaceutical exporter, the paper stated, noting the strategic legislative history of maintaining critical safeguards to prevent ‘patent evergreening’ and allowing for generic manufacture of drugs. It also found that the country has increasingly focused on strengthening domestic manufacturing capacity. There are concerns over global trade policies affecting prices and the availability of raw materials. A government incentive scheme has been introduced to promote domestic manufacturing of raw materials, and as of 2025, production has commenced for 26 molecules that were previously imported.
The paper notes that metformin and sulfonylureas continue to form the foundation of type 2 diabetes management in India - both are included in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM). While DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase 4) inhibitors, SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA have all been introduced, they are not currently in the NLEM. Initial uptake of these drugs was constrained by pricing. Following the competitive entry by multiple domestic manufacturers, the price of semaglutide, for instance in India, has dropped considerably now, and there has been a huge increase in sales; however, absolute monthly costs remain high relative to the household income in India, and, crucially, these are not covered by insurance, as they are, to a great extent, in the U.S.
Quick availability of generic and biosimilar drugs, deliberate regulatory and distribution strategies such as the government’s Jan Aushadi Kendras, and market competition have allowed for affordable drugs in India, the paper highlighted.
What does it propose for other LMICs?
Building local manufacturing capacity as a strategic public health investment, balancing patent governance that encourages easier access to newer molecules, predictable and structured price regulation, good distribution networks at reasonable retail prices and aligning pharmaceutical policy with health financing and ongoing monitoring of medicine quality, prices, prescription patterns and patient access can all help with improving access to affordable medicines, the paper noted. These core principles could also apply to high-income countries facing drug prices, the paper said.
Challenges ahead
Challenges that remain include urban-rural disparities in distribution and availability of medicines; tight regulations potentially affecting chances of drug innovation; differences in quality between generics and difficulties in maintaining strict pharmacovigilance; as well as limited formal evaluation of government schemes to look at their long-term impact on clinical outcomes.

No one wants to worry about a break-in. But no one wants to end up paying fees every month just to check their video doorbell feed or find out their window was broken, and most smart security systems (even the original ones that weren't touted as smart!) rely on your fear to have you paying month after month for the promise of catching burglars and stopping intruders for you.
These systems do work, and they can give you a lot of peace of mind. This comes with a hefty price tag, though, and plenty of people would be more than happy with a system they build themselves sans monthly fees. If you're not interested in a system that will call the police or fire department if you don't respond fast enough to something that turns out to be minor, or don't want to have strangers looking through your security cameras at your property, I'm here to help with that.
This guide collects a handful of our favorite smart home security accessories that won't paywall you left and right, and will give you local storage options for video so you aren't locked into the cloud. This way you can build the system that works for you. Here's everything I recommend if you want smart home security without the subscriptions.
What Exactly Is a Smart Home Security System?
Smart security systems can look like whatever you want, in my opinion, but there are a lot of starter kits you've probably seen. Smart-home brands like Abode and SimpliSafe have starter packs you've likely seen before with motion sensors, door sensors, and security hubs that sound an alarm when one of those sensors is triggered.
But smart home security can go way beyond that. Most systems let you add on cameras and even video doorbells to monitor movement around your home and catch people at your door who shouldn't be there. (This is also a handy way to know when it’s a package delivery or another random salesperson.) These systems are usually modular and customizable, whether you DIY or go with a brand. Overall, the goal is to protect and monitor your home through motion sensors and video feeds.
Home security brands usually have various subscription options and some kind of self-monitored, subscription-free tier, but you usually lose out on a variety of features to encourage you to subscribe.
What Do Smart Home Security Systems and a Subscription Get You?
I remember running into the issue of paywalled features for the first time a few years ago when I was testing Abode's smart lock. I liked the lock, but I woke up to unclear notifications that happened in the dead of night. Had the lock been hacked? Had it sensed itself being manually opened when we were asleep? There was no way to tell because Abode’s base level would only tell me the lock was interacted with without explaining how. I signed up for the Abode membership that day to be able to review the events, and luckily it was just a loss of Wi-Fi connection and reestablishment that happened within a minute of each other. Crisis averted.
The main thing that subscription services paywall is video storage, which allows you to review past events at your home. Sometimes it can also be notifications, whether that's the type of notification or the ability to review notification history. What is or is not paywalled largely depends on the brand and its offerings. Professional live monitoring, however, is almost always paywalled, whether that's an agent calling police when an alarm has been triggered or an agent reviewing flagged footage (e.g., motion alerts) to either notify you of a situation or call emergency services on your behalf. That’s one thing you can't DIY—if you’re on vacation or otherwise not able to call police if there's an issue, you're out of luck.
Base stations from home security companies like ADT, SimpliSafe, and Vivint will act as a smart-home hub to connect and control sensors and other devices, and be able to sound an alarm. It might have a keypad that you can use to arm and disarm the system too.
A lot of subscription services also have a higher tier that gives you an on-staff specialist who will review live footage if a camera is triggered, or even use the microphone to speak to an intruder. It's a useful feature if it's something you're worried about, but those subscriptions can cost as much as a casual grocery trip each month.
Do You Need a Smart Home Security System Starter Kit?
You don't need a formal, branded home security kit to protect your home, but if you're interested in window and motion sensors that will trigger and sound an alarm, you might want one. You can buy a kit and even have a brand representative come and install the devices for you. (But as someone who's seen the bill for those, I'd recommend installing everything yourself, since it has to be connected to your phone and personal accounts anyway.)
If you're just looking to know who's at your door, get alerted when a window is opened, or prove you have trespassers with video footage, DIY-ing your own system with a handful of devices that fit the needs you're looking for is a fine solution. Personally, I worry most about my front door, while someone else might worry about trespassers in their backyard. Buying accessories à la carte allows you to get exactly what you want without paying extra.
Best Subscription-Free Security Devices to Build Your Own System
Smart locks are my most-used smart-home item by far. Having a smart lock makes it so easy for my entire family to access our home, including my 4-year-old, who has memorized the code. Smart locks make it easy to confirm your door is locked when it should be, and you can see the access history to know who's opening it and when. These are two of my favorite options that don't require any sort of subscription to get event history in an app, but you will need to buy a separate Wi-Fi hub or bridge for both if you want remote access. However, that's a one-time purchase instead of a forever one.
Most video doorbells have a no-subscription option, but you'll usually lose out on video storage, so you can't scroll back and see what happened when an alert went off. You'll also miss out on some notification types and features like package detection. I think doorbells and video cameras are impacted the most by the loss of features without a subscription, since so many then lose the ability to show you what happened that day or who rang the bell. These video doorbells below get around that with local storage options, so your footage is saved to a microSD card rather than the cloud. However, if you don't properly secure the camera, you could lose the footage and camera both, since all data is stored in the device.
Similar to video doorbells, you'll often run into subscription fees for security cameras in order to store footage in the cloud and review it. Instead, choose one of these cameras for the inside or outside of your home that allows local storage, so you can live subscription-free. We've got a whole guide to subscription-free security cameras if you want more options. Again, make sure the camera is secured so you don't lose the camera and footage in one go.
Motion sensors are a primary feature of most smart home security kits, but they usually don't need a subscription fee to work—when a sensor is triggered, the base station will sound an alarm. The subscription really just allows for an agent to call your local authorities if the alarm sounds; otherwise, you'll just get a notification on your phone to find out if someone's where they shouldn't be.
If you're looking for motion sensors that will activate smart-home features like turning on a switch when you walk by, these aren't it. These are designed to set off an immediate alarm when any motion is detected. Check out our guide to the Best Motion Sensors for more ideas there.
This is another popular feature of smart home security kits. It's great for getting an alert on a door that doesn't have a smart lock, or wouldn't be regularly locked. Even better for windows or sliding doors that have no other way to alert you if they're opened.

Crackdown on big money donations to parties, Grattan Institute says
Krishani Dhanji
Major parties should get less money to spend at elections, and new independents should get drastically more, says the Grattan Institute, urging a rethink of donation caps to prevent an election spending “arms race”.
Labor and the Coalition negotiated a new set of donation laws that independents called a “stitch up”, giving major parties a cap of $90 million each to spend, and placing a per-electorate cap of $800,000.
A new Grattan Institute report says the major party cap should be more than halved, to to $40 million. It argues the $800,000 seat cap should remain for incumbents and established-party candidates, but new entrants should get an extra 50% to spend.
Grattan says the Australian Electoral Commission and Australian Bureau of Statistics spend around $30m on big campaigns such as getting Australians to enrol to vote – so they argue $40m for big parties is pretty generous.
And to give you a sense of what $90m buys - Clive Palmer spent $89m during the 2019 election.
The report says:
Big-money elections mean politicians spend more time and effort on fundraising, and political parties become reliant on major donors to fund their campaigns. This creates fertile conditions for wealthy interests to have undue influence over policy making. Capping electoral expenditure puts a ceiling on money in politics.
Political parties collectively declared almost half a billion dollars in expenditure in the year leading up to the 2025 federal election. And this was not a one-off. They declared expenditure of more than $400 million in the lead-up to both the 2022 and 2019 federal elections as well.
Under the government’s newly legislated rules, the tax payer funding for parties increased from $3.38 for every first preference vote for parties and independents that achieved at least 4% of votes, to $5 - which Grattan argues won’t be necessary if the overall spending cap was reduced, saving public money.

Why are some songs grayed out on Apple Music (And how to fix it)
Here's what to do if some of your favorite songs are suddenly unavailable.
There's nothing better than listening to your favorite album, which is why it's so unsettling when tracks stop playing on your Apple device. And when you take a look at the track listing, you may find some of your tracks are grayed out. What's happening?
Often this is because your device is offline. Typically, you'll regain access once you get online again.
Licensing is another common cause. The music industry is built around a territorial licensing system, with labels owning different rights and then selling them or staggering release schedules –- sometimes even on AI-generated tracks.
This territorial licensing model means artists or labels sometimes remove tracks from Apple Music's catalog, or don't make them available in a specific region at all. When that happens, the song will not be available and will appear grayed out. There is nothing you or Apple can do about that.
How to check if it is a licensing problem
To check if a track's licensing has been revoked, open Apple Music/iTunes, click Songs in the sidebar, right-click the column headers, (where it says Name), and check the box for Cloud Status, which shows:
- No Longer Available: Track likely removed by artist or label
- Exclamation mark (!): A local sync issue
- Waiting: Sync is incomplete
There are other causes that the following guide will help you address.
Technical problems and how to solve them
If your tracks are still grayed out and you've verified that it's not a licensing issue, here are some other things you can try.
Switch it off and on again
I always recommend a full restart of your device. That's as easy as switching your Mac or PC off and on again, or running a force reset on your iPad or iPhone. Turning things off and switching them on again solves a lot of consumer tech problems.
Delete and redownload the track
Select the track, delete it and then search for it in Apple Music and download it again. If the track is unavailable, it has probably been removed from the platform.
Check for sync errors
The Music app may have developed a glitch; let's fix it:
- iPhone or iPad: Open Settings > Apps > Music and switch Sync Library off. Wait 30 seconds, turn it on again and open Apple Music.
- Mac: Open Apple Music, choose Settings > General in the menu bar, and uncheck the Sync Library item. Wait a few seconds, then turn it on again.
- Windows: Click the gear or profile icon, choose Settings and then select the General tab at the top of that window. Find Sync Library, turn it off, click OK and re-enable it after a few seconds.
How to solve content and Apple account problems
Still having trouble? The issue could run deeper than your phone's settings. Here's how to see whether it's a problem with your Apple account.
Content Restrictions
To protect minors, Apple Music's Content Restrictions feature prevents playback of explicit-tagged tracks. Override this in Settings > Content Restrictions in Apple Music on Windows, or in System Settings > Content & Privacy on Apple devices. Just set it to allow explicit content.
Check your Apple Account
Another reason music sometimes seems to disappear is because songs were purchased using a different Apple account than the one you are currently using. You'll regain access once you log out of your current account and log in with the correct one.
Reset your Apple Account
As a last resort, you can try signing out of your Apple account on your device in Settings > Apple Account > Media & Purchases and tapping the Sign Out button before signing in again.

India had the highest number of children with no sanitation service in schools, with 50 million out of the world total of 244 million as of 2025, according to a new global report. Only Nigeria (34 million), Ethiopia (26 million), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (11 million) or Indonesia (8 million) had a comparatively large number of schoolchildren who had no access to sanitation service.
The data from ‘Progress on drinking water, sanitation and hygiene in schools 2015-2025’ shows the progress as well as the challenges India is facing in meeting the water, sanitation and hygiene goals that are part of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) set for 2030.
14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service
The report can also be seen as a decadal report card on the Swachh Bharat Mission, which was launched in India on October 2, 2014. The report cites the achievement of India which saw a 14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service.
Lack of hygiene service
The WHO/UNICEF report that is part of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) shows that globally, 362 million children still had no hygiene service at their school in 2025. Of these, 20 million were from India.
It is not just lack of access that the WHO report flags about India but also gaps in data. “There is now sufficient data to estimate trends in basic hygiene coverage between 2015 and 2025 for all SDG regions except Central and Southern Asia where there were insufficient recent data to generate estimates for India, and therefore the region, beyond 2024.”
Drinking water
On the brighter side, India is among the 28 out of 62 countries that are on track to achieve universal coverage of basic drinking water in schools by 2030.
As of 2025, there were 258 million children who still had no drinking water service at their school. The number of children from Indian schools made up 12 million of this number or about 1 out 20 children in the world. The report shows that India has made a big progress in basic drinking water services in 2025 and average rates of change between 2015 and 2025. India, Panama, Syrian Arab Republic, Togo and Tuvalu increased coverage by over 4% per year, “demonstrating that rapid progress is possible”.
However, the report found that while gaps in basic water coverage persists between school levels and between rural and urban areas, this did not apply to India, Cambodia and Fiji.

United Nations, Sep 23: US President Donald Trump has said that his administration strongly supports the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEEC), saying there is a need to shift energy infrastructure away from Iranian checkpoints amid multiple strikes on West Asian countries.
Trump made these remarks while addressing a multilateral meeting with the Gulf Cooperation Council on Tuesday on the margins of the high-level UN General Assembly session.
"Iran's terrorist attacks on commercial shipping in neighbouring countries have shown the need to shift Middle East energy infrastructure away from the Iranian checkpoints," Trump said.
"That's why my administration strongly supports the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor and other places... the form of getting oil out, whether it's pipelines or anything else, and together we're on the verge of overcoming challenges that have plagued this region for decades,” he said.
The India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) is a multinational multi-modal connectivity and infrastructure initiative that was officially unveiled on September 9, 2023, during the G20 Summit in New Delhi. It is aimed at boosting connectivity, trade, and sustainability across South Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.

Looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular faces rape and drugging charges
Braden Peters, known online as Clavicular, faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted on the rape charge
Controversial “looksmaxxing” influencer, Clavicular, is facing rape and drugging charges stemming from an incident in Massachusetts last year, according to online court records.
Clavicular, 20, whose real name is Braden Peters, has been charged with one count of rape, one count of drugging someone for sexual intercourse and one count of procuring liquor for someone under 21 years old, according to court records viewed by The Independent.
The alleged incident took place on May 23, 2025, in Chatham, a seaside town on Cape Cod, according to the charges filed on September 8. Details about the allegations were not immediately known.
Online court records did not list an attorney for the influencer. Mitchell Jackson, a representative for Clavicular, told NBC News that The Bulwark, which first reported the charges, was “exaggerating,” and that Clavicular had not been served with an arrest warrant.
“Braden Peters has not been physically served. As usual the Bulwark is exaggerating,” Jackson told the outlet. Jackson did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Independent.
Clavicular gained notoriety for a trend among young men known as “looksmaxxing,” which Merriam-Webster Dictionary recently defined as “The practice of taking one or more sometimes extreme or dangerous measures intended to increase one’s physical attractiveness.”
The influencer and streamer, who has over 1 million followers on social media, gets his name from the clavicle, or collarbone, which is a highly prized feature within the looksmaxxing community.
Clavicular was sued in April by a teenage influencer in Florida who accused him of battery.
At the time, an attorney for Peters, Steve Kramer, said: “Mr. Peters denies the claims and disputes the characterization of events. He will respond through the appropriate legal channels and intends to vigorously defend himself.”
Online records do not indicate whether the charges of rape, drugging or procurement of alcohol for someone under the age of 21 were related to the allegations in that lawsuit.
Clavicular took to X Monday night to address the allegations, resharing The Bulwark’s article and writing, “What is this s***? Community notes?”
A community note underneath noted that “a community note is not needed in the quoted tweet as Clavicular has indeed been charged.”
If convicted on the rape charge, he faces up to 20 years in prison and would be required to register as a sex offender.
He is scheduled to be arraigned on October 14, according to online court records.

Gyaneshgate: Congress's scathing attack on Election Commissioner amid EC row
Congress escalated its attack on Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar after reports of internal dissent over the Special Intensive Revision. The row has intensified questions over the poll panel's independence and the voter roll exercise.
The Congress on Wednesday stepped up its attack on Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar amid reports of differences within the Election Commission over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. The party dubbed the row 'Gyaneshgate' and alleged that Kumar's actions had the full support of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah.
The attack came after a report in The Indian Express said two election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, repeatedly raised questions within the three-member panel over issues linked to the Special Intensive Revision exercise.
Later in the day, the Election Commission said differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberations in any institution, and that all its orders carry full legal sanction and follow established statutory procedures.
In a post on X, Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the chief election commissioner had lost "all administrative and moral right to continue in office".
"The CEC has proved to be an absolute disgrace to the Constitutional post he holds. His integrity of purpose, impartiality of intent and independence of action have always been extremely dubious," Ramesh alleged.
He said 73 opposition MPs had moved an impeachment motion against the CEC on April 24 and that it was still pending.
"Meanwhile, today he stands brutally exposed by his own two colleagues. And undoubtedly, opposition MPs in both Houses will now move impeachment motions if there is a special session, since the Monsoon Session has not been prorogued for an unprecedented 43 days," he said.
Ramesh also alleged, "Mr Gyanesh Kumar has functioned as a hatchet man for the Union Home Minister, who, in turn, is the designated executor of the PM's wishes. What the CEC has been doing is with the full knowledge, support and, in fact, at the instigation of the PM and HM themselves. #Gyaneshgate has been orchestrated by G2. Of that there can be no doubt".
According to the report cited by the Congress, the national rollout of the Special Intensive Revision has been under the supervision of all three commissioners, including CEC Kumar. But Sandhu and Joshi formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions taken and orders issued, which they said were done without their knowledge.
Ramesh also referred to the Supreme Court's split verdict on Wednesday on whether the selection committee to appoint election commissioners is valid.
"Justice Datta has, through pointed and straightforward questions, highlighted the degree of Central government control over the committee. He has rightly asked, can a PM's nominee go against the PM?" he said.
"The validity of the selection committee will now be examined by a larger bench, but Justice Datta's judgment confirms that the CEC must be free from the government's control if it is to be effective," he added.
Referring to the Anoop Baranwal vs Union of India case, Ramesh said the Supreme Court in March 2023 had directed that the CEC and election commissioners be appointed by the President on the recommendations of a committee comprising the prime minister, the leader of opposition and the Chief Justice of India.
Later that year, he said, the Modi government replaced the CJI with a Cabinet minister through the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, changing the court-mandated selection process.
He also said, "The Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha raised the issue of 'vote chori' over 15 months ago. He stands vindicated more than ever before".
Under fire over the red flag raised by two commissioners on the Special Intensive Revision exercise, the Election Commission said every officer of the poll panel, along with the three commissioners, is fully authorised to give suggestions for improving the electoral system.
It said any operational queries or inputs raised by Commission members during draft stages are part of standard administrative practice aimed at safeguarding voter rights, and that the suggestions made by the commissioners were for further improving the electoral process.
The day's developments saw the Congress sharpen its criticism of the CEC over the Special Intensive Revision exercise, while the Election Commission maintained that internal suggestions and differing views are part of its normal functioning and that its decisions follow due procedure.

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

Apple links landmarks on its Maps app to Hidden Histories podcast episodes
They’re part of the app's Guides feature and are available for select landmarks in five US cities.
Apple now links to Hidden Histories podcast episodes within Maps for select landmarks in five US cities. As Apple Insider has noticed, certain landmarks in San Francisco, Los Angeles, New York City, Chicago and Washington, DC now show a panel in Maps that links straight to podcasts about their histories when you view their information in the app.
When you tap the panel in Maps, it'll take you to an interface where you'll see the rest of the landmarks in the city with linked podcast guides. The New York ones, for instance, include talks on Times Square, the Statue of Liberty, Central Park, the Museum of Broadway, Grand Central Terminal, the Charging Bull, Studio 54 and Tin Pan Alley. The Los Angeles podcasts include episodes on the history of the Hollywood Sign and the Hollywood Walk of Fame, while San Francisco's include Alcatraz and the Farallon Islands.
The Hidden Histories podcasts live under the Guides section in the Maps app. Like other things under Guides, such as lists of places to go curated by various publishers, you can tap the + icon and add podcasts to your collection. You can then revisit and listen to them another day by pulling up the panel from the bottom part of Maps and then looking at the "Your Guides" section.

'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
- Published
Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.
The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.
Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.
The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.
Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation.
"I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.
When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin.
The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window.
"One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.
Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.
The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.
Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.
The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.
As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.
He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe.
"People were calling for help, some were already very weak."
But no-one came to help, he and others allege.
"While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency.
"We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door.
"We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."
Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.
The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye.
"The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.
As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja.
A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened.
It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable.
No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said.
As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event.

The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put has put healthcare in Africa and the Global South “under growing strain” a new report warns.
The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region.
The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions.
A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden.
The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m.
External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly.
The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment.
Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year.
At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m following the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions.
The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable.
“The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.”
Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”.
“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.”
The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. Some 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of over 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation.
The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know.
The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.

Hello there and welcome to a new week. STAT reporter Andrew Joseph here in London filling in for Mr. Pharmalot for the day. Before we get to the headlines, an extra dose of encouragement to check out all the great pieces that STAT has to offer today, from Reed Jobs opining on the NIH budget to our new trust-in-science reporter Nick Florko outlining his own experience grappling with, as he puts it, “how frustrating it is to realize that modern medicine does not have all the answers.” Now to those headlines. …
Novo Nordisk is seeking to assure investors that it can regain its momentum in the coming years, outlining plans to expand its pipeline and find new products that it could sell more like consumer goods than traditional medicines, building off what’s occurring with its obesity treatments, STAT shares. At the company’s capital markets day in London, CEO Mike Doustdar said Novo would launch at least five multi-blockbusters by 2030 and deliver revenue growth on par with other major pharma firms. He also presented a strategy that involved investing more in disease areas outside diabetes and obesity and said the company “will be more active within business development,” an acknowledgment of investors’ concerns that Novo was too reliant on its landmark GLP-1 drugs and needed to develop other products.
Drugs called orexin agonists have been hailed for their ability to treat rare sleep disorders, but with new data, Alkermes is showing for the first time that the new class of therapies may benefit people with ADHD, STAT writes. In a randomized Phase 1 study, the company’s new drug, called ALKS 7290, was well tolerated and showed a signal of efficacy. Participants in the study started with a median score of 39 on a diagnostic known as the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale, indicating that they had moderate to severe symptoms. After two weeks, those taking a high dose of 50 milligrams of ALKS 7290 experienced a 19-point reduction on the scale, indicating that their symptoms had become mild.

Mikel Arteta has agreed an improved new contract with Premier League champions Arsenal.
The Spaniard's current deal expires at the end of this season but talks over a new contract have been ongoing for a number of months.
BBC Sport reported earlier this month that an agreement between all parties was close.

There is no confirmation over the length of his new contract but it is set to take him into at least his 10th year at the club following his arrival in December 2019.

There’s always a danger in over-complicating products. Simple is so often best. The apocryphal story of NASA spending millions crafting a space pen while Soviet cosmonauts used a pencil is often cited as a prime example, even if it’s actually not true. Perhaps it’s not surprising that Dyson has got into hot water trying to reinvent the electric toothbrush.
The Chinese invented the first bristle toothbrush during the Ming dynasty. That concept muddled along quite nicely until 1937, when Tomlinson Moseley filed a patent for the earliest electric toothbrush. After more than 400 years, the Motodent marked the beginning of an evolutionary shift from manual brushing to powered oral care.
Having had considerable success reimagining established product categories such as stick vacuums and premium hair dryers—though not so much air-purifying headphones—the company earlier this month, with great fanfare, unveiled the next leap forward for teeth: the $499 Dyson CameraJet with a tiny camera to aim streams of rinsing fluid into the gaps between your teeth.
Others, like the Waterpik Sonic-Fusion 2.0, have already been daring (or foolhardy) enough to combine brushing and water flossing. However, Dyson upped the ante further by adding a macro-lens camera, allowing its “Gap Optical Targeting system,” trained on 470,000 dental images, to identify within 100 milliseconds precisely where to squirt fluid from the 12.5 milliliters of mouth rinse stored in its on-board reservoir.
It’s taken Dyson six years, 38 patents, and an awful lot of money to make this camera-squirt-brush doohickey work. However, something has gone badly wrong with the CameraJet. So wrong that despite James Dyson globally launching the product at a Paris event mere weeks ago, you can no longer, as far as WIRED can ascertain, buy the CameraJet anywhere.
The CameraJet launched in US stores on September 8. Just a day later, reports began outlining the first user complaints of water in the battery compartment and failures within 30 seconds of use. Consumer Reports’ own review unit stopped working less than 24 hours after unboxing. On September 11, French outlet Numerama reported that the French Dyson site and stores had reportedly stopped selling the toothbrush. By September 15, stores in the US, UK, and Singapore, where Dyson’s headquarters now reside, had followed suit.

Gautam Adani and family topped the Hurun India Rich List 2026 with a net worth of over ₹9.22 lakh crore, followed by Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani and family with ₹8.63 lakh crore.
Adani, whose business interests span the energy sector, had Ahmedabad as his listed base, while Ambani with Reliance Industries had Mumbai as his listed base. Roshni Nadar Malhotra and family of HCL ranked fifth with ₹2.78 lakh crore, while Kumar Mangalam Birla and family, of the Aditya Birla group, ranked sixth with ₹2.69 lakh crore.

Deepina Pal, 26, has been living with chronic kidney disease since she was 16 and has been on dialysis for nine years. She takes about 10–12 different kinds of medicines every day for multiple autoimmune and other chronic conditions, including medicines for blood pressure, cholesterol, thyroid and heart conditions, as well as migraine and other problems. Some need to be taken three times a day.
She sets alarms and records her medicines on her phone. When she was first prescribed medication for blood pressure, she became extremely drowsy and slept for long periods. Her family later understood that her blood pressure was falling. For people on dialysis, regular blood tests can lead to changes in medication.
Deepina’s experience reveals an important factor when it comes to taking many medications: the number of medicines does not, by itself, mean that treatment is inappropriate. The safety concern is whether every medicine remains necessary, effective and suitable as a person’s health changes.
Multiple conditions, several medicines
Polypharmacy is generally described as the regular use of five or more medicines; the use of 10 or more is often termed hyperpolypharmacy. It is particularly common among older people living with multiple chronic conditions, although complex treatment regimens can occur at any age.
A review of 27 studies involving 11,649 older adults in India found pooled rates of polypharmacy and hyperpolypharmacy of 49% and 31%, respectively.
“Not every case of polypharmacy is inappropriate,” says S. Manicka Saravanan, consultant, geriatric medicine, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. A person living with diabetes, hypertension and heart disease, for example may need several medicines. The concern only arises when medicines no longer have a clear benefit, duplicate one another, interact adversely or create a treatment burden that outweighs their benefit.
The World Health Organization identifies medication safety in polypharmacy as one of its priority areas under its Medication Without Harm initiative.
The risks
Smitha Jain, consultant, internal medicine, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, says problems can arise when medicines prescribed by different specialists are considered separately rather than as one treatment plan.
A patient may inadvertently receive duplicate medicines, particularly when several doctors prescribe for different conditions. Drug combinations can also cause harm. Some medicines used in heart failure or for blood pressure can affect potassium and kidney function; antifungal drugs can interact with anti-epileptic medicines, while some combinations can increase blood-thinner levels and the risk of bleeding.
Taking an extra dose can also be dangerous. An additional diabetes medicine may cause hypoglycaemia, while missing certain medicines, such as anti-epileptic drugs, can trigger seizures.
Older adults are particularly vulnerable because age-related changes, kidney or liver impairment, frailty, cognitive problems and multiple illnesses can alter how medicines are handled by the body. Side effects such as low blood pressure, low sodium, dizziness and confusion can increase the risk of falls.
Review and safety checks
A medication review should ask why each medicine was started, whether it is still needed, whether the dose remains appropriate, and whether there are side effects or interactions, says Dr. Saravanan. Kidney and liver function, nutrition, cognition, mobility, falls risk, cost and difficulties with swallowing or complex timings should also be considered.
Doctors recommend that patients bring all their medicines to appointments, a “brown bag” review can uncover duplicate prescriptions as well as over-the-counter, herbal or alternative products that doctors may not know about.
An updated medication list should be shared between specialists, particularly after hospitalisation or a change in treatment. Pharmacists can also help identify interactions and dosing problems. Pill organisers and alarms may reduce missed or repeated doses.
Some medicines may eventually be reduced or stopped when their benefits no longer outweigh their risks. This process, known as deprescribing, should be done carefully and not by stopping medicines abruptly. Electronic prescribing systems can flag some interactions and duplicate medicines, but clinical judgement remains the most important.
The aim is not simply to reduce the number of medicines, but to ensure that each one has a clear purpose and that the overall treatment remains safe as the patient’s circumstances change.

The story so far: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) summoned Meta officials for a hearing on Wednesday (September 9, 2026) as a part of an inquiry on child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) on Instagram. An investigation by British public broadcaster BBC threw up many ads that linked out to CSEAM on other platforms. The IT Ministry has also summoned the company on the issue.
What did the BBC investigation show?
In July, BBC reported that the organisation saw dozens of ads promoting CSEAM on Instagram with a test account. CSEAM is banned around the world, and attracts strict criminal penalties. Meta said in a statement, “Before these cases were brought to our attention, our enforcement systems had already identified and disabled several of the violating ads and the accounts behind them.”
Also Read: Google to report child abuse content directly to Indian authorities
The company said that it automatically removes millions of CSAM posting accounts each year, but that “no system is perfect and that determined criminals will continue to try to exploit our platform”. This month, the Tech Transparency Project reported that it found hundreds of CSAM ads on Facebook and Instagram, including some that were served to India.
Why are CSEAM ads appearing on Instagram?
While social media platforms prohibit CSEAM, automatic moderation systems, that use some AI to detect unlawful media, are not able to catch all violative submissions. The Tech Transparency Project, a US-based nonprofit, said that what Meta was doing was not enough even within the scope of what it could. The nonprofit said that even in cases where Meta was taking down CSEAM, it was tagging the ads as adult sexual content, and so “may be undercounting instances of child sexual abuse”.
While the firm revised this information for ads reported by TTP, “did not fix the flow of child exploitation content in its advertising system,” and continued to show CSEAM ads to certain audiences, the nonprofit said. One of the ads appeared to feature an unidentified “underaged European royal,” TTP said.
Amusing or addictive? The algorithms powering our social feeds
Many such ads were placed by “resellers” for ad spots on Meta’s platforms based in China, who account for billions of dollars of ad revenue. TTP pointed to a Reuters report that indicated that ads going through this channel were subject to a more relaxed enforcement regime, where the platform earned $18 billion in 2024. This channel is intended for Chinese firms who want to advertise to overseas customers.
Even with a human reporting CSEAM posts, action was not guaranteed, TTP found. “With 57% (73) of the CSAM ads reported to Meta, the company sent back a message that said, “We’ve taken a look and found that this ad doesn’t go against our Advertising Standards”,”, TTP said.
What was NCPCR’s reaction to the report?
NCPCR issued a notice on July 3, the same day the BBC report came out, demanding an explanation from the company. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) also sought an explanation from the company.
Shortly after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s July 23 video message to Indian youth was briefly removed from Facebook due to an “error,” MeitY summoned Meta’s global public affairs director Joel Kaplan to demand an explanation on that removal. In that meeting, the BBC reporting was also discussed. The summoning came as the government sent a massive volume of takedown notices for Instagram posts on the Jantar Mantar protests, and footage from the protests and the ensuing police crackdown went viral.
Meta provided written responses to both MeitY and NCPCR. The latter declined a Right to Information request by The Hindu for a copy of the company’s response, arguing that providing this information would impede its investigation.
After the written response, Meta officials were summoned by NCPCR this month. Neither side provided a description of the meeting.
What powers does NCPCR have to conduct an inquiry like this?
Like the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the NCPCR’s founding law, the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, gives the body the powers of a civil court under the Criminal Procedure Code (replaced recently by the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita Bill, 2023).
As such, it has the statutory power to demand explanations on issues of child safety from private organisations and can demand reports from law enforcement.
NCPCR’s remit includes “matters relating to children in need of special care and protection including children in distress,marginalized and disadvantaged children, children in conflict with law, juveniles, children without family and children of prisoners and recommend appropriate remedial measures,” and to “[i]nquire into complaints [relating to] non implementation of laws providing for protection and development of children,” the commission said.
NCPCR has in the past issued notices to firms like Netflix in response to the show Bombay Begums, and to Bourn Vita maker Mondelez over sugar content in their malt powder.
