- Another way to play multiplayer on Minecraft Java includes creating or renting a dedicated server or using Realms to host a 24/7 online world.
Playing Minecraft alone can be fun, but exploring the new biomes and surviving the night with your friends is where the chaotic nature of the game steps in. Thankfully, there are multiple ways to call in your friends or even join an online server for the entertaining mini-games. So, whether you want to create a local LAN connection, join a public server, or use Realms, this guide on how to play multiplayer on Minecraft Java will help you out.
Requirements to Play Multiplayer on Minecraft Java
Before hopping into a multiplayer world in Minecraft, make sure that you have the following requirements met:
- An official copy of Minecraft: Java Edition and a Microsoft account connected to its purchase.
- A stable internet connection and the same compatible versions for all players for a LAN connection.
- If you’re joining a public Minecraft server, you’ll need its IP address.
- If you’re joining a Realm, you’ll need its invitation from the owner. Creating a Minecraft Realm will cost you a subscription fee after the 30-day free trial period.
Important Note: Minecraft Java and Bedrock Edition use different multiplayer systems in some cases, and this guide focuses on the former for Windows, macOS, and Linux systems.
How to Play Multiplayer on Minecraft Java Using LAN
LAN is the simplest way to play multiplayer in Minecraft Java with your friends. However, it requires all the devices to be connected to the same Wi-Fi connection or router. So, here’s how to play Minecraft multiplayer using LAN:
- Launch Minecraft Java Edition and select Singleplayer from the main menu.
- Choose an existing world or create a new one. Once inside, go to the pause menu.
- Click on World Options and toggle on the LAN button. Click on Apply Changes.
- Now, your friends can launch the game, select the Multiplayer option from the main menu, and your world will be available on their local network.
- Any player on the same network will now be able to join your world through this option.
How to Play Multiplayer on Minecraft Java Using Servers
Not everyone likes to pay for additional services in a game, and fortunately there’s a way to make a Minecraft server for free. Additionally, you can also join a public Minecraft server if you’re looking for more than just vanilla gameplay. So, here’s a detailed process for it.
- From the main menu of Minecraft, click on Multiplayer and then the Add Server button.
- Enter the name of the server and paste its IP address or server URL in the address field.
- Click Done to save the server, then select it from the multiplayer list to enter it.
- Alternatively, you can also create your own server in Minecraft by downloading the official Java software.
- More details on creating your own server and sharing its address are stated in the guide linked above for your reference.
How to Play Multiplayer on Minecraft Java Using Friends Feature
Recently, a built-in social feature was added to the Java Edition after the Minecraft Chaos Cubed update. This allows you to call your friends to join the same local world you’re in using a peer-to-peer connection. Although it requires an internet connection, it’s simpler than setting up your own server and also doesn’t rely on a local network for all players. So, here’s how to do it:
- Launch the Minecraft single-player world you want to invite your friends.
- Go to the pause menu and click on the Friends icon.
- In this list, enter the profile name of your friend and click on the envelope icon to send a request.
- Ask your friend to accept the request, then you can send them an invitation to join your world.
Before completing the above steps, make sure that you have all the options in the Friends List turned on. These settings can be changed by clicking on the Options button in the main menu and selecting the Online button. For more help, our guide on how to add friends in Minecraft will help you out.
How to Play Multiplayer on Minecraft Java Using Realms
Minecraft Realms is Mojang’s official subscription-based multiplayer hosting service. It allows you to maintain an online world that invited friends can access without needing to run a server on your computer. The best part of Realms is that these servers stay online 24/7, so the owner doesn’t need to come online at all times. So, here are the steps you need to proceed with:
- Launch Minecraft Java on your system and click on Minecraft Realms in the main menu.
- You can try Realms for the first 30-days for free before purchasing the subscription model.
- Alternatively, if your friend has purchased the Realm, they can send you an invite, and you can accept it from the notifications.
- Our guide on how to join a Minecraft server explains joining a Realm server in great detail to help you out.
You can also try out the best Minecraft server hosting services for playing multiplayer in the Java Edition. Unlike Realms, these are third-party services that offer a similar 24/7 online server on a subscription-based model.
While all of the above methods are a pain in the head for adding Minecraft mods and plugins, Realms and third-party server hosting services offer a seamless experience if you want a modded world.
And that is all you need to learn about how to play multiplayer in Minecraft Java. So, which method are you going to consider from the above? Tell us in the comments below.
How to play multiplayer on Minecraft 26.3 in 2026?
You can play multiplayer on Minecraft Java in 2026 by joining a public server, hosting a private server using LAN, inviting friends through the supported feature, or joining a Minecraft Realm.
How to play multiplayer Minecraft Java on different networks?
To play Minecraft Java with friends on different networks, you can join a public server, use a hosted private server, or play on Minecraft Realms.

In May, Apple agreed to pay out $250 million as part of a class action lawsuit over claims the company overhyped its Apple Intelligence tools, specifically the long-delayed Siri AI overhaul.
Although the revamped Siri AI voice assistant is now available for owners of newer iPhones via iOS 27, you may still be eligible to claim cash back for past purchases. This settlement covers customers in the US who made their purchases from June 10, 2024, to March 29, 2025, and bought certain iPhone 15 or iPhone 16 models from Apple. If you qualify, you might receive up to $95 for each phone.
This settlement revolves around Apple’s promotion of Siri features to sell iPhones. “I expected to receive a Siri Apple Intelligence feature and did not receive it,” reads part of the statement you have to sign when filling out the claim form. As part of the settlement, Apple denies any wrongdoing.
“We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” read part of Apple’s statement from May about the settlement.
To file a claim, visit the dedicated website: smartphoneaisettlement.com. Click the blue button in the top-right corner of the page labeled File A Claim. First, you’ll be asked whether you have a Claim ID and PIN to enter. It’s not required for you to already have this info on hand. On the final page, you’ll need either your iPhone’s serial number or Apple Account ID on hand to file the claim.
Not sure where your serial number is located? Open the Settings app, tap General, then choose About. Your serial number will be a string of letters and numbers near the top of the screen.
You can choose to receive the settlement money through PayPal, Venmo, an electronic bank transfer, or a paper check. If you have multiple devices and want to make claims for all of them, then you’ll need to fill out the form again for every eligible device. iPhone owners have until December 21 to make their claims.

Teen social media bans are hot these days, with new regulations installed or soon to come in Australia, Indonesia, and the European Union. But how will we know these rules are working? And what does “working” even mean?
Researcher Camilla Iannone asked a group of young people for advice on how to answer those questions. Their feedback reframed the whole debate for her. “Rather than focusing solely on whether social media is harmful and whether we need a ban, they repeatedly asked us to look at what role social media currently plays in young people’s lives, and what might replace it if access is restricted,” she writes in a new First Opinion.
Read more on the questions teens had for researchers, and what kinds of data they’d like to see.
We write a lot at STAT about artificial intelligence and medicine. But I hadn’t seen a paper quite like this one before. In it, Penn State researchers probed how AI would choose whoshould receive a donor kidney, one of the thorniest issues in medical ethics. “Often, there is no single objective correct answer,” the researchers wrote. “Rather the decisions rely on nuanced human and moral judgements.”
But when they asked several prominent large language models to choose between possible kidney recipients, they found that AI diverged from human judgement in a few key ways: The AI was less indecisive than humans, “tending toward deterministic recommendations even when abstention is explicitly permitted.” It also rarely chose against the majority choice, which could “fail to capture the plurality inherent in moral values.”
I’m curious whether and how AI is finding its way into medical ethics, and whether this research lines up with real-world experiences. How are you thinking about AI and medical ethics? Thoughts, examples, and other research welcome!

Should it be ‘Pinky and the Brains’ now?
We all know about left brain and right brain. But a new paper suggests a more surprising division — our brains might have developed from two distinct organs.
To draw that conclusion, Stanford University researchers examined how the brains of mouse embryos develop. They found that at the earliest stages of growth, the hindbrain expresses discrete genes and a different chromatin configuration than the midbrain and forebrain. That raises some interesting possibilities.
“Although the brain is often construed as a single organ, the brain may itself derive from two parallel progenitors that emerge early in development and that, respectively, form the forebrain/midbrain versus the hindbrain,” the researchers write. “Analogously, the heart derives from two parallel progenitors, the first and second heart fields, which converge to form a single organ.”
The researchers hope their discovery will make it easier to grow hindbrain neurons, which support the study of diseases like spinal muscular atrophy and ALS. Read more here.
New federal autism committee head has financial ties to leucovorin
Move over, Sylvia Fogel. It’s John Gaitanis’s turn to steer autism research.
Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has installed Gaitanis, a pediatric neurologist, as the new chair of the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee, which helps the federal government decide how to allocate roughly $2 billion in autism research.
Gaitanis, who recently began a stint at the National Institutes of Health’s child health institute, is best known for co-founding Meadow Biosciences. The telehealth startup is centered around helping autistic kids access leucovorin — a drug that President Trump touted during a news conference last year even though the clinical evidence that it helps improve speech is sparse.
Fogel will remain on the autism council. During her tenure as chair, she got into testy exchanges with other autism committee members, pushed for doubling autism research funding, and oversaw the creation of a new strategic plan that ditches genetic research for investigations into environmental causes, including vaccines. — O. The sobering number in the CDC’s latest mortality report
This morning, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released new demographic data on 2024’s leading causes of death. Most of the killers — heart disease, cancer, and unintentional injuries top the list — remained unchanged from 2023. But suicide moved into the top ten, accounting for 1.6% of all deaths in 2024. It was the seventh most common cause of death for men, and the second leading cause of death for Americans between 10 and 24.
Johns Hopkins professor Paul Nestadt, medical director of the Center for Suicide Prevention, offered some helpful context, writing in an email that suicide has crept up the cause of death list “more because Covid deaths shrank than any particular increase in suicide rates.” What has been rising, he said, is the proportion of suicides by firearm. “Right along with that, we see increases in suicide specifically in the populations that are having the most new increases in firearm ownership: Black Americans,” he added.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Wipro Consumer Care & Lighting announced the acquisition of Dermatouch, one of India’s fastest-growing, science-backed premium skincare brands, marking its entry into India’s fast-growing premium skincare market. This marks Wipro Consumer Care’s 18th acquisition globally and its third strategic acquisition this year.
This move reflects Wipro Consumer Care’s continued focus on building leadership in high-growth consumer categories by expanding into segments where consumers are increasingly seeking effective, dermatologist recommended solutions backed by science and efficacy. Building on its global skincare expertise through brands such as Derma Lab, Dr. Dermis and Bio-essence, the acquisition represents Wipro Consumer Care’s strategic entry into India’s premium skincare segment.
Founded by Anish Nagpal and Amit Purswani, Dermatouch has emerged as one of India’s fast-growing, made-in-India, concern-based pharmacy skincare brands, focused on addressing a wide spectrum of evolving skin concerns and consumer needs. Built around concerns such as pigmentation, acne, brightening and sun protection, the brand offers science-backed skincare solutions across formats ranging from face washes, soaps and serums to creams, moisturisers and sunscreens. Dermatouch has built its proposition around efficacy, accessibility and a deep understanding of evolving skincare needs, with its products gaining strong consumer acceptance and being increasingly recommended by dermatologists. The brand has built its presence through its direct-to-consumer platform, online marketplaces and an expanding offline retail network.
Their revenues in FY 26 were Rs.131 Cr (~US$ 13.6 Mn) with a growth of 114% over FY25. Wipro will be acquiring a 60% stake at an Enterprise value of INR 387.5 Cr, with balance 40% to be acquired over the next 3 years. Anish Nagpal, Amit Purswani and the current management team of Dermatouch will continue to run the business during this period.
Dermatouch has built its proposition around a fundamental shift in consumer behavior: skincare is increasingly moving from beauty-led choice to efficacy-led choice. The pace of this adoption is reflected in the brand’s growth—from selling approximately 60,000 products a month just 2 years ago to over 60,000 products every day today.
Commenting on the acquisition, Kumar Chander, CEO, Wipro Consumer Care & Lighting and MD, Wipro Enterprises, said, “Dermatouch represents an exciting opportunity for us as our first foray into digital brands. We have been clear that we would only look at Digital brands that have the potential to expand offline, which Dermatouch has already proven. The brand has earned significant consumer trust in a short span of time, and we see considerable potential to scale it further by combining its innovation-led approach with Wipro’s capabilities. We welcome Anish and Amit to the Wipro family and look forward to the next phase of growth together.”
“Partnering with Wipro marks a monumental milestone in Dermatouch’s journey. Since inception, our mission has been to build a trusted, science-backed and efficacy-led skincare brand focused on addressing real consumer concerns. Wipro’s legacy of trust, consumer-first philosophy and decades of experience in building and scaling successful brands across global markets makes it an ideal partner for our next phase of growth. Its extensive distribution network, and deep research capabilities will enable us to take Dermatouch to newer heights, and make it a truly global brand,” said Anish Nagpal and Amit Purswani, Co-founders, Dermatouch.
“Dermatouch aligns perfectly with our strategy to capture high-growth segments in personal care. The brand has cultivated customer loyalty through its science-backed portfolio and deep understanding of evolving consumer needs. By combining Dermatouch’s strengths with Wipro Consumer Care’s capabilities in R&D, distribution and innovation, we believe there is extensive scope to accelerate growth in India’s fast-growing premium skincare market,” said Sumit Keshan, Head of M&A, India and Managing Partner, Wipro Consumer Ventures at Wipro Consumer Care & Lighting.
Built with a dermatology-led approach, the portfolio combines carefully selected active ingredients with an efficacy-led philosophy to offer accessible, high-performance solutions designed for diverse skin types.
This announcement also follows Wipro Consumer Care & Lighting’s recent acquisition of Good Home and Eva from TTK Healthcare, as well as S brands in Philippines, reinforcing the company’s continued focus on strengthening its presence in high-potential consumer categories.
About Wipro Consumer Care and Lighting
Wipro Consumer Care and Lighting, a part of Wipro Enterprises, is among the fastest-growing FMCG businesses in India and has achieved revenues of INR 10,800 Cr in FY25-26. The business includes personal wash products, toiletries, facial care products, home care products, electrical wire devices, domestic and commercial lighting, seating solutions, and foods business. With more than 50% of its revenue coming from international businesses, over 10,000 employees, and women comprising 41% of its workforce, the company has a prominent brand presence and significant market share across categories in India and Southeast Asia. The company is also expanding its footprint across the Middle East, Africa, and other developing markets.
For more information, visit www.wiproconsumercare.com

The Election Commission of India on Wednesday defended its decision-making process, saying that differing views and observations within an institution are a normal part of deliberation before a final decision is taken. The poll panel's response came amid a political row after an Indian Express report highlighting objections raised by two Election Commissioners over several decisions during the rollout of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls “Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system,” the poll panel said. The EC, in its eight-point official statement, said that focusing on specific internal notes and observations over a 10-month period, while leaving out the “much larger body” of approvals, decisions and initiatives, presents only “one part of the picture”. The Indian Express report had claimed that the two Commissioners objected to the Election Commission's steps 14 times in 10 months amid the rollout of Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exervcise. It stressed that not just the three Election Commissioners but every officer of the Commission is authorised to offer suggestions aimed at improving the electoral system. The report trigerred a political row with Congress party saying that Gyanesh Kumar has no right to stay in office and must resign. Many of the leaders also called for Kumar's removal and impeachment. Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi alleged that the BJP, the RSS and the Election Commission which organised "vote chori" have committed an act of treason. "Vote chori is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on our Constitution," Gandhi said. "The BJP, RSS and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason. Justice will be served," the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha said on X. The poll panel also pointed to the breadth of its work in recent months, saying it had taken numerous decisions, issued instructions, introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken electoral reforms, including electoral-roll revision and SIR across the country. The EC also said all these decisions were the outcome of unanimous decisions of the full Commission over the past year. The Commission reiterated that it remains committed to carrying out its constitutional duties with “complete integrity”, while underlining its role in advancing India's democracy. “The Election Commission of India remains fully committed to executing its constitutional duties with complete integrity, recognizing its vital role in advancing our democracy,” it said. The objections by the two EC's, according to a report in The Indian Express, covered issues including the addition of new voters, deletion and restoration of names, changes to Form 6, and the functioning of technology used to manage electoral rolls. TMC Rajya Sabha leader Derek O'Brien said on X, "Five months ago, 60 Rajya Sabha MPs (50 needed) wrote to Chairman RS moving Motion to remove CEC Gyanesh Kumar. After big news break today that two Election Commissioners objected to many of CEC's actions, it's time to bring out the RS Motion today. Impeach CEC to save democracy". The story so far: The Union Health Ministry has said that stem cell therapy for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) cannot be offered as routine or commercial treatment and can be used only as part of a duly approved clinical trial. The advisory, issued on September 16 to States and Union Territories that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, follows a landmark Supreme Court judgment in January that examined the use of stem cells for autism.
What exactly has the government said?
The Health Ministry has reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for disease conditions or indications included in the Ministry’s approved list. Autism is not among those indications.
For ASD specifically, the Ministry has said that therapeutic use of any type of stem cell must remain restricted to duly approved clinical trials, following the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, and other applicable regulatory requirements. It should not be offered as a routine, standard or commercial clinical service.
The advisory is an attempt to ensure enforcement of an existing regulatory framework, particularly after the Supreme Court ruling.
Why is this significant for autism?
Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition. There is currently no established stem cell treatment that has been shown to cure autism or to provide sufficient evidence of benefit to make it a standard treatment.
The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), in its evidence review on stem cell therapy for ASD, examined the available scientific evidence and concluded that it did not support using stem cells in addition to behavioural and supportive therapies. It recommended that stem cell therapy for autism should not be offered as standard or routine therapy and that its therapeutic use should be restricted to approved clinical trials.
This distinction is important — a treatment being investigated in a clinical trial does not mean that it has been established as an effective treatment. A clinical trial is the mechanism through which safety and efficacy are tested.
What did the Supreme Court say?
The issue came before the Supreme Court in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors., decided on January 30, 2026.
The petition raised concerns about the commercial promotion and administration of stem cell “therapy” for autism. The court examined the scientific and regulatory position and held that, given the evidence available at present, stem cell therapy for ASD could not be offered by medical practitioners as a clinical service outside an approved and monitored clinical trial or research setting.
The court also said that, until further research establishes stem cell therapy as a sound and relevant medical practice for ASD, offering it as routine clinical treatment would not meet the reasonable standard of care expected of medical practitioners.
The court recognised the difficult situation faced by families of people with autism who may look for experimental treatments when conventional interventions do not produce the hoped-for results.
It therefore also addressed patients who were already undergoing such treatment before the judgment. Rather than abruptly discontinuing treatment, the court directed the Health Ministry to work out a mechanism, in consultation with AIIMS and the National Medical Commission, to provide the best possible solution and facilitate their continuation until they could be redirected to institutions conducting clinical trials.
So is all stem cell therapy prohibited in India?
No, that is not what this latest advisory states. The latest advisory does not say that stem cells can never be used clinically. It draws a distinction between approved standard care and experimental use.
The Ministry’s current approved list covers 18 adult and 14 paediatric indications. These include several blood cancers and blood disorders, as well as conditions such as multiple sclerosis and systemic sclerosis. For these indications, the relevant treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation performed appropriately; the Ministry’s list specifically states that mesenchymal stem-cell transplantation is not recommended for any disease condition.
Autism is not on this list.
The 2017 National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research also make a fundamental distinction between established haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and experimental applications. They state that, apart from approved indications, stem-cell use in humans must be within an approved and monitored clinical trial.
What is the way forward for use of stem cells in children with autism?
The advisory states that this therapy cannot be simply prescribe or administer as a routine therapy/treatment.
If stem cells are being investigated for ASD, the treatment has to be part of a properly designed and approved clinical trial. Such research requires the appropriate regulatory and ethical approvals. Depending on the nature and manipulation of the stem cells, different regulatory requirements apply.
This is the key difference between research and treatment being that a clinic cannot describe an experimental intervention as an established therapy and charge patients for it as ordinary clinical care.
What about clinics already offering it?
The Health Ministry has asked State and District regulatory authorities to ensure compliance and to disseminate the Supreme Court’s directions to government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion or administration.
The National Medical Commission (NMC), in an advisory dated September 5, has separately reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for approved indications. It has said that unauthorised administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement beyond those indications would constitute professional misconduct. State Medical Councils have been asked to examine complaints and take disciplinary action where professional misconduct is established following due process.
There can also be consequences for clinical establishments. The Health Ministry has referred to Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, which provide for cancellation of registration and penalties in applicable jurisdictions.
What should parents understand from this?
The advisory does not mean that research into stem cells and autism has stopped. It means that such research has to remain research until there is convincing evidence that establishes safety and efficacy.
For parents, perhaps the most important distinction is between a clinic saying that stem cells are being studied for autism and saying that stem cells are an established treatment for autism.
The first is a legitimate area of scientific investigation, subject to approvals. The second is not supported by the present evidence or India’s regulatory framework. ICMR’s assessment remains that stem-cell therapy should not be offered as routine treatment for ASD.
The September advisory puts renewed emphasis on enforcing the distinction between an experimental intervention being tested under scientific oversight and a commercial treatment being sold to families as established care.

A Hyderabad-based man has slammed the Indian passport, alleging no advantage while travelling abroad. He said that having an Indian passport gives no benefits despite paying up to ₹1 crore in tax every year. He called it “absolutely useless”. The post was shared on X by entrepreneur Jitender Emmani. He added that most Indians chase other passports to avoid the issues. "Can’t go anywhere good without waiting for days for the Visa or submitting a thousand pages. No wonder so many Indians are chasing other passports," he added. Emmani, who is the founder of Cozy Farms, said that having a United States visa stamp on an Indian passport makes it easier for holders to travel. However, securing a visa stamp from the States itself can be challenging. "A valid US visa is the shortcut many use. Why do we need a US stamp to let an Indian Passport let in anywhere," he added. The man further shared how high taxation in India comes with no benefits, even in terms of travel. He said that he pays somewhere between ₹75 lakh to 1 crore directly or indirectly as tax in a year. "I pay almost 75L - 1 Cr in taxes directly and Indirectly a year and have zero advantages both locally or internationally. We need to start fixing our country’s situation and stop blaming the past for few more decades," he concluded. His post has now gone viral across social media, gaining mixed reviews. "For the first time someone echoed my anguish deep down like an inner battle. God knows how much I paid as taxes and yet the services I get are pissport. 'Father of Nunavut' has one more fight left: to live in the territory he helped create
Time is ticking to secure funding that would allow John Amagoalik to age at home
"I'll never go back," John Amagoalik said of an assisted living facility in Ottawa, where he was sent to live by Nunavut's government in February 2025.
The territory's Department of Health transferred him to Embassy West Senior Living after an infection left no choice but to amputate part of his right leg.
"The worst part was the loneliness," Amagoalik recalled in an interview with CBC News as he sat in a wheelchair at his temporary home in Iqaluit with his wife, Evie, on Sept. 7.
"The strange surroundings. That was the worst part, being so far away from home and not ... being able to be with my many grandchildren."
Amagoalik is turning 79 in November and has multiple chronic age-related issues. He also has a difficult time talking.
He's frail, but he's still a fighter.
After a lifetime of struggle that included being forced to attend residential schools and advocating for Inuit rights and self-determination, Amagoalik is in his last fight: to age in the territory he helped create.
"It's been my life," he said, when asked what Nunavut means to him. "And I feel fortunate in being part of it."
'Father of Nunavut'
John Amagoalik is revered as the "Father of Nunavut" for his work spanning over three decades beginning in the 1970s — earning him the Order of Nunavut and the Order of Canada.
Among his many roles, he advocated for Inuit as an adviser with the Tunngavik Federation of Nunavut before it became Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. He was also on the executive council of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in the 1980s, and served as president of what was then the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, now Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami.
Amagoalik led the land claims settlement process with Nunavut Tunngavik after ratification in 1993. He also chaired the Nunavut Implementation Commission that designed the public government of Nunavut before the territory was created in 1999.
It's the very government his Victoria-based lawyer and longtime friend, Steve Kelliher, said is now failing him. So he's helping Amagoalik take the Nunavut government to court.
Kelliher, who first worked with Amagoalik in the 1970s formulating Nunavut's future government, said his friend is still as much a force today as he was back then.
But when he and another friend, Mark Stiles of Ottawa — who first met Amagoalik in 1975 while working in the land claims office of the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada — visited Amagoalik at Embassy West in March, they felt he needed their help.
"I said, 'Well, how do you like it here, John?' And he said, 'I hate it,'" Kelliher said.
So he asked Amagoalik if he wanted help to return home. "He said, 'Do anything to get me out of here, to get me back to Iqaluit.'"
So they did.
First, they delivered a letter to the territory’s health minister, signed by Amagoalik and dated March 31, pleading to return home. Amagoalik claims he never agreed to the move being permanent.
When the minister, Janet Pitsiulaaq Brewster, didn't take any action on his request to return home, they formed the John A. Committee and brought in Iqaluit lawyer Anne Crawford.
The committee raised $30,000 for a consultant to develop Amagoalik's plan of care, buy medical equipment and supplies, and pay for eight to 10 hours of daily private home care from personal support workers.
It also secured an accessible unit at a subsidized rate of $2,000 a month that has space for his hospital bed and an elevator. The Amagoaliks' public housing unit has stairs that would be too difficult for him to use.
The committee also arranged air transportation donated by an airline to fly Amagoalik to Iqaluit. On June 12, 16 months after he arrived in Ottawa, he returned home.
An uncertain future
But despite all of the hard work to bring Amagoalik back to Nunavut, his future is still uncertain.
The funds raised by the committee were only meant to be for the short term, and Anne Crawford said the money is running out.
"Which we did tell the government at the time, this will not last forever. And therefore, can you talk to us about how and what we can do going forward to continue to support him and live in his home community?"
The request to the territorial government for $16,000 a month to cover accommodations in the accessible unit and up to 10 hours a day of support worker care was declined. However, the government can provide a maximum of two hours per week of personal support worker care.
The committee says its research shows that Nunavut was spending about $30,000 a month for Amagoalik’s care at Embassy West.
The Health Department told CBC News that it can't comment on his care in order to protect his privacy. Brewster, the health minister, also declined to be interviewed.
But a communications manager provided a written statement saying the government has not refused to provide publicly funded health care to Amagoalik and that it continues to work in "good faith to support him."
"So we have no alternative but to appeal to the courts to compel them to do the right thing," Kelliher said, calling the situation "despicable."
"If we've got no money, we'll go beat the bushes," he said. Amagoalik "deserves better. He's earned it. He is an exception. Who treats their leaders like that? Not the Inuit. I don't believe it."
On Sept. 16, two notices of application for judicial review were filed in the Nunavut Court of Justice on behalf of Amagoalik.
"One for judicial review of the assistant deputy minister's letter, the decision not to fund John's care and housing," Kelliher said. "And an application for urgent relief to compel them to do so until the matter is fully heard, which could take months."
Lack of care facilities for seniors
Amagoalik's care situation is emblematic of a wider problem in Nunavut. The vast territory, which covers a total area of just over two million square kilometres and is home to roughly 40,000 people, has only six seniors' facilities spread across its three regions.
The government says it's expanding two more long-term care facilities in Nunavut.
- Amagoalik among 6 northerners appointed to Order of Canada
- John Amagoalik, ‘Father of Nunavut,’ honoured in Iqaluit
Currently, 73 elders from Nunavut are being cared for at Embassy West Senior Living, the only out-of-territory facility contracted by the government for more complex needs.
"We don't want to continue seeing our elders getting flown to Ottawa,” said Gloria Uluqsi, president of Nunavut Tunngavik. "I think they can do better. I think we as a team can do better for our elders."

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

Moldova to impose 60-day energy and water emergency due to drought and rising costs
Moldova’s parliament has declared a 60-day state of emergency in the country’s energy and water sectors amid severely low water levels on the Dniester River and global conflicts that are driving up energy costs
CHISINAU, Moldova -- Moldova voted on Tuesday to impose a 60-day state of emergency on its energy and water sectors due to severely low water levels on the Dniester River and global conflicts that are driving up energy costs.
Moldova is facing “a severe hydrological deficit” on both the Dniester and Prut rivers, which threatens the European Union candidate country’s water supply, according to the Ministry of Environment, which said the measures would give the authorities the power to intervene faster and apply temporary measures where necessary to maintain supplies.
“Particular attention is paid to the situation on the Dniester River, which is one of the main water sources of the Republic of Moldova,” the ministry said.
The 101-seat legislature approved the measure in a 54-20 vote, with 22 lawmakers not casting ballots. The emergency takes effect on Saturday.
The decision comes a day after President Maia Sandu chaired a National Security Council meeting on the “impact of the international energy crisis” on Moldova and “measures to strengthen national energy resilience” ahead of winter.
Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said on Tuesday that a “perfect storm” of issues, such as drought, conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, and the destruction of refineries, has led to rising energy costs and put pressure on Moldova’s energy sector.
Moldova depends heavily on imported natural gas and electricity. Similar states of alert, which expire on Friday, have been in place in both sectors since July, when a severe drought began to grip Europe.
“I’m not saying that tomorrow we’ll run out of gas, diesel, electricity or water,” Tofan said. “The problem is that we are entering the cold season with several major risks overlapping at the same time.”
Tofan said about 22 cubic meters of water per second were flowing into the Novodnistrovsk reservoir upstream in Ukraine, well below the minimum of 60 cubic meters per second that he said was needed.
Environment Minister Gheorghe Hajder said restrictions on nonessential water use may be necessary. “We must have all the tools required to intervene,” he said.
Moldova declared a state of emergency in the energy sector in March after Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid disconnected a key power line linking Moldova to Romania. That same month, thousands of Moldovans were left without water after a Russian strike on the Novodnistrovsk hydropower plant resulted in pollution on the Dniester.

Anthropic and OpenAI announce more powerful (and cheaper) AI models
After a lot of back and forth about slowing the pace of AI development, both companies are releasing new models.
The conversation in the AI industry has largely been focused on slowing down AI development or "pacing the frontier," but that apparently won't stop Anthropic and OpenAI from releasing new models. Both companies are iterating on their previous releases, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra, with new models that offer similar levels of performance but at lower costs.
In the case of Claude, Anthropic says its new Opus 5.5 model is better at handling complex work, "finding and fixing inefficiencies in software" and financial analysis and business work — all pitches laser-targeted at Anthropic's enterprise customers. Anthropic's benchmarks claim Opus 5.5 also scored better at agentic coding than GPT-6 Astra on both Terminal-Bench 4.0 and FrontierCode v1.1 (Main), which could make it more appealing for developers.
Improvements extend outside of the tasks the model can handle and to how it works: Anthropic claims Opus 5.5 produces writing that's easier to understand, and that it "attempted to circumvent boundaries around 85 percent less often" than past models, suggesting it'll disobey directions less often. Equally important, the company claims it costs less per token to use ($4 for input tokens and $20 for output tokens, compared to the $5 input and $25 output of Opus 5).
OpenAI's new GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models are similarly focused on efficiency. The new models were trained using similar methods to GPT-6 Astra and offer improvements across professional work, coding and computer use, but for up to 50 percent cheaper than the promotional pricing of their GPT-5.6 counterparts. Specifically, GPT-6 Sol input tokens cost $2, while output tokens cost $10. For Luna, input tokens cost $0.10, while output tokens cost $0.50.
In terms of improvements, both new GPT-6 models are better at getting facts right, with Sol making about half as many mistakes as its predecessor, according to OpenAI. In coding, the company says GPT-6 Sol is able to match the performance of Fable 5.1 at a lower cost, too. The new models also communicate more clearly, and thanks to improvements to prompt caching, OpenAI says they can reuse more context and respond faster.
OpenAI says the GPT-6 models are more aligned than before based on the company's homegrown tests. For example, they lie less about the results of their coding work and deny even more attempts to bypass safeguards when they receive an unsafe command. Like Anthropic, OpenAI has also proposed its own criteria for third-party evaluators to use when judging the progress and safety of AI development. Whether these proposals will lead to some kind of industry-wide standard remains to be seen though.
Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model is available to developers now through Claude, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are both available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise customers. Free users and Go subscribers will have access to only GPT-6 Luna in the company's desktop app.
