When asked if a boycott of Sunday's Israel game will be discussed among the squad on Friday, O'Shea said: "For us, the decision was made by the FAI, Uefa and the Government. For us as players, that's not our decision.
"We're Irish players and when called upon we come and represent our country and that's important to know too.
"Obviously when we come together, we'll speak openly about what we feel and what we feel is right. And yeah, that'll be given its time on Friday."
Making headlines 'not so clever from me' - Hallgrimsson
Earlier this week, Israel's football governing body accused Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimmson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity" regarding comments he made about facing Israel.
Last week, Hallgrimsson said: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide. We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."
While the FAI did not respond publicly, Taoiseach Micheal Martin [Irish prime minister] said Israel FA's comments were "unacceptable" and "should be withdrawn".
Addressing the matter on Wednesday, Hallgrimsson expressed gratitude for the support he has received while admitting "it was not clever" of him to generate headlines in the build-up to the Kosovo match.
"Obviously, we are grateful for all the support that we have," said the Icelander, who has been in charge since 2024.
"Creating and taking over maybe the headlines at the moment, what I said [in the] last press meeting we had is taking the attention away from maybe what's most important," he said.
"We are playing an important game against Kosovo. So that was not the purpose and from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention like this.
"I need to be focused on the game, the players need to be focused on the game. But to answer the question, we're thankful for all the support we get. It's a tricky time for us."
Armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.
In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Israel has repeatedly denied that it has committed genocide, as well as war crimes and crimes against humanity. It says its military operations in Gaza have been conducted in self-defence and in accordance with international law.

EXCLUSIVE: Here’s the trailer for Season 2 of Apple TV‘s German dark comedy Where’s Wanda?.
The sophomore season starring Heike Makatsch (Love Actually), Axel Stein (The Vault), Lea Drinda (The Gryphon), Leo Simon and and Nikeata Thompson (Späti) debuts globally on October 21, and this is the exclusive trailer ahead of the launch. Episodes will drop weekly through December 9, as previous announced.
The UFA Fiction German-language comedy-drama picks up after the events of the first season, which saw Carlotta and Dedo Klatt (Makatsch and Stein) searching for their lost daughter Wanda (Drinda). As the season opens, Wanda is seemingly caught red-handed standing over a dead body and is hauled off to jail.
Carlotta and Dedo have to do everything in their power to prove her innocence and avoid losing her again, with their investigation taking them to the heart of their sleepy suburban town, Sundersheim.
Watch on Deadline
In the trailer we see a shaken Wanda in jail. The scene morphs back to the murder scene, as Wanda finds a body dead backstage at a funfair. As the curtains pull back, she is revealed standing over the corpse with a bloodied trophy in her hands as the audience gasps. From there, her parents hatch their crazy plan to set her free and reveal the killer.
“We end Season 1 with Wanda returning to her family, which is a great relief for them,” said Where’s Wanda? exec producer Nataly Kudiabor in an exclusive interview. “We had already announced that Wanda will be in prison in Season 2, and that has a huge impact on the family,” she said. “They have just got their daughter back, and now they have to deal with what this will do to them.
“It also affects the family’s position in Sundersheim. What are the neighbours thinking? What do the people in Sundersheim think? Is it right that their daughter is in prison? There are a lot of questions being asked.”
Sam Riley, Alexandra Maria Lara, Harriet Herbig-Matten, Gisa Flake, David Schütter, Palina Rojinski Suzanne von Borsody, Kostja Ullmann, Devid Striesow, Frederic Balonier, Sascha Geršak, Torben Liebrecht , Aaron Maldonado-Morales and Anton Dreger are also cast in Season 2.
Oliver Lansley created, written and executive produced season 2, alongside UFA Fiction co-Managing Director and executive producer Nataly Kudiabor and Oliver Ossege. The series was co-created and based on a story by Zoltan Spirandelli, though he was not involved in Season 2, we understand. Tobi Baumann and Christian Ditter.
We sat down for an exclusive interview with Kudiabor this week, who said Drinda’s titular character would be far more present in Season 2.
“We always felt that Wanda was the heart of the show, so we wanted her to return and to give her more screen time,” she said. “Lea Drinda is a fantastic actress, and this time she isn’t hidden away for several episodes – she is there from the beginning.”
Kudiabor revealed there would be “surprises” for the audience. “We love our surprises. For example, new neighbours move in: the Kimballs, played by Sam Riley and Alexandra Maria Lara, who are internationally known. They are a couple in real life, and we cast them as a couple in the show, which I think was a great idea. They bring a new layer to the series.”
She added there would be “more twists and turns,” saying: “Oliver is very good at leading the audience in one direction and then revealing something unexpected from another side. There are also lots of interesting new characters in Sundersheim whom audiences haven’t seen before.”
Kudiabor said that if Season 1 was about “the search, the neighbours and everything people were hiding in Sundersheim,” Season 2 was about “what the crisis is doing to the family and how they rebuild afterwards.”
Working with Apple TV
Where’s Wanda? was the first German-language original to come from Apple TV, with the likes of Constellation and Berlin ER following later. Prior to the show’s launch, there was a feeling within the German television production community that the global streamer’s future in Germany hinged on its success, with several privately voicing the opinion to Deadline at the time.
The Season 2 renewal was validation the dark comedy had cut through, and Kudiabor praised the collaborative nature of Apple’s execs, with UFA Fiction in regular communication with Jay Hunt’s London office throughout the process. She noted that having an English writer in Lansley was “really helpful” to the flow of the development.
“We were very excited to make Apple TV+’s first German original,” she said. “It’s great to work for a streamer with so many excellent shows. I’m a big fan of Apple’s productions, and quality is very important to them.
“They always challenge us to do our best in terms of storytelling and production value, and it’s a great experience to be challenged and to keep getting better. Sometimes you think you know best, but ultimately it’s teamwork.”
She compared the first mover experience to that of Wiedemann & Berg when it made Dark as Netflix’s debut German original.
“If you’re the first show in a market for a streamer, you have to learn how to work together,” said Kudiabor. “I imagine it was a similar experience for Netflix when it made Dark. In the second season, the process was extremely nice and easy because we already knew each other and understood how things worked. There was a lot of trust in us, which was really nice.”
German market in flux
UFA Fiction, known for the likes of the Deutschland and Ku’damm franchises, has been on a roll over recent years, with Wanda? and Prime Video YA smash Maxton Hall – The World Between Us driving its streamer slate, with the likes of Disney+ miniseries Sam – A Saxon and Netflix movie Rising High also cutting through.
However, the Fremantle-owned company could be seen as an outlier in the German production market. Last week at Seriesly Berlin, much of the chatter was about a general lack of funding outside of the global streamers, and whether international co-production could fill the gaps. With the likes of Sky Deutschland exiting the originals market in the past half-decade, things remain tough.
“Streamers and commissioners are flooded with good ideas,” said Kudiabor. “What do you need to stand out? We’re really trying to work on that. I’m not saying we achieve it all the time, but we’re giving it our best, and perhaps our work shows that this approach is working for us.”
She attributed UFA’s hot streak on “a mixture of luck, timing, having the right talent and finding the right story,” and hinted at several upcoming projects.
“At the moment, we’re working for Amazon, with two shows launching there,” she said. “We’re working with Disney and have some developments with them, and we’ve just worked with Apple. We’re also working with HBO, so there are a lot of opportunities.
“But it’s also about excellence. We’re challenging ourselves to ask, before we go out: Is this really the best story we have? Is this the best talent? Is there something else we can do before we go shopping?”
Kudiabor admitted the success of Maxton Hall, which became Prime Video’s most-watched international original series.
“The first season was amazing, but I don’t think we expected such sensational success,” she said. “I loved the second season, but wait for the third – it’s even more mind-blowing. The fans are so engaged and give their feedback through social media, which is crazy. Our main actors are now big stars, and it’s really a ride.
“It’s a once-in-a-lifetime moment. When you go to the premieres, it feels like a real event: The fans are going crazy and they really want to be part of it.”
As for the future, Kudiabor said UFA Fiction will look to work with more production companies across the Fremantle group, as TV consolidated giants look to use their assets to create co-productions.
“I’ve been speaking with colleagues in the Netherlands, for example, because our markets are quite similar and they have great shows coming out there,” said Kudiabor. “We recently had a meeting here to look for a project we could make together, so we want to develop something jointly. We’re also speaking with some UK companies.”
Meanwhile, UFA Fiction is hoping Apple sees a long-term future for Where’s Wanda?. “Creatively, we have lots of ideas, but of course I can’t speak for Apple,” said Kudiabor. “Right now, we’re just happy to be returning for a second season. We hope to excite the viewers, and then we’ll take it from there.”

A video showing a large crowd gathered on a road and a flyover is being widely shared on social media, claiming that it shows the crowd at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event in Indore on 19 September 2026 (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows people gathered for Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event held on 19 September 2026 in Indore, Madhya Pradesh.
Fact: The viral video is old and unrelated to Rahul Gandhi’s event. It shows a rally organised in Indore on 9 August 2026 to mark World Tribal Day. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a Facebook post by Vinoddj Vlog posted on 10 August 2026. The account confirmed in the comments that the video was recorded during the Adivasi Diwas (World Tribal Day) celebrations in Indore. Further, we found a YouTube video uploaded on 9 August 2026 by @DineshSolanki_indori, which features the same truck and location seen in the viral video. This video also identified the visuals as being from the World Tribal Day celebrations in Indore. This confirms that the video predates Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event, which was held in Indore on 19 September 2026.
Further, we also found similar visuals shared by Lokesh Mujalda, president of Jai Adivasi Yuva Shakti (JAYS), on Instagram on 9 August 2026. The post stated that a large number of people had gathered in Indore for World Tribal Day celebrations.
We identified the location seen in the viral video as Bhanwarkuan Square in Indore, which was one of the locations along the route of the World Tribal Day procession. A comparison between both can be seen below.
Media also reported that thousands of people participated in the World tribal day procession that took place in Indore (here, here). Actual visuals showing the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event can be seen here and here.
To sum up, an old video of the World Tribal Day rally is being shared as visuals of crowd at Rahul
Gandhi’s Indore event.

We are in the midst of a loneliness epidemic: More than half of Americans say they feel isolated, and we’re getting together less and less. In 2023, only about 4 percent of adults said they went to a party on a weekend or holiday.
Why we should all be partying more
The historical case for partying it up, explained.
According to Imogen Willetts, a party historian and author of the book Up All Night: A History of Going Out, this moment is an outlier.
“For most of human history, the experiences that we associate with nightlife — drinking, dancing, music, hedonism — those experiences were simply part of religion because religion was so all-encompassing,” she told Vox.
If parties are so ingrained in humankind, then, what are we missing when we don’t get out the door on a Friday night anymore? And what lessons can we learn from the turnups of yore? We get into all of that and more — including how to throw a great party and how to be a good guest — on the latest episode Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Willetts, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
Can you talk about the role religion played in early nightlife? Because I think we often think of religion and partying as two separate things, but that was not the case for all of history, was it?
[Religion] contained people’s hedonistic instinct. There was nothing really outside of it. And so there’s even evidence, which I love thinking about this, that the churchgoing experience in medieval England was actually quite rowdy and quite raucous.
On feast days there would be drinking, there would be dancing. And there’s one theory that wooden pews were introduced in Wells Cathedral in England to subdue the dancing because it was so raucous. And so in some sense, it takes us a while to get to nightlife because we sort of didn’t need it for a very long time. Religion contained hedonism quite comfortably within it.
Seventeenth-century Japan, I would say, is the beginning of modern nightlife because we have these commercial party scenes, nightlife environments, which have nothing to do with religion,
“Whether it’s at a sports match or a concert stadium, and even within religion — that is collective effervescence.”
Crucially, they’re also separate from court. Another part of party scenes is court spectacle — think Louis XIV and Versailles and all of that stuff that was contained within these monarchical structures. So the first real nightlife destination is Yoshiwara, which was built on the outskirts of Edo, which is now Tokyo.
The idea of church being a place to party is so interesting. I do get the same feeling I get at church when I’m on the dance floor and I hear Kaytranada. I can imagine how these religious experiences allowed people to access that feeling of release through music and through dance.
An expression that I came across when researching the book that I think really wonderfully kind of captures the essence of nightlife and partying is this term coined by the sociologist Émile Durkheim in 1912, which is “collective effervescence.” That’s the feeling that we experience during peak communal experiences.
Whether it’s at a sports match or a concert stadium, and even within religion — that is collective effervescence. That is the same sensation, that surge of euphoria that people feel on dance floors. I think parties and nightlife are such an important way to access this very important human feeling, particularly in societies that are increasingly atheist or increasingly secular.
We need nightlife to have these communal euphoric experiences and feel part of something bigger than ourselves.
You’ve written about how, yes, parties are fun, but they’re also at the epicenter of some pretty important cultural and societal shifts.
I think nightlife is very uniquely poised to allow for experimentation and innovation and transgression. Also, in a very practical way, if you’re part of the abstract expressionist scene of mid-century New York or something, you need somewhere to meet and talk to people and figure out how you’re going to sell your work that’s like nothing people have ever seen before.
These social spaces play a really, really important role in culture. The abstract expressionist artists were hanging out in the Cedar Tavern, and then you have things like the Viennese Secession Movement and Cabaret Fledermaus was part of that meeting space.
Similarly, you get things like dance and music that’s very much created for dance floors, for clubbing, for nightlife: the can-can and then disco and then techno. Nightlife has been so crucial to the propulsion of culture.
A lot of this is happening in the club, but what about parties happening in private homes?
One of the great examples of people opening up their homes in a sense of turning the home into a club was turn-of-the-century New Orleans. On Saturday nights, people would host fish fries: Basically, when you would open up your home to the public, you would charge entry at the door. Once inside, people were treated to this amazing spread of food, drink, and there would be bands that would perform. It was often a way for households who were struggling with rent payments to earn some extra cash.
It happened again in Harlem in the 1920s. Langston Hughes writes about the Saturday night rent parties, where people’s apartments would be opened up in the exact same way. He said they were more interesting than anything that was going on in the cabarets and the clubs. He was going to those as often as he could and collecting the invitations for them.
People would write their address on business cards, leave them in different shops and pubs and hairdressers or whatever, and then you would pick them up and then go to the party. Langston Hughes collected them, and they now are randomly in a Yale archive of all places.
As you think of parties over the centuries, are there elements that all the best parties have in common?
At their very core essence, you need good music, you need good lighting, and I think also you need to create this atmosphere where the sense that anything can happen. What you want is for the people that are at your party to feel like they can behave differently or do something a little bit wild.
I think that there’s something very satisfying in experiencing a domestic world upturned. I think seeing the kitchen become a gloomy cocktail bar, the living room becoming a dance floor — there’s something very satisfying in experiencing that.
It goes back to what the heart of nightlife culture or party culture is all about. We want to shed our daily lives. You want that sense of slight disorder that makes people feel alive.

The Imperial Japanese Army secretly considered imposing martial law in Tokyo in January 1945, during the final stages of World War II, amid concerns that large-scale U.S. air raids would severely disrupt public order, according to a newly reviewed historical document.
The study, however, significantly underestimated the likely scale of destruction from such air raids. Martial law, which would have allowed the military to assume administrative authority and other powers, was ultimately never imposed.
According to the document, the army estimated that more than 13,700 people would be killed in two air raids. In the Great Tokyo Air Raid of March 10, 1945, however, around 100,000 people, mainly in downtown areas, were killed — far exceeding the estimate.

Ukraine anger as EU removes Russian oligarchs from sanctions list
- Published
The European Union is to remove sanctions on two oligarchs imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to reports, prompting anger in Ukraine.
France had campaigned for Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be taken off the list, citing "national security concerns". Luxembourg called for the removal of Russian-Israeli businessman Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the country for the release of frozen assets.
Latvia initially opposed the deal but agreed to a compromise, part of which involved extending sanctions on nearly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years.
Ukrainian officials said the move was "unacceptable" and sent the wrong signal to Moscow.
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on X.
He urged all EU member states to instead announce national sanctions on the two individuals. Latvia has already said it would do so.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov earlier welcomed the prospect of the two oligarchs being taken off the list, claiming the EU's sanctions were illegal and all Russians should be removed.
Usmanov founded USM Holding company, an investment group that owns iron, steel and copper suppliers, and the Megafon telecommunications company. He has in the past had ties with the English Premier League clubs Arsenal and Everton.
The EU froze his assets in 2022, describing him as "a pro-Kremlin oligarch with particularly close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin". Usmanov said the decision was "unfair".
It has been reported that France's initiative was linked to a prospective prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan.
Fridman, a Russian-Israeli citizen born in Ukraine, is the founder of the Alfa Group investment conglomerate, with key interests in energy and banking. The EU has described him as a top Russian financier and enabler of Putin's inner circle.
Fridman himself said at the time of Russia's full-scale invasion that the conflict should end as soon as possible, but avoided outright condemnation of President Putin.
His Russian-Latvian business partner Pyotr Aven was stripped of Latvia's highest civilian honour in 2022 for failing to condemn the invasion of Ukraine.
This may have influenced Latvia's opposition to the move, vetoing it in a vote by EU ambassadors on Monday.
However, on Tuesday it changed its vote to an abstention as a compromise was reached. The new deal involved extending sanctions on some remaining 2,600 individuals and entities to three years. Until now, sanctions had to be renewed every six months.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also announced that France had agreed to start talks with Latvia about joining a French nuclear deterrence initiative and strengthen its military presence in Latvia.

Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.
Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. You can save up to 14 percent on plans for the first three months, whether you're signing up as an individual or as a business. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.
Save up to 14% Off These Google Workspace Promo Codes 2026
There are some notable differences between each Workspace plan – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.
What Is the Best Google Workspace Plan?
Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.
Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.
Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.
Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.
Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.
At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.
Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.
Why Teams Love Using Google Workspace Flows with Google Workspace
Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e., update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.
You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.
Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.
Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.
Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow-up message. No apps or links are needed.
Does Google Workspace Offer a Free Trial?
Even with a discount, Google offers a free trial for all new Workspace subscribers. Your first 14 days are free, regardless of which plan you choose, and even with the promotional pricing, you can sign up using our links at the top of this article. Just make sure to cancel if you don’t want to continue. After 14 days, you’ll be billed, and that will be the start of your new billing cycle.

Hurricane Polo has become one of the world’s strongest storms this year as it threatens to lash Mexico’s Pacific Coast with heavy rain and winds.
Polo’s top winds reached 180 miles (290 kilometers) per hour, making it a Category 5 storm in the five-step, Saffir-Simpson scale.
The intensification ties Polo with Super Typhoons Bavi and Sinlaku for the title of the Northern Hemisphere’s strongest storm this year, said Phil Klotzbach, a hurricane researcher and seasonal forecaster with Colorado State University.
By central pressure, Polo is now the second-most powerful system ever recorded in the eastern Pacific, Klotzbach said. Category 5 Patricia, also a compact hurricane, in 2015 had a lower pressure.
The storm, which is forecast to miss Mexico’s coast, could continue to strengthen, the US National Hurricane Center warned.
“The hurricane is expected to remain very intense through this week and, in fact, maintain Category 5 strength for a couple of days,” Richard Pasch, a senior hurricane specialist at the center, wrote in a forecast. “On the forecast track, the core of Polo is expected to be near the coast of southwestern Mexico through the middle of this week, although it is forecast to remain offshore.”
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged coastal residents to remain alert in case the storm changes course.
In 2023, Hurricane Otis struck Acapulco as a Category 5 storm, killing at least 52 people and causing some $20 billion in damage. Mexico’s west coast is often pummeled by destructive storms during the eastern Pacific hurricane season that begins on May 15 and runs through Nov. 30.
Mexico’s meteorological agency said Polo’s broad circulation would bring intense rain with as much as 6 inches (15 centimeters) in some cities, and strong winds across much of the coast, particularly in the states of Guerrero, Oaxaca, Michoacán and Colima. The ports of Lázaro Cárdenas and Manzanillo are located in the latter two states.
The agency also warned of dangerous 20-foot waves and very rough seas.
Polo was about 355 miles south-southeast of Manzanillo and has stopped moving. Tropical storm warnings have been issued from Tecpan de Galeana to Punta San Telmo, and a watch has been extended westward to Playa Perula.
Polo is a relatively compact hurricane – its strongest winds extend only 35 miles from its center.

It is sometimes called "momnesia," "mommy brain," "pregnancy brain" or "baby brain" — the forgetfulness, mental fogginess and cognitive changes that many women may experience during pregnancy. For instance, a woman might walk into the kitchen and forget why she did, or perhaps misplace her car keys in the bathroom.
Scientists know it is a real biological phenomenon, and now have found a possible explanation, identifying a specific brain circuit that becomes disrupted under the sustained high levels of oestrogen that accompany pregnancy.
They conducted experiments using laboratory mice designed to mimic the sustained elevated oestrogen experienced during pregnancy, finding that this led to temporary memory impairment in the animals without mood changes.
Underlying this in the mice, they found, was how the high oestrogen affected a neuronal pathway between two brain structures — the hypothalamus, which acts as a control center and integrative hub, and the hippocampus, which is central to memory formation.
High oestrogen increased the activity of hypothalamus neurons, which in turn suppressed activity in the hippocampus and impaired memory, they found.
"Momnesia" becomes most evident in late pregnancy and may continue into the postpartum period but usually dissipates after childbirth. Short-term and long-term memory can be affected, including spatial, social and verbal memory such as having difficulty remembering names or words, or struggling to recall familiar information.
"It is not serious or medically disabling, although it does affect daily functioning and confidence," said Zheng Sun, a professor of medicine at Baylor College of Medicine specialising in endocrinology and molecular biology and one of the leaders of the study published in the journal Science Bulletin.
"Typical examples include forgetting why one entered a room, misplacing an item, losing the thread of a conversation or needing reminders for appointments. It is widespread. About 80% of pregnant women notice those changes, but that figure largely reflects self-report and subjective experience rather than objective testing," Dr. Sun said.
The findings suggest that the phenomenon does not represent a general decline in cognitive ability.
"The important point is that pregnancy does not simply make someone 'less intelligent.' The effects appear to be more subtle and specific to certain cognitive tasks," said Yanlin He, director of the Brain Glycemic and Metabolism Control Laboratory at Louisiana State University's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and another of the study leaders.
Mouse experiments
The mouse experiments shed light on what is happening in the brain. Oestrogen is a hormone that governs a woman's pregnancy, menstrual cycle and puberty, spurring physical changes that help the body support the fetus, foster fetal development and prepare for childbirth. Its levels increase during pregnancy, peaking in the third trimester.
The researchers found that a protein called "oestrogen receptor alpha" transmits estrogen's signals into cells in the hypothalamus.
This region has abundant brain cells called GABAergic neurons that typically transmit calming signals to other parts of the brain. The study showed that high oestrogen levels over-activate the inhibitory signals by these neurons in the mice, and this directly affected the hippocampus.
The researchers performed memory tests including object and location recognition, finding impairment in mice given high oestrogen levels compared to those that were not.
When the researchers experimentally turned off the hypothalamus-to-hippocampus neuronal pathway, the mice no longer experienced oestrogen-induced memory problems. But experimentally activating the same pathway impaired memory in the mice, even without higher amounts of oestrogen present.
"When we genetically removed estrogen receptors from these hypothalamic neurons, estrogen-induced and pregnancy-induced memory problems in mice were also reversed. We suspect that a similar circuit may play a similar role in humans, although you cannot do this type of invasive study directly in humans," Dr. Sun said.
The researchers complemented the mouse experiments with a study assessing memory performance in 70 women, including some across different stages of pregnancy and some who were not pregnant, using tests of long-term, short-term and working memory. These tests revealed memory impairments that manifested during late pregnancy, correlating with high circulating oestrogen levels.
"Importantly, higher circulating estrogen levels were associated with poorer performance on several memory-related measures even after accounting for other potential contributing factors. This provides human evidence consistent with the mechanism we identified in mice," Dr. He said.
"However, we should emphasise that we did not directly manipulate or measure this specific neural circuit in pregnant women. Therefore, the human findings support the hypothesis but do not establish the same level of causality as the mouse experiments," Dr. He said.

Haridwar, September 23, 2026: Surendra Koli, who spent nearly two decades in jail before being acquitted in all 13 cases linked to the 2006 Nithari killings, died by suicide, according to his post-mortem report, Uttarakhand Police said on Wednesday.
Koli was found dead at a tea stall in Haridwar on September 18. Police said the post-mortem examination found that he died of asphyxia due to ante-mortem hanging and that the investigation had so far found no evidence suggesting another person was involved.
Autopsy Points To Suicide
“The autopsy report of Surendra Koli states it as a suicidal death. The cause of death is specified as asphyxia due to ante-mortem hanging. During the investigation also, no other forensic evidence, CCTV footage of any suspect person or suspicious activity came to light,” City Police Station in-charge Kundan Singh Rana said.
No suicide note was recovered. Koli had rented the tea stall in Haridwar’s Sapt Rishi area just three days before his death.
His brother, Chandan Koli, submitted a complaint at the Saptarishi police outpost in Haridwar on Sunday, seeking a high-level investigation into the death. He alleged that his brother had died under suspicious circumstances.
The demand for a high-level probe and the police findings present contrasting aspects of the case. While Koli’s family has raised questions about the circumstances surrounding his death, police have said the post-mortem findings and evidence gathered during the investigation point to suicide.
Family Raises Questions
After Koli’s body was recovered, police began an investigation and sent it for a post-mortem examination to establish the cause of death. The examination was conducted on September 19.
Following the examination, Koli’s brothers and son performed his final rites at the Khadkhadi Cremation Ganga Ghat in Haridwar, Hindustan Times reports.
Police said the investigation found no forensic evidence, CCTV footage involving a suspect or suspicious activity indicating the involvement of another person in Koli’s death.
Koli had walked out of jail on November 12, 2025, wearing a powder-blue shirt, black trousers and a navy-blue jacket.
A New Life In Haridwar
Anil Sharma, who had rented the tea stall to Koli in Haridwar’s Kumbh Mela area, said Koli had introduced himself as “Sada Ram” and told him that he had previously worked in Roshanabad.
Neighbouring shopkeepers said Sada Ram appeared to have been looking ahead to the next year’s Ardh Kumbh fair and hoped to maximise his earnings during the four-month event.
The tea stall is in the core Mela zone, an area with a large number of temples, ashrams, dharamshalas, maths and hotels. Sharma had rented the stall to Koli for Rs 7,000 a month and taken an advance of Rs 14,000.
Police identified Koli as a resident of Magrukhal in the Bhikiasain area of Almora.
From Nithari Case To Acquittal
Koli had worked as a domestic help at the Noida home of businessman Moninder Singh Pandher.
The Nithari case came to light in 2006 after skeletons, skulls and bones were discovered in drains and the backyard of Pandher’s bungalow in Noida’s Sector 31. The discovery triggered nationwide outrage amid suspicions over the disappearances and murders of several children and women.
Also Watch:
Koli and Pandher were arrested on December 29, 2006, and charged with rape, murder, abduction, trafficking and destruction of evidence.
Koli subsequently spent nearly two decades in jail before being acquitted in all 13 cases linked to the Nithari killings. His death, less than a year after his release, has now prompted questions from his family even as police maintain that the medical and forensic findings indicate suicide.

Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious
- Published
An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.
That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians.
But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza.
And on 4 October, the Republic will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia.
No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis.
So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football?
Venue changes have not quietened protests
As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza.
The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott.
Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income.
As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures.
No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary.
Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly.
The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil".
Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin.
The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest.
In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years.
The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition.
Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean.
FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide".
"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."
In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity".
The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations".
Irish support for Palestinians is long-standing
The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023.
More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN).
In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice.
The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers.
On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population."
Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.
Last summer a UN commission of inquiry found that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and this year a further investigation determined that the country has deliberately targeted children with military force, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations it has committed genocide.
The Republic of Ireland is not the only nation to have expressed reluctance to face Israel in international football.
In 2024, Belgium refused to host Israel on home soil, and the match was held instead in Debrecen.
The president of the Norwegian Football Association, Lise Klaveness, made a public statement last year saying Israel should be suspended from European competitions, and Turkey also called for Israel to be banned.
BBC Sport reported last autumn that Uefa executives were considering a vote on whether to ban Israel, under pressure from representatives from a number of nations.
But any plan to hold a vote was pulled when the first phase of a ceasefire was announced last October.

Engineer gets 160 hours’ community service over Queen Mary Hospital lift defects
Engineer convicted of submitting misleading documents and improperly issuing safety certificates after 24 lifts at Hong Kong hospital were found defective
A Hong Kong-registered lift engineer held liable for faulty installation work at Queen Mary Hospital’s new block has been sentenced to 160 hours of community service after being convicted of submitting misleading documents and improperly issuing safety certificates.
Eastern Court sentenced Law Wing-chai, 54, on Wednesday for two summary offences under the Lifts and Escalators Ordinance. The sentence came a month after authorities revealed that 24 of the 28 lifts in the new block of Hong Kong Island’s largest hospital had serious defects, delaying services.
In August, the Architectural Services Department said the faults had caused lifts to start or stop unevenly, halt at floor levels, or fail to open their doors. The problems included damaged electronic components, faulty wiring connections and poor installation workmanship.

President Xi encourages China-US youth ties after exchange
In the run-up to his US visit, President Xi replied to American students who attended a cultural exchange, encouraging deeper mutual understanding and friendship.
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Nearly 100 students from 10 US universities who travelled through China under Future Makers 2026 jointly wrote to President Xi Jinping after the programme, sharing what they had seen and experienced during the trip.
In his reply to the students, Xi encouraged young people from both countries to promote friendship and co-operation and deepen mutual understanding between the two peoples.
People-to-people exchanges can create space for that understanding by allowing participants to transcend impressions formed from afar, ask questions directly and discover common ground through everyday interaction. Over time, such encounters can help strengthen trust and create more channels for dialogue between the two societies.
That role for people-to-people contact has received renewed attention at the highest level. During their meeting in Beijing in May, Xi and US President Donald Trump agreed that the two countries should expand exchanges and co-operation in areas including tourism and people-to-people ties.
For 170 young people from China and the US, that principle became personal during a week travelling through Shandong and Beijing. Some arrived knowing China mainly through books, television, university courses or impressions formed thousands of miles away. Sometimes, seeing really is believing.
Future Makers 2026 brought 100 students from 10 US universities together with 70 young people from Beijing and Shandong. Co-hosted by the Beijing NGO Network for International Exchanges and the Ng Teng Fong Charitable Foundation, the philanthropic arm of Sino Group, the programme combined cultural and technology visits with direct exchanges between students from both countries.
Student, University of WashingtonSeeing different sides of China
The journey began in Jinan, where participants attended the Asia-Pacific Civil Society Conference during China’s 2026 APEC host year. They then travelled to Qufu, the birthplace of Confucius, visiting Nishan Sacred Land and the Temple and Mansion of Confucius, trying Chinese calligraphy and discussing “harmony in diversity” with students from Qufu Normal University.
Beijing offered another encounter with China’s past at the Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven and Mutianyu section of the Great Wall, before the itinerary turned towards a very modern China. Students watched humanoid robots in action at Beijing E-Town Robot World, visited the Beijing High-Level Autonomous Driving Demonstration Area and toured Xiaomi’s EV factory.
Within days, they had gone from Confucian thought to AI, and from imperial architecture to an EV production line.
That juxtaposition of ancient traditions and modern China left participants with vivid memories. Asyifa Isvari, a Harvard Kennedy School student, said travelling through China offered perspectives that were different from discussing the country as an abstract subject in the classroom.
Even though we come from different countries, it has been amazing to see those differences and still build such strong connections. 
Grace, Central Michigan University
From countries to people
The destinations provided the introduction. The conversations gave the journey its deeper purpose.
At Qufu Normal University and Tsinghua University, dialogue sessions covered cultural identity, innovation, sustainability, youth leadership and Asia Pacific co-operation. Outside formal sessions, students had meals together, discussed university life and swapped favourite films, music and jokes.
Some similarities were surprisingly ordinary. University of Washington students discovered that their Chinese peers followed basketball, played some of the same video games and watched some of the same films.
Daryl Ng, Director of the Ng Teng Fong Charitable Foundation and Chairman of Sino Group, joined participants during their visit to the Temple of Heaven and over lunch, providing opportunities for more informal exchanges.
Xi’s reply was a source of encouragement for the organisers and participants, said Ng, who also thanked the Beijing NGO Network for International Exchanges for its long-standing work in promoting international exchanges and providing opportunities for young people from different backgrounds to learn from one another.
He also welcomed the students’ efforts to share their experiences after returning home, helping others gain a better understanding of China. The Foundation, he said, would continue supporting international youth exchanges and dialogue and make use of Hong Kong’s role as a “super-connector” to encourage further exchanges between China and the rest of the world.
A UC Davis student recalled meeting Chinese students who began the week as strangers and became genuine friends. They spent time together, discovered common interests and formed relationships she intended to maintain after returning home.
Yanqi Lake is where the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting was held in 2014, the previous time China hosted APEC. Twelve years later, the students returned during China’s 2026 APEC host year, this time with spades in their hands.
The activity also introduced ecological conservation and green development into a week that had taken students through China’s history, culture and technology.
The metaphor was not lost on the participants. One American University student spoke of planting trees while also planting the seeds of friendship. Another said the friendships established in China could continue growing long after the journey ended.

OpenAI and Anthropic both recently released new models aimed at lowering costs. Anthropic announced Opus 5.5, the latest version of its main mass-market workhorse model, used for tasks like coding and other complex knowledge work.
And OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol and Luna, the latest versions of its middle-of-the-road or smaller models focused on efficiency and speed.
These new releases are not about groundbreaking new capabilities. Rather, they’re about efficiency. As both OpenAI and Anthropic target enterprise customers, they’re racing to compete with open-weight models as organizations have explored changing their practices and using model routers to use these pricey, frontier models less in favor of cheaper alternatives.
Anthropic and OpenAI argue that these new releases push the envelope at the frontier (albeit mostly in modest ways), while bringing costs substantially down.
Opus 5.5: A more affordable, more competitive flagship
Opus 5.5 is at the higher end of the models announced today, but the wider context here is that Anthropic is playing a bit of catch-up in its race with OpenAI. OpenAI earlier this month released GPT-6 Astra, which has sometimes been modestly beating Opus 5 in benchmarks and user sentiment. (By price and capability, Astra is competing with both Opus and Fable.)
Benchmarks by Anthropic and its partners now show Opus 5.5 performing better at coding and knowledge work than GPT-6 Astra in some cases, albeit modestly.
The real story here is cost. From Anthropic’s announcement: “Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5. Cache reads (which make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs) are $0.20 per million tokens, 60% less than Opus 5. Opus 5.5 also generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.”

Qualcomm is making not one but two versions of its flagship Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chip
The extreme variant comes with 50 percent more shared memory, wider codec support and better video capture.
Now that most of the major smartphone releases are done for the year, Qualcomm is preparing for the next generation of handsets with its upcoming flagship mobile chip and this time it will be available in two versions: the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.
Based on a 2nm process node, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 features an eight-core Oryon CPU composed of two prime cores with clockspeeds of up to 5GHz. The chip also has 16MB of what Qualcomm is calling Flex Cache, which the company says allows the processor to dynamically allocate the cache pool to improve single-threaded performance. Elsewhere, the chip features an Adreno GPU that's 35 percent faster than the previous generation while also providing faster rendering speeds in games. Meanwhile, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6's NPU is 14 percent faster and offers 20 percent better performance-per-watt for machine learning-based tasks.
When it comes to camera features, Qualcomm says the chip's new Spectra image signal processor (ISP) natively supports 8K video capture at up to 30 fps. Photography has also gotten a bump, as the chip can handle single image capture at up to 320-megapixels or triple cameras at up to 64MP with "zero shutter lag." Qualcomm also says its Elite Color Engine will bring more cinematic color science to videos and support for real-time 3D look up tables. Additionally, the company's Intelligent Pixel Control tech allows the camera to better understand the context of a shot, so it can more accurately respond and adjust camera settings to deliver optimal results. As for its connectivity, as you'd expect from a new SoC, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6's X105 5G modem offers a range of 5G communications including sub-6Ghz and mmWave, along with integrated support for ultra wideband connectivity, Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 8.
Finally, while the extreme version of the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 is based on the same underlying architecture, it has a few extra features, including that ability to run AI models with more than 30 billion parameters, support for both the APV and VVC video codecs, 18MB of high performance memory and better video recording that tops out at 8K at 60fps (or slow-motion at 4K at up to 240 fps). Gamers will also get an added benefit from Qualcomm's new Matrix Cores in its Adreno GPU, which offers AI-powered super resolution and frame generation for boosting graphics quality and framerates.
So far, it remains to be seen how many next-gen phones will be powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and it's important to remember that even though the chip may support a specific tool or feature, it's ultimately up to the device makers to implement them on retail products. That said, Motorola has already committed to using the SD8 Gen 6 in its upcoming Signature 27 phone. And with Qualcomm's previous gen flagship chip holding the performance crown among Android handsets, this new offering looks like it will be the go-to processor for next year's premium mobile devices.

With secularism sidelined in Quebec election campaign, here's where the parties stand
Voters both for and against controversial laws want action
After losing her job over Quebec's controversial religious symbols ban, teacher Fatemeh Anvari says secularism is her top campaign issue in the province's election.
“Something that has to do with my personal freedoms, my rights and the rights of so many – it would be at the forefront,” Anvari said.
“I lost my teaching job only because I was wearing a hijab and the law didn’t allow that."
It’s the same story for Bouchera Chelbi, a Montreal teacher who under Bill 21 was allowed to keep her current job because of an acquired rights clause, but cannot move jobs or get a promotion.
“Because of this bill, I'm denied many advantages that anybody can have, at least anybody who's not wearing a religious symbol,” Chelbi said.
“This is not because I'm not competent enough. This is not because I'm not qualified enough. It is because of the way I choose to dress."
Ahead of Quebec's general election on Oct. 5, Chelbi says she'd like all five main political party leaders to take into consideration "that there are real human beings impacted by these bills."
Supreme Court decision looming
The previous Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government passed various laws during its eight year mandate – bills 21, 94 and 9 – that banned police, prosecutors, judges, teachers, other school employees, and publicly-funded daycare workers from wearing religious symbols at work.
The ban even extends to parent volunteers at schools.
The CAQ also banned prayer rooms in schools and universities, barred public institutions from serving exclusively kosher or halal menus, and put restrictions on group prayers in public.
One of the reasons secularism hasn’t come up much in this campaign may be because everyone’s waiting for a Supreme Court decision that will ultimately decide its fate in the province.
Quebec’s secularism laws are – in theory – protected from legal challenges because the CAQ pre-emptively invoked the constitutional notwithstanding clause when it passed them.
The Supreme Court is currently weighing whether the clause can actually be used that way, and a decision is likely in the next few months.
That decision will directly affect how the next government deals with secularism laws.
Some groups want more secularism measures
People such as Anvari and Chelbi, who’ve experienced major consequences of secularism laws, don’t want the next government to wait for the Supreme Court decision to act. They're calling for the laws to be repealed as soon as possible.
Meanwhile, some groups that support the province's secularism laws want to know they'll be protected.
“Evidently, we’re not talking enough about it. It’s Quebec's autonomy that’s at stake,” said Daniel Baril, president of the group Mouvement laïque québécois, a provincial secularism group.
He wants the ban on wearing religious symbols at school expanded to include not just teachers and staff but students as well.
“It’s a method used to engage in religious proselytism in schools, and it creates tensions and conflicts,” he said.
Nadia El-Mabrouk, president of another pro-secularism group, the Rassemblement pour la laïcité, told CBC the group wrote to all the political parties at the start of the campaign proposing more secularism measures, but has yet to hear back.
Her group is pushing for a national secularism day, stricter enforcement of existing laws, and an end to religious tax breaks and livestock slaughter exemptions.
“Unfortunately, we are seeing a backlash, so we need political parties that stand firm,” she said.
CBC reached out to all the parties and asked whether they would strengthen secularism laws, weaken them, or maintain the status quo. Here's what they said:
CAQ would further measures if 'necessary'
The CAQ, which passed the existing secularism laws, is promising to maintain them, and to continue to use the notwithstanding clause to protect them from legal challenges.
“These are all necessary laws to affirm and preserve the secular nature of the state, which is so dear to Quebecers,” the party said in an email.
The CAQ was also the only party that hinted at strengthening the laws.
“We have no intention of backing down from our commitment to secularism, and should further measures prove necessary, we will not hesitate to implement them,” the party said.
PQ, Conservatives would maintain and protect laws
The PQ and the Conservative Party of Quebec also both promised to maintain current secularism laws and to use the notwithstanding clause to protect them, although neither party mentioned any further measures.
Still, both suggested the notwithstanding clause would be a big part of their plans even beyond secularism laws.
“As long as Quebec remains part of Canada, the Parti Québécois reserves the right to invoke the notwithstanding clause for any law it deems legitimate,” the PQ said in a statement.
The Conservatives went further.
“We will systematically invoke the notwithstanding clause in every law we pass in order to protect the choices of the National Assembly,” the party said.
Liberals would maintain, but not protect laws
Somewhere in the middle is the Quebec Liberal Party (PLQ).
“The PLQ is in favour of state secularism, but does not plan to adopt new measures regarding current prohibitions,” the party said in a statement.
The party says it favours a milder version of state secularism first proposed by the Bouchard-Taylor commission in 2008, which would limit the ban on wearing religious symbols at work to people in positions of authority – judges, prosecutors and police – but not teachers or any other civil servants.
The party didn't commit to changing or repealing any of the secularism laws, but it did say it would not renew the notwithstanding clause protecting Bill 21 when it expires in 2029, which would leave the law open to being struck down in a court challenge.
Québec Solidaire would repeal laws
The party with the strongest stance against secularism laws is Québec Solidaire.
“Québec Solidaire believes that the freedom-curbing measures of bills 21, 94 and 9 do not strengthen the secular nature of the state in any way, and that is why we are committed to repealing them,” the party said in a statement.
It also said it would regulate the use of the notwithstanding clause to protect rights and freedoms of Quebecers.
Québec Solidaire said there are better ways to strengthen state secularism, such as ending public funding for religious schools.

Obama often criticized Fox News. He also did fewer interviews with Fox News and took fewer questions from its correspondents compared to other news networks. His administration also said it was willing to exclude Fox News from interviews. Some accused his administration of blocking the network's access in one instance, but a spokesperson claimed it was a communication error and the administration backtracked.
However, the Obama administration never outright blocked, banned or ejected Fox News reporters from press briefings.
In September 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump banned three major news outlets — CNN, MSNOW and Politico — from the White House. The outlets subsequently filed a lawsuit accusing the administration of violating the First Amendment.
Soon after, former President Barack Obama condemned Trump's ban and speculated about the consequences if he had banned Fox News during his administration. In response, some people online claimed Obama had retaliated against Fox News (archived) in a similar way during his first term. For example, television personality Piers Morgan wrote on X (archived), "Obama did ban Fox, and waged almost constant war against press freedom."
(X user @PiersMorgan)
As Snopes previously reported in 2018, while Obama criticized Fox News and snubbed the network's requests for interviews, he never banned the network outright from the White House. As such, we rate this claim as mostly false.
In October 2009, a New York Times report (archived) stated Obama's Treasury Department attempted to exclude Fox News from a roundtable interview with the executive-pay czar Kenneth R. Feinberg. Major news networks were sharing a "pool" camera crew for these interviews. According to the report, other networks protested Fox's exclusion.
However, a 2009 Talking Points Memo report referred to the situation as a "miscommunication." The report said:
TPMDC dug into it, and here's what happened. Feinberg did a pen and pad with reporters to brief them on cutting executive compensation. TV correspondents, as they do with everything, asked to get the comments on camera. Treasury officials agreed and made a list of the networks who asked (Fox was not among them).
But logistically, all of the cameras could not get set up in time or with ease for the Feinberg interview, so they opted for a round robin where the networks use one pool camera. Treasury called the White House pool crew and gave them the list of the networks who'd asked for the interview.
The network pool crew noticed Fox wasn't on the list, was told that they hadn't asked and the crew said they needed to be included. Treasury called the White House and asked top Obama adviser Anita Dunn. Dunn said yes and Fox's Major Garrett was among the correspondents to interview Feinberg last night.
A Treasury spokesperson told Talking Points Memo, "There was no plot to exclude Fox News, and they had the same interview that their competitors did. Much ado about absolutely nothing." Fox News did conduct the interview with Feinberg.
The Obama administration didn't hold back in its criticism of Fox News in the aftermath of the controversy. When questioned by NBC News about the administration's tone regarding Fox News, Obama said:
We're going to take the media as it comes. And if media is operating basically as a talk radio format, then that's one thing, and if it's operating as a news outlet, then that's another. But it's not something I'm losing a lot of sleep over.
Obama spokesperson Josh Earnest reportedly admitted that the White House had demonstrated its "willingness to exclude Fox News" from interviews, but that it had not done so, according to Talking Points Memo. Earnest added, "The president and other high ranking officials and people like Ken Feinberg have done interviews with Fox in the past and will do them in the future."
In a 2010 interview with Rolling Stone, Obama accused Fox News of focusing more on its point of view than objectivity. "It's a point of view," Obama said, "that I think is ultimately destructive for the long-term growth of a country that has a vibrant middle class and is competitive in the world."
As Snopes previously reported, former Fox News White House correspondent Major Garrett asserted that though there was "never an effort to shut me out of the briefing room," ongoing tensions between the Obama administration and Fox News hindered his ability to do his job. In a November 2018 interview with The Hill, he said:
The White House would always pull me aside and say "well, really, Major, we're not at war with you," and I said "stop talking to me like that because when you're at war with my network you by definition are questioning and assailing my journalistic credibility and the work I do here every day," he said. "So don't tell me it's not about me, it is about me."
"Now, they never tried to pull my pass, but they had this sort of arms-length relationship to Fox and tried to demonize it on a daily basis. So that's another part of American history and journalism in the White House press corps I think at least should be noted at this moment," he said.
As we previously reported, Fox News' White House correspondents were called on less during press briefings compared to other major television networks. In September 2009, when Obama made the talk show rounds to talk about healthcare reform, he snubbed "Fox News Sunday" and did not appear on the show until his last year in office in 2016.
In 2013, The Washington Post reported that Obama's Department of Justice surveilled a Fox News reporter and obtained a search warrant for his emails while conducting an investigation into national security leaks in 2009. The investigation also looked into other reporters but appeared to specifically target Fox News.
The Obama administration never banned Fox News outright, but no love was lost between the two groups. While Fox News accused the administration of cutting it out of one interview, the administration blamed it on miscommunication and gave the network access while not hiding its disdain for the network.
For further reading, Snopes previously covered the misrepresented claim that former U.S. President Joe Biden cut reporters from the press pool.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Trump gets a Greenland deal
But the island is still a part of Denmark.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s campaign to take over Greenland has reached a peaceful end — for now.
What happened? Trump signed a new security agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland while at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, outlining an expanded US military presence on the island.
The deal is the result of months-long negotiations between the two countries and Greenland, which is a semi-autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. Crucially, it reaffirms the “sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Denmark and Greenland, something Trump has spent the last year-and-a-half-plus threatening to sweep away.
What’s the context? Trump returned to office last year proclaiming that US “ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity” for US national security, even though Denmark — and by extension Greenland — is a NATO ally.
That rhetoric quickly escalated, and by this January, Trump was suggesting that the US could even use force to take the island. “If we don’t do it the easy way,” he said — buying Greenland from Denmark, or perhaps bribing its residents to secede — “we’re going to do it the hard way.”
This, understandably, freaked Europe out, prompting multiple countries to deploy small numbers of troops to Greenland.
Does this mean Trump is done trying to take over? We can always hope. It’s possible Trump will claim this as a win and move on, even though Tuesday’s deal doesn’t fundamentally change the nature of the US-Greenland relationship. (Last week, he referred to it as “a dream come true” for the US.)
That being said, Trump’s desire to own Greenland always made more sense as an attempted legacy move than anything else, whatever his professed justifications. So while he might be happy to take the win for now, with the war in Iran still on and the midterms fast approaching, it shouldn’t be surprising if he’s clamoring for ownership again before his term is up.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
