Krakatau, a volcanic island in Indonesia, killed more than 30,000 people when it erupted in 1883. One might assume that volcanic debris posed the major threat, yet many of the victims died from a tsunami caused by the volcanic eruption instead.
Volcanoes at sea can pose hazards quite different from those on land, as their impact can vary depending on how the volcanic activity interacts with seawater. In the deep ocean, high water pressure can suppress explosive volcanic activity, making eruptions less destructive. But closer to the surface, the lower water pressure and the high temperatures of volcanic material can cause violent explosions. Yet scientists still do not fully understand the conditions under which volcanic activity can cause a tsunami.
To better understand these risks, an international team of researchers examined the 2022 Hunga eruption in Tonga, focusing on the rapid caldera collapse that may have amplified its powerful tsunami. Calderas form when the ground above a magma reservoir collapses as the magma drains away. Comparisons of seafloor topography before and after the eruption showed that a roughly four-kilometer-wide caldera sank by about a kilometer during the eruption.
The researchers argue that the rapid collapse of the entire caldera may have enhanced the massive tsunami. Even a relatively small caldera like Hunga may be capable of producing a dangerous tsunami, depending on the speed and nature of its collapse. This suggests that other underwater volcanoes may also have the potential to generate dangerous tsunamis. Still, the paper warns that “The dynamics of submarine caldera-forming eruptions and, thus, the hazards they pose are not well understood, owing to the relative inaccessibility of the resulting calderas and eruption products.”
A roof too thin to hold
The Hunga volcano’s eruption on January 15, 2022, ranks among the most powerful volcanic events this century. The eruption column soared more than 55 km, pushing vaporized seawater up into the stratosphere, and the pressure wave from the explosion was detected across the globe. The accompanying tsunami is estimated to have reached heights of 40 meters within about 100 km from the source. It is the highest tsunami ever recorded from an underwater volcanic eruption.

Academic libraries across the globe are stuffed with hundreds of thousands of Ancient Greek papyrus fragments. Though many are so damaged that their meaning is probably lost, scholars have the ability to restore the rest by methodically filling in missing words or phrases. To accelerate that laborious task, researchers have turned to artificial intelligence.
On Wednesday, the Austrian Academy of Science will release “the world’s first advanced large language model for Ancient Greek,” developed in partnership with French AI lab Mistral and technology services firm Sail Reply. The model, Apollo, is trained on roughly 600 million historical Greek words drawn from manuscripts, papyri, and inscriptions.
The model will be freely available to academics through a chatbot interface. The ambition is to help scholars to more rapidly identify papyrus fragments relevant to their specific sub-disciplines, as well as promising new avenues of research. Where documents are tattered and torn, Apollo is built to fill in the blanks with the most statistically likely words or passages, potentially revealing hidden details about historical events and practices.
Dimitris Vlitas, partner at Sail Reply, tells WIRED that unlocking knowledge in this way “was unthinkable a year ago.”
Until now, restoring a tattered piece of papyrus has required a skilled academic to first identify the word divisions—there are no gaps in Ancient Greek writing—then accurately date the document, weigh the appropriate socio-political contexts, and consult reference materials to help choose suitable words to fill in the gaps. “There are very few people in the world who are that good at Greek history,” says Stephen Colvin, a professor of classics and historical linguistics at University College London.
But all of that specialized knowledge is baked into Apollo. “When it sees Homer, it supplements Homeric Greek. When it sees an inscription in Doric dialect, it uses Doric dialect,” says Anna Dolganov, a historian and papyrologist at the Austrian Academy of Science.
Academics who find themselves bogged down in painstaking reconstruction work expect Apollo to accelerate things, allowing them to focus on the implications of historical documents, rather than figuring out what they say.
“I think it’s very exciting,” says Armand D'Angour, a professor of classical languages and literature at the University of Oxford, home to the world’s largest ancient papyrus collection. “If I had a machine telling me, ‘Here are the three possible words that could fit into that gap,’ it would speed up matters considerably.”
Apollo is unlikely to change the broad-strokes understanding of the ancient world; many papyri are yet to be restored precisely because they are mundane—personal letters, marital contracts, civil service papers. “If you were a layperson, you might think suddenly we’ll get a few new plays by Sophocles, but that’s not going to happen,” Colvin says. However, the model could help to uncover new details about life in antiquity and substantiate existing scholarly assumptions. “Every time something is produced, it adds a tiny element of knowledge about the ancient world,” D’Angour says.
If Apollo is a success, says Vlitas, the same technique could be readily applied to other ancient languages—Latin or Egyptian, say—or any other academic discipline that would benefit from the distillation and indexing of a large corpus of material. AI has had notable success in some areas; OpenAI recently said its AI models solved a 200-year-old math problem, while Google DeepMind released a vast dataset that maps how genetic mutations affect molecular biology, which it compiled using AI.
One concern might be that relying on a language model—which deals in probabilities—to fill in gaps in ancient documents risks polluting the historical record with errors. But to head off that issue, Apollo is built to propose a selection of word options for a scholar to select between. “The crucial point is that human competence needs to remain,” says Dolganov. “If we become totally reliant on AI transcriptions and interpretations of historical material, that’s when the problems start.”

OpenAI has hired three former Patreon execs to anchor its product strategy for creators. After starting the creator subscription platform 13 years ago, co-founder and technology chief Sam Yam announced on X that he’s joining OpenAI to lead Creator Product. He’s also bringing Patreon’s former product head Drew Rowny and engineering head Shannon Ma with him on the new venture, both of whom stepped down in the past few weeks.
OpenAI nabs key Patreon execs ahead of upcoming announcement
OpenAI now has the team behind the modern creator-subscription economy.
“We’re going to build together with Creators at OpenAI and share early access to a new set of tools that I think will be critically valuable to Creators and their communities,” Yam said in his announcement. “Pay attention to OpenAI DevDay next week! I’m becoming active today (and experimenting with some innovative early tools here!)”
Dev Day is set for Tuesday, September 29th, though Yam also links to a post from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that teases another big announcement will be coming this week.
Bringing key Patreon execs on board suggests that OpenAI is exploring ways to enter the creator monetization business, given Patreon effectively set the blueprint for the creator-subscription economy as we know it. Losing Yam is another blow for Patreon, which recently announced an extensive update roadmap to overhaul its user features after laying off 20 percent of its staff in January.

Country singer Rick Sollo and three others missing after helicopter disappears in Brazil
A Black Hawk military helicopter has been deployed to search for a possible crash site in a rural mountainous area
Musician Rick Sollo was among four people on board a helicopter that has disappeared in Brazil, it has been reported.
The twin-engine Bell 430 aircraft had departed from Porto Belo heading towards Sao Joaquim on Monday afternoon when the pilot lost contact with air traffic control, according to G1 Globo.
The three passengers have been identified as Sollo, 59, from the country music duo Rick and Renner, influencer Bruno Avelar and videographer Paulo Soares, according to a statement shared on Avelar’s social media. The pilot has not yet been named.
“To date, there is no official confirmation of an accident involving the aircraft,” it added. A further post said there were five people on board, bit did not identify the fifth person.
This came hours after Sollo posted a video on his Instagram story showing him boarding and landing an aircraft alongside Avelar.
A search and rescue operation has been launched in the mountainous region of Urubici, where air traffic last detected the helicopter.
In an appeal to residents, Avelar’s team urged them to listen out for “loud bangs and noises” and report any sightings of smoke and debris.
The Santa Catarina Fire Department first received a call about a possible aircraft crash at around 4pm on Monday.
At the time, a red weather alert for thunderstorms and heavy rainfall was issued for Urubici.

“Rainfall between 30 and 60 mm/h or 50 and 100 mm/day, strong winds (60–100 km/h), and hail. Risk of power outages, crop damage, fallen trees, and flooding,” said a downgraded weather warning issued at midnight.
The Brazilian Air Force (FAB) has deployed a Black Hawk military helicopter and an SC-105 Amazonas in the rural Vacas Gordas area to search for a possible wreckage, according to Sapicua Radio Agency.
Lieutenant Colonel Heloisa, commander of the 5th Military Fire Brigade Battalion of Santa Catarina, said about the search and rescue late last night: “The first search point is the point of the aircraft's last communication. A team has already arrived at the location, and nothing was found.
“We also have information on the last cell phone signal point of one of the people who were on that aircraft. At this moment, teams are moving to that location to carry out searches.”
Fire crews are expected to be carrying out searches in the area Tuesday, but the weather conditions are understood to be slowing down the operation.
The air forces added that "the priority of the operation is to locate the aircraft and its occupants in the shortest possible time, concentrating search efforts in the areas of highest probability and continuously adjusting the plan as new information is obtained."

సౌదీ అరేబియా రాజధాని రియాద్లోని విమానాశ్రయంపై వైమానిక దాడి జరగడంతో భారీగా మంటలు, దట్టమైన నల్లటి పొగ వ్యాపించాయంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: సౌదీ అరేబియాలోని రియాద్ విమానాశ్రయంపై జరిగిన వైమానిక దాడికి సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో రియాద్కు చెందినది కాదు. ఇది రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో జూన్ 2026లో డ్రోన్ దాడి వల్ల జరిగిన అగ్నిప్రమాదానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియో. సెప్టెంబర్ 2026లో రియాద్ విమానాశ్రయంపై హౌతీలు దాడి చేసినట్లు వార్తలు వస్తున్నప్పటికీ, వైరల్ వీడియో దానికి సంబంధించినది కాదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇవే దృశ్యాలను చూపుతున్న వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 18 జూన్ 2026 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. వీటి ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియో రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోకు చెందినది. మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్పై జరిగిన డ్రోన్ దాడి కారణంగా వ్యాపించిన మంటలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతోంది.

Trump turns to ‘national security’ crutch to defend his media ban citing coverage on Iran War and the ballroom
The Justice Department made the argument in a court filing on Tuesday, while urging a judge not to block Trump’s ban

The Justice Department argued in a court filing Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the authority to bar CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House on “national security” grounds, urging a federal judge not to suspend the restrictions.
The three outlets filed a lawsuit after Trump abruptly revoked their reporters’ White House access on Friday, arguing the restriction amounts to a “blatant violation” of the First Amendment. A hearing on their request for a temporary order restoring that access is scheduled for Wednesday.
In the DOJ’s telling, the ban doesn’t violate the First Amendment, because, it argued, “access to the White House is a privilege—not a right.”
“CNN, MSNOW, and Politico have long been granted privileged access to White House grounds,” department attorneys wrote in the court filing. “But the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”
Letters were sent to the three outlets outlining a “non-exhaustive list” of incidents in which their reporters “have threatened national security and spread falsehoods,” the filing states.
The letter cited stories on President Trump’s White House ballroom, weapons stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and Russian sanctions.
The president has previously invoked national security in justifying other actions, including the construction of his massive White House ballroom and of his planned 250-foot victory arch.
Trump abruptly announced on Friday that the three organizations were being banned from the White House “effective immediately.”
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
By the following morning, CNN, MS NOW and Politico all said that their journalists had been stopped from accessing the White House grounds, with some reporters stating that they were asked to hand over their badges.
On Monday, the outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump and several of his top aides, arguing that the ban violates the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, as well as the First Amendment, and calls for the press passes to be restored.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawsuit states.
“No official can deprive Plaintiffs of those interests on a whim—with no notice, no process, and no warning—as the President did here,” it continues.
The 80-year-old president has long had an extremely combative relationship with the press, accusing reporters of unfair and biased coverage, lobbing personal insults against them and insinuating that those he opposes should be punished.
Trump previously curtailed The Associated Press from accessing certain presidential spaces in 2025 after the outlet continued using the “Gulf of Mexico” despite Trump rebranding it as the “Gulf of America.” In 2018, Trump also revoked CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass following a contentious news conference.

ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోపై వివరణ ఇస్తూ సంజీవ్ కుమార్ ఒక వీడియోను విడుదల చేశారు. తాను ఒక పాఠశాలలో జరిగిన సాంస్కృతిక కార్యక్రమంలో పాల్గొన్న వీడియోను కొందరు ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా ఎడిట్ చేసి, తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారని ఆయన తెలిపారు. వాస్తవానికి, ఆ కార్యక్రమంలో విద్యార్థినులు మహిళా సాధికారతకు సంబంధించిన పాటపై ప్రదర్శన ఇస్తున్నారని చెప్పారు. అలాగే, తాను మంచినీళ్లు తాగుతున్న దృశ్యాలను మద్యం సేవిస్తున్నట్లుగా వక్రీకరించి తప్పుడు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారని ఆయన స్పష్టం చేశారు. ఇటువంటి అసత్య ప్రచారాలకు పాల్పడిన వారిపై సైబర్ క్రైమ్ పోలీసులకు ఫిర్యాదు చేసినట్లు ఆయన పేర్కొన్నారు.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Kim Woo Young was left dealing with a very unique problem when he first arrived in Japan following the Tokyo Summer Games five years ago, to begin working as coach of the country’s Olympic rifle shooting program.
“Although I was supposed to coach the shooters, I wasn’t allowed to touch any of their guns,” he recalls. It might seem strange but it was the law.
“The rules are very clear. If you don’t have a Japanese instructors license, then even a coach can’t touch guns that belonged to someone else,” recalls women’s rifle shooter Taichi Hinata, one of the first athletes he trained.
The only way Young, former national coach in South Korea could explain technique to his shooters was through words and gestures. “I could talk to them and I could show them what I needed them to do with pictures. It was very unusual but that is the law,” Young recalls.
Young would eventually have to study for 10 months to get a Japanese instructors license before he was allowed to handle his students shooting instruments. “I remember thinking it would be easier to simply take shooters and coach them outside Japan. It was very frustrating.” he recalls.

Young wasn’t having any trouble as he sat in the coaches chair behind his athletes at the Asian Games, though. Coming off a blank in Hangzhou in 2023, Japan’s already had one of their best ever performance in shooting events at the Asian Games in recent years.
On the opening day of competition, Taichi Hinata stunned Olympic champion Ban Hyojin of Korea, India’s Elavenil Valarivan and China’s triple gold medallist at last years World Championships Wang Zifei in the women’s 10m air rifle final. Hinata also partnered with Misaki Nobata and Shiori Hirata to take team bronze, ahead of South Korea’s vaunted women’s team on the opening day.
Then on Tuesday, Nobata partnering Naoki Hanakawa denied India a place on the podium, taking bronze in the 10m air rifle mixed team events. At the end of the rifle events, Japan has three medals – one of each kind – while Hinata’s gold is only the second in shooting since 2010 (the other came in the women’s trap). Currently Japan are only second to heavyweights China on the shooting medal tally.
It’s a performance that’s all the more impressive when you consider the hoops Japanese shooters and coaches have to jump through in their sport. Young’s journey to put his hands on his student’s air guns isn’t even that extreme, for Japanese gun laws are some of the strictest in the world and sporting instruments even for air guns are highly regulated.
There’s no distinction made between air guns used in the 10m rifle events or guns that fire explosive rounds like those used in the 50m event. Licenses are long, arduous and require applicants to clear multiple police verifications, get neighbours to vouch for character, written exams and psychological tests. Pistol licenses are capped at a number nationwide, junior shooters aren’t even allowed to own their own air guns and fire lasers at targets rather than pellets while the decision even to replace a gun requires months of paperwork.
There are hoops to be cleared that seem designed to dissuade all but the most determined.
ALSO READ | Mohammed Afsal: From 3am newspaper van rides to India’s 800m national record
“It’s very hard to be a sports shooter in Japan,” admits Nobata. “First of all, competitive shooting is a very niche sport in Japan, so most young people don’t even know about it. Because of this, the participant base is very small. Also the age at which people start tends to be higher. Due to licensing regulations, you can only own an air rifle yourself from age 18, and the same applies to small-bore rifles—you can’t possess one unless you’re 18 or older. So, the fact that the starting point is delayed creates a significant hurdle,” she says.
While there are shooting clubs around the country, they don’t train with the air guns of the sort that can be found across ranges in India. “We have shooting clubs in Japan but if you are under 18 years old, you aren’t even allowed to touch a gun. You can’t fire pellets out of an air gun. You train on laser simulators,” says Naoya Okada who competed in the men’s team and individual event.
When shooters turn of legal age and want to buy their own gun, they need to purchase it from specific stores only after getting a police license for that specific weapon. But first they need to clear a written exam and extensive police verification that lasts months.
“In the test, you have to be able to have to identify the various parts of the gun, you need to know what’s the weight of the trigger and other very minute details. But the test was also created at a time when it was thought that most guns were going to be bought for hunting purposes so you also have to answer questions on where to fire the gun. Later you have to appear before the police three times and you also need to get your neighbours to vouch for your character,” says Hiroka Monagan, a former national level shooter who is involved in press operations at the Aichi Prefecture shooting range where the shooting events of the Asian Games are being held.
If the licenses for rifle shooters are hard, they can get almost prohibitive for pistol shooters since that weapon has an unfortunate reputation with crime.
“There is a limit on the total number of pistol licenses available at any one time. The only time you can get a pistol license is if someone who already had it gives it up. The gun license rules are strict and they get stricter depending on which prefecture you are getting your license in. The rules in Osaka are particularly strict because there is a history of Yakuza (Japanese organised crime) over there. But it is very strict everywhere in Japan,” says an official who didn’t want to be named since he wasn’t authorised to speak to the media.
And while shooters elsewhere – as was the case with India’s Vidarsa Vinod - can simply swap weapons if they need to, that’s a lot harder in Japan. “Your gun license is specific to your gun. So if you want to use another weapon, you need to go through the procedure for another license for that once again,” says Hiroka.
Then there is the problem of finding a place to train. “We only have one shooting range for each prefecture. So if you don’t live nearby, it’s hard to train,” says Naoya.
ALSO READ | From 1951 to 2026: A brief history of the Asian Games
Indeed most shooters don’t train nearly as much as their international counterparts. “I think it’s very difficult for most shooters to train at a range for more than two days a week. For the rest of the time they have to do dry firing or practise with a gun that fires a laser,” says coach Young.
When informed that many Indian shooters have constructed impromptu ranges in their homes, there’s a sense of disbelief.
“Indian shooters have ranges inside their home? I don’t think you could do that in Japan,” says Japanese men’s shooter Naoki Okada. While the specifics aren’t always known, Japanese shooters are conscious they are at a disadvantage when it comes to simply practising their sport. It takes some getting used to. “I know India, for instance, has a huge number of people participating in the sport. Just like that, I used to feel intimidated when looking at the shooting scene overseas. I was surprised by how easy it was to be a competitive shooter out of Japan. but now I feel confident that I can compete at that level and count myself among the top athletes,” says Nobata.
Even with multiple medals including gold at the Asian Games, shooters like Nobata and Taichi don’t expect much to change with the sport in Japan. “I think it will get a little more popular on instagram or social media but it will still be a niche sport,” Taichi says.
But despite the challenges, the sport will continue to have takers in the country. “Compared to other sports, physical attributes like height or build don’t give you a massive advantage or disadvantage. I find it really appealing that we can compete on a level playing field right from the start. It’s hard to get a gun but what really matters is the person behind the gun,” says Nobata

Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from a drug overdose
- Published
Child star Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed by the Greenville County Coroner's Office in South Carolina.
The coroner's office said Panettiere's death was an accident and that no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to her death.
Panettiere died last month at the age of 36 after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina residence.
The star of US TV shows Heroes and Nashville had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse.
The coroner's office also found methocarbamol - a prescription muscle relaxant - and quetiapine - an antipsychotic medication that is used to treat certain mental health conditions.
Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone.
The coroner's office said emergency responders had "initiated advanced cardiac life support measures; however, resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful".
The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) was reportedly joining the local police department's investigation into the child star's death.
Panettiere's ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report from the day she died.
Just months before her death, Panettiere published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction and postpartum depression.
Panettiere has said she was introduced to drugs around the age of 16 during a red carpet appearance for Heroes when a member of her professional team gave her something called a "happy pill" for energy.
"I had no idea that this was not an appropriate thing, or what door that would open for me when it came to my addiction," she told People Magazine. "As I got older, the drugs and alcohol became something I almost couldn't live without."
Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition. Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother also struggled with substance abuse and used heroin and cocaine leading up to his death.

NEW DELHI: Banks will remain open on Sunday, September 27, to ensure customers have access to essential banking services ahead of a proposed three-day nationwide strike, the government said on Wednesday.
The move comes after the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) called for a nationwide strike from September 28 to 30. With September 26 and 27 falling on a weekend, the strike could otherwise lead to an extended disruption in banking services, the govt said.
“In view of the proposed three-day nationwide bank strike called by the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) from September 28 to 30, 2026, coinciding with the preceding weekend holidays of September 26 and 27, the government has taken proactive steps to safeguard the banking needs of citizens,” the finance ministry said in a statement.
“In order to ensure that the genuine banking needs of the public are not adversely affected for an extended period, all Public Sector Banks and Regional Rural Banks will function normally on Sunday, the 27th of September, 2026,” the ministry said.
“The Department reiterates that the welfare and convenience of bank customers remains the Government's foremost priority. The Government and bank managements have appealed to unions to defer the proposed strike, and have also taken measures to ensure that essential banking services continue un-interrupted,” it added.
The 
Reserve Bank of India
 has also approved the operation of bank branches, offices, ATM-linked branches and currency chests on September 27.
“Permission to operate Bank Branches and Currency Chests on Sunday, September 27, 2026. As requested in the above letter, with a view to ensuring that the genuine banking needs of the public are not adversely affected for an extended period, you have our approval for keeping the branches, offices, ATM link branches and Currency Chests of banks fully operational on Sunday, September 27, 2026," the apex bank said.
“The banks may be advised to ensure adherence to relevant legal requirements in this regard. A list of Currency Chests of private sector/foreign banks has been sent to you separately,” it added.
Also read: Nationwide strike - Banks to remain shut from Monday for three days
Why are bank unions planning a strike?
The UFBU has said bank operations could be disrupted across the country during the three-day strike from September 28 to 30. Since the strike follows the weekend holidays, customers could potentially face an effective five-day disruption in banking services.
The timing is also significant as September 30 marks the half-yearly closing of banks, when reconciliation, provisioning, and treasury and market operations are carried out.
The UFBU, which claims to represent around 90% of the banking workforce, has said it will proceed with the strike unless there is concrete progress on its key demand for five-day banking.
“Responding to the appeal made by the Department of Financial Services (DFS), Indian Banks' Association (IBA), Bank managements to defer the strike, we informed them that if there is any concrete and positive development towards implementation of our demand for introduction of 5 days banking, UFBU will consider the same,” the UFBU said in a statement following a meeting with the deputy chief labour commissioner.
UFBU's other demands include an update and improvement of pension, a uniform dearness allowance formula for all pensioners and an option for employees covered under the National Pension System (NPS) to move to the old pension scheme (OPS). Bank unions under the UFBU had also gone on a nationwide strike on September 11 over their demands.
The statement came after a conciliation meeting on Tuesday ended without a resolution. In the absence of such progress, the union said it would be “constrained” to go ahead with the proposed strike on September 28, 29 and 30.

US prosecutors are investigating cryptocurrency exchange Binance over possible violations of US sanctions on Iran and trading activity conducted through its platform, according to a person familiar with the matter, Reuters reported on 22 September.
The investigation is being led by federal prosecutors from the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York and the Justice Department’s criminal division in Washington. Bloomberg News first reported the probe, saying investigators are examining whether Binance knowingly allowed trading that breached US sanctions.
The US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York and the Justice Department’s criminal division declined to comment on the investigation.
Binance, meanwhile, said it maintains a zero-tolerance approach to sanctions violations and is cooperating with authorities.
“We fully cooperate with law enforcement, and we remain committed to rooting out and shutting down bad actors,” the company said in a statement to Reuters.
The latest investigation comes as Washington has intensified its sanctions campaign against Iranian entities and individuals accused of supporting Tehran and its regional proxies.
Earlier this month, federal prosecutors in Manhattan also sought the forfeiture of millions of dollars linked to Iranian oil sales that they alleged had been laundered through Binance. The new criminal probe appears to examine a related question: whether the exchange’s systems and controls adequately prevented prohibited Iran-linked trading.
Binance has already faced significant US enforcement action over its handling of sanctions and anti-money laundering requirements.
In November 2023, the company pleaded guilty to federal charges involving violations of the Bank Secrecy Act, operating as an unregistered money-transmitting business and violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
Binance agreed to pay more than $4.3 billion in penalties and forfeiture, while its then-chief executive and founder, Changpeng Zhao, also pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering programme.
The Justice Department said at the time that Binance knew it had users in comprehensively sanctioned jurisdictions, including Iran, as well as US users.
Prosecutors said the exchange failed to prevent transactions between the two groups, resulting in more than $898 million in trades between US users and users ordinarily resident in Iran between January 2018 and May 2022.
Zhao stepped down as CEO as part of the 2023 resolution and later served nearly four months in prison. In October 2025, President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao, according to the White House and Reuters.
The current investigation does not establish that Binance committed a new sanctions violation. Prosecutors are examining the matter, and no new criminal charges against the exchange have been announced.

Nvidia boss rejects AI extinction fears as 'doomsday narratives'
- Published
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has described warnings that AI could lead to humanity's extinction by the next decade as "doomsday narratives".
"2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world", Huang said in an interview with CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
Huang added: "Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible."
Warnings from researchers in recent weeks about potential risks posed by the technology escalated the debate about AI safety, with some industry executives calling for a slowdown in developing models.
His remarks follow claims posted on social media by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI developers believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade".
Coxon's concerns sparked debate about the technology's risks, including calls by top executives like Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman urging for AI's development to slow down.
Huang said that such predictions are "not grounded in science", adding that it is in Nvidia's best interest to ensure the industry builds its products responsibly.
"Our company's success is directly connected to the safe deployment of products and services," he said. "If we don't continue to do that, our value would be diminished."
Huang suggested AI firms talking about a "slow down" could be seeking liability protections for harms their products may cause.
"Go and read between the lines," he said. "They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have, and I think that that's a problem."
- Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone

Nvidia is a key player in the industry, developing cutting edge computer chips that are crucial for making AI models.
Last week, Huang appeared at a UK summit hosted by King Charles, who warned tech leaders of the "existential dangers" of AI.
"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," the King told the group.
In the US, President Donald Trump has downplayed concerns about AI's risks.
Trump made a surprise phone call to Huang while the Nvidia boss was speaking on stage at a tech conference in Los Angeles on 14 September.
During the call, Trump criticised calls to slow the pace of AI development and dismissed fears as a "hoax".

Days after rival RentoMojo’s strong stock market debut, furniture and appliance rental startup Furlenco is reportedly gearing up for a potential ₹1,000-1,200 Cr IPO. The Bengaluru-based startup is seeking a valuation of around ₹7,000 Cr (about $732.2 Mn) through the proposed issue, the Economic Times reported, citing sources. However, the final valuation is expected to be decided closer to the IPO, depending on market conditions and investor feedback during roadshows. Furlenco is looking to launch the IPO in FY28 and is expected to soon appoint ICICI Securities as an advisor for the public issue, the report added. Questions sent to Furlenco remained unanswered at the time of publication. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. The IPO plans come after Furlenco turned profitable in FY25 and further expanded its bottom line in FY26. Founded in 2012 by Ajith Mohan Karimpana, Furlenco operates a subscription-driven furniture and appliance rental platform. It offers more than 300 SKUs across 28 cities, including Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi NCR, Chennai, and Kolkata. Besides rentals, the startup also sells new furniture. Its operating revenue surged 61.9% to ₹370.4 Cr in FY26 from ₹228.7 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its net profit jumped nearly 20X to ₹59.5 Cr from ₹3.1 Cr in FY25. The company’s EBITDA nearly doubled to ₹129.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹66.4 Cr in FY25, while its EBITDA margin expanded to 35.01%. Furniture and office equipment rentals accounted for around 92% of Furlenco’s operating revenue in FY26. Rental income jumped 64% YoY to ₹341.1 Cr, while revenue from furniture sales rose 38% to ₹29.4 Cr. Meanwhile, total expenditure increased 45.1% YoY to ₹343.9 Cr from ₹236.9 Cr in FY25. The startup raised ₹125 Cr (about $15 Mn) in a funding round led by existing investor Sheela Foam, along with participation from Whiteoak and Madhu Kela, in December last year. The capital was earmarked towards strengthening its presence in existing markets, entering new markets and investing in product innovation, technology and customer experience. Furlenco has raised more than $290 Mn in funding to date from investors like Lightbox Ventures, Crescent Ventures, Whiteoak, and Madhu Kela. Furlenco Joins Growing Startup IPO Queue Furlenco’s IPO plans come shortly after primary rival RentoMojo raised ₹1,255.6 Cr through its public issue. The IPO closed with an overall subscription of 72.88X before RentoMojo’s shares listed at ₹482.45 on the NSE, a premium of 19.42% over the issue price of ₹404. Several other Indian startups are also preparing to tap the public markets. Digital lending platform Moneyview’s IPO will open for subscription on Thursday (September 24), while Snapdeal parent AceVector’s public issue will open on Friday (September 25). Used-car marketplace Spinny has also filed its draft IPO papers through the confidential route for a ₹2,500-₹3,000 Cr issue. Meanwhile, PhonePe is targeting an IPO by March 2027 after the government introduced MDR on certain UPI transactions. Other startups in the IPO pipeline include Kuku, Razorpay, OYO, Zetwerk, and Atomberg.

Facing criticism, Carney says he has a 'very clear mandate' to push through major economic changes
New bill designed to limit federal project reviews to one year, establish labour peace
Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government received a clear mandate from voters in the last general election — and in subsequent byelections — to "build Canada strong," and he's pressing ahead with changes to federal project approvals and the Labour Code despite criticism from some circles.
The comments come a day after the government tabled Bill C-39, a 246-page omnibus bill that seeks to end what critics maintain is an unwieldy approvals process for major projects and establish a one-year timeline for federal reviews.
The legislation also includes a provision clarifying that the labour minister can step in and end a work stoppage if it's deemed in the "national interest," which has drawn heat from organized labour leaders who say it infringes on the right to strike.
Carney said Canada is facing U.S. economic assaults and threats to its sovereignty and Ottawa's top priority is to turbocharge development to keep the economy going and people working.
"We've been very clear that we would focus on what we can control, and first and foremost is building at home, building Canada strong, building in a way that builds for all," Carney said.
"The government was elected on a very clear mandate."
- AnalysisA consequential fall in Parliament begins with familiar concerns and a new test
- Modi expected to visit Canada in December, Carney says
Carney established the Major Projects Office to help shepherd proposals like port expansions, mines, hydroelectric links and pipelines through the federal approvals process. More than two dozen projects and initiatives have been added to the list since it was established last year.
This latest legislative program is designed to streamline approvals for more projects needing a federal green light.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Carney said projects currently face a maze of bureaucratic red tape with multiple agencies sometimes responsible for different aspects of an approval.
Pointing to the more than decade-long fight to build a new rail bypass after the Lac-Mégantic disaster, Carney said he's taking steps to make the approvals process "much more efficient."
"A decision delayed is a project denied," Carney said. "If you're going to say no — decide it within a year."
Carney said timelines under the last government were so long that businesses effectively "stopped building."
"That's not good for Canadian independence. It's not good for Canadian workers. It means fewer jobs. It means a more expensive life for Canadian families," Carney said.
"This government has elected to turn that around."
Regarding union criticism that C-39's labour provisions gut workers' rights, Carney said the bill "absolutely reinforces the right to strike," but it does include new clauses clarifying when a minister can step in to end job action.
Before this legislation, Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code stated that the minister could direct the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB) to "do such things as the minister deems necessary" to maintain or secure industrial peace in federally regulated workplaces.
With the proposed legislative changes, the wording would be somewhat less vague: a minister can direct an end to strikes within its jurisdiction if that action "adversely affects or may adversely affect the national interest."
The government insists this provision will be deployed only in extraordinary circumstances, but unions maintain that the language is ripe for abuse and will incentivize employers to hold out on cutting a deal with workers while waiting for the government to step in.
"A right you cannot exercise is not a right," said Bea Bruske, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress.
"Canada's unions fought for the right to strike, and we will fight to defend it.”
NDP Leader Avi Lewis said he's concerned about what could be federal overreach in the collective bargaining process.
"The NDP stands shoulder-to-shoulder with Canada's labour movement," he said in a statement.
Some industry groups, meanwhile, are thrilled with Ottawa's economic proposals.
"The legislation directly targets two longstanding barriers to Canada's prosperity: slow and unpredictable project approvals and labour instability affecting critical supply chains," said Adam Legge, the president of the Business Council of Alberta.
"These actions signal a renewed and much appreciated focus from Ottawa on creating the conditions to grow, invest, hire and compete."
The federal Conservatives have not said how their caucus will vote on this new legislation — and it did not feature prominently in their question period attacks on Tuesday — but leader Pierre Poilievre has criticized what's been proposed.
He said a "real bill" designed to turbocharge the economy would "scrap all anti-development laws."

Minecraft Dungeons 2 is bringing more than just chaotic, co-op adventures with your friends. There’s a brand new dimension, dangerous mobs, and several stylish cosmetic rewards: the Minecraft Dungeons 2 capes. If you’re a fellow cape collector like the rest of us, there are plenty of choices, starting with the Hero Cape, the Corrupted Creeper Cape, and even a Special one. So, go through this guide to learn about all the capes you can collect in Minecraft Dungeons 2.
List of All Minecraft Dungeons 2 Capes and How to Get Them
There are currently five announced capes for Minecraft Dungeons 2. While all five are designed for the sequel, only the Hero Cape and Twisted Cape have been confirmed for Minecraft Java and Bedrock Edition. That said, here’s a quick overview of every Minecraft Dungeons 2 cape and how you can obtain it:
| Cape | How to Get It | Available in Java/Bedrock | 
|---|---|---|
| Hero Cape | Play Minecraft Dungeons and Minecraft Dungeons 2 | Yes | 
| Twisted Cape | Pre-order Minecraft Dungeons 2 before launch | Yes | 
| Soul Cape | Purchase the Deluxe Edition of Minecraft Dungeons 2 | No | 
| Corrupted Creeper Cape | Watch eligible Minecraft livestreams on Twitch or TikTok | No | 
| Special Cape | TBA | No | 
Now let’s take a closer look at how to obtain each of the above capes in Minecraft Dungeons 2:
Hero Cape
The Hero Cape might be the most classy-looking of all the Minecraft Dungeons 2 capes. Whether it’s due to the red and gold detailing or due to the cape being added to the original Minecraft Dungeons game, it surely deserves to be in your collection. So, here’s how you can obtain the Hero Cape:
- Play the original Minecraft Dungeons game and launch Minecraft Dungeons 2 once it has been released.
- Use the same Microsoft account in the sequel, and you will be able to unlock the cape.
- Our guide on the Hero Cape in Minecraft will give you a detailed process of obtaining it in the vanilla versions.
Twisted Cape
The Twisted Cape takes a bit darker approach with a skeleton rib design on a deep blue background. While it may look unsettling, you might love to equip this cape once you’re clearing out the rooms in the Deep Dark area in Minecraft Dungeons 2. So, here’s how to obtain it:
- Purchase the Minecraft Dungeons 2 pre-order before its release.
- Launch the game on September 29, 2026, or after that to claim the Twisted Cape inside the game.
- If you want to use this cape in the vanilla versions, our guide on how to get Minecraft Dungeons 2 Capes in Java and Bedrock can help you out.
Soul Cape
The Soul Cape is a premium cosmetic included with the Deluxe Edition of Minecraft Dungeons 2. It has a dark blue background, but the glowing Soul covers most of the cape’s center. Naturally, it’s quite easy to get this cape, as you just need to follow the steps below:
- Purchase the Minecraft Dungeons 2 Deluxe Edition and launch the game once it releases.
- Inside, you will be able to get the Soul Cape as a reward for making this exclusive purchase, along with future DLCs, hero skins, the Blub pet companion, and more.
Corrupted Creeper Cape
The Corrupted Creeper Cape should be a familiar face to both Minecraft players and non-Minecraft players alike, considering the fact that you’ve watched the Minecraft Movie. While this cape was first distributed as card codes through the in-person Xbox Gamescom event, a Gleam campaign later started giving out free codes to the first 1 million players before being taken down shortly.
Fortunately, Mojang has brought back the reward through a limited-time watch quest, and you can get this cape by following the steps below:
- Watch any eligible Minecraft livestream with the ‘Drops Enabled‘ tag on Twitch.
- Alternatively, you can also watch a Minecraft livestream with Game Rewards enabled on TikTok.
- However, you must complete either of the above tasks between September 21 and 26, 2026.
- Once you’ve completed the watch-time requirement, you can check your rewards section to find the cape code.
- Once the game launches, you can redeem the cape code to get the Corrupted Creeper Cape in Minecraft Dungeons 2.
Special Cape
The Special Cape remains one of the most mysterious cosmetics among the announced Minecraft Dungeons 2 capes. While Mojang has revealed its existence, the exact details on how to acquire it haven’t been fully explained.
The Special Cape has a deep blue background, a typical Deep Dark aesthetic, along with golden yellow and light blue borders. As of now, you must wait until further announcements are made by Mojang. Who knows? They might consider revealing the Special Cape redemption process in the upcoming Minecraft Live in September 2026.
That is all for the Minecraft Dungeons 2 capes and how to obtain each of them in the game. So, which one among the above is your favorite? Tell us in the comments below.

Firm behind some of Trump’s top social media accounts sues co-founder for blowing $3m on slot machines
Derek Utley, formerly the chair and CFO of X Strategies, is accused of funding a lavish lifestyle and fueling a gambling addiction with money embezzled from the company
A company that runs some of President Donald Trump's social media accounts is suing its co-founder for allegedly embezzling at least $5 million — including at least $3 million he's accused of blowing on slot machines.
X Strategies alleges that former chair and chief financial officer Derek Utley stole millions of dollars to fund an increasingly lavish lifestyle and fuel a gambling addiction, according to a lawsuit first reported Tuesday by Politico.
“In just 2025 alone, Utley gambled $29,000,000 of the Company’s money at slots at a single casino, ultimately losing $3,000,000,” according to the lawsuit filed Friday in U.S. District Court in West Palm Beach, Florida.
Utley also allegedly bought luxury sports cars and designer clothes, rented “opulent condominiums,” took extravagant vacations and attended events with an entourage, all “funded by money he embezzled from X Strategies,” the lawsuit alleges.
X Strategies maintains the Trump War Room and Team Trump accounts on X, and also helps manage Trump's presence on TikTok, according to Politico.
Utley didn't immediately respond to an inquiry The Independent sent to Washington, D.C.-based Tower Strategies, where he's listed as a partner.
But he told Politico, “I dispute these allegations in the complaint and will address them through the legal process. I have no further comment at this time.”
In an email to The Independent, X Strategies CEO Alex Bruesewitz declined to comment. The White House didn't immediately respond to an inquiry.
Utley and Bruesewitz founded West Palm Beach, Florida-based X Strategies in 2017 when they were 32 and 19, respectively, according to court papers.
Utley's roles gave him “exclusive access” to the company's bank accounts and financial records, and at some point he began “concocting a scheme to embezzle money from X Strategies,” the lawsuit alleges.
The alleged thefts were uncovered earlier this year after the company hired Michael Seifert as its president, and he found X Strategies "should have had millions of dollars more in cash than it actually did," according to the lawsuit.
Utley "voluntarily resigned" his executive positions on April 3 and gave up his 50 percent interest in the company, but was allowed to keep working there until he was fired for allegedly falsifying medical records to seek a six-month paid leave to recover from a purported car crash, court papers allege.
The lawsuit also lists Utley's former girlfriend, Anna Weisheimer, as a co-defendant who allegedly helped him “launder funds embezzled from X Strategies.”
In response to an inquiry from The Independent, Weisheimer — a social media model and Pilates instructor who's also known as Anna DiCenzo — denied any wrongdoing.
“I have absolutely nothing to do with the drama between Alex and Derek. I briefly dated Derek, during which time I asked him to purchase a Pilates studio for me. He ultimately decided not to, and our relationship ended shortly thereafter,” she said in an email. “I have requested that I be removed from this lawsuit immediately, as I have no involvement in the issues between these two gentlemen.”

But the Korean giant has many, many models at varying prices, so what's the best Samsung phone? We sort it out here in this guide. Check out our mobile guides, including the Best Samsung Galaxy S26 Cases, Best Samsung Galaxy S25 Cases, Best Android Phones, Best Cheap Phones, Best Pixel Phones, and Best Folding Phones.
Updated September 2026: We’ve added the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8, Galaxy A37, and Galaxy Z Flip8; mentioned the Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra and Galaxy S26 FE; removed some older devices; updated the best time to buy section; and updated prices.
Why Buy Samsung?
The best part of the Android world is the choice of hardware. Want a phone with a headphone jack? Sure! Want a phone that fast-charges in around 30 minutes? It exists. So why stick with the stalwart Samsung?
In our experience and research, Samsung's smartphones have a track record of reliability, and because it's a major player, it has a wider network of authorized repair centers than competing Android manufacturers. Yes, there was the Galaxy Note 7 fiasco and even the issues with the first-gen Galaxy Fold, but Samsung now has a customer satisfaction score equal to Apple's, according to the American Customer Satisfaction Index. That said, we haven't read great things about the company's US customer support team.
With its flagship phones, you get top-of-the-line specs, exceptional build quality, and long software support. We primarily pick Pixel phones over Samsung because we prefer Google's software experience, but there are plenty of people who like Samsung's take on Android. As always, keep an open mind and consider all your options.
Is Now the Best Time to Buy?
Samsung announced its new foldable range in August, and it won't upgrade the S-series until next year. If you're after the best Samsung phone, now's a good time to buy. But keep the company's launch time frames in mind if you want the latest and greatest.
- The flagship Galaxy S series launches at the start of the year during Samsung's Galaxy Unpacked event. The Galaxy S26 series went on sale March 11.
- The budget Galaxy A series typically arrives in the spring. There are several A-series phones, so they usually dribble out during the first few months of the year. In 2026, the company launched the Galaxy A17 in January, and the Galaxy A37 and Galaxy A57 went on sale in April.
- The folding Galaxy Z series always lands in the summer, and 2026's event was in August, when the company unveiled the Galaxy Z Fold8, Z Fold8 Ultra, and Z Flip8.
- The midrange Galaxy FE series is the “Fan Edition,” but this is more or less a slightly cheaper variant of the Galaxy S-series. The Galaxy S26 FE was just released this month (September 2026).
Consider these dates as you shop, because you may want to hold off for the new model, or it can help inform you about when to expect the best discounts.
How Long Are Samsung Phones Supported?
Android phones used to have disastrously poor software support. Two years after you bought your $1,000 phone, it would no longer receive software updates. Thankfully, Google began promising longer software update cycles for its Pixel phones, which pushed Samsung to match it.
The following Samsung phones will receive seven years of software updates from their release date, which includes Android operating system updates and monthly security patches. The latter keeps your phone secure, and new OS versions can add new features.
- Galaxy S26 FE, S26, Galaxy S26+, Galaxy S26 Ultra
- Galaxy S25 FE, Galaxy S25, Galaxy S25+, Galaxy S25 Edge, and Galaxy S25 Ultra
- Galaxy S24 FE, Galaxy S24, Galaxy S24+, and Galaxy S24 Ultra
- Galaxy Z Fold8, Z Fold8 Ultra, and Z Flip8
- Galaxy Z Fold7, Z Flip7, Z Flip7 FE,
- Galaxy Z Fold6, and Z Flip6
Samsung's Galaxy A-series phones, from the A16 and up, will receive six years of updates. Most other older Samsung devices, like some in the Galaxy A-series or older flagships, will receive four years of OS updates and five years of security patches starting from the release date. This varies because Samsung has kept changing its policy year over year, but you can find more information here.
To find out if your Samsung phone has a pending update, go to Settings > Software update > Download and install. It should check for any updates and download them, then you'll see an option to install. Make sure you back up your phone before installing any update. We have a guide here.
Why We Recommend Buying Unlocked
Most people buy phones directly from their carrier, but if you're reading this guide, we suggest you buy an unlocked smartphone. When you buy a carrier phone, it's “locked” to that network. That means if you want to switch carriers, like moving from Verizon to T-Mobile, you'll have to ask your carrier to unlock the device, and this can be a huge headache. (Especially if you're traveling and want to use an international SIM card.) Carriers usually have a few requirements to unlock a phone, like making sure your device is paid off or waiting a set period of time. Unlocked phones, on the other hand, don't have this problem. You're free to use whatever carrier you want, whenever.
Carriers also mask the true cost of a smartphone. AT&T may entice you with a $ 36-per-month payment for a shiny new Samsung flagship, but in reality, that means you're paying $1,300 for a smartphone over 36 months. Did you really want to spend that much? Or will a cheaper phone suffice? Also, you're more likely to get software updates faster as they come directly from Samsung, and there's often far less preinstalled bloatware to deal with.
All in all, buy unlocked! You can buy unlocked Galaxy phones directly from Samsung and most third-party retailers like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart.
The Settings to Change on Your New Samsung Phone
Samsung has an annoying habit of announcing a bunch of cool new features with its smartphones, then leaving them turned off by default. If you've never fiddled with your phone's settings, there's a good chance you're missing a lot of fun, helpful features.
This can include things like changing the navigation from onscreen buttons to gesture navigation, adding the battery percentage icon next to the battery bar, or keeping the display always on instead of requiring a tap on the screen. Good news for you! Since our reviewers routinely switch phones, we drummed up a list of the most important settings to change when you get a Samsung phone. Read it here. Pro tip: We can't stand Samsung's default keyboard, so we almost always switch to Google's Gboard instead.
Explaining “Qi2 Ready” Samsung Phones
Qi2 is the new wireless charging standard—it takes a page from Apple's MagSafe technology and embeds magnets directly into the smartphone, allowing it to connect to accessories and chargers magnetically, even the same ones available for iPhones. It could increase accessory compatibility across devices, which is a good thing. The magnets ensure precise charging, so you never worry about a misaligned phone that won't charge. It offers better efficiency and can potentially charge faster. We have more details in our Qi2 explainer here.
Confusingly, Samsung's 2025 and 2026 flagship phones are “Qi2 Ready” and technically not true Qi2 smartphones. This means they can support Qi2 when paired with a magnetic case, but on their own, the S25 and S26 series don't have built-in magnets (you can still charge wirelessly). It's disappointing and creates more confusion. We've already encountered some cases with varying degrees of magnetic strength, and some cases don't quite work with basic Qi wireless charging stands.

Qualcomm Snapdragon vs. Exynos Chipsets
A Samsung phone sold in the US may not be the same as a Samsung phone sold in the UK. That's because Samsung's Galaxy S-series flagship phones have long relied on two different processors. Devices sold in the US and select markets are powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon processors, while other regions use Samsung's homegrown Exynos chipsets.
The performance gap between these processors isn't as wide anymore, but there have been issues in the past. Exynos chips tended to overheat a few years ago, though they sometimes offer slightly better battery life than their Qualcomm counterparts. This also greatly affected camera quality, since the chip handles image processing. Again, none of this is as big an issue as it used to be, but it's worth keeping in mind as you shop.
Other Samsung Phones to Consider
If you don't see a Samsung phone mentioned in this guide, it may be because it isn't sold in the US and is a little harder to source for testing. But here are a few other Samsung phones we've tested.
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra for $2,100: An incremental upgrade over the Z Fold7, the Z Fold8 Ultra is for foldable phone fans who want the best and are willing to pay for it. The familiar book-style form factor offers a 6.5-inch cover screen, like a regular candy bar phone, and opens to give a tablet-sized 8-inch display with a fainter crease than before and a stronger hinge. Naturally, you get top-notch performance, all-day battery life, and Samsung’s best camera in a folding phone, with a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and 10-megapixel telephoto lens.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE for $700: The Samsung Galaxy S26 FE is a perfectly decent phone with good battery life, a lovely big display, and a solid triple-camera system, but nothing about it justifies the extra $100 over last year’s almost identical S25 FE. The processor is slightly better, but that’s about it. In fact, Samsung downgraded the USB-C port to USB 2.0 in the S26 FE, so we think you’d be better off buying the S25 FE above while it’s still available.
Z Fold7 for $2,000 or Z Flip7 for $1,100: If you want a Samsung foldable without the eye-watering price tag, consider 2025’s Galaxy Z Fold7 or Galaxy Z Flip7 if you can find them discounted. The Fold7 is a little thicker with a more prominent crease in the screen. The battery life isn’t great, and the ultrawide camera is weaker, but there isn’t a huge difference between it and the Fold8 Ultra. It’s a similar story for the Flip7, with the Flip8 bringing minor hinge improvements, a refined, lighter design with a less noticeable crease, a faster processor, and more useful software features for the outer display.
Samsung Galaxy S25 Edge for $1,300: Have you ever wanted a really thin and lightweight phone? No? Well, Samsung has an option for you anyway. The Galaxy S25 Edge was a unique one-off last year (it's doubtful we'll see a successor) and matches several features of the Galaxy S25 Ultra, like a titanium frame, stronger front glass, and 4K 120 frames per second video recording. All the cameras even have autofocus. But it made several sacrifices to achieve its amazingly slim 5.8-mm frame (for context, the S25 Ultra is 8.2-mm thick). There's no stylus, no telephoto camera, and worst of all, the battery capacity has been slashed. We've seen this before—thin phones have always compromised on battery life, and this is no different. We constantly had to baby this phone's 3,900-mAh battery with mixed usage, and that's just not acceptable. (The iPhone Air did it better.) If you find yourself constantly near a power source and think you'll enjoy the slim and light design, then go for it.
Samsung Galaxy A17 5G for $249: On paper, the Galaxy A17 seems like a really great deal. It offers six years of software support, an AMOLED screen, expandable storage, and a decent camera. Unfortunately, it's held back by lackluster performance. The problem is the very limited 4 GB of RAM in the US model, which ruins the overall experience. If you had to use your smartphone in an emergency, I would not trust the A17 to be reliable. But if your needs are extremely minimal, it may suffice.
If you're looking to save some cash, it's fine to buy Samsung's Galaxy S24 range from 2024, as long as the prices are a good deal lower than the original MSRP. (They're hard to find at most major retailers.) These phones will still get support for a while, and they're pretty great. I don't think it's worth buying anything older.
Should You Invest in Samsung’s Ecosystem?
Samsung is one of the few smartphone manufacturers that can match Apple's hardware ecosystem. The company makes smartphones, but you can also expand your experience with a Galaxy Watch8 smartwatch, Galaxy Buds4 Pro earbuds, Galaxy Ring fitness ring, Galaxy Tab S11, and even a Windows-powered Galaxy laptop.
There are perks, like some features on the Galaxy Ring and Watch8 being available only when paired with a Samsung phone, and its earbuds automatically switching between Samsung devices based on what you're using. There aren't many exclusive features when using a Galaxy phone with a Galaxy laptop, but capabilities like Quick Share let you send photos and documents between your devices (even to iPhones via AirDrop!).
Again, it's not necessary, and these other devices might not be the right ones for you within their respective categories, but if you're chasing hardware parity, you have that option with Samsung.
What Is Galaxy AI?
With the Galaxy S24 series, Samsung launched “Galaxy AI," a selection of artificial intelligence features, many of which are powered by Google's Gemini large language models. These enable smart features that may be helpful in your day-to-day, like real-time translations during phone calls, real-time transcriptions in Samsung's Voice Recorder app, the ability to summarize long paragraphs of text in the Samsung Notes app, or changing a sentence's tone with the Samsung Keyboard.
In the Galaxy S25 series, Galaxy AI expanded to include Gemini as the default voice assistant and the ability for Gemini to work with multiple apps simultaneously. It also debuted Drawing Assist, which lets you sketch or enter a prompt and get an AI-generated image. Now you can also use video in real time with Gemini, even from the cover screen of the Galaxy Z Flip7.
And in the Galaxy S26 series, the AI features got even more helpful. The Document Scanner built into the camera app can now erase fingers and creases and minimize distortion before converting the photo into a PDF. Audio Eraser is now available in any media app to reduce distracting background sounds in videos, so you can hear the subject clearly. And there's now built-in call screening to better filter out robocalls. Samsung also debuted Google's Task Automations in the Gemini assistant, allowing you to ask Gemini to book you an Uber or order something from DoorDash, Uber Eats, or GrubHub, though it's pretty slow.
You can find many of these features in Settings > Galaxy AI to toggle them on or off. We also have an explainer on how to limit Galaxy AI to on-device processing.
What Is Samsung DeX?
Samsung's DeX (short for “desktop experience”) launched in 2017, and it lets you plug your Samsung phone into an external monitor and launch a desktop version of Android, all powered by the phone. You can find a list of compatible Samsung phones here—the Flip7 is the first Galaxy Flip to support DeX—and you'll need a monitor, mouse, and keyboard, plus a cable to connect the phone to the monitor. (You can also cast DeX to select screens wirelessly.)
In DeX mode, you can resize Android apps and open them all in separate windows. It's a proper computing platform, though you probably won't want to use this as a permanent laptop replacement or anything of the sort. It's great if you're visiting another office, or working out of a coffee shop or airplane (if you have a portable display). We have a whole guide to setting up and using DeX here.
What Happened to the Galaxy Z TriFold?
I have not tested Samsung's Galaxy Z TriFold, and it seems I never will. (I had some brief hands-on time with it at CES 2026, but Samsung did not provide WIRED with a test unit.) This folding phone, which had an MSRP of $2,800, officially went on sale in the US at the end of January, but three months later Samsung discontinued it because of high manufacturing costs.
Yes, unfolding it from a fairly compact phone to a massive 10-inch tablet was amazing and the stuff of dreams, but it didn't justify the high price; you can buy a killer phone and excellent tablet for way less than $3,000. The luxury of having them in one pocket is incredible, but more than a $1,000 incredible? I think the TriFold is the true “phablet” Samsung promised so long ago, and the folding mechanism is novel and a marvelous feat. Hopefully, when the smartphone market picks back up, Samsung will revisit this design. It's great for productivity junkies who frequently juggle multiple apps. Alas, it's just a dream now. You'll have to stick with the standard Z Fold. —Julian Chokkattu
How We Test Phones
WIRED has been covering Samsung smartphones since they entered the market. With each Samsung smartphone we test, our reviewers always put their personal SIM card inside and spend as long as they can (a few weeks) using the phone as their own. We do camera testing and compare the results with similarly priced devices; we benchmark performance and play graphically demanding games to see how they fare; we try out all the new features; and we even take calls to make sure they go through and that voice quality is fine.

British Columbia has sued OpenAI in California, saying a mass shooting at a school in the province could have been prevented if the company had warned local law enforcement that the shooter had used ChatGPT to plan the massacre.
The lawsuit filed in San Francisco federal court on Monday names OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, as defendants. It is seeking damages to fund recovery efforts in the province after the February attack, as well as an order directing changes to the way the company handles ChatGPT conversations that could lead to violence.
Nine people, primarily children, were killed in the school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. The shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, had been flagged by the company’s safety team after her conversations about gun violence, but the company did not alert police.
Altman published a letter to the community saying he was “deeply sorry” OpenAI had not contacted law enforcement. He promised reforms, but never followed through, despite efforts from British Columbia’s attorney general to engage, the lawsuit says.
The school where the shooting took place is in the process of being demolished, and the province has been forced to absorb the costs of a replacement school, mental health care and other effects of the shooting, according to the lawsuit.
A spokesperson for OpenAI, Drew Pusateri, called the Tumbler Ridge shooting an unspeakable tragedy. “OpenAI remains committed to working collaboratively with government and law enforcement officials, and continuing to advance our ongoing safety work.”
British Columbia’s lawsuit comes after more than 30 family members of victims and others affected by the attack filed lawsuits in California, accusing the company of opting out of a chance to prevent the shooting.
Van Rootselaar shot her mother and stepbrother at home before killing an educational assistant and five students aged 12 and 13 at her former school on 10 February, according to police. Van Rootselaar, who was 18, then died by suicide.
Van Rootselaar’s interactions with ChatGPT were first flagged by the company in June 2025. Safety team members recommended contacting police, but Altman and other OpenAI leadership overruled them, the lawsuit says, citing OpenAI whistleblowers who spoke to the Wall Street Journal in the wake of the shooting.
The shooter’s account was deactivated, but she was able to get a new account and continue using the platform to plan her attack.
After publication of the Wall Street Journal article, the company said the account was flagged by systems that identify “misuses of our models in furtherance of violent activities”, but the issues did not meet its internal criteria for reporting to law enforcement.
The lawsuit comes after a series of cases against OpenAI have been filed in US state and federal courts in recent months over claims ChatGPT facilitated violence, including lawsuits related to a mass shooting at Florida State University last year.
In June, Florida became the first state to sue OpenAI over safety risks, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, which the lawsuit said had harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users.
OpenAI, which has denied the claims, has said it trains its models to refuse requests that could “meaningfully enable violence”, and notifies law enforcement when conversations suggest “an imminent and credible risk of harm to others”.
