Of the 13 reported acts of kindness in the Facebook post, nine were true, mostly true or probably true.
Two of the claimed acts of kindness were false, and one was unproven. Lynne Patton, a former Eric Trump Foundation employee whom Trump appointed to roles in both of his presidential administrations, carried out one of the reported acts.
In September 2026, a Facebook post (archived) circulated online that listed 13 claimed "acts of kindness" that U.S. President Donald Trump purportedly carried out before running for office.
The introduction to the post read:
For thirty years before he ran for office, Donald Trump quietly paid mortgages, flew sick children across the country, and wrote checks to strangers who needed help. You will not find those stories on the evening news. So here they are.
Start with what people who knew him before politics say. He has never had a drink. He has never smoked. He has never used drugs. He built his business on long hours, and the people who worked for him will tell you he outworked all of them. Nobody called him a bigot until the day he announced for president. That timing tells you something about the accusation.
Now to the record.
The claim about Trump's reported acts of kindness spread on Facebook (archived, archived), X (archived) and Threads (archived). Snopes readers contacted us, asking if the claim was true.
Of the 13 reported acts of kindness in the Facebook post, nine were true, mostly true or probably true, two were false and one was unproven. One of the alleged acts was actually carried out by Lynne Patton, a long-time employee of the Eric Trump Foundation whom Trump later appointed to roles in both of his administrations.
Given the above, we rate this claim a mixture of true and false or unproven elements. Below, we investigate each claim in the post.
Annabel Hill's farm: True
In 1986, a Georgia widow named Annabell Hill was about to lose the family farm at a foreclosure auction. Trump saw her story on the news, picked up the phone, called the auction, and stopped the sale. Then he sent her the money to keep the farm.
Snopes investigated this claim in September 2026 and found it to be true. According to reporting at the time, Hill's farm had been up for auction twice. Her husband, Leonard D. Hill, died by suicide in February 1986 to try to save the farm using the payout from his life insurance. That sum did not cover the debts, and his widow faced a second auction that September.
That was reportedly when Trump stepped in, called the bank to block a foreclosure auction and started fundraising for Hill. The fundraising was successful, with Trump himself covering at least $39,000 of the $170,000 needed. Because of the fundraising efforts, Hill's family was able to keep the farm.
A private plane for Andrew Ten: True
In 1988, an Orthodox Jewish family in Los Angeles had a three-year-old son named Andrew Ten who needed treatment in New York. The boy could not survive without a full life-support setup, and no airline would carry it. His father asked Trump for help. Trump put the family on his own jet and got them there.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2015 and found it to be true based on a report published by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in 1988 that said Ten's father had appealed to Trump for help transporting his ill son to access medical treatment in the New York area.
The Times of Israel later reported that Ten died in 1998. In 2014, the Securities and Exchange Commission fined Ten's father, Harold Ten, in an alleged scheme to "profit from the imminent deaths of terminally ill patients in nursing homes and hospice care."
Trump sent plane to fly Marines: False
In 1991, two hundred Marines came home from Desert Storm to Camp Lejeune and found out the military had no aircraft to fly them the rest of the way to Florida. Trump's airline, the Trump Shuttle, made two runs between North Carolina and Miami and got every one of them back to their families.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2016 and found it false. Though some Marines did fly from Miami to North Carolina on a Trump-branded plane after Operation Desert Storm in 1991, Trump did not own Trump Shuttle or its planes at the time because he had defaulted on the loans he used to buy the fleet. Rather, the military chartered some of the planes that still bore the Trump logo to fly the Marines without involvement from Trump.
A flat tire and a mortgage payment: False
In 1995, a passing driver in New Jersey pulled over to help change a flat on Trump's limo. Trump asked what he could do in return. The man only wanted flowers sent to his wife. A few weeks later, the story goes, the flowers came with a note saying the couple's mortgage had been paid off. People have been repeating that one for three decades.
This claim is an urban legend that Snopes first debunked in 1998. It has also circulated using other celebrities' names. According to an Aug. 15, 1997, report in the Toronto Globe and Mail, an assistant at Trump's New York office told the paper the story "isn't true."
Mar-a-Lago welcomed Black people and Jews: True
In 1996, Trump sued the town of Palm Beach, Florida. The town had been leaning on his Mar-a-Lago club for one reason. He let in Jewish members and Black members, and the older clubs did not. Abraham Foxman, who ran the Anti-Defamation League at the time, said Trump shined a light on the ugly side of Palm Beach that the glitter usually hid. Foxman also said other clubs started admitting Jews and Blacks after Trump forced the issue.
Snopes investigated a similar claim in 2016, finding it true that Trump allowed Black people and Jews to access Mar-a-Lago while other clubs in Florida did not. The Wall Street Journal reported in 1997 that after Trump sued Palm Beach alleging discrimination against his club because it admitted Black and Jewish members, other clubs had started to admit Jewish patrons.
However, the WSJ reported in April 1997 that Palm Beach denied it was discriminating against Mar-a-Lago because of its membership and that restrictions imposed on the club were part of a zoning matter. The outcome of the lawsuit was unclear.
Ultimately, Trump's decision to allow Jewish and Black members turned out to also benefit his business, helping him fight Palm Beach's restrictions and also allowing him to attract a different crowd than existing clubs already catered to.
According to the Wall Street Journal article, Foxman did speak the quote the Facebook post attributed to him, saying Trump "put the light on Palm Beach. Not on the beauty and the glitter, but on its seamier side of discrimination."
Money for a girl with brittle bone disease: True
In 2000, Trump was watching Maury Povich and saw a little girl named Megan who lived with brittle bone disease. He said her attitude got to him. He called the show and sent her family a large check.
According to a recording of a Dec. 19, 2000, episode of "Maury," the talk-show hosted by Povich, an 11-year-old girl named Megan and her mother received a check and video greeting from Trump.
The clip of the show Snopes viewed did not elaborate on Megan's illness or the exact size of Trump's check. During the clip, Trump called Megan "beautiful, inside and out" and told her to "keep up that attitude."
Povich, when handing over Trump's check to Megan, said Trump didn't give out "chump change" and referenced "all those zeros" but did not say the exact amount.
In 2020, to mark the 30th anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act, Trump's campaign shared a news release that highlighted several moments he reportedly supported Americans with disabilities. One of these highlights was about Megan and said she had brittle bone disease.
Jennifer Hudson stayed free at Trump hotel: Probably true
In 2008, Jennifer Hudson's mother, brother, and nephew were murdered in Chicago. Trump moved Hudson and her family into his Chicago hotel at no charge and had his security team watch over them while they grieved.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2016. E! Online reported on Oct. 31, 2008, that Hudson checked into the Trump International Hotel & Tower on Oct. 24, following the murder of her mother, brother and nephew by her former brother-in-law.
The outlet reported that Trump himself was paying for the stay, something Trump also told People magazine on Nov. 10. It was unclear how long Hudson stayed at Trump's hotel.
Hudson has never publicly refuted Trump's claim that he paid for her stay or named herself or anyone else other than Trump as having paid.
A check for bus driver who saved woman from suicide: True
In 2013, a Buffalo bus driver named Darnell Barton saw a woman standing at the edge of a bridge. He stopped the bus, walked over, put an arm around her, and talked her back to safety. Trump read about it and mailed Barton a check, because he thought a man like that deserved a reward.
Snopes found this claim to be true in 2016. A Buffalo radio station reported photos from a ceremony on Nov. 7, 2013, during which Barton received the $10,000 check (archived) that Trump had promised on social media after Barton's Oct. 18 rescue of an apparently suicidal woman he spotted while driving his bus.
Money for a Marine arrested in Mexico: True
In 2014, Marine Sgt. Andrew Tahmooressi spent seven months in a Mexican prison after he took a wrong turn at the border with legally owned guns in his truck. President Obama never placed the call to Mexico that the sergeant's family begged for. Trump sent Tahmooressi a check for $25,000 to help him rebuild his life once he got home.
Snopes previously investigated this claim in 2018. We found at the time that Tahmooressi was arrested after he crossed the Mexican border while carrying guns and ammunition that he legally owned in the U.S. — but wasn't permitted to carry in Mexico — and was imprisoned for seven months.
We could not substantiate his claims about abuse and mistreatment by Mexican authorities that also circulated at the time.
The House Committee on Foreign Affairs reported on Oct. 31, 2014, that Tahmooressi had been released from Mexican jail. Trump pledged (archived) on social media on Nov. 10, 2014, that he would send Tahmooressi a check for $25,000. We reported in 2016 that Trump made good on his promise the next day, writing to Tahmooressi:
You have served our country with fortitude and dignity, and we are fortunate to have someone like you as a brave Marine and protector of our wonderful nation. We are proud of you and I wish you and your family the very best for many years to come.
According to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs and reporting by the Los Angeles Times, Republican and Democratic politicians alike had pushed for Tahmooressi's release. Any involvement or lack thereof by then-President Barack Obama was unclear.
College money for beauty queen's son: True
In 2016, Melissa Young stood at a Trump rally in Wisconsin and cried while she thanked him. She had competed as Miss Wisconsin USA in 2005, then got sick with an illness that has no cure. During her worst stretch, a handwritten note arrived from Trump calling her the bravest woman he knew. She said the doors Trump opened for her ended up giving her Mexican-American son a full ride to college.
During a Trump campaign rally in Janesville, Wisconsin, on March 29, 2016, Young told the then-candidate that his organizations, including the Miss USA pageant and the since-defunct crowdfunding platform FundAnything.com, had helped secure her Mexican-American son a full ride to college.
Young, who competed as Miss Wisconsin in the Miss USA pageant in 2005, said she suffered from an incurable illness and that at one point when she was in hospital, Trump sent her a handwritten letter addressed to the "bravest woman I know."
In 2016, Snopes reported on Young's story and the open letter to Trump she posted on Facebook (archived) in July 2015. That letter explained that Miss USA 2005 Chelsea Cooley had started a fundraiser for Young's son after attending the launch of FundAnything.com, which would allow him a full ride to college.
It was unclear whether Trump personally paid anything into Cooley's fundraiser for Young's son. (The claim does not say specifically that he did.)
Young posted (archived) on Facebook in August 2026 that her son would be a high school senior that coming school year.
Lynne Patton's reply to claims Trump was racist: True
That same year, Lynne Patton, a Black executive at the Trump Organization, put out a video answering the people calling her boss a racist. She admitted she had fought addiction for years. She said the Trump family never pushed her out. They stood by her the whole way.
Patton, who was at the time the vice president of the Eric Trump Foundation, spoke at the July 20, 2016, Republican National Convention in Cleveland, Ohio. Before she took the stage, a five-minute video essay played in which Patton criticized "repeated and reprehensible" attempts to "align my boss and his family with racist hate-mongering groups campaigns and messaging" (time code 0:14).
Patton called the Trump family, "one of the most generous, compassionate and philanthropic families I've ever had the privilege of knowing" (time code 0:39).
Patton's video essay and following appearance did not include mention of addiction. This part of the claim may have come from her later media appearances. For example, in April 2025, Patton discussed her history with cocaine addiction with Lara Trump, Eric Trump's wife, on Fox News. During that interview, Patton also talked about how the Trump family had supported her through her addiction.
After Donald Trump won the 2016 presidential election, he appointed Patton to a role in the Department of Housing and Urban Development overseeing a region covering New York and New Jersey. During his second administration, Trump appointed Patton as deputy assistant to the president and director of minority outreach.
Patton previously served a suspension from government work for a violation of the Hatch Act, which regulates the partisan political activities of federal employees, during her time at HUD.
Cancer treatment for campaign volunteer's father: Mostly true
Also in 2016, a young Illinois volunteer named Shane Bouvet told reporters that Trump had stepped in to cover his father's cancer treatment. His father, Donald Bouvet, beat the cancer. Trump has stayed in touch with the family ever since.
Trump met with Bouvet and his father, Donald, on Feb. 9, 2018. The president said he had first read about Shane Bouvet in The Washington Post ahead of his January 2017 inauguration.
The Post reported at the time that Bouvet was a Trump supporter and volunteer social media coordinator for the Trump campaign in Illinois. The article noted that Bouvet's father had cancer and that Bouvet and his mother both faced layoffs and difficulties finding well-paid work.
Trump said in February 2018:
I said, "I'd like to meet him." Nice young man, had a lot of difficulty. And I gave him some money for himself — $10,000. His father, Donald — good name — was suffering and really on a pretty final path toward losing his life with cancer. Shane took the $10,000, and, rather than spending it on himself, he gave it to his father. And his father went to a very good cancer clinic or hospital because he was at hospitals before and they didn't do so well.
Trump continued:
And they did a fantastic job, and Donald is now cancer-free. And I think it's an incredible story where a son would give 100 percent of the money to his father, who he loves, obviously.
As such, though Bouvet ended up spending Trump's money on cancer treatment for his father, Trump suggested that was not how he intended the money to be spent when he gave it to Bouvet. It was unclear whether Trump remained in contact with the Bouvet family at the time of this writing.
Loans to Black entrepreneurs: Unproven
And there is a story that has floated around New York business circles for years. A Black business owner could not get a loan anywhere in the city. Someone told him to go see Trump. Trump lent him the money and told him to pay it back when he could. The man came back later with a check and said the business was doing well. Trump tore the check up.
Snopes could not determine the source of this rumor. An oft-cited source was the Joe Brown, a former TV judge, who appeared on a podcast in 2019. When asked on the podcast whether Trump was a racist, Brown said (time code 1:07:43):
I don't think so. I have talked to a number of Black entrepreneurs who, back in the late '80s and '90s were, early '90s, were trying to get financing. They couldn't. Somebody told them to go check with Donald Trump. So they come back and tell me they got a loan from Donald Trump. He gave him a term loan: Show up with the interest in the principal [unintelligible] but they had to go see him in person. They independently relayed this tale that when they saw him he said, "That's what you're supposed to pay me, this is our agreement?" say "Yeah," and then tore the check up, shook their hands and "Congratulations, now run your business."
We found no evidence that Trump, his campaign or individual business owners had ever publicly confirmed giving or receiving such loans. We attempted to contact Brown to ask if he could put us in contact with Black business owners who received loans from Trump in the early 1990s. We also contacted the Trump Organization to ask about the rumor. We await replies to our queries.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report

How Premier League teams have really started - according to xG
- Published
How have Premier League teams really started?
At this stage last season Liverpool were top, with five wins out of five, and Tottenham were third. Given that they finished fifth and 17th respectively, it shows that the table shouldn't be taken too seriously this early on.
While any statistics should be taken with a pinch of salt - given such a small sample size of games and the fact that some teams have had more difficult starts than others - they do provide a more accurate picture of how the season could unfold.
Expected goals (xG) tells us how much teams have dominated games, based on the number and quality of shots they've taken and faced. Basically, how well they've performed in general before finishing, shot-stopping and plain old luck come into play.
And Premier League history shows us that the more a team dominates games, the more points they win in the long run.
It's best to exclude penalties as refereeing decisions and defensive clumsiness give a false impression of how good teams actually are at attacking and defending, especially at this early stage.
Champions Arsenal may have suffered their biggest defeat in three years last weekend at Brighton but they've still been the best team overall based on xG difference.
Leaders Manchester City are not too far behind them in terms of how much they've dominated their games, while there's nothing fortunate about unbeaten Brentford's impressive start to the season.
Manchester United constantly seem to flip between feast and famine, when often they've simply been fine. Despite their underwhelming start, only three teams have a higher xG difference so far.
The likes of Nottingham Forest and Bournemouth have also been better than their position in the early table suggests.
At the other end, Aston Villa, Crystal Palace and Newcastle have been the least impressive in terms of their overall performance, with the latter perhaps the most surprising given their position in the top half.
It's still early days, so there's no need to panic just yet, but it shows that those teams have a lot of room to improve - something Villa did to great effect after a slow start last season by finishing fourth.
Worryingly for the established sides though, the promoted teams seem like they won't be going down without a fight, with both Hull and Ipswich making genuinely solid starts to the campaign.
Pecked by the Seagulls
Looking at teams' numbers going forward, Brighton have the best attack so far based on the number and quality of chances they've had, followed by Manchester City, Brentford and Manchester United.
Although the Gunners are more admired for their defensive prowess, it's still surprising that eight teams have a higher xG than champions Arsenal, while Liverpool and Chelsea also rank in mid-table.
Brighton not only have the highest xG but have also been one of the most ruthless sides in front of goal, scoring 15 non-penalty goals from their 10.7 xG.
The only team to be more clinical than the Seagulls is their avian cousins the Magpies, who actually have the lowest xG in the league so far.
Newcastle have scored twice as many goals as a team historically would given the chances they've had - 9 goals from 4.5 xG - but head coach Matthias Jaissle will no doubt want his team to create more and not have to rely on such sharp finishing as the season goes on.
In contrast, Coventry, Sunderland, Nottingham Forest and Tottenham have all scored three goals fewer than they really should have given the opportunities they've had in their first five games.
It'll be interesting to see whether those teams genuinely have a problem with their finishing or if their luck in front of goal simply begins to change in the games to come.
Same old Arsenal... mostly
As mentioned earlier, champions Arsenal are renowned for their defence and they still have by far the best backline in the league - even taking their heavy defeat by Brighton into account.
While Forest head coach Oliver Glasner has work to do to get his side scoring goals, he's already instilled a solid foundation to build from at the back, as has Andoni Iraola at Liverpool.
There's a lot of construction work needed in the capital as Crystal Palace, Fulham and Chelsea have all been far too open at the back so far this season, although Xabi Alonso's side are not quite as terrible as the 12 goals they've conceded suggests.
Brighton's brilliance going forward has come at the cost of them not being particularly solid in defence, with Fabian Hurzeler's team perhaps a little fortunate not to have conceded more often.
Everton and Leeds have also conceded three goals fewer than expected given the chances they've faced, although both sides have been among the strongest defensively overall.
Just five games into the new campaign, it's too early to be making any concrete claims about how sides will perform but their underlying numbers have given us a glimpse of what might be in store this season.

How to use Google's Find Hub to locate your Android phone
You don’t even need another Android device to access the hub.
Google, just like Apple, has a tracking network that can help you locate missing Android phones, tablets and accessories. It's called the Find Hub, and it's the first thing you should check if your Android device goes missing. You don't even need another Android device to access it — you can just as easily load the Find Hub on a browser on your computer or a smartphone. For this piece, we're going to focus on how to use the Find Hub to find a missing Android phone and what to do when you locate it.
Make sure your phone can be located
The first thing you should do is ensure your phone can be located in case it does go missing. To start with, always keep your phone updated with the latest software. If you're good on that front, check that you're logged into a Google account you still have access to by going to Settings on your phone then tapping your name and then your profile info. You can find the Google account you're using with your phone there. Make sure to verify your email address, as well.
Again, from Settings, go to Location and make sure it's switched on. After that, go back to the Settings page and go to Security or Security and Privacy. From there, go to Find Hub or to Lost Device Protection > Find My Mobile and make sure that Allow device to be located or Allow this phone to be found is ticked on.
You'll also find an option that says Find your offline devices or Offline Finding. Switch that on so that you can still use Find Hub to see your device's most recently recorded location even if it's offline. Take note that you would have to set a PIN, pattern or password on your phone to be able to use the offline finding feature. If you have a supported model, like a newer Pixel phone, Find Hub can even locate your device several hours after it's turned off. Just tick on With network in busy places only or With network everywhere under Find your offline devices, if either is available. Your Bluetooth and Location must also be on.
The options' wording will depend on your device's brand and its custom software interface, but they will mostly likely sound similar to the ones above.
How to use Find Hub
If you do lose your phone, open the Find Hub app on another Android device or a Wear OS smartwatch, or go to the Find Hub website on a browser. Sign in with the Google account logged into your phone and then go to the Devices tab. From there, you can see where your missing device was last located. If it's within 10 meters from where you are, you can launch Maps from the Find Hub interface to get directions to its last location. You can also remotely trigger your phone from the hub to Play a sound to make it easier to find, even if it's set to silent.
In case your phone was stolen or if you lost it far from your current location, you can take more drastic measures to protect your privacy and security. From the hub, you can tap Mark as lost to lock your device with your PIN, pattern or password. It can also secure your data with two-step verification, as long as the missing phone is running Android 17 and up and has fingerprint or Face Unlock. When you choose to mark your device as lost, you'll be able to enter your contact info and a message to display on the lock screen of your phone. However, take note that thieves and scammers could use the information you display to trick you into unlocking the phone for them.
If you've lost hope of ever recovering your phone and would just like to protect your data, you can Factory Reset it remotely from Find Hub. You can think of it as your last resort and nuclear option, because it will permanently delete all the data on your device and will also remove it from the Find Hub, so you cannot use the feature to find your phone anymore.

A month-long citizen science initiative involving school students across Assam’s Kamrup Metropolitan district has resulted in the documentation of 1,517 species of flora and fauna.
Guwahati is the headquarters of the 1,528-sq. km Kamrup Metropolitan district, comprising three development blocks and five revenue circles.
Help Earth, a Guwahati-based biodiversity conservation organisation, conducted a 30-day taxonomic survey in association with the Assam Climate Change Management Society. Students from seven schools participated in the exercise, titled Guwahati Bioblitz 2025. Its results were announced on Tuesday (September 22, 2026).
“The survey was conceived as an intensive biodiversity documentation (exercise) to encourage students to discover, document, and understand the biological diversity within a largely urban landscape. Students were allowed to explore and observe their surroundings and contribute scientifically useful records,” said Help Earth general secretary Jayaditya Purkayastha.
According to the data released at a school in Guwahati’s Barsajai area, 48 students logged 5,932 observations and documented 1,517 unique species.
The final tally comprised 993 plant species, 221 insect species, 117 bird species, 25 mammal species, and 10 reptile species.
The survey introduced the participants to biodiversity awareness, field exploration, digital photography, species identification using iNaturalist app, monitoring, and continued engagement with biodiversity.
“The initiative was designed not merely as a competition, but as a platform to develop a lasting habit of observation, documentation, and appreciation of nature among young learners. The broader vision presented during the programme was to transform biodiversity assessment from a one-time activity into a continuous learning and monitoring process, with schools functioning as living classrooms,” Mr Purkayastha said.
“Large-scale biodiversity conservation through student participation can go a long way in promoting ecological literacy and the exploration of urban microhabitats, from school grounds to surrounding areas,” said Amlan Kumar Dey, the principal of Maharishi Vidya Mandir III, where the concluding programme of Bioblitz 2025 was organised.

There's growing concern that Trump may deploy the National Guard ahead of elections
With Election Day less than 50 days away, a growing number of Democratic lawmakers, retired military leaders and civil society organizations are seeking assurance from members of the Trump administration that the U.S. military will not be deployed to or around polling places — while also preparing for such a move to occur.
Having armed federal agents — like the FBI or Immigration and Customs Enforcement — or military troops near the polls is clearly barred by federal law, but President Trump and several other key officials have recently sidestepped direct lines of questioning around the issue.
Some have even suggested that such a presence might be necessary to ensure trust in the vote, a claim that voting officials across the United States deny. Those voting officials say they plan on administering the midterm elections as usual and have been working hard to assure voters that plans are in place if armed federal officials do show up.
The concern over federal interference at the polls has led to a wave of unprecedented action by civil rights groups, unions and political organizations, including multiple lawsuits, Freedom of Information Act requests and public service announcements to voters about what to watch for on Election Day. And many are specifically ringing alarm bells over the possible involvement of the U.S. military, particularly the National Guard.
Trump's extraordinary use of the National Guard on U.S. soil has already upended democratic norms in the U.S. and unnerved civil rights groups. And experts say the U.S. Supreme Court's recent rejection of Trump's executive order attempting to limit mail voting has backed him into a corner.
"Quite frankly, as this president's options are dwindling, the idea that he might use the military becomes even more of our concern," says retired Air Force military lawyer Maj. Gen. Steven Lepper.
Lepper is part of the Former Judge Advocates Working Group, made up of several dozen retired military lawyers. The group has been tracking the president's executive orders and military deployments and has written several reports to Congress about its worries.
"Either this administration is trying to limit the ways in which votes can be cast, or they're setting up a situation where a scenario could be concocted to justify the use of military force," Lepper says. In particular, he notes the executive order declaring antifa a terrorist organization. He says that this could be used amid disruption at polling places to justify invoking the Insurrection Act — something Trump has repeatedly threatened to do.
When asked directly by a reporter in May about deploying the National Guard or ICE, Trump didn't rule it out, saying he would do "anything necessary" to make sure there are "honest elections."
NPR reached out to the White House for clarification on the comment but did not receive a direct response.
The National Guard can legally be used to support elections in many capacities — like logistical or cybersecurity purposes — when ordered by state governors. But the president deploying troops or federal armed agents to polling places is illegal.
It's a situation that would almost certainly face immediate legal challenges — like all of Trump's domestic military deployments — but, as Lepper points out, such challenges take time to work their way through the courts.
"There's no do-over," Lepper says. "There's no way the courts can basically reverse the impact of something like [election interference]."
Democrats pressure Trump administration
It's not just Lepper and his colleagues raising the concern.
In March, several Democratic members of the Senate Armed Services Committee sought assurances from Gen. Gregory Guillot, the commander of U.S. Northern Command, who would be in charge of federal troops if such an order came from the president.
When asked by Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois what guardrails are in place in that situation, Guillot said he very clearly understands the laws.
"If given the order, I would look at it very closely," Guillot answered, later adding that he didn't think troops should be "anywhere near" polling places.
Last month, the Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration for failure to respond to Freedom of Information Act requests seeking records about any plans to seize ballots in the midterm elections.
In recent weeks, Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan directly pressed several military leaders and federal agencies to confirm that U.S. troops won't be sent to polling places. Only the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Gen. Dan Caine, has responded, saying that there are "no plans" to send U.S. troops to the polls.
Immigration enforcement
There is also growing concern about immigration enforcement agents being used to intimidate voters, something that's also illegal.
The Department of Homeland Security has told NPR that it is "not planning operations targeting polling locations." This month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE agents could serve warrants at polling places. And that, too, could include the military accompanying the agents, although that is also considered by most legal experts to be illegal.
An internal DHS memo from last year that was recently made public shows that the administration has outlined a way to circumvent a law that prevents the military from performing law enforcement duties, including immigration enforcement, known as the Posse Comitatus Act. The memo lays out a specific path to deputize federalized National Guard members as immigration enforcement officers — something many members of the administration, like Stephen Miller, have long stated as a goal.
"This memo is designed as a work-around to say, 'Here is how we can get this done without violating federal law,'" says Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight, the nonpartisan, nonprofit watchdog group that obtained the memo through a Freedom of Information Act request.
The memo, which NPR has read, does not explicitly say anything about elections or polling places. But Chukwu says that given the administration's escalating claims around voter fraud by unauthorized immigrants, it's important to read it in that context.
"We should be planning for this to potentially be the way that they justify deploying National Guard to the polling places around the country," she says.
When asked about the memo, DHS told NPR it "speaks for itself."

It could have been a scene from Cape Fear: a quiet evening, an ordinary home, a sudden intrusion by a stranger convinced that the law has betrayed him.
In early July 2022, Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington and her husband were watching television at their Seattle home when men drove past their house screaming threats: vile, racialized, and unmistakably political. They called the police. The men left. Thirty minutes later, one returned, blasting music and approaching the porch. When officers arrived, they found him armed with a loaded handgun, a round already chambered. A neighbor heard him shout, “Go back to India. I am going to kill you.”
Jayapal later described the episode not as an aberration but as evidence of a broader transformation in American politics—a climate in which grievance increasingly functions as permission and intimidation is framed as justified political expression. The threats did not stop. Nor is Jayapal alone. For years, Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia lived under constant threat as one of Donald Trump’s most aggressive defenders in Congress. She reported hundreds of death threats, largely from ideological opponents.
But when Greene publicly broke with Trump—over the Epstein files, Gaza, and what “America first” had come to mean—the direction of the threats shifted. After Trump labeled her “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” messages arrived threatening her son by name. One threatened her assassination. Another claimed that a plane ticket had already been purchased. In November 2025, Greene announced her resignation from Congress, citing threats to her family. “I think that comes to a point,” she said, “where any American can look at that and say that’s a high bar and way too much to ask.”
What Jayapal and Greene have in common is not ideology, temperament, or policy; it is exposure. Both became targets in an era in which political violence is no longer confined to the fringe, no longer clearly condemned by leaders, no longer monopolized by either the right or the left—and increasingly treated as a legitimate instrument of political pressure.
What happened to Jayapal and Greene is no longer exceptional; it is revealing. Their experiences point to a deeper transformation: Political violence has moved closer to the center of American political life, touching elected officials across parties and becoming a recurring feature of contemporary conflict rather than a rare deviation.
Since 2016, Americans have argued fiercely not only about whether political violence is rising but about who is responsible. One dominant narrative attributes the problem primarily to the radical right: white nationalism, militias, election denial. A competing narrative insists that violence emanates just as strongly from the radical left, manifested in riots, assaults on police, and organized disruption in cities and on campuses. These claims are not merely rhetorical; they shape public trust, elite behavior, law enforcement priorities, and—most dangerously—the willingness of partisans to condemn violence committed by those they regard as allies. But what does the evidence actually show?
America’s political violence problem is neither one-sided nor symmetrical. Taken together, the evidence from federal threat assessments, terrorism databases, protest incident data, and congressional security records points toward the same conclusion. Political violence in the United States declined for nearly two decades after the 1990s and then rose sharply beginning around 2016. For decades prior to that year, politically motivated violence was concentrated overwhelmingly on the far right. Today, violence associated with the right and left is closer to balance, even as it takes very different forms. Right-wing violence has been substantially more frequent and far deadlier than left-wing violence since 2016—aimed at elections, federal institutions, and public officials—while left-wing violence has been more common in mass protest settings, from the 2020 George Floyd unrest to clashes over immigration enforcement, typically involving property destruction and confrontations with police.
Although uncertainty remains at the margins, the evidence strongly suggests that since roughly 2016, political violence on both the right and the left has reached levels unseen in the United States since the upheavals of the 1960s. These patterns reflect not a single ideology but the deeper forces of violent populism: hardened identities, perceived existential threats, collapsing institutional trust, and elite rhetoric that frames politics as a struggle between enemies rather than fellow citizens.
Much of the public disagreement about whether political violence is rising and who is responsible for it stems not from ideology alone but from competing definitions about what should be counted.
In scholarly literature, political violence is generally defined as the use or credible threat of physical force for political ends. Those ends may include coercion, intimidation, punishment, or symbolic signaling intended to influence public behavior, political outcomes, or institutional authority. Under this definition fall assassination attempts, armed assaults on public officials, bombings, arson attacks, violent intimidation, riots against buildings with explicit political aims, and organized plots to use force against political targets.
Just as important are the exclusions. Political violence does not include ordinary criminal activity lacking political motivation, interpersonal violence driven by private disputes, or lawful protest—even when protests are disruptive, angry, or unlawful. Nor does it include harsh rhetoric alone, however inflammatory, unless it is paired with a credible threat of force. These boundaries matter, because collapsing political violence into crime or protest obscures its distinct causes and consequences.
The hardest problem is determining intent. Political violence is defined not only by what happens but by why it happens—and intent is often ambiguous. When a crowd burns a police precinct, is the act political rebellion, criminal opportunism, or both? When a gunman attacks a synagogue, is the motive ideological antisemitism, personal grievance, or mental illness layered atop political belief? When an individual sends a death threat to a lawmaker, is it expressive rage, partisan trolling, or preparation for real-world violence?
Reasonable scholars answer these questions differently, often using dissimilar evidentiary thresholds. Some datasets require explicit ideological statements; others infer political intent from targets, symbols, or timing. Some classify riots as political violence only when their organizers articulate political goals; others focus on behavior rather than rhetoric. None of these choices is neutral, and each shapes the resulting picture.
These definitional choices explain why prominent datasets sometimes appear to disagree. Federal law enforcement datasets emphasize lethality, capability, and threats to national institutions. Protest-oriented datasets capture frequency and geographic spread. Terrorism databases prioritize ideological framing and tactical similarity to global movements. Each captures something real—and each misses something important.
For this reason, no single dataset can settle the debate. Accordingly, my work triangulates across several sources, combining federal threat assessments, incident-level databases, congressional security data, and survey research. The goal is not to produce a definitive body count but to identify patterns that recur across independent measures: who is targeted, how violence is carried out, how lethal it is, and how those patterns have changed since 2016.
This approach does not eliminate uncertainty. But it does attempt to move beyond partisan narratives and toward a more accurate understanding of how political violence in America has evolved—and why arguments over its meaning have become almost as intense as the violence itself.
The most authoritative window into political violence in the United States comes not from media tallies or advocacy groups but from the federal agencies charged with tracking national security threats—above all, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Yet even here, readers encounter a fundamental problem: There is no single, formal US government definition of “political violence.” Instead, federal agencies operate with overlapping categories—domestic terrorism, domestic violent extremism, hate crimes, threats against officials, and antigovernment violence—each shaped by legal constraints, investigative mandates, and statutory language rather than a unified conceptual framework.
This definitional fragmentation matters. Unlike many countries, the United States does not criminalize “domestic terrorism” as a stand-alone offense; the relevant statute (18 U.S.C., § 2331) defines “international terrorism” and “domestic terrorism” descriptively but does not by itself create a prosecutable offense. As a result, the FBI does not report a simple annual count of domestic terrorism incidents. Instead, the statistics reflect investigations, disrupted plots, arrests, and threat assessments organized around ideological motivation, such as racially and ethnically motivated violent extremism, antigovernment or antiauthority extremism, and hostile acts against government structures. The absence of a single metric has fueled public confusion and partisan cherry-picking, with critics on all sides accusing the FBI of either exaggerating or minimizing particular threats.
Despite these constraints, a consistent picture emerges from FBI testimony, annual threat assessments, and congressional reporting since 2016. Across political administrations, FBI directors have warned that domestic violent extremism is a persistent and elevated threat, with particular emphasis on right-wing ideologies—especially white supremacist and ethno-nationalist violence—as the most lethal category among domestic violent threats. This assessment is grounded not in ideology per se but in outcomes: The majority of fatal attacks tied to political or ideological motives in recent years have originated in right-wing ecosystems, often carried out by lone actors inspired by online propaganda rather than formal organizations.
At the same time, federal reporting makes clear that political violence is not monopolized by the right. The FBI and DHS have also documented significant spikes in violence associated with mass protest movements, assaults on law enforcement, arson, and attacks on government facilities during periods of intense unrest—most notably in 2020, when protests following the killing of George Floyd were accompanied by substantial violent confrontations in many cities. These events are more commonly linked to left-wing or anti-authority contexts, tend to cluster geographically, and are far less likely to result in mass casualties. The distinction federal agencies draw is therefore not between “violent” and “nonviolent” sides but between forms of violence that differ in frequency, lethality, and strategic orientation.
A further frustration is temporal. Much of the FBI’s publicly accessible data lags behind current events. Detailed breakdowns often stop several years short of the present, while ongoing investigations limit transparency about more recent trends. As a result, scholars and policymakers must rely on testimony, qualitative assessments, and partial datasets to infer patterns after 2021—a gap that has widened in the wake of intensified threats against public officials and institutions. This delay has created a disconnect between the lived experience of escalating threats—particularly against elected officials—and the statistical record available to the public.
These limitations should not be mistaken for insignificance. On the contrary, the persistence of the same core warnings across multiple administrations, political contexts, and leadership teams suggests institutional continuity rather than partisan distortion. While the FBI cannot provide a clean annual count of “political violence,” its threat assessments provide something arguably more important: a comparative judgment about which forms of violence are most likely to kill, destabilize institutions, and undermine democratic governance.
When federal threat assessments are read alongside terrorism databases, incident-level coding, congressional security data, and survey research, the contours of political violence since 2016 come into focus—even if the exact numbers remain contested. The challenge is not the absence of evidence but the difficulty of integrating imperfect sources into an honest and comprehensive account.

A tropical storm off the south-west coast of Mexico has intensified into a category 5 monster in fewer than 24 hours, fueled by stronger than usual El Niño weather patterns in the Pacific Ocean.
Hurricane Polo was sending out maximum sustained winds of 165mph (266km/h) on Tuesday as its center churned about 215 miles (346km) south of the coastal city of Zihuatanejo, in Guerrero state.
On Monday, Polo was only a tropical storm with winds below 74mph (120km/h). Its rapid and sudden growth is testament to the dominance of this year’s so-called super El Niño, which set a record on Monday as the most extreme on record, and has amplified a number of extreme weather events globally.
Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center in Miami said Mexico was likely to avoid a direct hit, but warned that further intensification was likely, and that life-threatening flooding and mudslides were possible inland, along with dangerous surf and rip current conditions.
El Niño occurs when extended ocean temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific, and near the equator, rise above their historical average.
Meteorologists say the phenomenon increases disruptive winds and curtails other conditions favorable to storm development in the Atlantic basin, which remains quiet with less than three months to go in this year’s hurricane season.
Conversely, it promotes increased activity in the Pacific, where the 2026 El Niño remains one of the strongest on record.
“The water temperatures in two separate areas, the north-central Pacific and off the Mexican coast, are running well above average,” Paul Pastelok, AccuWeather’s lead long-range meteorologist, said in the online weather service’s fall hurricane outlook last month.
“We are seeing a strong impact in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins, with extreme wind shear limiting Atlantic storm development, while the Pacific remains quite active, as we expected back in the spring.”
Hurricane Polo’s single-day intensification also fits into the assessment of University of Miami senior research associate Brian McNoldy on his tropical Atlantic blog that El Niño, which he said was only “moderate” towards the beginning of September, was “forecast to become very strong, likely the strongest on record, by later this fall and into winter”.
Polo is the 18th named storm, and seventh hurricane, of the 2026 Pacific season, which runs from 15 May until 30 November.
By contrast, the Atlantic basin, which has a six-month season from June until November, has seen only six named tropical storms and no hurricanes so far.
It is the first time in 112 years that no Atlantic hurricanes have formed by 21 September, and 2026 could join 1907 and 1914 as the only years without one being recorded.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

UK pauses multimillion-pound payments to Mauritius as Trump blasts ‘terrible’ Chagos deal
Andy Burnham said the government would ‘work hard’ to find a ‘resolution between the different sides’

Multimillion-pound payments to Mauritius have been paused while the UK government re-evaluates its agreement to relinquish sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago, according to the Defence Secretary.
Wes Streeting stated that the accord transferring the Chagos Islands to Mauritius "can’t go ahead without American support", following comments from US president Donald Trump branding the pact "terrible".
Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, the cabinet minister confirmed that annual disbursements amounting to at least £120 million will not be provided "at this stage".
Last May, the UK government finalised a treaty transferring sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius.
The 99-year agreement committed Britain to paying £165 million annually for the first three years, decreasing to £120 million a year thereafter, to ensure the continued presence of a joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia.
During discussions with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in New York on Tuesday, Mr Trump referred to the islands as "a very important piece of real estate, militarily and strategically".
Referring to the treaty, he told reporters at the United Nations General Assembly fringe meeting: “I don’t support it.
“I think it’s a terrible deal.”
After their meeting, Mr Burnham said the government would “work hard” to find a “resolution between the different sides”.
Mr Streeting said on Wednesday: “This deal, as it is currently constituted, can’t go ahead without American support.
“So, we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government.
“And the reason why that is important is because we are trying to safeguard not just now but for the longer term the base at Diego Garcia and the capability it provides the United Kingdom and the United States for our national and collective security.”
Asked whether the yearly payment would go ahead, the Defence Secretary said: “Not at this stage.
“We’ve got to get to a point where we can agree a deal.”
Mr Streeting added that a financial agreement would be “a price worth paying” if it secured the UK’s long-term ability to use the military base.
Asked on BBC Breakfast whether the government was reviewing the deal, Mr Streeting replied: “Yes, we have to, because the US doesn’t support it.
“What President Trump said yesterday wasn’t new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing.”
Mauritius’s claim to the Chagos Archipelago was backed by an International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling in 2019.
Mr Streeting earlier told Times Radio that while the ICJ’s ruling was “advisory now, there is a potential further course of legal action avenue open to the government of Mauritius”.
He warned that further action was “too great a risk to carry on”, in case the UK and US had to give up their military presence on the islands.
He said the administration led by former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer “got to a point where they clearly believed they did have the support of all parties involved” before concerns were raised in Washington.
“I’m not pretending that’s an easy position and that resolving this is not going to be difficult,” Mr Streeting said.
“It is difficult and necessarily painstaking work, but it is necessary.”
He added: “The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand and hoping it (will) go away, I would caution, is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world.”

A claim (archived) circulated online in September 2026 that a U.S. Secret Service agent said working for President Donald Trump had "ruined" him because of the president's kindness.
According to one Facebook user, the agent in question said:
Trump RUINED me for this job. Not because he's difficult — but because he's completely different. Trump knows my NAME. Other Presidents called me "agent." Trump calls me by my actual name.
The same claim, text and image also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived, archived, archived).
We previously investigated this rumor in March 2026 and found it false. We found then that the rumor originated from the "Garvit pandey" Facebook page, which appeared to mass-produce baseless stories about Trump using unrelated images. Snopes had previously found another such story from that page to be false.
There was no credible reporting to support the claim at the time of this writing (archived, archived, archived).The text and images that accompanied the claim appeared to have been generated or edited using artificial intelligence. This, taken together with the unreliable nature of the claim's source, led us to rate this claim false.
Users who create content like the story about the alleged Secret Service agent capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up claims, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has previously reported on the business strategy.)
A Secret Service spokesperson told Snopes via phone in March 2026 that they could not comment on the interview's authenticity without an agent's name, which neither "Garvit pandey" nor later posts included.
We contacted a manager of the "Garvit pandey" Facebook page ask for more details about the story or an explanation of why it shared the alleged quote without a disclaimer that it was false. We had not gotten a reply by September 2026.
Text and images provided clues to story's falsehood
The post on the "Garvit pandey" Facebook page displayed several signs of AI-generated text. For example, the text used all caps on some words for emphasis, a tool not generally used in traditional reporting. Pangram, a highly regarded artificial intelligence detector for images and text, assessed the Facebook post's text to be fully AI.
Let us note here: These types of AI detection tools are fallible. Snopes cautions people against using them for definitive answers on media's authenticity without supporting evidence.
Aside from likely AI-generated text, the post that circulated in September 2026 appeared to use edited or fake images that showed Trump with Secret Service agents.
Two of the images in the collage showed agents surrounding Trump at a rally in Dayton, Ohio, in 2016. However, the Facebook post used a version of one of those photos with a different background.
An authentic portrait of James M. Murray, a Trump-appointed former head of the Secret Service who stepped down in 2022, also appeared with a different background in the September 2026 Facebook post. Another image that showed Trump looking down with an agent standing behind him (upper left corner) also appeared to have been enhanced from the original and given a different background.
Pangram found the entire collage to be fully AI.
'Garvit pandey' page spreads fake stories about Trump
Snopes previously investigated the "Garvit pandey" page that originally shared the false story in March 2026. Our review found several users accusing the page of posting AI-generated stories. We also found that posts on the page contained common markers of AI-generated stories like excessive use of emojis, repetition of one core message and calls to action. The story about the Secret Service agent included all of these markers.
The above factors led us to conclude that stories on the page were either falsified or misattributed.
The fictional story about the Secret Service agent heaping praise on Trump resembled glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental."
Snopes has previously investigated other rumors involving the Secret Service, including whether a "reptilian" agent guarded former U.S. President Barack Obama and whether the service went "broke" paying for agents to guard the Trump family.

Pentagon officially adds one more soldier death to US count from Iran war
Internal Defense Department tallies indicate that as many as 23 US service members have died in the region since February, far exceeding the Pentagon’s official public numbers

The Pentagon updated its official casualty database to list 19 total U.S. military deaths related to the war with Iran after quietly adding a new fatality.
The change occurred following the death of a female Army officer who suffered a fatal medical emergency Friday while traveling to the Middle East, as reported by The Washington Post.
A U.S. defense official speaking on the condition of anonymity told the outlet that the casualty was logged into the database sometime after Monday afternoon. The death was reported earlier by Task & Purpose. Her identity has not been released.
The addition brings the total number of documented fatalities in the Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS, to 19, up from 18 recorded earlier in the week. The database also lists more than 820 service members wounded in action.
However, current and former officials indicate the public count remains incomplete. Five U.S. officials told the publication last week that at least 22 service members have died in the region since military action began on February 28, while a sixth official placed the figure at 23.
Some of those unrecorded deaths involve military personnel deployed to the region during active hostilities, even if not directly killed in combat.
In response to reports regarding the accounting discrepancies, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth rejected claims of intentional omissions.
“Even if we wanted to attempt to hide a combat death, we never would and we never could,” Hegseth said.
The accounting methods used by the Defense Department have drawn scrutiny throughout the conflict. Earlier this year, four service members killed in action were temporarily left off the official count.
Discrepancies in casualty counts carry logistical consequences beyond public record-keeping. The military conducts a formal “line of duty” inquiry for every death to determine whether it occurred during active duty, a designation that directly dictates the financial survivor benefits allocated to military families.
Within the DCAS system, 14 of the listed deaths are categorized under Operation Epic Fury, the official administration title for the military campaign against Iran.
An additional five deaths — including the female officer added this week — are listed under a separate “Overseas Operations” category, which includes casualties that occurred after a brief July ceasefire collapsed.
In addition, the Pentagon issued press releases earlier in the war acknowledging the deaths of two service members in the Middle East at bases targeted by Iranian strikes, though neither name appears in the DCAS registry.
The conflict, now in its seventh month, continues to face widespread skepticism among the public and lawmakers.
“The Washington war machine is trying to turn Iran into another Iraq,” Representative Nancy Mace, a South Carolina Republican, said in March. “Our troops are not to be used for another endless war.”
A recent Fox News poll found 60 percent of voters believed the military action in Iran was a wrong decision, while 71 percent indicated they did not believe the administration had a clear plan to end the hostilities.
In July, President Donald Trump attended a dignified transfer ceremony at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware for four service members killed during operations tied to the war.
The soldiers honored included Army 1st Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Hawaii, Army Private Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Texas, Army Sergeant Angel S. Rampersad, 28, of New York, and Army Sergeant Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, of North Carolina.
Feehan, Gonzales and Rampersad died following an attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, while Swinton was killed during a controlled detonation of a downed drone in Iraq.
Speaking to reporters on his way to the ceremony, Trump called the event “one of the hardest things to do as a president.”
“There’s no games, there’s no nothing — that’s their child,” Trump said. “And all you can do is throw out your heart.”
The Independent has contacted the Pentagon for comment.

Sport is a kind of conquest. Rulers often get one significant, special coronation that cements their legacy before their followers. Sport, though, offers that sensational feeling of ‘taking over the horizon’ on a platter, again and again, patiently allowing those who persevere to have their fill.
The Indian women’s cricket team knows the feeling, with two such anointments in the span of a week, when it was undisputedly crowned the best in Asia — a record-extending eighth Women’s Asia Cup title in Dubai and a savoured gold medal at the Asian Games in Japan, both against the same opponent: Sri Lanka. Two summit clashes, two similar submissions to authority.
A marauding top order headlined India’s unopposed quest for glory, both in Dubai and Nagoya. The tempestuous youngster in Shafali Verma has well and truly given way to a wiser allrounder, hungry to contribute to a win in every way possible.
Smriti Mandhana rose to the zenith of international cricket, leaving behind names who had influenced her in the sport. Sree Charani’s incredible year kept getting better as she hacked down a number of records while reigning supreme in the T20I rankings.
ALSO READ | Smriti Mandhana breaks record for most runs in women’s T20Is
Nothing came in the way: be it feeble attempts at a fightback from weaker opponents, an unforgiving travel itinerary that barely gave the team breathing space between the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, modest accommodation provisions or threats of a Japanese typhoon that ultimately steered clear of the Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin City.
Mismatch aplenty
Take away the passions of sporting merit from the consumption of these two tournaments, and the chronology and character pools are nearly identical. The traditional Asian top four — India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Bangladesh — are paired against starry-eyed gladiators emerging from the Qualifiers. Valiant campaigns and campaigners come up against the Full Members, akin to bringing a knife to a gunfight, and eventually get found out.
In the Asia Cup, Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong China and UAE asked the occasional tough question but were ushered out of contention without much mercy. One’s heart beats and breaks for the underdogs and keeps you invested long enough before you realise how every competition day across editions feels the same — lopsided contests, a glaring mismatch in resources and infrastructure, and a tape growing increasingly stale in an impatient consumer market where sport is primarily produced for broadcast.
The story was no different at the Asiad. While the big four — courtesy of some continuity gathered over their travels across the continent — found their rhythm, Thailand was the only constant among the rest, with Malaysia, China and Japan completing the pack. These are not random draws; qualifying tournaments guarded the gates to these stages. But as much as things change, teams improve or find their footing in the global game, the overall imbalance between the Associates and the Full Members stays the same.
ALSO READ | India wins first gold medal of Asian Games 2026 after women’s cricket team beats Sri Lanka in final
Asian teams are playing more fixtures, a welcome change from years of calendars filled with blots of emptiness. The focus now is on the quality of opponent one can afford to face.
Within the Asian fold itself, a tiered system operates where the likes of India, in particular, barely face Associates. So regardless of how futile a pampered cricket fan might think these tournaments are, they are, so far at least, the only avenues for teams to experience a top-class global opponent.
The knowledge transfer, by itself, becomes the biggest takeaway for so many of these teams. Images of Hong Kong players flocking around India’s senior players and Japan and China players lining up for photographs with women they had only watched in videos or heard about in lore passing over from the subcontinent made for heartening visuals. Hong Kong China’s Marina Lamplough’s videos through the Asia Cup, in which she showed glimpses of how the team took notes from the Indian openers’ style and strategy, are one such example.
But that’s as deep as the engagement goes. India’s ‘responsibility’ to democratise its presence in the Asian circuit now has the hurdle of a packed calendar standing before it.
In the Asian Games and Asia Cup, the eastern cricketing wave doesn’t realise what it has, Netherlands skipper Babette de Leede pointed out, highlighting Asia’s advantage over other continental groupings.
“You know how Asia has the Asian Games and the Asia Cup? We don’t have any of that in Europe. It would be great because you get more games. Look at the difference between the number of games we play and the number Australia or India play. We do have entities like the European Cricket Network... the T10 tournament they organise. Those numbers are developing. And now there’s the European T20 Premier League too. If there was something like that for us in Europe, it would be quite cool,” she told Sportstar on the sidelines of the T20 World Cup earlier this year.
ALSO READ | How Japanese women prepared for a moment of blossoming
The wish for integration isn’t random. With cricket making the Los Angeles Summer Games, the ecosystem hopes this is the start of a long stay in the Olympic roster. In 2028, six teams each will compete in the men’s and women’s events, with rankings deciding the majority of the slots and qualifiers filling the gaps. The Asian Games is no different: an eight-team tournament that begins at the quarterfinal stage in a continental showpiece involving 46 countries.
In Aichi-Nagoya, China didn’t even get to play, despite making the cut, after rain washed out its quarterfinal against Bangladesh, the latter advancing due to higher seeding. Cricket’s intense weather vulnerabilities leave teams on the bigger stage of amateur sport short-changed when months of preparation and dreams can drown in a downpour.
Work at the roots
The International Cricket Council, especially after the recent FIFA World Cup, has made its intention of expanding cricket to counter football, covertly and overtly, known. Development initiatives with Associates, infrastructure assistance and advocacy have spruced up since the turn of the decade.
The Indonesian ecosystem is a direct beneficiary, having landed Asian Cricket Council membership a few years ago. Cricket chief Abhiram Singh Yadav credits the role of former ACC president and incumbent ICC chair Jay Shah for making room for Indonesia at the high tables of Asian cricket.
“Mr. Shah thinks quite broadly about the game. He sees the potential of global markets. Indonesia is a country with a population of over 200 million. We are a G20 member. That recognition also came through in Mr. Sanjog Gupta’s (ICC CEO) visit. Both are working towards developing emerging markets and looking at non-traditional cricketing nations. With the sport now in the Olympics, this is the only way we can make cricket inclusive,” Yadav told Sportstar.
“Cricket wants to work towards becoming bigger than FIFA, and that requires looking deep into different international markets. As an Associate member, we want to support that vision. Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Japan and Korea are promising markets, and we want to be a model for others to follow,” Yadav added. UAE, too, has a promising women’s side drawing heavily from the expat Indian population in the Gulf. While the national side benefits from their quality, the Emirates Cricket Board has been trying to foster an interest in the sport among natives too.
ALSO READ | Asian Games 2026: Shafali Verma scores her maiden T20I century during Bangladesh semifinal
“I won’t say that it’s a challenge,” Emirates Cricket Board COO Subhan Ahmed told Sportstar. “If you look at the overall demographics of this country, about 80 per cent of the population is expat. So it’s natural that the sports that they have played back home and that culture travels. The infrastructure here has grown because of it. We have 62 grounds across the seven states in the Emirates. There are some Full Members who do not have that kind of base. The local Emirati population is always a part of our plans. We don’t envisage a complete takeover by the local population, but we do anticipate greater participation given how much it can do for overall community unity here,” he added.
Indonesia, too, faced the same predicament of leaning entirely on the diaspora, but Yadav underlined that the setup is on a war footing to ensure cricket can become a 100 per cent localised sport.
Sports tourism has emerged as a way to galvanise smaller boards, as Yadav pointed out earlier, allowing them to tap newer markets within cricket. Sanjog Gupta has also identified China as a potential cash cow, hoping to convert at least some of its 1.4 billion people into cricket fanatics.
The ICC pumped USD 1.5 million into cricket in the nation, broadcast World Cup games in Mandarin to whet the appetite for the game, and has also seen the cricketing system build three top-level cricket venues, including a new 1,500-seat stadium in Taicang that is primed to host domestic and international matches and provide a training base for the national teams. The Marylebone Cricket Club has chimed in with support, saying it will send a women’s team there for an overseas tour next year.
The women’s national team, made almost entirely of homegrown players, has climbed 10 spots in the rankings over the last two years, which only underlines why that faith isn’t misplaced. That Asiad washout stings that much more now, right?
Dissonance at the top
The one-sided nature of this fairytale Asian romp was known to all before the curtains rose. But even for the world’s most successful team, backed by the world’s richest board and cricketing circulatory system, multi-sport events bring with them nostalgia and old-time achievement.
Indian skipper Harmanpreet Kaur, for instance, grew up in Punjab, where tales of legendary Olympians were often served alongside a child’s daily meals. The Games — of the Asian, Commonwealth and Olympic kind — hold a special place. It’s why her creaking knees want to carry on till she makes it to Los Angeles 2028, till that Olympic gold finds its way to her neck.
ALSO READ | Asian Games a teaser to 2028 Los Angeles Olympics: India Women’s head coach Amol Muzumdar
While parallels can be drawn between India’s comfort and dominance here and what might lie ahead at the Olympics, that would be an oversimplification. At the end of the day, Olympic cricket — as it stands — is still a T20 knockout tournament, the sport’s most fickle format. It cares not for past laurels. Fortune only favours the brave here, as India learned at the Birmingham CWG when it watched Australia don gold while it made do, grudgingly, with silver.
For all the expansion, the view from the top remains fairly myopic. Players being dragged into the political theatre of handshakes and trophy tug-of-war took the sheen off what is, in theory, one of the most promising learning opportunities for teams on the fringes of the power core. If one wants to be doggedly apolitical, two high-importance tournaments in 2026 without television referrals and held at a single venue are no vote of confidence in the efforts of the custodians of the sport. The ICC can’t wash its hands off either, as the inaugural Women’s Champions Trophy — taken away from Sri Lanka due to political interference in administration — is due to be held across just two Tier 2 Indian venues.
While the prosperous continue to prosper, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh face tumultuous transitions within and outside the team. Outside India, franchise cricket is not a reality or a liberating financial avenue for any other Asian nation. FairBreak Global, an ICC-based independent initiative that brought several Asian Associate nations much-needed game time with stars from SENA countries, is now defunct.
Indonesia, for all its ambition, still played the Asia Cup without a shirt sponsor, while a Full Member nation like Afghanistan is still being shielded from accountability for failing the cardinal principle of said membership — mandatorily fielding a women’s team.
Hierarchy masquerades as competition in Asian cricket, with one crown after another for those already on top, while the rest are left arguing over scraps of legitimacy. Showpieces without follow-ups, expansion without equity and Olympic ambition without Olympic-standard competitiveness will only widen the gap the game is desperate to bridge.
