How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto says the World Athletics Championship will be "coming home", with Nairobi set to make history after being selected as the first African city to host the event in 2029.
Ruto hailed the winning bid as a "victory for generations of athletes" who have made the nation "synonymous with excellence" on the track and road.
Nairobi beat London and Rome to the hosting rights, with Munich selected to stage the 2031 edition.
After missing out on the 2025 World Championships to Tokyo, a series of factors helped Kenya see off its European rivals this time around.
A sport 'woven into the fabric' of the nation
When World Athletics president Lord Coe announced the decision in Budapest on Tuesday, he described Kenya's bid as "compelling and emotional".
The East African nation is the second-most successful nation in the history of the World Championships with 72 gold medals, placing it behind the United States.
The vast majority of those glories, alongside 38 Olympic gold medals, have come in middle- and long-distance running.
Lord Coe said that athletics is "woven into the fabric" of the nation and that Kenyans have helped "shape the history" of the sport.
He name-checked several runners including two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge - who was involved in the lobbying for Kenya's bid - men's 800m world record holder David Rudisha and multiple world and Olympic medallist Faith Kipyegon.
A passionate fanbase is also one of the country's great strengths.
Some 68% of Kenyans surveyed by World Athletics rated their interest in athletics as high, compared with a global average of 39%.
Athletics is the country's second-most followed sport, behind only football, and when World Athletics assessed its social media channels, Kenya was the fourth-highest nation in terms of followers.
Upgraded facilities
Kenya's previous bid for the 2025 edition fell down largely on the facilities which the country possessed.
This time around, the Kasarani Stadium will have gone through a complete structural upgrade well before the world's top athletes descend on Nairobi.
The 48,000-capacity venue will be used when Kenya co-hosts football's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) next June and July alongside Tanzania and Uganda.
"We learned from the 2025 bid because there were areas that we did not score well," Barnaba Korir, who worked on the successful bid, told the BBC World Service.
"Because of that, we managed to improve on those areas.
"I'm happy that the infrastructure that we have already developed will also meet the standards that we have seen all over the world."
Hotel space is one area not expected to be a problem, with Nairobi a regular host for large conventions.
"Kenya is also known for its very dynamic hospitality, the tourism sector," Elijah Mwangi, principal secretary at the State Department for Sports, told the BBC.
"It has a game park within the city, so we are waiting to welcome everybody."
President Ruto made financial and security guarantees in order to secure the Championships.
"We thank World Athletics for the confidence it has placed in Kenya," Ruto said.
"We will honour that confidence by delivering an unforgettable championship worthy of our athletes, our country and our continent."
Expanding athletics
Lord Coe became president of World Athletics (then known as the IAAF) in 2015 and has pledged to grow the sport around the globe.
During his time in office the World Championships have been hosted in Qatar (2019), the United States (2022) and Tokyo, while China's capital Beijing will stage them in 2027.
Kenya has successfully hosted age-grade events in Nairobi and the World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, while the World Athletics Relays were held in Botswana's capital Gaborone in May.
With Coe's third term in office coming to an end next year, one official involved in Kenya's bid, speaking before the host announcement, said it was "unthinkable" that Nairobi would not succeed.
"With this decision we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide," Coe said.
"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances.
Coe hailed the "quality, ambition and commitment" of all four bidding cities.
London, Munich and Rome have all previously held the Olympics, with the World Championships in London as recently as 2017, but the chance to break new ground in Africa was clearly compelling.
UK Athletics chief executive Jack Buckner said his team was "deeply disappointed" to see London miss out.
What is needed next?
Kenya now faces logistical and organisational challenges over the next three years as it prepares to deliver Africa's first World Championships.
With the 2027 Afcon looming large on the horizon, Nairobi will have a chance to test-run getting fans in and out of the Kasarani Stadium, which lies about a half-hour drive from the city's central business district.
The venue does not have any rail connections but Korir says World Athletics officials were "very satisfied" by Kenya's transport plan.
There were instances of overcrowding when the stadium hosted Kenya games at football's African Nations Championships last year, which led to the capacity being reduced for some matches.
Delays in preparations for Afcon have raised concerns, and the funding for the World Championships will come entirely from the Kenyan government.
Mwangi revealed that $78m (£58.5m) is the current estimate for the government's contribution, with sponsorship deals also playing a role.
"We are prepared to ensure that whatever is expected to be paid, it is paid in the due time," he added.
Presidential elections are scheduled for next year, but Korir is confident organisers will secure the "huge" and "legally binding" figure earmarked even if there is a change in government.
"Whatever the government assigns now will be observed by the next government. It is an international agreement," he said.
Then comes ticketing, first to make sure the local population are not priced out and then to ensure the stands are filled.
The cheapest tickets for the Under-18 World Championships in 2017 were priced at 200 Kenyan shillings ($1.15, £1.14) but attendances were low until entry was made free.
World Athletics generated $522m in revenue from Tokyo 2025, with a total of 619,000 tickets sold over the nine days of competition, while London sold a record 705,000 tickets in 2017.
In passing up the opportunity of returning to the British capital, World Athletics has chosen expansion over guaranteed ticket sales, but attendances will be scrutinised - especially after the sparse numbers seen in the stands in Doha in 2019.
Korir, however, is confident the Kasarani Stadium "will be full" on "every day" of competition, including morning sessions, if sales begin early enough.
Meanwhile, Kenya has endured a spate of doping scandals in recent years, with 11 individuals banned by the Athletics Integrity Unit so far this year alone.
The pressure is now on the East African nation to deliver on its promises in the build-up to Nairobi 2029 and ensure the Championships pass off without any major issues.
Additional reporting by Ian Williams and Celestine Karoney.

Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC
- Published
Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.
He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.
Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad.
"We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," Sinkevičius told the BBC.
"We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."
Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat".
It comes just a week after Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.
Though the origins of the drone have not been confirmed, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it came from the direction of Belarus, Lithuania's neighbour and a key Russian ally.
The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace.
"We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."
Moscow did not comment on the incident.
Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5.5, its latest flagship AI model, touting stronger performance, lower running costs, faster output, and enhanced safeguards. Anthropic said Claude Opus 5.5 performs at the level of its more powerful Claude Fable 5.1 model on most tasks while costing 40% less to run on typical workloads than its predecessor, Claude Opus 5. The new model also generates output over 30% faster. Claude Opus 5.5 is priced at $4 per Mn input tokens and $20 per Mn output tokens, 20% lower than Opus 5. However, Anthropic estimates that typical workloads will cost about 40% less because the new model also uses fewer tokens to complete tasks. Cache reads, which Anthropic said constitute a majority of the costs associated with agentic and coding workloads, are priced 60% lower at $0.20 per Mn tokens. Anthropic is positioning Opus 5.5 for agentic coding, computer use, and knowledge work. On the CursorBench 4.0 coding benchmark, the model scored 52.5% at its default effort setting, compared with GPT-5.6 Sol’s top score of 41.7%, while costing about one-third as much per task, according to the company. The company also said Opus 5.5 communicates more naturally than previous models, puts important information upfront, avoids jargon, and follows users’ writing instructions more consistently. The model is available to Claude Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise subscribers. Developers can access it through the Claude Platform, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. The launch comes less than three weeks after OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra, positioning the model as a major step towards more autonomous AI systems. Astra can navigate websites, interact with software, work with documents and spreadsheets, write and test code, and execute multi-step workflows. The launch will be followed by Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, which will be released in the coming weeks, bringing many of the same performance, speed and safety improvements. AI Safeguards In Focus For Anthropic Earlier this month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on AI companies to “pace the frontier”, arguing that safety practices and public policy need to keep up with rapidly advancing model capabilities. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also expressed support for slowing AI development under certain circumstances. Anthropic said Opus 5.5 is its first model release since it called for pacing frontier AI development. The model underwent predeployment evaluations by external organisations, including Frontier Design and nonprofit research organisation METR. The latter said its preliminary evaluation focused on the model’s potential impact on AI R&D and did not assess its alignment properties. Separately, Anthropic said Opus 5.5 scored better than previous systems in internal safety tests and was about 85% less likely than Opus 5 or Mythos 5.1 to attempt to bypass containment boundaries in a dedicated evaluation. The debate over frontier AI regulation and safeguards has gained urgency following incidents involving AI agents operating beyond their intended restrictions, alongside growing concerns over AI being used for cyberattacks, fraud and other malicious activities.

You can get Google Pixel’s Rambler AI voice typing on many Android phones without root by patching a supported Gboard version with Morphe. Once enabled, Rambler can clean up speech, remove filler words, fix grammar, add punctuation, and format dictated text using AI.
If there is one feature that truly revolutionized because of AI, it is voice typing. Voice typing did exist way before AI, but it was very basic. It only converted the spoken audio directly into text, which included all the filler words, missing punctuation, grammar mistakes, and more. It basically turned whatever you spoke into text.
But with AI, voice typing goes through one extra step, where all your typing is fed to the AI models, which remove all filler words and format the sentence structure. It fundamentally eliminates the need for you to copy text into multiple apps, fix the grammar and sentence structure, and then copy it again to wherever you need it.
Third-party voice dictation apps went ahead and also included support for different formatting styles based on the app you are using, and they support almost every app.
However, the AI voice dictation feature truly gained traction after Google introduced the Pixel 11’s Rambler feature, which is very similar to AI voice dictation apps that use AI to refine the speech-to-text output.
However, currently, this feature is officially available on Pixel 11 series devices. You can see the full requirements here. But with a single patch for your Google Gboard, you can get this feature on a supported Android device. In this video, you are going to learn exactly how to get the Google Pixel’s Rambler feature on another Android device without root.

How to Get Pixel 11 Rambler Voice Typing on Any Android Without Root
Before we get started, here are the prerequisites
Download the supported Gboard 18.0.3.954559732-release-arm64-v8a APK from here, or you can skip this if you want to download the supported version directly from Morphe

- Android 10+ (Android 12+ recommended)
- Requires Sideloading enabled
Download the Morphe app for Android. It lets you patch your apps. For those who are unaware, patching is basically modifying the app and adding features that don’t exist.
Step 1: Download the Morphe app on your Android phone. Visit the official Morphe GitHub page and tap Download. Or download directly from the official Morphe site
Step 2: Once downloaded, install the app.
Step 3: Open the Morphe app and tap on Sources.

Step 5: Wait for the source to load and tap on the Gboard app.
Step 6: Now tap on Yes, Help me find an APK, tap on Download APK, and download the app. Don’t install it.
Step 7: Now go back to the Morphe app, tap on Open APK file, and select the Gboard 18.0.3.954559732-release-arm64-v8a APK or later you downloaded above, and Morphe will start patching the app.
Step 8: Once patched, tap Install the app and allow Morphe to install the app on your device.
Step 9: Now open the patched Gboard and enable it. You need to set it as the default keyboard on some Android phones to use it, or you can go through the permission setup and switch to this keyboard later.
Step 10: Now open the patched Gboard and tap on Settings, scroll down, and tap on Patches.
Step 11: Tap on Advanced Voice Typing and enable the Enable Advanced Voice Typing option.
Step 12: Once enabled, go back to Voice Typing Settings and then select the Rambler feature.
Step 13: Now, to use the feature, you need to force stop the app. To do that, go to the patched Gboard app, long-press on it, tap on the i icon, then tap on the Force Stop option, and then confirm. These steps may vary depending on your smartphone brand and Android version.
Step 14: Now open any app where you can type, bring up patched Gboard, tap on the microphone icon, and start using Rambler.

FAQs on Using Google Rambler on Non-Pixel Phones
1. Is it safe to use a patched version of Gboard with my Google account?
Yes, it is safe to install if you follow my steps exactly and only use the resources I included in this guide. For safety, I also highly recommend checking the app before installing using Google Play Protect or using third-party antivirus scanner tools like VirusTotal.
2. Will Rambler continue working after Gboard or Android gets updated?
Yes, since you are using a separate Gboard patched version, updating the original Gmail app won’t affect this patched version. However, the patched version also needs to be updated in case Google blocks access to the Rambler feature for other devices.
3. Can I switch back to the official Gboard later without losing my keyboard settings?
You won’t lose any settings; you can simply switch back to the original Gboard if you want to anytime.

Yes, the Google Pixel Rambler feature uses cloud processing to fix sentences; however, Google says this data is not saved, stored, or shared and is deleted immediately after the processed text is delivered.

For the second time this year, the Department of Health and Human Services announced a new set of strategies to speed a shift toward human-based research methods and reduce the use of animals in medical testing.
The Food and Drug Administration issued a final rule stating that research methods other than animal testing can be used when “appropriate” for determining the safety of drugs and biologics. Specifically, the rule replaces terms like “animal tests” and “animal studies” with “nonclinical tests” and “nonclinical studies.”
“We are moving HHS toward a new era of biomedical research that puts human biology at the center of science,” health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a statement. “We are modernizing outdated regulations, investing in human-based technologies, and breaking down barriers that have kept researchers dependent on animal models when better tools are available.”

Trump bought and sold SpaceX stock in July, financial disclosure shows
The satellite, space, and AI business achieved a valuation of $1.77 trillion on June 12 after pricing the largest US initial public offering in history
Recent public financial disclosures reveal that President Donald Trump purchased up to $50,000 in SpaceX stock and later unloaded up to $15,000 worth of the holdings in July, marking his latest transactions involving the Elon Musk-led defense contractor.
Documented in an ethics filing signed on September 8, the president acquired between $15,001 and $50,000 worth of shares in the company on July 10.
He subsequently divested between $1,001 and $15,000 in stock on July 17.
These recent stock dealings deepen the financial ties between the president and the rocket enterprise owned by his former adviser, arriving as the federal administration weighs regulatory decisions capable of influencing the firm's business prospects.
The satellite, space, and AI business achieved a valuation of $1.77 trillion on June 12 after pricing the largest US initial public offering in history.
Trump had also bought shares in the company that same month, as previously reported by Reuters.
Between July 10 and July 17, the span covering the president's buy and sell dates, SpaceX stock dropped 15%.
Addressing earlier disclosures, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Reuters that independent financial management firms oversee the president's investments, mirroring benchmark trackers "such as the Schwab 1000."
A spokesperson for Trump did not immediately reply to requests for comment regarding the July transactions.
The Office of Government Ethics published the document online Tuesday. The transactions formed part of more than 1,000 investments executed by the president throughout July.
Because federal reporting guidelines require officials to list asset values within defined ranges, the exact total of Trump's financial stake remains unspecified.
As a key U.S. military contractor, SpaceX routinely submits applications for federal regulatory approvals.

A journalist once barred from the White House says this media ban is different
Former CNN correspondent Jim Acosta on White House's ban of 3 media outlets
Jim Acosta knows what it is like to be kicked out of the White House.
In 2018, President Trump revoked Acosta's press pass after a contentious news conference, when Acosta was CNN's chief White House correspondent. A federal judge temporarily restored his access, and the White House ultimately backed down.
Now, with CNN, MS NOW and Politico barred from the White House, Acosta says the stakes are broader, and so is the response. The three organizations have sued, alleging violations of their First and Fifth Amendment rights. Major television networks also declined to replace CNN in the White House video pool.
NPR is not using audio from White House events until further notice, in solidarity with several news organizations barred from White House grounds.
"This is aimed at three specific news organizations, and we just can't allow that to happen," Acosta told Morning Edition. "And so, it's a good thing to see the press showing some solidarity."
Acosta said that solidarity should have come sooner, pointing to restrictions imposed on the Associated Press after it refused to use Trump's preferred name, Gulf of America, for the Gulf of Mexico.
Trump has said the outlets were barred because of coverage he considers unfair and overly negative.The White House has also cited a study by the conservative media watchdog group Media Research Center saying 92% of coverage of Trump during the first 100 days of his second term was negative. The administration argues that the First Amendment protects the outlets' right to publish but does not entitle them to White House access.
Acosta rejected the idea that journalists should think of coverage as positive or negative, saying their job is to report news that matters to the public. He said Trump's objections, "by and large," are to being fact-checked.
"Do we just allow truth to become lies and lies to become truth," Acosta asked, "or are we there to provide sort of a safety valve for the American people to make sure they're getting fair, accurate information at all times, no matter who's in charge, without fear or favor?"

IPO-bound B2B seafood brand Captain Fresh crossed the ₹5,000 Cr revenue mark in FY26, while its adjusted EBITDA nearly tripled as the company continued to remain profitable for the second consecutive year. The Bengaluru-based company reported a consolidated net revenue of ₹5,169 Cr in FY26, up 52% from ₹3,397 Cr in FY25. Adjusted EBITDA rose 2.7X to ₹371 Cr from ₹136 Cr in the previous fiscal, it said in a statement. Captain Fresh’s gross margin also expanded to 23.5% in FY26 from 17% in FY25. While the company did not disclose its FY26 bottom line, it claimed it remained PAT-positive. Captain Fresh is yet to file its audited financial statements for the fiscal year. In FY25, it posted a net profit of ₹42 Cr. The company claimed that it is now on track to achieve ₹10,000 Cr in revenue in FY27, with its focus shifting towards scaling its existing portfolio and infrastructure. “FY26 stress tested the industry in the form of tariffs and an unsettled trade environment, and we came out stronger than we went in,” group CFO and whole-time director Mathew George said. Captain Fresh had ₹2,300 Cr debt at the end of FY26, of which ₹440 Cr was long-term debt, while the remainder comprised working capital financing. Its debt-to-equity ratio stood at 1.6 during the year, which it is also targeting to reduce to 1.3-1.5. The company said it carried higher inventory during FY26 to ensure uninterrupted customer supply amid global disruptions. This, it said, was the reason behind its higher working capital requirements during the fiscal. As operating conditions normalise, Captain Fresh expects this inventory build-up to reverse. Captain Fresh said its receivables are insured and that none of them were disputed during the period under review. Zooming Into Captain Fresh’s Business Founded in 2020 by Utham Gowda, Captain Fresh began as a tech-led B2B seafood supply chain platform and has since expanded into a global packaged seafood business. It operates a portfolio of seafood brands across Europe and North America. Its European processing footprint includes Frime in Spain, Koral in Poland, Senecrus in France and CFT in Denmark through a joint venture. In North America, it distributes through CenSea, Ocean Garden and Ocean Edge, largely across foodservice channels. The company sources seafood from more than 30 countries across three oceans. In FY26, Ecuador accounted for 17% of sourcing, followed by Indonesia at 15%, India at 12%, and Vietnam at 9%. Captain Fresh said it serves nearly 2,500 customers, including more than 50 of the world’s largest seafood buyers. Captain Fresh’s Delayed IPO Plans The FY26 performance comes as Captain Fresh continues to prepare for a potential public listing. After converting into a public entity in June 2025, it confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI for a $400 Mn IPO in August 2025, comprising a $200 Mn fresh issue and a $150-200 Mn offer-for-sale component. However, it withdrew the IPO papers in December 2025, citing delays in obtaining regulatory clearances for a European acquisition. The company said it planned to refile after securing the approvals. The acquisition in question was completed in March 2026, when Captain Fresh acquired Spanish tuna processor Frime. However, it is yet to refile its IPO papers. The company subsequently raised ₹290 Cr in debt from Blue Earth Capital to scale manufacturing, global distribution and hiring. Captain Fresh has raised nearly $250 Mn to date from investors including Accel, Tiger Global, Prosus Ventures, Z47, Evolvence Group, and British International Investment.

Shares of ecommerce major Meesho surged as much as 9.3% during the intraday trading after brokerage UBS maintained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock and raised its target price to ₹260 from ₹210. The stock touched an intraday high of ₹239.45 on the BSE. It was trading 8.9% higher at ₹238.55 at 11:25 IST. At the current price, UBS’ revised target implies a further upside of around 9%. At its current price, the stock is trading nearly 115% above its IPO issue price of ₹111 and about 6% below its 52-week high of ₹254.65.

Imagine handing an AI agent a task you would normally give to a junior employee: open the company’s software, find the right customer record, fill in a form, check a few details and send the result back. You simply assign AI the job and let it work. OpenAI claims to have achieved just that, with the launch of GPT-6 Astra earlier this month. Unlike a chatbot that simply responds to prompts, Astra can take on a task and work through a computer like a human would. OpenAI calls Astra its most intelligent and aligned model yet. But what drew more attention was OpenAI president Greg Brockman’s proclamation of the arrival of “the AGI era” at a press briefing following the launch. OpenAI is not alone in pushing AI towards greater autonomy. Zhipu, a major Chinese AI company, says its general language model, GLM, helped build the computing infrastructure it now runs on. Google DeepMind and Anthropic are also developing AI agents capable of taking action, albeit with their own limits and safeguards. But none of them has explicitly claimed that their models have achieved AGI. If everyone is moving in the same direction, why is there still no consensus that the AGI era has arrived? Perhaps because there is no fixed definition of AGI, and no universally agreed threshold for what would count as reaching it. Therefore, in this edition of The AI Shift, we explore whether we have already crossed the AGI threshold, and if not, how far we are from reaching it. But first... What Is AGI? AGI stands for artificial general intelligence. But there is no universally accepted definition of what it actually means. OpenAI’s public document on its principles defines AGI as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. Its benchmark is based on how much economically valuable work a system can do, rather than how it thinks. However, Mayank Verma, the global head of data & AI at Xebia, an AI-first consulting and software engineering firm, calls AGI “a state rather than a point”. According to him, there is also no agreed checklist, and each large lab sets its own thresholds. OpenAI tests whether its models can find and exploit previously unknown software vulnerabilities, with Astra becoming the first to cross its highest bar on that evaluation. Anthropic uses safety levels to determine what safeguards are required before deploying increasingly capable models. Google DeepMind tracks critical capabilities across areas including autonomy, biosecurity, cybersecurity and AI research. These evaluations can tell us what a model is capable of but do not establish that a system is generally intelligent. The closest neutral measure comes from METR, a non-profit that evaluates AI. It tracks how long a task an agent can complete on its own, and that number doubles every few months, now reaching 14-hour tasks. The Big AGI Debate The claims are coming from the top. Earlier this month, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang posted on X that “AGI has arrived”, pointing to the scale of Astra’s training run while utilising NVIDIA’s Grace Blackwell GPUs. Paras Chopra, founder of Bengaluru-based AI research lab Lossfunk, takes a practical view. “Different people have different definitions of AGI, but for all practical purposes I believe we have AGI,” he said, arguing that the labs’ growing focus on self-improvement is evidence of the shift. DeepMind cofounder Shane Legg has also signalled that the AGI conversation has moved beyond theories. But others reject the premise. Yann LeCun, a pioneer of modern AI, told the India AI Impact Summit in February that AGI is overhyped. Umakant Soni, cofounder and CEO of Bharat1.ai, a Bengaluru-based AI research initiative, agrees. “AGI is a marketing term and doesn't mean anything. What we should talk about is actual usable intelligence. How useful is AI in our daily life," Soni said For Soni, the point is not replacing people but solving problems — from an ageing population and climate change to what he calls the “birth lottery” — by using AI to accelerate scientific breakthroughs. Between the camps sits the view Xebia’s Verma brings from large enterprises. “Businesses are not waiting for the answer. Agents already produce better presentations than people do. A definition does not really matter for businesses.” However, for AI labs, defining AGI could determine how we understand what comes next. What’s Next In The Age Of AGI? The debate over AGI is giving way to another question: what comes next? OpenAI’s Sam Altman already talks about early superintelligence: systems that beat people across the board. Zhipu raised about $5 Bn this month to train the next generation of intelligence inside environments the previous one built. OpenAI says it already has an automated research intern and is aiming for a fully automated AI researcher by March 2028. But the progress is arriving alongside a growing record of failures. In July, OpenAI said its models had escaped a sealed test environment and reached outside systems, calling the incident a cautionary tale. Anthropic disclosed a similar case soon after. In September, Spain’s data protection agency disclosed its first data breach involving an autonomous agent, which modified personal data. "Agents are already more powerful than what we think," said Verma, and since the July episode happened inside a sandbox with guardrails, the next round of spending will go into control and decision boundaries. As AI gets closer to acting on its own, the challenge will be to make our safeguards as capable as the systems they are meant to control — so that general intelligence works for us, not against us. Top Stories From India & Around The World Pocket FM’s AI Bet: The audio streaming startup is targeting a 15%-20% EBITDA margin against about 5% now on the back of AI-led efficiencies. It also plans to enter Japan and South Korea within six to eight months and is weighing AI anime, interactive stories and gaming formats. OpenAI & Anthropic Back Pacing Frontier AI: The frontier labs have endorsed independent evaluations, common safety standards and closer government-industry coordination on frontier development. The risk here is if the largest labs shape those rules, costs and compliance burdens could make it harder for smaller rivals to compete, a live question for India's AI startups. Amazon Blocks Meta's Muse: Close on the heels of Meta recently launching AI assistant Muse, the ecommerce giant began showing shoppers a pop-up over the weekend stating that continued access by an unauthorised AI agent violates its conditions of use. This follows Amazon's earlier action against Perplexity's shopping bot. VerifAIX Bags $5 Mn: The AI-based chip verification platform has raised about ₹48 Cr in a seed round co-led by Endiya Partners and Bluehill VC. The 2024-founded startup checks whether AI-generated chip designs match their original specifications, and will use the funds to grow its engineering teams in the US, India and Israel. The Weekly Buzz: Claude Builds Claude Anthropic has published data that shows that Claude now leads roughly 26% of the company’s own AI research and development work, up from under 1% in February. The internal “R&D Automation Index” tracks how much of the pipeline for successor models is already driven by the current AI system rather than human researchers. The sharp rise is one of the clearest public signals yet that recursive self-improvement has moved from theoretical concern into daily lab practice. Claude is no longer only assisting with isolated tasks; it is increasingly directing substantial portions of the work that will produce the next generation of models. At the same time, Anthropic is reportedly accelerating plans for a November IPO and weighing an earlier model release to stay competitive. The combination of rapid internal automation and continued commercial urgency highlights the dual pressure facing frontier labs: using their own systems to accelerate progress while still claiming to manage the risks that acceleration creates. Whether the 26% figure represents controlled leverage or the early stages of a faster feedback loop remains the central open question. Startup In The Spotlight: Base14 Founded in 2025 by Nilakanta Mallick, Ranjan Sakalley and Irfan Shah, Bengaluru-based Base14 is building a unified observability platform to give engineering teams a single view of their software infrastructure. As software systems grow more complex, engineering teams end up running separate tools for logs, metrics, performance and traces. That splits their data across dashboards, inflates monitoring costs and makes it harder to trace the root cause when something breaks in production. Instead of stitching those tools together, base14 brings telemetry data across logs, metrics, traces, RUM, APM and LLM/AI data into one layer through its platform Scout, so teams keep live production context in a single place. Scout uses that unified data layer to monitor applications, flag anomalies and debug production issues, and the startup claims the platform handles full-cardinality data without sampling while reducing observability costs significantly compared with legacy platforms. The startup is also expanding into AI-native developer infrastructure with Scope, a prompt-management and evaluation platform that lets teams version, test and deploy prompts while tracking latency, cost and output quality. Early customers include Glomo, DPDZero and Zinc Learning Labs. With those early customers, base14 is tapping India's application performance management market, which generated $291.1 Mn in revenue in 2024 and is expected to reach $723.4 Mn by 2030 as AI scales, driving demand for observability and granular data insights. Prompt Of The Week What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work? Here’s Anuj Gupta, founder & CEO of KiteFishAI, with a prompt he uses to challenge assumptions, stress-test ideas and make better decisions while building an AI company: “You are my toughest strategic thinking partner, not my assistant. Here is the situation: I need you to: Identify the assumptions behind my thinking and which ones may be wrong Give me the strongest argument against my current point of view Tell me what I may be overlooking, underestimating or taking for granted Separate facts, assumptions, signals and opinions Think through the second- and third-order consequences of my options Identify how different stakeholders could react and what incentives may influence them Give me 3 possible strategic paths, including one that challenges how I have framed the problem Recommend the path you believe has the highest strategic value and explain why Do not optimise for agreeing with me. Optimise for helping me make a better decision.” Editor’s Note: Some prompts may need to be adjusted by users for best results or may not work as intended for certain users.

Cities and counties around the US are angry at the Trump administration over a proposal to override local rules that govern the deployment of wired broadband networks.
The Federal Communications Commission has been taking public comments on a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that proposes to preempt state and local permitting rules. The FCC argues that too many local governments “excessively delay approvals and seek to extract exorbitant sums from providers, resulting in costs that render some deployments infeasible.”
The FCC plan is supported by broadband providers, but local governments told the FCC that it would override rules that protect public safety. Local governments say the plan is illegal and that the FCC should instead focus on how Internet providers thwart competition with permit-hoarding and other tactics that prevent competitors from deploying networks.
The FCC docket has drawn many comments from leaders of individual municipalities, and from groups representing local governments nationwide. They object to FCC plans to impose a 120-day deadline for processing permits and to proposed limits on fees and compensation that local governments can require from providers.
“Local permitting is not a barrier to broadband deployment—it is an essential public safety function protecting residents, taxpayers, and all users of finite, multi-tenant public rights-of-way. The complex coordination required to safely deploy wireline telecommunications infrastructure in, above, and below public roadways cannot be reduced to an arbitrary federal deadline,” said a September 21 filing by the United States Conference of Mayors, National Association of Counties, National League of Cities, and National Association of Telecommunications Officers and Advisors.
Cities say ISPs drag feet in deployment
While the FCC says it is trying to speed up broadband deployment, local governments say ISPs themselves are often to blame for delays. The groups representing local governments urged the FCC to issue new rules that apply to the providers and suggested a requirement that ISPs deploy networks within 180 days of local authorization.
“We ask the commission to address provider delays, failures to deploy, and permit-hoarding,” the groups told the FCC. They wrote that ISPs often fail to promptly deploy networks after obtaining approvals from local governments:
Local governments’ efforts to attract telecommunications infrastructure investment to their communities often lead to frustration due to applicants’ permit-hoarding and other bad-faith actions by providers intended to crowd out competition in sought-after locations and routes, regardless of the provider’s actual intent to deploy and provide service or upgrades. Providers are aware that local governments have limited resources and existing legal obligations to review and process complete permits in a timely manner, and will generally do so in the order they are received. When a provider stakes “claimed” space on a pole or structure through permits, requests for make-ready work, or other actions—regardless of actual intent or ability to deploy in a timely fashion—this limits the ability of other providers to deploy in those same locations, particularly if a city must make decisions and recommendations based on elements such as the physical capacity of a structure given the assumption that the provider that has completed the permitting process will deploy soon.
Another filing submitted by the League of California Cities said the FCC has no authority to adopt the proposal. “Federal preemption of traditional state and local authority over public property, construction, public safety, permitting, and rights-of-way management should rest on clear congressional authorization,” the filing said. “The commission should not infer broad preemptive authority where Congress did not expressly provide it.”
The FCC claimed authority to preempt local rules under Section 253 of the Communications Act, which says that no state or local requirement “may prohibit or have the effect of prohibiting the ability of any entity to provide any interstate or intrastate telecommunications service.” The FCC argues that certain permitting rules have the effect of prohibiting broadband deployment.
FCC claims authority under Title II
Section 253 is part of Title II, which gives the FCC authority to regulate telecommunications companies as common carriers. While Democratic FCC leaders in previous administrations used Title II to regulate broadband providers and impose net neutrality rules, a 2025 appeals court decision determined that broadband is an “information service” and can’t be regulated as a telecommunications service.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has consistently opposed Title II regulation of broadband providers, maintaining that broadband is not a telecommunications service. With Carr now relying on Title II to preempt local broadband rules, his FCC plan argues that the infrastructure deployed by broadband providers is used for “both telecommunications and non-telecommunications services.”
A filing by Minnesota cities said the current FCC is making the same mistake it made during the first Trump administration, when its attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws was blocked in court. Without Title II regulation of broadband providers, the FCC can’t convert “a federal policy of nonregulation into independent preemptive authority,” the Minnesota cities’ filing said.
If the FCC finalizes its new preemption plan, city and state governments could sue and ask a court to rule that the agency exceeded its authority.
Preemption plan
The FCC said its preemption plan would “establish a rebuttable presumption that state and local governments have effectively prohibited the provision of wireline telecommunications services if they fail to process all authorizations for use of public rights-of-way to provide wireline telecommunications services or to deploy wireline telecommunications infrastructure within 120 days.”
The FCC intends to limit fees charged by state and local governments “to a reasonable approximation of the government’s actual, direct costs of managing the rights-of-way.” The FCC is proposing to establish “safe harbor fee levels that presumptively comply” with the standard but hasn’t settled on specific amounts yet.
The FCC plan would also limit the value of in-kind compensation demanded by state and local governments and prohibit localities from imposing additional requirements or fees “on the basis that the wireline telecommunications infrastructure may be used to provide other services.”
The filing by the United States Conference of Mayors and other groups pointed out that federal agencies, such as the Bureau of Land Management and US Forest Service, have a 270-day deadline for processing permits related to wireless and fiber deployments on federal property. There is no consequence if the agencies don’t meet those deadlines, and there are many delays due to staffing shortages, the groups’ filing said.
The federal standard of 270 days shows that the FCC’s “120-day proposal is arbitrary and bears no connection to the realities of permitting processes and procedures,” the filing said. Meanwhile, the proposed limits on fees would override local governments’ ability to obtain reasonable compensation for private, commercial use of public property, the filing said. The groups said the plan “raises significant federalism concerns” and doesn’t fully account “for the actual costs and burdens of right-of-way deployment borne by local governments.”
ISPs want even shorter deadlines
Cable providers support the FCC proposal. “Unreasonable delays in issuing authorizations for access and use of public right-of-way and infrastructure materially inhibit the provision of telecommunications services,” wrote America’s Communications Association, which represents small and medium-size cable companies.
The cable lobby group said 120 days should be an “outer bound” and that some kinds of “simple” right-of-way permits should have a 45-day deadline. Telco lobby group USTelecom urged the FCC to limit fees and said that 60- and 90-day deadlines would provide cities and towns with enough time to review applications.
The deadline for the first round of comments passed yesterday, and the FCC will accept reply comments until November 5. The FCC would finalize new rules sometime after that, assuming it doesn’t drop the proposal entirely.
Carr appears intent on approving some form of the plan. “There are some jurisdictions where providers continue to face lengthy delays, excessive fees, and unpredictable permitting processes that can postpone projects for months or even years,” Carr said in June, when the FCC issued the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking.
Carr acknowledged that cities and towns may be frustrated by provider delays. But he proposed that ISPs be given “incentives” to build networks faster, rather than face new legal requirements. Carr said the FCC call for comments asks for input on “how we can incentivize providers to act quickly on any granted authorizations so that state and local governments have more certainty that deployments will be completed and that their resources are being correctly applied.”
Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez approved the step of asking the public for input but signaled she would vote against the final proposal. “I am dubious about the commission’s authority under Section 253 to use rulemaking to preempt states and localities when it comes to their management of rights of way and fees charged to providers,” she said. Gomez also noted that “states and localities face large volumes of requests that they may or may not have the resources to respond to as rapidly as providers would like.”
Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

Luxury spending is holding up in parts of Asia even as the AI-fueled stock-market rallies that helped create new wealth have stumbled.
In South Korea and Japan, affluent consumers are still spending on jewelry, watches, and other luxury goods after huge gains in AI-linked stocks swelled household wealth.
The trend is most apparent in South Korea, where Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and other technology companies powered a historic stock-market rally earlier this year.
Markets have since turned volatile, but consumer spending has proved more resilient.
"Buoyant revenues for technology firms have helped to drive large bonuses and dividend payouts, as well as wealth effects from rising stock prices, the combined impact of which has boosted consumption spending in the first half of 2026," Rajiv Biswas, CEO of Asia-Pacific Economics, told Business Insider.
Korean spending slowed in July before rebounding in September, a dip the bank attributed partly to market swings, Kathleen Oh, the chief Korea and Taiwan economist at Morgan Stanley, wrote in a September 17 report. She added that consumer confidence in the spending recovery remained intact.
The bank raised its forecast for private consumption growth this year to 2.6% from 2.2%, citing stronger household incomes, fiscal support, rising wealth, and inbound tourism.
Department stores and luxury companies are going strong
The resilience is showing up at department stores.
At Shinsegae, one of South Korea's biggest high-end department-store operators, same-store sales rose 15% from a year earlier in August, according to Bank of America, with luxury sales up 20%. Revenue from international customers jumped 82%.
The strength fits a pattern BofA has found in past market cycles. Korean department-store sales tend to follow increases in household equity investment, with the relationship strongest at a lag of about a year.
Luxury companies are seeing strong demand, too.
LVMH reported strong first-half growth in Asia outside Japan. CEO Bernard Arnault highlighted the "remarkable performance" of Louis Vuitton's new stores in Seoul and Beijing as one factor behind faster growth in the second quarter.
Richemont, the owner of Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, also reported strong demand. Asia-Pacific sales rose 21% in the quarter ended June, with South Korea and Taiwan among its strongest markets.
But the latest numbers suggest the spending boom is cooling after a blockbuster first half that sent both luxury sales and shares of South Korea's major department-store operators soaring alongside the broader market.
"Demand is no longer uniformly strong, but it is not breaking either," JPMorgan analysts wrote in a September 18 report.
Luxury demand had cooled since July as market volatility increased, with jewelry, watches, and top-tier brands holding up better than the broader category, the analysts added.
More AI money could still reach consumers
Stock-market gains are only one way the AI boom is reaching Korean households.
Morgan Stanley now expects the country's semiconductor windfall to spread more broadly through investment, government finances, and household income.
"Korea is poised to monetize the semis super-cycle on a scale and with durability of historic proportions," its economists wrote, saying the benefits could spread through the economy over the next three to five years.
Employee pay is one channel.
Morgan Stanley estimates Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix could generate 66.7 trillion won, or $49 billion, in combined gross employee compensation this year, rising to 107.6 trillion won in 2027 and 114.9 trillion won in 2028.
Average annual liquid bonus capacity between 2026 and 2028 could be about 20 times the 2025 level, the bank added.
That leaves another source of spending power even if stock-market gains become less reliable.
Japan's big spenders
Japan's high-end retailers are also seeing affluent domestic shoppers spend as the country's stock market has also rallied strongly this year, with AI-linked chip and equipment makers among the biggest winners.
At Takashimaya, one of Japan's largest high-end department-store chains, in-store sales rose 3.9% in August from a year earlier.
Meanwhile, Richemont's sales in Japan surged 36% in the quarter ended June, driven by both domestic customers and tourists. Hermès reported an 11% increase in first-half Japanese sales at constant exchange rates.
Biswas said the AI wealth effect is likely to be more muted in Japan.
"The majority of Japanese households have low direct exposure to the stock market, with a strong focus on low-risk fixed income assets," he said.
Taiwan offers a longer-running example.
Around Hsinchu Science Park — home to TSMC and hundreds of companies in its semiconductor supply chain — years of chip wealth have fueled demand for housing, luxury retail, and premium services.
Former farmland has given way to luxury apartment towers, while home prices have climbed beyond the reach of many longtime residents.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to travel to the United States in December to attend the G20 Leaders' Summit in Florida, India Today reported on Wednesday.
The summit is scheduled for 14 and 15 December at the Trump National Doral Miami resort, where US President Donald Trump will host leaders of the world's major economies.
The Indian government has not yet made a formal announcement on Modi's possible visit.
PM Modi-Donald Trump meeting likely on G20 sidelines
If Modi travels to Florida, he is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Trump on the sidelines of the G20 Summit, as per the report.
Earlier this year, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor had indicated that Modi would be among the leaders Trump would want to meet at the G20.
The possible meeting comes at a sensitive time for India-US relations, particularly over trade and India's continued purchase of Russian crude oil.
The US has been considering additional measures against countries buying Russian oil.
 
A recent Reuters report said a US sanctions bill proposes tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue to make significant purchases of Russian oil, with India among those affected.
 
Trade talks remain key issue
Trade is expected to be one of the important issues in India-US discussions. The two countries have been negotiating a broader trade agreement while also cooperating in areas such as defence, technology, energy and critical minerals.
 
The December meeting could therefore provide an opportunity for the two leaders to discuss the state of bilateral trade and broader strategic ties, according to media reports.
 
The G20 gathering could also provide an opportunity for a meeting of Quad leaders — India, the US, Japan and Australia.
 
PM Modi to visit Canada, says Canadian PM Mark Carney
Modi's possible visit to the US could be followed by a trip to Canada around the time of the G20 Summit, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carneysaid on Tuesday.
 
Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Carney said India and Canada are making "good progress" in trade negotiations and are looking to conclude a deal by the end of the year, news agencies reported.
 
Notably, the two countries are negotiating a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, with the next round of talks scheduled to begin soon.

On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced its revamped social media team, appointing Deepak Mhaskey as the national social media convenor, and Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav as co-convenors.
While curiosity grew as to who these newly appointed individuals were and their past work and association with the party, social media users were quick to notice that immediately after the announcement, Gandhi, Dwivedi and Yadav made their X accounts private and there was no trace of Bhatt on the internet.
While all the other IT cell members are back to being active on X, albeit after deleting hundreds of thousands of old posts, Alok Bhatt is the only one in the group whose X handle remains inaccessible or ‘protected’ even a month after the new team was announced.
The only remnants of Bhatt’s online presence are the now-disabled X account, screenshots from his X posts and some articles in Right-wing outlets like OpIndia, Organiser and Swarajya.
Alt News found that in the past, Bhatt had been called out for controversial tweets several times. In archived screenshots of his posts from the past, the BJP functionary can be seen using sexist, Islamophobic, and derogatory language, some of which can be seen below:
Who is Alok Bhatt?
Bhatt, who claims to hail from Dehradun, has worn many hats over the course of his career. According to his LinkedIn profile, he graduated from Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University (HNBGU) in Uttarakhand and went on to work with several organisations, including NIIT University, where he served as financial controller until April 2010.
In 2010, he founded Nature Connect Outdoors — an education and adventure non-profit organisation that deals in outdoor education and skill development, including treks, camping, and rafting expeditions. According to the website’s bio, Bhatt had “shunned his corporate career” to follow his passion, which culminated in the formation of the NGO. The organisation is still functional.
According to details available on Zauba Corp, Bhatt is a Chartered Accountant (CA) and the partner of a firm of CAs called RSAC & CO LLP, incorporated in May 2021.
Bhatt has also served as the economic adviser to former Uttarakhand chief minister Trivendra Singh Rawat. However, it’s not clear when he was appointed and when exactly his tenure ended. He wrote an article for Firstpost defending the ministry of housing and urban affairs over the controversial Central Vista project. The author bio designated him as ‘Economic Advisor’ to Rawat.
In 2020, after a district officer’s press release promoting inter-caste and interfaith marriages drew criticism from social media users, Bhatt had reportedly tweeted: “No one from the government has spoken in support of promoting interfaith marriages. No one in the BJP government in their wildest dreams will support anything that is made out here.”
We sent an email and called up Bhatt several times to know more from him, but he did not respond.
Long-standing Association With BJP
Bhatt’s X handle, @alok_bhatt, was followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In fact, Modi quote-tweeted one of Bhatt’s posts in 2024, where he urged people to watch the film Sabarmati Report.
Bhatt was also invited to PM Modi’s swearing-in ceremony in the past. In 2024, Right-wing influencer Vikas Pandey shared an image with Bhatt alongside former BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma, member of the economic advisory council to the PM, Sanjeev Sanyal, and others, with the caption “First swearing in”.
Pics from first swearing in @amishra77 @NupurSharmaBJP @sanjeevsanyal @alok_bhatt pic.twitter.com/YADSZm1lCT
— Vikas Pandey (Sankrityayan) (@MODIfiedVikas) June 9, 2024
We also found an X post from 2015 where Bhatt can be seen with the Prime Minister.
Matter of pride 4 me when friends meets the man of millenium @narendramodi @alok_bhatt @kaushkrahul @tajinderbagga pic.twitter.com/LG2e1lGsNT
— Vishnu Dhanuka (Modi ka Parivar) (@VishnuDhanuka) July 2, 2015
In April 2022, Right-wing influencer Shefali Vaidya, who has been fact-checked by Alt News several times in the past, posted an image with Bhatt on X saying that she had met the latter and “his lovely family” in Uttarakhand.
No Uttarakhand trip would have been complete without meeting @alok_bhatt and his lovely family! pic.twitter.com/1QHMaJk9OY
— Shefali Vaidya. 🇮🇳 (@ShefVaidya) April 2, 2022
X Handle Suspended for Violating Guidelines
Alt News found at least three instances, in 2018, 2019, and 2020, where X (then Twitter) had initiated action against Bhatt’s handle for violation of community guidelines, and at least two of those three actions were owing to hateful content.
In 2018, Bhatt declared that all the “killers of Pandits, Rapists of Pandits, Terrorists killing in Kashmir, instigators of Godhra, and bombers of Mumbai were all Muslims, and thus Islam was the problem”. His account had then been ‘limited’.
Why is @alok_bhatt blocked by twitter for a week when blue-ticked racist bigots like Audrey Truschke are still on Twitter despite their naked Hinduphobia? @TwitterIndia pic.twitter.com/3qlnNiVWhj
— Shefali Vaidya. 🇮🇳 (@ShefVaidya) April 20, 2018
In 2019, Bhatt declared in a post that “their boys could take on Jihadis” but needed police action for “rumour mongers” like activist Shehla Rashid. “These jihadi accomplices are running a hate campaign aided and abetted by Media…please help our state dispel rumours,” the tweet read. His account was suspended after this. Political analyst and Right-wing influencer Suresh Nakhua took to Twitter to condemn the move.
Just because @alok_bhatt exposed lies of Shehla Liar Rashid, @twitter has suspended the handle.#BringBackAlokBhatt pic.twitter.com/YJpuOAxQjZ

His account was suspended again in 2020.
What’s this @TwitterIndia ? @alok_bhatt has tweeted about Hindu girls being kidnapped, r@ped and forcefully converted to !slam in Pakistan and his account has been suspended, What kind of nonsense is this? Explain!#BringBackAlokBhatt pic.twitter.com/w4T3epRn6t
— संवैधानिक डकैत (@Shivam_h9) May 29, 2020
The Pamphlet-Savitr Analytics-Alok Bhatt Connection
In 2022, Bhatt took on a directorial role at Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation, a company that was incorporated in April 26 that year, with Bhatt and Ashish Nautiyal initially named as directors. According to documents filed with the Union ministry of corporate affairs (MCA), Bhatt holds 9,500 shares, or 95 per cent of the company, while Nautiyal holds the remaining 500 shares, or 5 per cent.
Interestingly, Nautiyal is also the founding editor of the Right-wing media outlet, The Pamphlet.
Savitr Analytics has no website or online presence. We went through its financial records filed with the MCA for the financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25, and found that it was registered as a Section 8 company, i.e., a non-profit. In the 2024-25 financial year, its total revenue from operations was Rs 2.7 crore.
The organisation’s revenue across all three years comes from ‘sale of services’, and the rows for ‘Grants or donations received (relevant for Sec 8 companies)’, present in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 filings, are left blank in 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, the row does not exist.
Under ‘Corporate Information’, they state ‘Research and awareness about Indian culture and heritage…’, ‘Promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, and environmental protection…’ and ‘Advancement of education, learning, and skills development…’ as their activities.
There was a category called ‘professional expenses’ in the 2022-23 filing that was later relabeled as ‘content production expenses’. Rs. 41,48,600 was spent in the first year, Rs. 95,36,600 (filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the second year, and Rs. 1,38,53,200 (also filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the third year.
Next, we found that an individual named Ridhika Aggarwal stated on LinkedIn that she worked as a content writer for Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation until August 2023. We went through her X timeline (linked to her LinkedIn profile) and found that she wrote at least three articles for The Pamphlet during her tenure at Savitr. None of the articles are currently available on the website.
Ridhika is also listed as a non-official member of a steering committee formed by the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change in 2023.
The Pamphlet, previously known as The Indian Affairs, posted for the first time on Facebook in April 2022, which is the same time when Savitr Analytics was incorporated.
ठीक 2 साल पहले देहरादून में आज ही के दिन @Pamphlet_in ऑफिस निर्माण की शुरुआत हो गई थी, उत्तराखण्ड चुनाव निपटने के बाद मैं २० दिन के अपने नैनीताल और लैंसडाउन प्रवास के बाद दून घाटी में उतरा था।
आज ही के दिन साल 2019 में लोकसभा चुनाव का रिजल्ट भी आया था और प्रधानमंत्री… pic.twitter.com/6lAVSW3twN

The Pamphlet claims to “cut through the noise of the modern information ecosystem by offering readers and viewers clarity, depth and perspective on issues that shape India and the world.” Its reports have seem to be echoing pro-BJP narratives. An August 11 video report, for instance, was captioned: “Questions raised in the public domain regarding the credentials of two CJP leaders, Abhijeet Dipke and Saurav Das, have brought up several serious concerns”. It questioned Dipke’s Boston University degree, academic timeline and funding, as well as Das’ property, tenancy, rent, police verification, and electoral records.
During the CJP protests, another report took a swipe at Mohammed Junaid, who had been feeding protesters, with the reporter noting that “such bhaijaans were also seen” at the protest sites in Shaheen Bagh and Farmers’ stir. Thumbnails of these reports carried AI-generated visuals of individuals critical of the Union government, their faces distorted through AI to portray them in a negative light. This is a tactic common across Right-wing outlets and social media troll handles.
More recently, the outlet, alongside Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, Law Beat, The Jaipur Dialogues and The Sunday Guardian, was summoned by the Delhi high court over a Rs 2 crore privacy suit by Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das, who alleged that they had disclosed his home address and other personal details online.
