If the tech industry sought to create a method of seducing users into sending their deepest, most sensitive secrets to a server in a faraway data center, it would be hard-pressed to create a better honeypot than an AI chatbot.
OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, and their countless smaller competitors have become therapists, sounding boards, and virtual confession booths for millions of people around the world. Almost all of those AI models are set by default to collect and store that highly private data with, in many cases, no restrictions on how it’s shared or sold, used to further train the tools, or handed over to any lawsuit plaintiff or law enforcement agency that demands it through a legal process.
“You have this intelligent thing staring back at you, and you’re basically telling it, one question at a time, every possible thing there is to know about your life,” says Matt Green, a privacy- and security-focused computer science professor at Johns Hopkins University. “You're giving it this huge profile on you.”
A decade ago, text messages represented perhaps the most personal, sensitive data that most people shared from their devices, says cryptographer and software developer Moxie Marlinspike. The surveillance dangers invited by unprotected texting are what pushed him in 2014 to create Signal, the end-to-end encrypted messenger now used by well over a hundred million people. Now, he says, that critical point of privacy vulnerability has shifted to people’s interactions with AI.
“Those same things I was concerned about with messaging are happening in the AI space, but several orders of magnitude more significantly,” says Marlinspike. “People are integrating AI into their personal lives. They talk with it about their deepest insecurities, their finances, their health, their relationships.”
So earlier this year, Marlinspike launched Confer, an AI chatbot designed to allow users to ask it anything while preserving their privacy, using cryptography to technically prevent the service’s own server from being able to surveil or log their conversations. “Confer is designed to be a service where you can explore ideas without your own thoughts potentially conspiring against you someday,” he wrote in a blog post introducing it.
Marlinspike’s private AI tool is, in fact, just one standout among a new generation of AI services that promise to remedy the pervasive privacy invasion that these chatbots represent. Some advertise that they never record conversations as a policy. Others offer to anonymize them. A few, like Confer, seek to create actual technological guardrails that restrict their own access to users’ secrets.
The result of that nascent competition to create less surveillance-prone AI is a growing crowd of tools, often ones that offer confusing assurances for users as they seek to adopt an increasingly unavoidable technology without losing control of their secrets. Here’s WIRED’s guide to using AI with your privacy intact.
Zero Data Retention
When you start typing into one of the big three AI chatbots—ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini—it’s safest to start with a baseline expectation of approximately zero real privacy from anyone who is determined to access your conversation records and has a legal path to obtaining them. That includes the owner of the service, advertisers or other companies they partner with, contractors who help fine-tune the systems, law enforcement agencies, or even someone who manages to subpoena the records as part of a civil lawsuit.
The simplest, strong exception to that rule is a contract between you—or more likely, your employer—and an AI provider that legally prevents them from retaining those records, a provision that’s come to be known as zero data retention, or ZDR. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google all offer ZDR policies for their enterprise versions, which when enabled generally require that they immediately delete records of users’ interactions with a chatbot as soon as they’re processed.
Even these ZDR policies, which are only available for paid enterprise and developer accounts rather than for average users, have significant exceptions. Anthropic, for instance, doesn’t offer ZDR for its most sophisticated “Mythos-class” models like Fable 5.1, due to what it describes as the potential for misuse like scamming or hacking and even “autonomous misbehavior,” such as AI agents independently hacking targets to carry out their unwitting users’ requests, as has occurred in several high-profile AI-driven breaches.
OpenAI also announced last month that its ZDR implementations will analyze user activity prior to deletion—on the customer’s systems rather than its own, it says—and, if it detects abuse, flag it for the customer organization. OpenAI says its system, known as Private Safety Processing, will even alert OpenAI’s staff if it detects abuse in some cases, though without revealing the content of the conversation to them. Google, too, warns that it logs some Gemini prompts for abuse monitoring even with ZDR enabled, but without the user’s Google ID or IP address included—though that “sanitized” data can in some cases still pinpoint a particular person when the request itself includes identifiable information.
Policies, Promises, and Proxies
Regardless of those protections and exceptions, the paid, enterprise-level, contractual promises of ZDR are out of reach for the vast majority of non-corporate AI users. Instead, many consumer-targeted AI services ask us to settle for the far weaker, pinky-swear promises they’ve made not to log our conversations.
Privacy-focused cloud services company Proton, for instance, offers the AI chatbot Lumo, which it describes as “AI where every conversation is private.” That privacy, however, isn’t based on the technical guarantees of end-to-end encryption, like Proton’s other services such as Proton Mail and Proton Drive. Instead, it simply promises not to log users’ conversations, and users have to trust that Proton will adhere to that privacy policy—which, in Proton’s case, is at least backed by the company’s long track record as a privacy-focused company. “A promise is not as good as a mathematical guarantee,” Yen told WIRED in an interview last month, “but a promise made by the right people is still actually quite substantial.”
Other privacy-focused AI services like Venice.ai and Duck.ai, the AI chatbot offered by long-running private search engine DuckDuckGo, offer similar vows about keeping no logs of your conversations. Both services, however, relay your chat requests to other services such as Claude or ChatGPT, essentially acting as a proxy for your conversation that limits what information the underlying AI model can collect about you.
(Duck.ai lets the user choose which third-party model they’re using. Venice.ai appears to automatically route conversations to different services based on the request, without always making clear to the user which one it’s using, as well as answering queries with an AI model hosted on its own infrastructure in some cases. Venice.ai also touts other privacy features, like using “trusted execution environment” systems to cryptographically prevent logging of conversations—more on that below—but when WIRED attempted to reach out to Venice.ai’s staff to ask more questions about these privacy features, its AI response bot only repeatedly referred us to a nonworking email address.)
Using an anonymity proxy offers some privacy protection compared with using ChatGPT or Claude directly. Yet when they relay your requests to those services, Duck.ai and Venice.ai’s own promises about their retention of data become significantly less meaningful, points out Johns Hopkins’ Green. That’s because your chat messages can still be collected by that underlying AI model and, even stripped of any identifying metadata, those messages can often contain identifiable information.
Ask about the best coffee shops in your neighborhood, for instance, and you’ve immediately revealed information about where you live, Green points out. “All that stuff tied together is basically a fingerprint for you,” says Green.
Trusted Execution Environments and On-Device AI
Far better than privacy promises, policies, or anonymizing relays are actual technological restrictions that prevent an AI service from reading your conversations—a guarantee that the service not only does not snoop on or record your chats, but that it cannot. That’s where cryptography comes in.
Unlike encrypted messaging or storage, where the server hosting a service never sees any unencrypted data, interactions with an AI model can’t yet be truly end-to-end encrypted like a Signal or WhatsApp conversation. Currently, working AI models can only process unencrypted prompts. So instead, some AI services are offering the next best thing, what’s known as a trusted execution environment, or TEE. In that system, the server running the AI model uses a hardware setup—most often Nvidia’s Confidential Computing—in which the user’s queries are processed on isolated hardware, and the server can cryptographically prove that the rest of the system has no access to that segregated enclave of secrets.
Confer, the private AI chatbot launched by Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike, uses that Nvidia-based TEE setup— along with an authentication system based on passkeys and open-source code that anyone can audit—to offer what are perhaps the strongest consumer-level privacy protections currently available in an AI chatbot.
Meta, too, uses a TEE to offer a more private version of the Meta AI chatbot included in WhatsApp—a privacy system that Confer’s Marlinspike has said he is helping Meta to develop. Start typing into the “Ask Meta AI or Search” bar in your WhatsApp app, and an “Ask” button will appear on the right side of the text field with the Meta AI logo. Tap it and then tap the speech bubble with a lock that appears on the top right of that Meta AI chat screen, and you’ll enter a new chat screen that’s protected with a TEE system, which Meta says prevents it from keeping any record of it. That Incognito system is by no means truly end-to-end encrypted like the rest of WhatsApp’s messaging, but it appears to be Meta’s attempt at integrating AI into WhatsApp while approximating the privacy promises it offers to users in their conversations with other humans.
Unlike the Meta AI integrated into WhatsApp, Meta’s newer AI agent called Muse doesn’t yet offer a TEE-based privacy system. Instead, it promises only to run in a segregated virtual machine (VM) in the cloud, where Meta says its ad systems won’t be able to access your data and you can opt out of your data being used to train Meta’s AI. The company says, however, that it’s working on releasing Muse Confidential VM later this year, which Meta tells WIRED “is intended to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data” in a user’s Muse virtual machine.
Apple also offers a privacy-preserving AI system of its own design with some TEE-like properties, what it calls Private Cloud Compute (PCC), to enforce its promise that it can’t read users’ conversations with its Apple Intelligence AI service. When you ask Apple Intelligence or Siri a query that’s processed on its servers, your personal device cryptographically checks that the server is running an unaltered version of Apple’s PCC code, which is designed to keep no logs and isolate your data from any remote access. (It’s also possible to ask Apple Intelligence or Siri to query ChatGPT or other third-party AI services. When you do, just as with other tools that relay your queries, you won’t get that same PCC level of protection, but Apple will also check with you before sending your request to a third-party service.) For most simple queries, however, Apple uses a more limited, on-device AI model that doesn’t share any of your secrets beyond your phone, computer, or smartwatch, but also isn’t as fully featured as a typical server-based model.
On that note, there are plenty of other AI tools that run locally on your computer, too, such as Ollama, LMStudio, or LocalAI. All of them ensure—by the simple fact that no data ever leaves your computer—a level of privacy that’s tough to obtain with any cloud-based AI tool. But Green warns that what you gain in privacy with locally hosted artificial intelligence, you lose in, well, intelligence. Expect these self-hosted AI tools to be frequently stumped and to hallucinate far more often than the modern, cloud-hosted AI models most users are accustomed to. “You can run these on any laptop,” Green says. “They’re just dumb as rocks.”
The Price of Privacy
That intelligence-versus-privacy question is, of course, just one of the trade-offs that privacy-conscious AI users face as they choose their preferred tool. Price is another.
Confer, for instance, uses a freemium model, charging $34.99 a month for its cheapest tier after users run out of the roughly 20 to 25 queries a day it offers for free. That’s more than the $20 a month Claude and ChatGPT charge for their cheapest paid tiers. But Marlinspike says that price premium in fact captures the actual cost of running an AI model without the subsidies that come from an expectation of future profits from data collection or advertising. “It’s more expensive, but it's the real cost,” Marlinspike says, “whereas other paid providers are subsidizing the cost with monetization of our data in one way or another.”
Given the serious energy and hardware costs of running frontier AI models, the advent of more privacy-preserving AI raises the question of how companies that don’t monetize user data will sustain themselves, Green notes. Without those data-collection-driven profits, he says, it’s not yet clear whether companies that provide more private AI services will find a sustainable business model—or whether some will eventually give up or even undermine their data protection promises down the road.
In other words, AI that doesn’t exploit your data is possible. But it may be far pricier than you think. “If you want real privacy,” Green says, “you might have to pay for it.”

Rabbit, the company behind the underwhelming R1 device, is rolling out a standalone AI agent that you don’t need its hardware to use, as reported earlier by Wired. The startup says its new OS3 “agentic operating system” runs in the cloud but operates locally across Windows, Mac, and Linux devices.
Rabbit’s new AI agent doesn’t need an R1 to run
The startup’s AI agent can operate locally across Windows, Mac, and Linux devices.
According to Rabbit, you can add up to five devices to one account, along with your preferred AI models. OS3 will automatically determine the devices, files, apps, and AI models it needs to complete a task. You can also access OS3 through its dedicated desktop site, a paired messaging app like Telegram or iMessage, as well as on Rabbit’s R1 device.
Though Rabbit founder Jesse Lyu tells Wired that the startup has stopped manufacturing R1 devices, it isn’t giving up on AI hardware entirely. It’s instead focusing on a new vibe-coding “cyberdeck” that will run OS3 when it launches within “months,” Wired reports.
Rabbit claims its OS3 system won’t store, copy, use, or sell your data. It notes that it will still keep your chats and memories stemming from them on its servers. Other AI providers linked to OS3 will also handle your data under their own privacy rules.

Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has celebrated a “historic” meeting with Donald Trump in New York, posing for a smiley photo with the US president less than nine months after he ordered the abduction of her boss, Nicolás Maduro.
The former foes met at a five-star hotel in Manhattan a few blocks from Trump Tower late on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly. The hotel is about 7 miles from the Brooklyn prison where Maduro has been held since he was snatched during a special forces raid on Caracas.
On the eve of Tuesday’s encounter, an American reporter asked Rodríguez if she would be visiting Maduro, under whom she served as vice-president, during her stay in New York. She did not reply.
But Venezuela’s interim leader did find time to meet Trump at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel, with the get-together seen as a key part of Rodríguez’s push for international legitimacy after years of diplomatic isolation under Maduro’s dictatorship. On Wednesday she is expected to address the annual UN assembly.
“We held a historic meeting with … Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote on Instagram, in a 133-word statement that made no mention of her incarcerated ally.
Oliver Blanco, one of Rodríguez’s top diplomats, claimed the meeting marked “a new stage of dialogue and understanding between both countries” and was “an important step toward new opportunities for our country and our people”. Blanco also posted a cheery photo in which both he and Trump smiled and gave the thumbs up to the camera.
A White House aide said the meeting was also attended by top US officials including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Hours earlier, Rodríguez had sat in the general assembly hall watching Trump celebrate the “massive military operation” during which Maduro – whom he called an “outlaw dictator” and “a real criminal” – was captured. “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils,” Trump bragged of the recent oil deal between the US and Venezuela, as she appeared to wince.
Some observers also detected signs of discomfort in the body language captured in the photo of Trump and Rodríguez, who appears to be clenching her left fist as she poses beside the grinning US president.
Some of Rodríguez’s critics in Venezuela called her treatment by Trump an unmitigated humiliation for a socialist party politician who has spent years railing against Yankee imperialism.
After Maduro’s capture, Trump warned that Rodríguez would “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro” if she did not toe the US line. Since then, Rodríguez has made a series of major concessions, including ceding control of Venezuela’s oil revenues to Washington and agreeing to a controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal that Trump on Tuesday called “the largest oil deal in history”.
One opposition figure denounced the Rodríguez/Trump meeting as an encounter between a “shameless puppet and her unscrupulous puppeteer”.
But Rodríguez has succeeded in consolidating power, with Trump seemingly more focused on gaining access to Venezuela’s natural resources than pushing for a fresh presidential election that would move the South American country back towards democracy.
Trump has repeatedly praised Rodríguez’s “fantastic” and “terrific” leadership while sidelining her main rival, the opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado, who left Venezuela late last year to receive her Nobel peace prize in Oslo, has been unable to return and is exiled in Panama. She reportedly made three attempts to return to Venezuela this week, but failed.
Before Tuesday’s tête-à-tête, the presidents of the US and Venezuela had last met in 2015, when Barack Obama and Maduro spoke briefly during a regional summit in Panama. In the decade that followed, Maduro became an international pariah as he led his country into economic chaos and increasingly authoritarian rule, and Venezuela was hit by punishing international sanctions.
At the 2015 summit, Obama conceded that the days in which “the US could meddle with impunity” in Latin America were over. But Trump has dramatically different ideas and has been forging ahead with attempts to reassert US dominance in a region it has long considered its back yard.
As well as capturing Venezuela’s government and trying to topple Cuba’s communist government by strangling its economy, Trump’s push for hegemony has also seen the US accused of trying to swing Brazil’s presidential election in favour of the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro through diplomatic and economic pressure.
Addressing the UN assembly on Tuesday, the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, hit back at such efforts, without directly citing the US. “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians,” said Lula who is facing a tough battle to win re-election in October’s vote.
“Brazil doesn’t fit into anyone’s back yard,” added Lula, who also called for fresh elections in Venezuela. He did not meet Rodríguez during her visit to New York but said the “people of Venezuela deserve to decide their own future”.

Florida teacher accused of trying to ‘cancel’ an 8th grader because of the student’s conservative views
Liz Ballard, a Pine View School history teacher, would frequently discuss politics in her classroom and have one of her students be the conservative voice against his parents’ wishes
A Florida teacher has been accused of trying to “cancel” an eighth-grade student because of the child’s conservative views.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, who is running for re-election, called for Liz Ballard, a Pine View School history teacher, to be fired and her educator certificate revoked if the allegations against her were found to be true.
Uthmeier wrote in a letter to Ballard’s district, Sarasota County Schools, Monday that his Office of Parental Rights was informed that Ballard “allegedly harassed, disparaged, and deliberately tried to ‘cancel’ an eighth-grade student for his conservative views.”
The student allegedly told Ballard that his parents forbid him to take part in political discussions that frequently happened in her classroom. But Ballard “ignored the parents’ wishes and continued to engage this student as the conservative perspective in the classroom,” read the letter, which the attorney general shared on X.
Ballard is also accused of calling the student a “misogynist” and spreading the label around the school. She also allegedly publicly questioned the “suitability and influence” of the child’s father.
Sarasota County is predominantly Republican. There are more than 164,000 registered Republicans, more than 81,000 registered Democrats and more than 73,000 with no party affiliation in the county, according to the Florida Division of Elections.
Utehmeier said if the allegations against Ballard are corroborated and if there is no reason to question their reliability, the teacher’s “conduct violated Florida law, School Board policy, and basic ethical principles for educators.”
The attorney general asked Sarasota County Schools Superintendent Terry Connor and the school district’s board to tell his office by October 1 what actions they have taken or will take to address the situation.
Superintendent Connor confirmed that the district received Uthmeier’s letter in a statement shared with The Independent.
“We take the concerns seriously and will respond to the Attorney General's Office,” Connor said.
“Every student deserves a classroom where they feel safe, respected, and free to learn. No student should face harassment, humiliation, or retaliation because of their beliefs or their family's views,” the statement continued. “Respect for students and parents is fundamental to the trust our community places in our schools.”
Speaking on the allegations, Connor said the district will “examine the relevant facts and records, ensure a fair process for all involved, and take appropriate action based on the findings and requirements.”
The district did not address Ballard’s current employment status.

What to know about the agreement signed by President Trump and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland
U.S. President Donald Trump and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland have signed an agreement about Greenland's status
U.S. President Donald Trump and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement about the status of the Arctic island after months of threats by Trump to seize the semiautonomous territory of a NATO ally.
The deal was officially signed Tuesday in New York, after U.S., Greenlandic and Danish officials had quietly negotiated for months behind the scenes — searching both for solutions to address some of Trump’s security concerns about the territory, as well as alleviating Danish and Greenlandic fears of being taken over by the U.S.
The three parties expressed satisfaction with the deal at the signing ceremony — but what exactly does it say?
Washington is allowed to “modernize and expand” its activities at the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest, according to the agreement.
The U.S. can also set up “defense areas” at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east, and “may establish additional defense areas in Greenland and strengthen its military operations or facilities.”
The accord calls for wide U.S. military mobility on Greenland’s territory, including “undersea access," noting that “ the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”
The agreement reaffirms “the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark,” and recognizes the Greenlanders' "right to self-determination.”
The agreement says all three parties “support a stronger NATO engagement in the Arctic, including as regards planning, presence, exercises, and joint intelligence gathering.”
It allows U.S. military access to Greenland to defend the NATO area, Greenland itself and the American continent — including through a “Golden Dome defense system."
The deal spells out that “no state that is not a member of NATO shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland."
In the preamble, the signatories recognize “the need to protect the pristine environment of Greenland.” It also stresses “the economic, social, and cultural rights of the people of Greenland, including with respect to their lands and their way of life, including hunting, fishing, and other traditional, cultural, historical, future activities.”
The accord “does not have an end date” and, if Greenland chooses to become independent, it will agree to remain in NATO and take on Denmark’s rights and obligations under the deal.
The deal will only “enter into force” once the “necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed.”

In August and September 2026, a popular meme claimed to show the alleged contradictory positions of Alice Weidel, leader of the far-right German political party Alternative for Germany, known in Germany by the abbreviation AfD. The meme states that Weidel is anti-immigration yet has an immigrant wife, supports anti-LGBTQ+ policies but is a lesbian, and opposes adoption for LGBTQ+ families despite having adopted two children.
The claim states:
Alice Weidel becomes the first leader in the world who is anti-immigration but has an immigrant wife, is anti-LGBTQ+ but is a lesbian herself, opposes LGBT adoption but has adopted two children, and is a hardcore German nationalist but lives in Switzerland.
While Weidel has stood by her party's positions on immigration and LGBTQ+ issues—while expressing minor disagreements on occasion—we have not been able to verify certain details of her personal life directly from her, and as a result we have relied on her interviews and reporting from other sources. Snopes reached out to AfD to learn more and will update this post accordingly. Until we have more information, we will keep this claim unrated.
Below we break down the truth behind several of the above claims. The above meme is largely true in that Weidel has a Sri Lankan-born wife with Swiss citizenship, while also supporting anti-immigration policies. Despite her party's anti-LGBTQ+ policies, she has said there is "no contradiction" between her personal life, her belief that same-sex couples deserve equality, and her public advocacy for a "traditional" family.
While Weidel is at the time of this writing the most prominent leader internationally associating with a party that contradicts her personal lifestyle, she is not the only public figure to follow this pattern. For example, U.S. President Donald Trump's ally and former Acting Director for National Intelligence, Richard Grenell, is openly gay despite having opposed pro-LGBTQ+ policies.
Weidel's family life
A 2021 interview with the German politician's Sri Lankan-born wife, Sarah Bossard, noted that the couple was in a registered partnership. We should note that as of July 1, 2022, same-sex marriages are 
In a televised interview, Weidel said Bossard, whom she referred to as her wife, became Swiss through adoption as a child, not through "migration":
INTERVIEWER: You brought your wife along; she was born in Sri Lanka. Is that sort of thing ever discussed at home — given that it touches on something fundamental?
WEIDEL: It's not about skin color. And my wife — as you've just done yourself — is labeled as having a "migration background." My wife is Swiss and was adopted; consequently, she doesn't view herself as having a migration background.
In a 2021 interview, Bossard noted that she grew up in Biel, Switzerland. A 2025 NBC News report said the couple resided in Willerzel, a village in Switzerland. A 2025 Time magazine profile noted they have a home in Switzerland and their sons attend school there.
According to The New York Times, they are raising two sons together. According to the Financial Times, their sons are adopted. Pink News, an outlet focused on LGBTQ+ news, said Bossard gave birth to the sons and Weidel adopted them. Snopes was unable to determine the exact circumstances of the sons' adoption and whether they are biologically related to either parent.
AfD's positions on LGBTQ+ rights, immigration and adoption
Weidel's AfD party opposes same-sex marriage and does not support same-sex adoption, according to German news outlet DW. The party website states:
We, the AfD, as the only serious political force, have the will to counter the family policy failures of recent decades with clear political measures. We will put the family, consisting of father, mother and as many children as possible, back in the center of political and social thinking and action. With us, parents get the best possible conditions for starting and managing a family and our children the best possible chances of good and healthy development.
Weidel addressed her party position in an interview:
Well, we live in a completely different reality now. Same-sex relationships should be treated as equal. But if I, as a politician, speak of a societal ideal—and that happens to be the traditional family—then I am entitled to advocate for it. There is no contradiction there.
Weidel also said the party position "was written by conservatives who might not see things exactly the way I do. As for me personally ... my children have the best upbringing and the best foundation — let them write whatever they want. I live a different reality."
She has also reportedly said, "I'm not queer, I'm just married to a woman who I've known for 20 years."
In a 2021 interview, Bossard criticized a campaign against marriage equality in Switzerland:
The campaign is not only distasteful, but completely misses our reality of life. I would have wished the committee would have more closely experienced the people and life constellations that it is criticizing. But that also shows what is still going on in the minds of some people. This is why marriage equality is an important step towards changing that.
AfD has a firm anti-immigration policy and calls for more local skilled workers. In 2025, in an interview with billionaire Elon Musk, Weidel said former German Chancellor Angela Merkel "ruined" the country after she "opened our borders through illegal immigration." Weidel also said Germany allowed migrants to "throw away" their passports and papers before entering the country in order to avoid deportations.
Snopes has previously reported on false claims that migrants committed mass sexual assaults in Germany.

Hunting hidden gems - is there anywhere in the world left to scout?
- Published
The world's biggest clubs were all aware of the teenage sensation turning heads for Universidad de Chile, the one dubbed his generation's Alexis Sanchez.
"When we signed Dario Osorio, it was not because no-one knew about him," Kristian Kjaer, technical director at Midtjylland, tells BBC Sport.
Osorio was on the radar of AC Milan, RB Leipzig, Salzburg and a number of other English and German clubs before he left Santiago for Denmark at the age of 19.
It was a carefully considered pathway. After three seasons in Scandinavia, the winger joined Crystal Palace on loan this summer with a £24m option to buy which would make him the most expensive sale in Danish Superliga history.
Midtjylland, where Brentford owner Matthew Benham was a majority stakeholder between 2014 and 2023, are renowned as one of the most innovative clubs in Europe for their use of analytics - from set-pieces to smart recruitment.
"We work on both pathways," explains Kjaer. "We have subjective scouting, more classic video scouting, live scouting, a network, people we trust in the club and also our partners. And then we have the data scouting.
"And Dario Osorio, we were aware of him long before we signed him."
From feet-on-the-ground to the increasing availability of footage, data analytics and artificial intelligence, Premier League clubs - whether buying direct from source or tracking players like Osorio's progress - have a large proportion of the world's emerging talent covered.
"That hidden gem kind of thing almost does not exist any more in football," says Kjaer. "Sometimes it does, but it's rare."
'Find me a player like Ashley Cole...'
"You would put this period as one of the most transformational in talent ID and recruitment," explains Sam Turner, head of operations at scouting and development platform Eyeball.
Clubs can now obtain an incredible level of detail on players across the globe before they have even made a senior appearance. Eyeball, for example, was founded five years ago to focus on those predominantly aged 13 to 21.
It is used by more than 60% of clubs in Europe's top five leagues, and a majority of Premier League sides, for access to more than 400,000 young players across 42 global markets from Europe to Africa and Latin America.
Winger Malick Yalcouye, a new 20-year-old star at Brighton, was tracked on the system since developing at Ivorian side ASEC Mimosas, likewise Bazoumana Toure, who is now at Newcastle.
The breadth of coverage is highlighted by other recent moves - Josue Caicedo left Ecuador's LDU Quito for Barcelona, Mustapha Nyassi swapped Gambia's Real de Banjul for Copenhagen and Nour Ashraf joined Leipzig from Egypt's ENPPI.
"The availability of data and footage has prompted a change in methodology," says Turner. "That has brought a load of benefits in terms of data-led recruitment, time saving, cost saving."
Eyeball takes north of 2,000 data points every match, typically from leading amateur clubs and elite academies who film and upload their fixtures.
The result is a huge database allowing analysts to watch all of a player's progressive passes, for example, discover who covered the most distance or simply ask 'find me a player like Ashley Cole'.
"There is always this human feel that can never be lost," adds Turner. "I like to think we have aided scouts and recruitment teams, supplemented them with the tools, data, information to be able to make more informed decisions on a more consistent basis."
Data, says Midtjylland's Kjaer, is "extremely important because it gives you an objective tool you can lean towards" when complemented by years of decision-making experience.
"We cannot just turn on the computer and it tell us who to sign and then we go sign them," he says. "We also need to know about the cultural background, the family background, to make sure they fit into our football club.
"Of course, data has given us opportunities. We sign young. So the sample size will simply be smaller for us because if we are waiting until it's big enough, Brighton and Liverpool and Brentford and other guys, they will sign the player in front of us."
Where are the emerging markets?
"We can find interesting players all around the world," explains Kjaer.
"I like us to be open-minded. We are particular in the way we play and the way we sell. And therefore, we need to find these players who fit that style of play.
"When you have done your due diligence and you feel certain, pull the trigger. The pace in decision-making is also a hidden gem."
One country regularly mentioned is Uzbekistan, who played in their first World Cup this summer, while Turner says Azerbaijan is pioneering a national talent network and "very forward-thinking and motivated to progress the game domestically".
Then there is Japan, which Turner calls a "guiding star" in youth development for a system which takes players from grassroots, to school and college football and then the professional game. Think Kaoru Mitoma's thesis on dribbling techniques.
For European clubs, it makes identifying young Japanese prospects more complex.
Latin America, too, remains a hotbed of talent.
As former Midtjylland chairman Rasmus Ankersen, who has since worked for Brentford and Southampton, wrote in his book The Gold Mine Effect, a club such as Cruzeiro will reject 4,000 players under the age of 15 for every one they take in.
Brazilian clubs are naturally protective of their assets.
"They know eventually players will leave," says Turner. "But it is allowing them to leave at the right age where those clubs can benefit locally. And we are very invested in that."
Much of the region, however, remains "untapped" but recording games creates opportunities.
"It's just a visibility piece for a lot of these players that means they don't get picked up," says Turner.
"We have gone a long way in solving that for a lot of markets, but there are many more that can be picked up with brilliant players everywhere."
One of those markets continues to be Africa.
"There'll be thousands," says Thomas Randolph, founder of Delphlyx, when asked whether talented African players may have missed out on big moves in the past.
Delphlyx works with Premier League clubs and ownership groups, and others across Europe, the United States and Mexico, to provide information on the best - and most relevant - 14 to 21-year-olds in West Africa, often through data, live scouting and private tournaments.
"We have over 19,000 players in Africa on our platform that you could just sit right here in London and watch, then pick up the phone, call one of them and organise a trial or a transfer. That just wasn't happening before," adds Randolph.
With a projected average age of just over 18, Randolph says the region is a "young, growing, developing space" - a "sporting mecca". Football remains the main passion, though NFL and NBA are starting to invest in certain countries.
But Randolph disputes the idea African scouting is now saturated, citing a number of areas that remain relatively undiscovered, often because of conflict or logistics, with scouts drawn to the region's biggest cities.
"Zadok Yohanna is a good example," explains Randolph. "He moved to Brighton recently. He comes from Ikon Allah, which is a tiny and relatively unknown academy in northern Nigeria.
"The southern bit of Senegal is where Sadio Mane is from, where [Lamine] Camara is from, who Chelsea tried to sign, and there's only one team down there. So within all these big countries, there are certain regions that are less scouted."
Historically, it was agents who brought players out of Africa rather than scouts discovering them, whereas Delphlyx aims to help clubs identify and analyse certain talent first so scouts can visit specific tournaments or showcases to watch targets.
Randolph mentions eastern Mali, Togo, Guinea-Bissau and Burkina Faso but Benin, situated between Nigeria and Togo, is of particular interest for the way the country has invested federation grants in football infrastructure and pitches.
"One place they've used the Fifa money very well is Benin," says Randolph. "It's now produced probably a future female Ballon d'Or winner - Romaine Gandonou, who's 15, just played at the Under-20 World Cup, and got the likes of PSG, Barcelona, everyone after her.
"Benin is going to be a country that over the next few years will become very interesting."
Some Premier League clubs are buying directly from Africa. At 18, Senegalese defender Mor Talla Ndiaye has already been on the bench for Liverpool after arriving from Amitie, owned by ex-Newcastle and Chelsea striker Demba Ba.
Ndiaye was spotted at last year's Under-17 World Cup, where Burkina Faso midfielder Mohamed Zongo also impressed. He will join Chelsea and Strasbourg owners BlueCo's project when he turns 18 in two years' time.
"The Under-17 World Cup is a big one," says Randolph. "If your African nation plays there and you do well, you're going to get a good move."
Scouts have also been at the recent Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying and Delphlyx has helped organise trials for players from Senegal and Gambia at Premier League clubs.
The pool is narrowed, however, because players must obtain a Governing Body Endorsement to be granted a work permit or - most likely - take one of a club's four Elite Significant Contribution spots, which essentially comes down to how many youth or senior internationals they have played.
It's part of the reason young players initially move to European countries where regulations are less stringent and why Randolph believes Scottish clubs, where the same criteria does not apply, should be looking into the African market the way Scandinavians do.
Nordsjaelland are unique in that the Right to Dream academy - founded in Ghana in 1999 by former Manchester United scout Tom Vernon - bought the Danish club seven years ago to provide a pathway for its biggest prospects, which have included Mohammed Kudus, Simon Adingra and Kamaldeen Sulemana.
Brighton's Yalcouye and Newcastle's Toure made their first moves to Swedish clubs IFK Goteborg and Hammarby, while Midtjylland have a partner club in Nigeria, FC Ebedei. Coventry's Frank Onyeka played for both on his way to the Premier League, as did Paul Onuachu, now at Trabzonspor.
Like with Osorio, and others such as Guinea-Bissau forward Franculino, who left this summer for Trabzonspor, or Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande, now at Nottingham Forest via Sporting, Midtjylland can highlight a track record of developing young players before selling them on.
"I see Midtjylland a bit like Silicon Valley for tech companies - we have produced so much talent over the years," explains Kjaer.
"We can focus only on the development. Of course, we need to win, but it's a bit more of a secure environment.
"What we say is, if you want to focus on your career as a football player, you have to come here because that is the only thing we do. That is what we are experts in."
Undiscovered talent on the doorstep?
There remains, however, undiscovered talent close to home. France, particularly Paris, boasts an incredibly rich talent pool.
A unique national youth league system, where amateur sides face professional academies - and regularly beat them - offers clubs the chance to witness unsigned prospects competing against the most gifted players in their age group.
"Scouts from all over the world come to Ile-de-France to look at players in our leagues," said Jamel Sandjak, president of the Ligue de Paris Ile-de-France, which boasts more than 1,000 clubs and 270,000 players.
"Most of the France national youth teams are full of our players. So our regional teams are playing at national level."
Last season, amateur side ES Nanterre, from the outskirts of Paris, won Championnat National Group B ahead of Champions League outfits Lens and Lille and second-tier clubs Reims, Bastia and Red Star.
Forward Exauce Luyindula was the division's top scorer for renowned amateurs AAS Sarcelles - where Riyad Mahrez played until he was 18 - and has since joined Ligue 2 Guingamp.
Other Eyeball partners enjoyed memorable victories, too. AFC Creil beat Lens at under-15 level, Olympique Rovenain's under-19s beat Nice and CS Bretigny's under-17s edged Paris St-Germain.
"Until recently, the vast majority of clubs were relying on the fact the best players are in the best academies or national talent systems, when actually a lot of those players were chosen by 12 or 13," explains Turner.
"A lot of the time that can be right, but also statistically the best players at 12 aren't always the best players at 18.
"There is such a high concentration of players in that region, there is not enough space. The best players aren't necessarily in the national systems."

India can't simply stop buying Russian oil. Nirmala Sitharaman explains why
India has remained one of the largest buyers of Russian crude since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine disrupted global energy markets.
India cannot simply stop buying Russian oil and switch to other suppliers, Nirmala Sitharaman has said. The Union finance minister cited global supply constraints and the needs of the country's 1.4 billion people.
At the BusinessLine Changemaker Awards on Tuesday, Sitharaman said moving away from Russian crude could drive up prices because the global supply pool remains limited.
“India can get out of Russia and say all right I'm buying oil from somewhere else. The moment you come out the available pool which is limited is going to shoot up in price,” she said. “It poses a severe challenge no doubt, but I think we will have to keep India's interest topmost,” she said.
Her remarks came days after US President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law. The legislation gives the US president powers to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that are major buyers of Russian oil and gas, putting India and China among the countries potentially exposed to the measure.
Sitharaman said India would continue to source energy from different parts of the world, based on availability and suitability, while keeping domestic energy security in mind.
“We will choose to source our energy requirement from every corner of the world, and that which suits us, suits not for anything else but for the availability,” she said.
ALSO READ | 'Russia’s economy depends on India': Zelensky says ending oil trade could stop Ukraine war
‘Oil pool itself is coming down’
Sitharaman pointed to recent disruptions in the global energy market. This included attacks and damage involving facilities in the Gulf region, which she said reduced available supplies.
“Today just look at it realistically with the attack in Saudi Arabia and some crossfire hit at some other Gulf-related refineries, the oil pool itself is coming down,” she said.
India was already diversifying its crude basket, she said, but replacing Russian oil would require supplies from several different sources to meet the country's demand.
“To replace all that we need 1.4 billion people, the requirement has to be met from so many different sources already we are diversifying our oil basket,” she said.
ALSO READ | Trump threatens to use Russia sanctions law putting India, China at risk of 100% tariffs
Indian refineries cannot process every type of crude
The finance minister also spoke of the technical constraints involved in switching suppliers. Indian refineries are largely configured to process medium crude where factors such as density and sulphur content affect whether a particular grade can be processed.
“So if you have to pick it up from somewhere else where it is available which cannot be even with some tweaking be treated by our refineries, what good is that for and whose cause are we then serving?” she said.
Sitharaman said the government therefore had to consider not just where crude was available, but also whether Indian refineries could process it.
ALSO READ | US law gives Trump power to impose 100% tariffs on India, China over Russian oil
US pressure over Russian oil
The comments come as Washington steps up pressure on countries continuing to buy Russian energy.
India has remained one of the largest buyers of Russian crude since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine disrupted global energy markets and Western sanctions changed the flow of oil.
New Delhi has maintained that its energy purchases are guided by market conditions and the country's energy security requirements.
Zelensky asks India to stop buying Russian oil
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also requested India and other major buyers to cut energy ties with Moscow. Russia's economy depended on countries including India, China and Turkey, he told The Wall Street Journal.
“Russia is basing its economy on India, sometimes Turkey and China. And it is obvious if these guys stop their energy trade with Russia, then it (Russia) will have to stop fighting the war,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky said ending energy trade with Moscow would increase pressure on Russia to end the war in Ukraine. He also said he hoped Trump would help bring the conflict to an end soon.
“I hope that we will end this (Russia-Ukraine war) and President Trump will help us to end this war. We need to do this as soon as possible, before winter, better before winter,” he said during a media interaction on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

More than 170,000 respiratory cases recorded in haze-choked Indonesia
- Published
Some 175,000 people in Indonesia have suffered from respiratory illness since August, its health ministry said, as it continues to battle wildfires that have raged for weeks.
More than 40,000 cases – which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia – involve toddlers.
Forest fires have blanketed parts of the country as well as neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore in toxic smog, pushing air quality indices into "unhealthy" territory.
Indonesia has deployed more than 54,000 officials and dozens of jets to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra for water bombing, but the vast territory and challenging peatland conditions make it hard to put out the fires, authorities say.
"From the air to the ground, all forces continue to move," Indonesia's Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya said on Monday.
"Everything is being done to extinguish the fires, reduce the impact of the smoke, and, most importantly, protect the public from the threat of forest and land fires."
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during its annual dry season, which usually runs from July through October.
This year, however, the fires and haze have been turbocharged by a so-called "Godzilla" El Nino, which has fuelled extremely dry conditions.
The independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas has detected around 734,000 hotspots across the country as of Wednesday - a figure that is more than 30% higher than that of 2019, one of Indonesia's worst wildfire seasons.
Since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land – nearly six times the size of Greater London – have been burned.
The wildfires have led to school closures and a surge in hospital admissions across Indonesia.
The number of people suffering wildfire-related respiratory illnesses had more than doubled to 113,336 by 9 September, up from 50,891 on 1 September, according to figures from the health ministry.
The toxic smog has also taken a toll on wildlife, including critically endangered orangutans.
Late last month, an Indonesia-based wildlife foundation shared footage showing an orangutan writhing on the ground on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan, one of Indonesia's hardest-hit provinces. The great ape, which was discovered by a farmer, was rescued and given emergency treatment for hypoxia, but later died.
Indigenous and civil society groups in West Kalimantan filed a class action suit last week against the central government and local administrations, accusing them of deliberate negligence for failing to properly tackle the wildfires scorching the province.
"This is a disaster that occurs every year. This recurring pattern proves our view that the defendants knew about the potential haze disaster and the risks of disaster from forest and land fires," the group's lawyer Glorio Sanen said in a statement at the time.
Indonesia has carried out several rounds of cloud-seeding operations in recent weeks, some conducted together with members of Japan's Self-Defense Forces who arrived in Borneo earlier this month to help with firefighting efforts.
Cloud seeding involves manipulating existing clouds, such as by dropping salt crystals or silver iodide into them, to help produce more rain. Meteorologists, however, are divided over the effectiveness of the practice.
In the Malaysian state of Sarawak, one of the worst-affected areas outside Indonesia, authorities launched a five-day cloud-seeding operation earlier this month.
Apart from tackling the ongoing haze, this exercise was aimed at boosting declining water levels at several hydropower dams ahead of a severe dry spell forecast for October.
"October might be hotter and drier," Sarawak's Deputy Premier Douglas Uggah Embas told reporters. "We want to increase the water levels as much as possible while we still can."
The haze has reached as far as parts of the Philippines, where local officials have urged residents to stay indoors as much as possible, and Singapore, where authorities have begun issuing daily haze advisories.

President Droupadi Murmu on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) urged popular film artists not to endorse products harmful to people's health, saying a “true star” spreads light, not darkness, highlighting the impact of words and actions of celebrities on young minds.
Ms. Murmu distributed the 72nd National Film Awards for 2024 in various categories of cinema at Ekta Nagar (Kevadia), near the Statue of Unity, in a glittering ceremony attended by top talents of the film industry.

"Please ensure that the workers, small-scale artists, assistants, and those struggling to make their mark, who contribute to this economy, receive both respect and social security," President Murmu added.

Describing film artists as key representatives of the creative economy, the President said highly popular artists possessed immense potential to influence citizens, especially the youth.

Government hospitals across Tamil Nadu are facing a shortage of surfactant medicines, a critical and life-saving medicine for pre-term babies.
The shortage has been persisting for the past few months, and several Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs) at government hospitals have been flagging it up for the Health Department.
Doctors said surfactant medicines are essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies in need of the therapy. They utilised external bovine or porcine surfactants (intratracheal) in pre-term babies. These surfactants were part of the speciality drug rate contract purchases of the Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation (TNMSC).
Inquiries with a number of hospitals and doctors revealed that a number of centres were facing short supply of surfactants in the past few months. Official sources confirmed that government hospitals, among them medical college hospitals in Theni, Dharmapuri, Tiruppur, Cuddalore, Tiruvannamalai, Vellore and Karur districts and in Chennai, reported surfactant vial shortage, while some hospitals said they had uninterrupted supply.
A doctor, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the shortage prevailed in the past three to four months owing to a number of factors. “First, we got no allotment. Secondly, some centres miscalculated their requirement, which is based on the average number of pre-term babies delivered, and thirdly, there was higher utilisation. This is a life-saving medicine essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies who are otherwise solid,” he said.
A doctor at another hospital said continuous supply was not assured, and shortage occurred frequently. “Currently, we are borrowing from other sub-centres which are referring babies to us. It is very difficult for us to manage newborn units without surfactants. Sometimes, we purchase them privately using SNCU funds to save the babies,” another doctor said.
A senior paediatrician said that after 34 weeks of gestation, the foetal lungs are generally mature enough to support exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide after birth. “However, in very pre-term babies, the alveoli, which are the tiny air sacs in the lungs, may not be sufficiently mature to function effectively on their own. Surfactant, a substance produced in the lungs, helps keep the alveoli open. But in babies born very prematurely, not enough surfactant may be produced, making it difficult for them to maintain adequate oxygen levels. Depending on the baby’s condition, doctors may use respiratory support such as CPAP or a mechanical ventilator. Surfactant is delivered directly into the lungs through the endotracheal tube to prevent hyaline membrane disease.”
Lung maturity in a newborn is critical as decreased oxygen could cause hypoxia and conditions such as retinopathy of prematurity and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, he said.
A Health Department source denied that there was any shortage. “There was no procurement delay. Some centres may have miscalculated their requirement, resulting in shortage, or may have utilised more vials. In such circumstances, they have obtained the required supply from neighbouring facilities. A six-month purchase order, worth nearly ₹9 crore, has been issued. Additionally, operational costs are provided for paediatricians to make local purchases whenever required,” he said.
Another official said the TNMSC has issued purchase orders and it will be supplied within two days. Officials said Cuddalore faced shortage and arrangements were made to send supplies from Coimbatore. The situation was being closely monitored, they said.

What is the White House pool and why is it in a row with Trump?
- Published
When Donald Trump unveiled a helipad at the White House on Monday, his remarks were barely audible in live footage of the event.
This was due to a row over an institution that rarely makes the news – the White House Press pool.
Yet it is at the heart of relations between the US president and the media, and this dispute could have constitutional implications, as well as potentially affecting coverage of the future presidential engagements.
Tensions are high. During Trump's visit to the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, he lashed out at a reporter from CNN - one of the media outlets he has come into conflict with.
What is the White House press pool?
It is a group of news organisations that combine resources to follow presidents wherever they are - in the Oval Office, at state dinners, on Air Force One or on holiday.
There are separate pools for TV, photographers and print and radio outlets, as well as a "new media" category.
The idea, conceived decades ago, is that having a pool saves on costs and space and it is not practical for hundreds of media outlets to follow the president around.
Members of the pool share their material - pictures and descriptions of the president's movements - with the wider media.
The pool is always on standby in case an event requires the president to speak to the nation.
This latest row centres on the TV pool which has five members - CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC.
It began on Friday when Trump said he was banning three outlets - CNN, Politico and MS NOW - from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news" and "fictions and lies" about his team.
A day later, reporters from those organisations found that their entry badges to the White House had been disabled.
On Monday, all the major US TV networks decided to pull out of White House pool duties - in effect boycotting presidential events.
That afternoon came the first test of this post-pool era - the new helipad at the White House.
With no pool cameras present, much of the media did not carry any pictures and for those that did, there was no microphone to clearly pick up the president's remarks.
But there were no such problems at Trump's meeting later that day with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, because it was not dependent on pool cameras and lots of media were there.
Why did US networks pull out of filming Trump?
Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds the rotating role covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC on Monday that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage" of President Trump.
In a joint statement, the five networks said: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.
"No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting."
The First Amendment of the US Constitution protects speech and press freedoms.
It forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
CNN, Politico and MS NOW have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports". A hearing is scheduled for Wednesday.
In a joint statement on Monday, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
Trump's speech to the United Nations on Tuesday was unaffected by the boycott because it was carried by outlets which are not part of the pool.
But the president's movements to and from his various New York events, which are usually filmed, could be subject to the blackout.
CNN appears to have taken the decision not to run Trump's UN speech live, despite it being made available through official UN sources. It should have been the pool news outlet with the president on Tuesday but is no longer travelling with him since his ban.
CNN Chief White House Correspondent Kaitlan Collins still attended the UN meetings, where she asked him a question as he spoke to reporters.
"I'm surprised CNN is here covering me… you should not be here covering me," Trump said, singling out Collins, whom he has frequently criticised and insulted in the past.
She responded by pointing out that the UN, not the White House, accredits journalists to cover the General Assembly.
How has Trump reacted and what is Trump TV?
Responding to news of the lawsuit, Trump called the outlets "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements.
"Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He added that his team would file an appeal. Meanwhile the White House has launched Trump TV, a 24/7 stream on YouTube.
Its description reads: "Watch the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place."
So far, the channel has primarily consisted of replays of previous Trump speeches and rallies.
For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York.
Unlike the traditional pool, however, that outlet is under no obligation to share material with others and has operated unilaterally for its audience.
Have there been previous examples of White House media bans?
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.
The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.
There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.
The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.
But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. Unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS NOW and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview.

ICC convicts former Central African Republic militia commander of torture
Judges at the International Criminal Court have convicted former Seleka rebel commander Mahamat Said Abdel Kani of persecution and torture as crimes against humanity committed while he ran a prison in Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Judges at the International Criminal Court on Wednesday convicted rebel commander Mahamat Said Abdel Kani of persecution and torture as crimes against humanity committed while he ran a prison in the Central African Republic.
Said, 56, wore jeans and a blue sweater and remained expressionless for most of the hourlong hearing as presiding Judge Miatta Maria Samba described the conditions prisoners endured at the facility in the capital, Bangui.
During the trial, witnesses described cramped cells with walls marked by “bullet holes and blood” and said they were whipped “until they soiled themselves,” Samba said. Other victims testified that they were confined in a windowless room under the floorboards of Said’s office.
The charges stemmed from fighting more than a decade ago between the predominantly Muslim Seleka rebels, who had seized power from then-President Francois Bozize, and a mainly Christian militia called the anti-Balaka.
Said pleaded not guilty to all charges when the proceedings began in 2021. His sentence, which could be as long as life in prison, will be decided at a later date.

Throughout 2026, people shared a rumor alleging Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix responded to U.S. President Donald Trump calling a reporter a pig. According to social media users' posts, the NFL quarterback publicly rebuked Trump, saying that "staying silent makes me part of the problem."
For example, on Sept. 20, a Facebook post (archived) read, "BREAKING NFL NEWS: Broncos star Bo Nix breaks his silence in shocking video response after 'Little Pig' comment to a female reporter shocks T.r.u.m.p — NFL superstar condemns disrespect towards women and sparks nationwide outrage."
The post featured a meme showing side-by-side images of Nix and Trump, with a purported Nix quote reading as follows:
When I watched that clip, something in me snapped. I play this game with fire and pride, but I was raised to respect every woman who cheers, works, and sacrifices behind the scenes. If a man with that much power can mock and demean them in front of the world, then staying silent makes me part of the problem. And I refuse to be part of that.
Other examples of the claim appeared on Facebook, Instagram and Threads. Snopes readers also searched this website in September 2026, specifically asking, "Did Bo Nix stand up for a female reporter?"
We first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo to locate possible evidence from credible sources about Nix publicly commenting on Trump. If the story was true, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters — or sports blogs — would have widely reported on it. That was not the case.
The rumor about Bo Nix responding to Trump was fictional, and as a result we've rated the claim false.
The claim appeared to take inspiration from a real remark Trump made in November 2025 while aboard Air Force One, when he told a female reporter asking a question, "Quiet. Quiet, piggy." 
People.com, citing a journalist's X post, reported the female journalist Trump addressed as "piggy" was Bloomberg reporter Catherine Lucey. The subject matter of Lucey's question pertained to asking Trump about his past relationship with deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
We emailed the Denver Broncos to ask if the organization would like to address the fake Nix quote and will update this article if we receive further details.
Digging into the rumor
In addition to social media posts, the untrue rumor about Nix publicly rebuking Trump appeared on a handful of generic-looking WordPress blogs. Those blogs lacked author names and credible information about their founding. An examination of the blogs found they were not reputable outlets, for example such as well-known newspapers or established news websites, or websites for local or national TV channels.
A scan of the text in one blog article with the artificial intelligence detection tool Pangram displayed the results, "We believe that this entire text is AI," as well as, "100% of this text is AI."
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. For Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as criticisms of the tool.
Creators of content like the fabricated Nix quote capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has previously reported on the business strategy.)
The fictional story about Nix standing up for women resembled glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental."
