How to set up 5.1 surround sound system for your Xbox
Modern TVs make surround sound Xbox audio easier, while older models have workarounds.
While it might not come to mind as quickly as 4K textures or smooth frame rates, being able to pair your Xbox Series X/S with a surround sound setup is a big advantage of modern gaming. Whether alerting you to nearby players in competitive shooters or upping the immersion in a story-driven title, a multichannel sound system is a big upgrade over stereo speakers.
For those interested in the best gear to upgrade your home theater setup, there's a good chance you own a modern TV with proper HDMI passthrough features. If that's the case, setting up surround sound on your Xbox is relatively easy. Folks using older TVs that lack eARC ports don't need to be left out in the cold, though; a cheap accessory can still treat your Xbox to full-blooded surround sound. We'll walk you through the process either way.
Tips for connecting your Xbox to a surround sound system
If you own a decent TV manufactured in the last few years, the easiest way to connect your Xbox console to a surround sound system is by hooking it up to your TV's eARC/ARC-capable HDMI port. To get the most out of your Xbox's current-gen visual features, you should connect to a TV that supports HDMI 2.1, making sure the HDMI cable supports this standard as well. This way, you can play supported games at 4K/120 fps — like Ori and the Will of the Wisps or The Touryst — while still enjoying surround sound.
The specific HDMI port on your TV that supports eARC will depend on the manufacturer. The slot you're looking for should be branded with "eARC/ARC". If it's not, check your TV's manual or head to the manufacturer's official listing online for precise specs.
Once you've connected your sound bar or home theater receiver to your TV's eARC port, it's time to tweak audio settings on your console by heading to Settings > General > Volume and audio output. Looking under Speaker audio, depending on what type of home theater setting you're working with, either the 5.1 uncompressed or 7.1 uncompressed option should provide immersive multi-channel audio. If those don't work, they may require more bandwidth than your setup offers. Try Bitstream out in that case.
If you own a Dolby Atmos system, install the Dolby Access app (it's free unless you're using headphones), then choose Dolby Atmos for home theater. This way, you'll get a more compelling sense of height in the soundscape for compatible games.
How to get surround sound on Xbox on older setups
If you're gaming on an older TV that doesn't support HDMI passthrough, you can still get surround sound on your Xbox, though it's not as smooth. In theory, an optical cable enables this, but neither Xbox Series X or S have an optical output. Thus, you'll need an HDMI audio extractor to get the setup working.
These aren't terribly expensive, though you'll need to get a model that supports at least 60Hz, or 120Hz if your TV supports it, to avoid artificially limiting performance since cheap ones are capped at 30Hz. Extractors split the audio and video signals, with the former being sent to your surround sound system and the latter going to your TV. To properly configure this optical cable workaround on your Xbox, go to Settings > General > Volume and audio output > Additional options/Audio setup, then choose a compatible format, like Dolby Digital. Though optical doesn't support 7.1 or lossless Dolby Atmos, it's perfectly capable of delivering 5.1 audio.
There's another option to achieve surround sound on your Xbox with older setups. Provided your AV receiver has HDMI inputs, you can plug your Series X/S directly into the receiver. A potential downside with this option is that older receivers likely won't support HDMI 2.1, meaning you won't be able to achieve a 4K/120Hz signal, while frame-smoothing VRR features are also off the table.
Is 5.1 or 7.1 surround sound better for gaming?
Technically, 7.1 has a higher audio immersion ceiling than 5.1 surround sound. That said, the difference between a well-calibrated 5.1 system and a budget 7.1 setup is slim. If you struggle to tell the differences between Dolby Digital, DTS and Atmos, a standard 5.1 home theater system will suit your Xbox needs just fine.
A 5.1 setup consists of a center speaker, one either side of it, a subwoofer and two surround speakers (normally placed behind where you sit). 7.1 systems throw in an extra two surround speakers, which can more precisely convey, say, the direction of footsteps if the developer has really put time into a game's audio. Either, many of the best Xbox games boast superb surround sound support. First-party efforts like Gears 5, Halo Infinite and Forza Horizon 6 all support Dolby Atmos. Hearing cars rapidly approaching in your surround channels can help you claim podium finishes.
While 7.1 systems can offer a slightly elevated audio experience compared to 5.1, there are some important practicalities to consider. The biggest is that you need more space to accommodate a 7.1 system. If you play your Xbox in a cramped lounge where floor space is at a premium, a 5.1 setup will be more practical than 7.1 while still delivering a compelling sound experience.

Australian man is accused of being Islamic State group propagandist who shared 10,000 files online
Authorities in Melbourne have accused a man of pledging allegiance to the Islamic State group and spreading extremist propaganda online
WELLINGTON, New Zealand -- A man in the Australian city of Melbourne is accused of pledging allegiance to the Islamic State group and spreading thousands of pieces of extremist propaganda online over a period of years, the authorities said on Wednesday.
He was the seventh man to be arrested in Victoria state since May over allegations of possessing or distributing IS content online. Australia's federal police didn't link the latest arrest to the other six and wouldn't say if they believed the man's case was connected.
The 65-year-old Australian citizen, whose name hasn't been released, was due to appear in a Melbourne court later on Wednesday. He's charged with being a member of a terrorist organization and with transmitting violent extremist material in an encrypted messaging app the authorities didn't name.
The maximum penalty for the offenses is 10 years in prison.
The authorities said the man had sent 10,000 files containing extremist content between 2015 and 2020, including material relating to executions, torture and IS propaganda. The federal police allege that he also shared information about avoiding detection from law enforcement and instructional guides on planning and conducting mass casualty attacks, a statement Wednesday said.
Acting Assistant Commissioner Paula Hudson told reporters in Canberra that the scale and distribution of the materials by the man “placed him as a principal distributor of ISIS propaganda within the group.”
“The material glorified acts of violence and terrorism, spreading hateful ideology that is designed to radicalize others,” Hudson said.
An investigation into the man began when border officials examined the man's luggage as he departed Australia for a six-month trip to Egypt in 2020, the authorities said. He wasn't known to have traveled abroad since 2020 and wasn't linked to any attack or plot, Hudson said.
Earlier this month, a 30-year-old Melbourne man was arrested and charged with possessing violent extremist content as he attempted to depart Australia for the Middle East, authorities said. The federal police allege he was part of an online group chat with five other Victoria state men arrested in May, who all face charges relating to possessing extremist material, including IS propaganda.
The Islamic State group is a scattered and considerably weaker group since a 2019 United States-led military intervention drove it out of territory it had seized in Iraq and Syria, but its cells remain active and it has inspired a number of independent attacks, including in western countries. In Australia, a mass shooting at a Hanukkah event in 2025, in which two men are accused of killing 15 Jewish people, was motivated by the shooters' IS affiliations, the authorities allege.
It's thought 200 Australians traveled to Syria and Iraq to join the Islamic State group between 2012 and 2019, according to a website for the country's national security agencies. Dozens more “assisted” IS by supporting those overseas or by planning or carrying out terrorist attacks in Australia, the website says.

Richard Marles says the Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong.
The acting prime minister said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” will be reviewed, however, he claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.
The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.
The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.
“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained on of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The Guardian has contacted the Pentagon.
While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.
“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.
Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence community that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.
More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F3-5 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

The story uses screenshots and not the actual viral video in view of its sensitive nature.
A 12-second long video is going viral on social media where a woman is seen bathing in river water while wearing a bikini.
The video was posted on September 15 by X user Barkha Trehan, who describes herself as ‘Activist | Voice Of Men | President, Purush Aayog’. She wrote, “Location : Haridwar. Madam: My Body My Choice. Your take ??” The video garnered over 1 million views. (Archive)
In her X bio, Trehan identifies herself as a “men’s rights activist” and the “president of Purush Aayog”. She also claims to be a TEDx speaker and a “Hindu entrepreneur”; she apparently also “directed a documentary titled The Curse of Manhood”.
Media outlet News 18 Hindi published a report with screenshots from the video pointing out that it had angered social media users. (Archive)
This same video was posted by content creator Piyali Banerjee, where she questioned the “basic decency” and “knowledge of clothing” of the woman.
Other social media users also shared the same video with similar captions, questing the woman for wearing a bikini in Haridwar, with misogynistic comments about her character.
The video is also viral on Instagram.
Fact Check
To verify its authenticity, we ran a reverse image search on a few keyframes from the viral clip. This search led us to a reel posted on Instagram on August 18. The 21-second long reel was uploaded by an account named ‘ishika_pandit’. It showed the same woman bathing at the same spot, but wearing completely different clothes.
This video matched the background of the viral clip with the steel railing on the river and the foundations of a bridge clearly visible in the background. The woman’s hand gestures also mirror the viral video, and the same two men are visible in both videos.
Based on these similarities, it can be concluded that the video uploaded on August 18 is the original footage. The woman in the original video is seen wearing a yellow suit, and not a bikini. Thus, the viral clip is a doctored version of the original video, manipulating the attire of the woman.
Some social media users highlighted the possibility of the viral clip being an AI-generated deepfake, claiming that the woman’s clothes had been purposely changed from a suit to a bikini. (Archive)

Taking a safe bet here that most of you who have heard of Louise Joy Brown have not heard at all of Jean Purdy, or her role in the birth of Baby Brown. Louise Brown was the first baby born of an IVF procedure on July 25, 1978. But this might not have been a joyful story, but for Jean Purdy.
Like all the heroines in this column, Jean Marian Purdy, a clinical embryologist and a critical part of the development of in vitro fertilisation, remained uncredited for a long while. Born in Cambridge, U.K., she went to work with physiologist Robert Edwards and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe at the Physiological Laboratory in Cambridge. They were working on a high-risk experiment and taking medical science where it had never been before – who would have thought babies could be created in test tubes before the trio managed to show that it is possible.
Purdy trained as a nurse in Addenbrooke Hopsital in Cambridge, and joined Edwards in 1968 as a research nurse and quickly became indispensable to the team. Going back to study the records later, scientists established that it was Purdy who managed the laboratory, prepared and tested culture media, and recorded and organised the data of the early IVF work in the lab. Besides this, the records also put her at the centre of patient care, in this case, supporting women who volunteered their eggs and wombs at a time when public sentiment was entirely against it.
Purdy was the first to recognise and describe the formation of the early human blastocyst – the cluster of cells that forms five or six days after a sperm fertilises an egg, in the culture, a key milestone in pre-implantation development. It represents the early stage of embryonic development, where the embryo implants itself into the wall of the uterus to establish a pregnancy. Purdy was the first to see the embryonic cells successfully dividing in the lab, soon these cells would go on to become on 25 July 1978, she was the first to see the embryonic cells that would become Louise Brown. This moment is significant, because it was the first indication that their pioneering technique had worked.
That was not all; between 1970 and 1985, until her death, she co-authored 26 academic papers with Edwards and others in leading journals, including Nature, documenting methods, outcomes and sophistication that made IVF safe and more reliable.
After NHS funding for IVF was withdrawn following early successes, Purdy helped establish the world’s first dedicated IVF clinic, Bourn Hall Clinic near Cambridge in 1980, and served as its technical director. Again, she helped standardise medical protocols for IVF and scale up treatment, overseeing the birth of more than 500 IVF babies before her death from cancer at just 39 years, in 1985.
In their article The Oldham Notebooks: an analysis of the development of IVF 1969–1978. V. The role of Jean Purdy reassessed, archived in PubMed, Martin H. Johnson and Kay Elder, look at her body of work in early fertility care. The authors pored over the Oldham Notebooks - 21 handwritten laboratory notebooks and loose records kept primarily by Purdy between 1969 and 1978. They concluded that: “Purdy’s interests were clearly focused on the research and development aspects, especially those exploring viable embryo development and improved transfer procedures. For example, in a film made in 1980 (Williams, 1980), she talks about a modification to the transfer cannula that she was trying. Thus, whilst Edwards provided the ideas and the intellectual stimulation and Steptoe the authoritative clinical skills, it is arguable that without Purdy’s systematic approach and dedicated contributions, the project at Oldham may have faltered.”
Despite all this, centuries of sexism weighing in on the scientific community, a classic example of the Matilda Effect, her role was minimised in public memory for decades. Even though Edwards and other colleagues objected to it, Purdy’s name was omitted from a commemorative plaque installed at Oldham Hopsitals, associated with IVF’s breakthrough. Correspondence from Edwards archived at Cambridge later described Purdy as “crucial” to their work, underscoring how her erasure contradicted the team’s own view of her importance. In fact, Edwards’ own records state his growing confidence in her and her essentiality in the team: Purdy was “being ‘particularly good with the patients’, and her ‘cooperation had become crucial. It was no longer just Patrick and me. We had become a threesome’.
However, only Edwards was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for IVF. While recognition for the work that Purdy did, has grown only recently, thanks in good measure to the research of Johnson and Elder, some things cannot be corrected any more. Now, some museums and clinics cite Purdy as the first clinical embryologist, and other institutions have begun naming awards and exhibitions after her. Sidelined again, this time, though her collaborators acknowledged her work, Purdy’s contributions were callously and credit consistently denied.
Though belated, it’s now time to undo the wrongs. It is time to say her name! Say Jean Purdy, shout it out from the rooftops!

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

O'Neill receives Celtic backing after 'painful' week

Celtic will "come together and support" manager Martin O'Neill after a "painful" week for the club, chief executive Michael Nicholson has said.
O'Neill had indicated that he would use the international break to consider his future following two defeats to Rangers, either side of a home loss to Ferencvaros in the Europa League.
In the wake of Sunday's 1-0 derby defeat at Celtic Park, 74-year-old O'Neill had said "it might be time to wrap it up".
However, Nicholson suggested the club will rally round the manager who has delivered nine trophies over two spells.
His remarks came with the latest financial figures revealing a drop of nearly £33m in revenue.
A loss of £4.8m is largely down to the failure to reach last year's Champions League and Celtic have missed out again, squandering a 4-0 aggregate lead in their play-off with LASK last month.
"Having started well in the Premiership this season, we experienced disappointment in the Champions League play-off," said Nicholson in a written statement accompanying the financial results.
"Reaching the league phase of the Champions League is an objective for us all, and we are sorry not to have achieved it.
"On top of that, the losses in the last week have been painful for us all. We will now come together and support Martin and the players, as we focus our efforts on achieving success domestically and in the Europa League."

Trump administration to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees over fraud claims
WASHINGTON — Vice President JD Vance and other Trump administration officials said Tuesday they plan to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging that the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program, or simply do not exist.
Vance said the discovery and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges, part of an administration-wide crackdown on fraud, would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings.
"We're actually making sure that the people receiving Obamacare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them," said Vance, who leads a government task force to eliminate fraud. He was flanked by Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, or CMS, and other administration officials.
Vance said the cancellation of approximately 315,000 enrollments covering 760,000 people was done in part because the government was not checking whether people enrolled were eligible. Vance said another 419,000 enrollments will get additional verification to make sure they are eligible for the benefit.
The Trump administration also announced a six-month suspension on new agents or brokers who sign up enrollees for healthcare coverage, who officials say commit a disproportionate amount of the fraud they uncovered.
Roughly 19.2 million Americans are actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans as of early 2026, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website. The number of enrollees grew during the COVID-19 pandemic when enhanced subsidies became available through the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act, both signed into law by former President Joe Biden.
Tuesday's announcement is the latest in an initiative by the Trump administration to address fraud around the country, including in federal healthcare programs, which officials say is needed to rein in runaway spending and protect taxpayers.
Some healthcare policy experts are calling for more transparency on how the Trump administration decided to cut hundreds of thousands of enrollees — and question how many people may have been wrongly cut from the program.
Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said "I think there's no question that somebody who was fraudulently enrolled should have their coverage canceled," however, "I think the question is whether this was the appropriate process by which to identify fraudulent enrollees, and also whether all of them were indeed fraudulently enrolled."
Cox said the elimination of the people from ACA programs was done outside of the normal regulatory process.
Ellen Montz, a former deputy administrator and director at the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight at CMS during the Biden administration said during her time in government, there was an ongoing effort to eliminate fraud from ACA programs.
"There's a lot of work to be done, and the Trump administration has done some good things that are targeting the actual fraudsters," she said. Adding that Tuesday's announcement lacked details on how the administration determined who to cut. " I would imagine we'll hear from some subset of consumers that ask: why did my enrollment get cancelled?" Montz said.
At the press conference, Tuesday, Vance referred to some enrollments lacking social security numbers or immigration documentation.
The announcement comes as stubbornly high inflation and rising healthcare costs pressure the Trump administration to come up with a plan to bring down costs for Americans as affordability remains a central issue in the fall midterm elections.
The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many Americans during Trump's second term, after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Biden's term.
Premiums doubled or tripled for many enrollees, prompting millions to downgrade their plans or exit the program entirely after the Republican-led Congress allowed the subsidies to expire this year.
The Government Accountability Office suggests fraud risks in the advance premium tax credit do exist - however it's unclear at what scale. The GAO conducted covert testing using fictitious ACA applicants enrolled in 2024 and 2025. A report released in December showed that the federal marketplace approved subsidized coverage for almost all of the GAO's 24 fake enrollees.
The White House referred The Associated Press to the Vice President's team for additional comment on bigger plans to address healthcare affordability. The Vice President's office and CMS did not respond to Associated Press requests for comment.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news of the Trump administration's plan to remove ACA enrollees from public exchanges.
Democratic lawmakers criticized the move to remove enrollees from ACA coverage.
Richard E. Neal, a Massachusetts Democrat and ranking member of the Ways and Means Committee, said "Republicans have already created the worst healthcare crisis ever, but every decision by the Trump Administration is designed to keep making it worse."
"As if making coverage harder to access through skyrocketing premiums and more red tape wasn't painful enough, they're doubling down to take it away entirely," Neal said.

Eight Sleep announced the next version of its “intelligent sleep system” designed to regulate the temperature of your bed in response to tracked health and sleep metrics like breathing and heart rate. The company calls its new Pod 6 system its “most significant hardware launch to date,” and it’s centered around a redesigned cooling hub that’s now small enough to hide beneath most beds. The new system is cheaper than Eight Sleep’s Pod 5 that launched in 2025, but is still by no means cheap.
Eight Sleep’s new cooling hub is small enough to hide under your bed
The Pod 6 intelligent sleep system cools or warms your bed faster while being smaller, smarter, and cheaper.
The Pod 6 is now available through Eight Sleep’s online store. The Standard version ranges in price from $2,699 for a full-size mattress to $2,999 for king and California king sizes. But for the first time Eight Sleep will offer a smaller Solo option for single sleepers with a cover that fits half of any size mattress for $1,999. The Pod 6 system is still compatible with Eight Sleep’s optional accessories, like its $999 cooling pillow cover, and there’s a mandatory subscription that ranges in price from $199 to $399 per year for two sleepers.
Eight Sleep claims the Pod 6’s control hub was “rebuilt from scratch, with the electrical, mechanical, and software systems re-engineered together,” resulting in it being half the size of previous versions while delivering more performance. The hub, which circulates temperature-controlled water through the mattress cover to help deliver a better night’s sleep, is now 20 percent faster at making temperature adjustments.
The Pod 6’s health and sleep tracking capabilities have also been upgraded with additional sensors. While last year’s Pod 5 featured two biometric sensors integrated into the mattress cover, the Pod 6 increases that to 18 sensors. It can track health metrics like heart rate, heart rate variability, breathing rate, sleep stages, and detect snoring for two individuals whether they’re sleeping next to each other or on opposite sides of the bed. The system is also smart enough to distinguish between adults, children, and pets. All of that collected data is used by Eight Sleep’s AI-powered Autopilot feature (which is what the subscription covers) to make automatic temperature adjustments throughout the night to maintain comfort without any manual input.

CLEVELAND — Amy Acton couldn’t speak.
Supporters of Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor of Ohio, were waiting for her remarks along the banks of the Black River, once known as the “river of fish tumors” because of the catfish deformed by steel mill slag. Now the river was being rehabilitated. Acton, a physician who vaulted to national fame when she led Ohio’s aggressive response to Covid-19 as the state’s director of public health back in 2020, was running with the promise to do the same for state politics.
The crowd, attending a Labor Day festival in the industrial city of Lorain, had spent the afternoon grazing on boba tea and pastelitos from food trucks while a live band covered ’90s hits like “Return of the Mack.” They didn’t yet know that Acton wasn’t going to make it onstage after all. Earlier that day, at a different campaign event about 90 miles east in Canfield, a man carrying two handguns, brass knuckles, and a Taser had barreled toward Acton while yelling her name, knocking over an elderly couple in the crowd. (The man, Patrick Havas, has since pleaded not guilty to charges including assault.)
Of all the high-profile electoral contests this November, the heated race for Ohio governor could be the most direct test of where public opinion in the heartland currently stands on health care, trust in science, and the lasting legacy of the Covid pandemic. Acton’s Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, is the billionaire founder and former CEO of biotech company Roivant who built his political profile as a 2024 presidential candidate in part on accusing the government of overreach in the pandemic — claims he’s made central to his current gubernatorial campaign as well.
STAT visited events for each candidate on the same day in August to get a sense of how Acton and Ramaswamy are tapping into American health anxieties, and how their messages are resonating with Ohioans. Acton stands by her decisions during the pandemic, but is betting that people in Ohio are ready to move on and instead focus on fixing problems like health care affordability and access. (Affordable Care Act enrollment in Ohio dropped by one-third in the past year following the expiration of federal subsidies, the most of any state.)

‘Almost unprecedented’ cuts in malaria funding will hurt UK pandemic planning, leading scientists say
‘The tools we have developed together are not only protecting children’s lives in Africa, but will help us protect and respond to similar risks in the UK,’ says one researcher
An “almost unprecedented” scaling back of funding for malaria science will harm the UK’s preparedness for future pandemics, leading scientists say.
Research targeting malaria has “spillover” effects that improve responses to wider health threats, according to experts polled for the first report of its kind.
The Malaria Science Index, a survey of the UK’s top researchers in the field, is published as world leaders meet in New York for a high-level meeting on pandemic preparedness alongside the United Nations General Assembly on Friday.
Some 80 per cent of respondents said they believed malaria science provided health benefits to the UK public, with the same proportion saying they thought it made the UK safer.
Heather Ferguson, professor of infectious disease ecology at the University of Glasgow, surveyed for the report, said: “Environmental changes are bringing mosquito-borne diseases much closer to home, and our ability to respond to these risks in the UK is strengthened by the training British scientists have from working shoulder-to-shoulder with experts in endemic countries.
“The technologies and tools we have developed together are not only protecting children’s lives in Africa, but will help us protect and respond to similar risks in the UK,” she added.
Professor Ferguson said that the obvious way to protect people in the UK from malaria was to eliminate it from Africa: “If we can control and eliminate malaria from its heartland, everyone benefits.”
The Oxford/AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine had its roots in research towards a malaria vaccine, and early results suggest antimalarial drug Atovaquone could help in treating some types of cancer.
Malaria is a life-threatening disease that is caused by a parasite and spread to humans by some types of mosquito. In 2024, there were an estimated 282 million malaria cases and 610,000 deaths, the majority of whom were children aged under five in Africa.
Almost all of the scientists polled saw funding shortfalls as a threat to the success of research, development and approval of future tools against malaria. They also identified them as the primary threat to implementing and scaling up those tools, beyond even climate change and extreme weather events
“Funding for global health has always been limited,” said one expert, “but the huge scale back of investment in support for this type of research in the last couple of years is almost unprecedented.”
Public funding for malaria research and development fell from $432m (£324m) in 2021 to $351m in 2024, according to figures from Impact Global Health. In the past two years, countries including the US and UK, both historically major donors in the fight against malaria, have announced widespread aid cuts.
Another scientist warned that continued research was vital to keep pace with a disease that is changing fast. The malaria parasite is evolving resistance to many antimalarial drugs, while mosquitoes are becoming resistant to existing insecticides, and new types of malaria-carrying mosquitoes are spreading across Africa.
“As governments and other agencies look to cut funding…there may be a temptation to cut funding to grassroots research and development to help support deployment of existing tools…This would be a huge mistake as innovation and discovery are absolutely critical to maintain the momentum in the fight against malaria,” they said.
The poll involved 35 of the UK’s top malaria scientists in both academia and industry. It was carried out by YouGov and led by Malaria No More UK, in partnership with Imperial College London, The Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine and The Innovative Vector Control Consortium. Because of the small size, they said the findings should only be treated as “indicative”.
Asked to point out the most promising tools in development involving UK scientists, 71 per cent highlighted drugs such as single-dose cures, and 69 per cent vaccines.
“With a new prime minister and cabinet in place, we hope the UK’s critical role as a malaria science superpower is maintained, primarily to end the disease for good but also to help protect the British public against threats to their health,” said Gareth Jenkins, managing director of Malaria No More UK.

Germany's saviour? How Klopp is looking to turn fortunes around
- Published
It has been quite the ride since Jurgen Klopp was announced as Germany's head coach in July.
In his first news conference, Klopp admonished the media, urging them to treat him fairly and refrain from any attacks against his family.
Last Thursday, during another media conference, Klopp called for "positive patriotism" amid political turmoil in the country.
When asked whether he considers himself an ambassador for Germany in his new role, Klopp's answer was a serious one.
"From my perspective as a sportsman, I can say that I would very much like to reclaim the flag for myself, for all of us," said Klopp.
"I want it so that when someone waves it, no-one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?' Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country."
His statement was made in light of the success of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The anti-immigration party has since scored another win in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Klopp's remarks were widely and positively discussed in the media - the German national team represents a diverse Germany, as several players come from a migrant background.
KIopp also remarked about the recent success of Alexander Zverev at the US Open, the women's basketball team at the European Championship and German athletes at the European Athletics Championships, saying sport can ensure "a sense of community".
He added: "This is our mission: we need to create a good atmosphere."
Klopp knows, intentionally or not, how to make headlines.
However, the German Football Association (DFB) didn't hire the former Liverpool boss on an annual salary of £6m to become a commentator on the state of Germany - but to transform a floundering national team.
- Klopp wants to 'reclaim' flag amid German elections 
  - Published5 days ago
- Klopp starts Germany reign by threatening to quit 
  - Published24 July
Between the two news conferences, Klopp looked like the busiest national team boss on the planet, making countless visits to league games and training facilities.
One day fans could see Klopp sitting in the stands of Dortmund's Signal Iduna Park, his old stomping ground and, not long after, they may have caught a picture of him in the VIP lounge of Mainz's stadium or somewhere near Eintracht Frankfurt's training pitch talking to players.
Klopp has approached this new job with open eyes. Initially, the charismatic 59-year-old drew up a list of 57 players who could have been selected for this first international break.
"Players will receive chances who don't even expect it yet," Klopp said in July.
His first selection wasn't short of surprises. In the flavour of a trial-and-error principle, Klopp and his staff decided to select two almost completely different squads for the upcoming four games.
The first squad, including Joshua Kimmich, Kai Havertz and Jamal Musiala, will face arch-rivals the Netherlands at Johan Cruyff Arena on Thursday (19:45 BST) and host Greece on Sunday.
The second squad, with Florian Wirtz and Aleksandar Pavlovic, face Serbia at home and Greece on the road in the second half of this international break. The only player who was selected for both is back-up goalkeeper Finn Dahmen.
'It could be wild, but I accept that'
The selection process means we will not see Germany's best starting XI this time around. Instead, Klopp clearly intends to try out new players, some of whom played in Germany's second tier only a few months ago.
Take, for example, Felix Keidel, a 23-year-old full-back-midfielder hybrid from recently promoted SV Elversberg.
A year ago, Keidel was as far away from the national team as the Oktoberfest from Rio Carnival.
Now Keidel - just like Mika Baur, Bambase Conte, Max Rosenfelder, Philipp Treu, and Vitaly Janelt - has the chance to show he could be a valuable cog in the machine.
Klopp has never built his success merely on star names - he has always taken a liking to undervalued and overlooked players.
He once signed an little-known Polish winger by the name of Lukasz Piszczek and moulded him into one of the best right-backs in Europe who would go toe-to-toe with Cristiano Ronaldo in his prime. And he helped transform Andy Robertson into a force on Liverpool's left side.
Klopp's style helps to elevate all the members of his squad - not just the most talented.
Fitness and mental readiness are highly important, and some newcomers might just have that to impress the new manager.
But man-marking is prevalent in Germany's top flight, while Klopp prefers his teams to close down the player in possession to create superior numbers around the ball. So some of the Bundesliga players will have to adapt quickly.
"It is not important who plays but how someone plays," Klopp said last week. "I expect a lot from the beginning. It could be a bit wild, but I accept that. It just has to be lively."
Klopp has chosen younger squads compared to the ones we saw in the past couple of years. Manuel Neuer, Antonio Rudiger and Pascal Gross have retired from international football, and other 30-somethings might just not receive a chance to get into the team again.
"I think it is about time to wish the new generation best of luck," Gross said after Brighton's win over Arsenal on Saturday. "I still enjoy playing football here in the club, but there's a change in Germany and rightfully so."
Both squads for this international break have an average age between 24 and 25. Youth and energy seem to be preferred.
"I have the desire to work with guys who cannot wait to wear this jersey, who want to play the kind of football everybody enjoys and who perform even better wearing the national team jersey," Klopp said.
We can expect from him to simplify Germany's approach to ball possession. Predecessor Julian Nagelsmann bent over backwards to hide some of the flaws he detected in his squad and thus created highly complex tactical systems.
On the contrary, Klopp intends to put an emphasis on the wings and break defences there. We saw what he was able to achieve with the likes of Mohamed Salah, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Sadio Mane from wide areas.
While underwhelming at the past couple of international tournaments, Germany still possess a deep talent pool. Cologne's rising star Said El Mala and 18-year-old Bayern Munich talent Lennart Karl will get chances to show their skills on the wings.
Freiburg's Derry Scherhant and Barcelona's Karim Adeyemi provide plenty of speed, just like Brentford's Kevin Schade who has returned to the squad after being left out for the World Cup. There is potential for an exciting Germany side we have not seen in quite a while.
Finally, the emotional component plays a role in Klopp's entire approach. He works towards a fresh start for the national team and a new spirit in the country.
Last Thursday, he wore a cap that read "One of 83 million". It was a clear indication he wants to unite all 83 million Germans behind this team and they are all in it together.
Klopp has spent plenty of time thus far attempting to shape narratives off the field - but now the spotlight turns to his ability to get the best out of his group of players on the pitch.

Angus Taylor has vowed to repeal a raft of emissions reduction and renewable energy policies, including several measures supported by or introduced under past Coalition governments, within a month of being elected prime minister, prompting accusations he would “let climate change rip”.
On Wednesday, Taylor’s energy spokesperson, Dan Tehan, announced a new bill would be introduced to parliament within 30 days after a Coalition win at the next federal election to ensure affordable, reliable and secure energy to Australians.
The bill, which contains a package of eight previously announced opposition policies, would remove safeguard mechanism and nuclear prohibitions, both introduced by previous Coalition governments.
It would also:
- 
  Scrap vehicle emissions standards.
- 
  Remove the legislated net zero by 2050 target.
- 
  Revoke four of six offshore wind energy zones due for completion by the late 2030s: the Hunter, Illawarra, Southern Ocean and Bunbury regions.
- 
  Introduce a renewable energy code of conduct for developers.
- 
  Require energy funding provided to states and territories prioritises energy affordability and reliability.
- 
  Change the Australian Energy Regulator’s main focus to affordability and reliability.
“Australia has done its bit,” Taylor said at a press conference when asked why it wanted to reverse laws driving down emissions.
“What we will continue to see is technologies emerging with lower emissions that Australians want to choose. That is fine, and that is great.”
Speaking at an energy forum on Wednesday, Tehan said the geopolitical changes in recent years, including the ongoing conflict over the strait of Hormuz, gave the Coalition the social licence to split energy from climate policy.
“I think the Australian people, and you can feel it in the mood of the nation at the moment, want us to be much more sovereign, capable, be able to stand on our own two feet, and make sure that we can deal with the world with a strong economy,” he said.
Tehan said the Coalition would “handle emissions reduction separately” with a policy released later this year.
The energy minister, Chris Bowen, said the plan would take a “chainsaw to the economy and household budgets” and “make Australia poorer, weaker and less secure from global shocks”.
“They want to take choice away from Australians – remove your ability to take control of your energy bills with a cheaper home battery, and pick a cheaper to run car,” he said.
Bowen said the Coalition’s plan to “stop renewables and household batteries” and extend the life of existing coal power stations would mean households would be “left to pick up the bill of global shocks”.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, described it as a “One Nation policy with a Liberal Party sticker on it”.
“Dan Tehan’s latest brain fade would put a wrecking ball through the economy,” he said.
“This is a plan for a smaller economy, lower wages, poorer workers and fewer jobs.”
The energy policy reversal was similarly criticised by Kooyong MP, Monique Ryan, and acting Greens leader, Mehreen Faruqi, for taking the country backwards.
“The Coalition’s plan is dumb, dangerous, and desperate climate denial which would make energy more expensive and unreliable,” Dr Ryan said.
Faruqi also took aim at Labor after its resources minister, Madeleine King, marked the opening of the Beetaloo basin with smiles.
“Australians deserve a safe climate future, but we won’t see that while the Labor government is capitulating to fossil fuels and the Coalition’s energy policy is written to prop up corporate profits,” she said.
Environment groups have condemned the Coalition’s announcement, with the Australian Conservation Foundation’s head of political advocacy, Gavan McFadzean, saying Australians deserved better.
“You can’t be anti-renewables and pro-energy reliability, because renewables with storage is the most reliable and affordable form of energy, while nuclear is the most expensive and would need to be publicly funded,” McFadzean said.
“To commit to slow the renewables transition is a breathtaking act of economic self-harm that would increase climate pollution and abandon jobs and investment in the future low carbon economy.”
The chief executive of the Climate Council, Amanda McKenzie, described the energy announcement as “pure ideology” underpinned by years of climate denial.
“The Coalition’s plan is to let climate change rip. It’s deadly negligence that would leave Australians facing more fires, floods and heatwaves,” she said.
“The Coalition wants to force Australians back into the most polluting cars in the world and increase our dependence on foreign oil.”
Farmers for Climate Action, a group representing more than 8,000 farmers across Australia, said they were “extremely disappointed”.
Harden sheep and crop farmer and FCA spokesperson Peter Holding, said giving up on pollution reduction was crazy.
“We are extremely disappointed in the Coalition today. You can’t say you’re looking after farmers while you axe pollution reduction policies, when we know more pollution means more fires and droughts, more climate change, and higher insurance costs,” he said.

Major news outlets banned by Trump will have their day in court
Sign up for NPR's Up First morning newsletter for the stories you need to start your day
Reporters try to hold President Trump and his administration accountable.
Now three major U.S. news outlets are asking a federal judge — a Trump appointee at that — to hold the president in check for what they say is an egregious violation of their First Amendment rights simply because he doesn't like how they cover him.
Trump has already signalled that he knows the judge may well rule against him: U.S. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly held in favor of Jim Acosta, then with CNN, in 2018 when Trump aides stripped him of his White House permanent credentials on similar grounds.
"Almost without question and, as usual, we'll go for appeal because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources, shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump's account on Truth Social posted Monday afternoon.
At the court hearing Wednesday afternoon, the three news outlets will ask Judge Kelly to return the credentials to their journalists.
CNN, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) and Politico sued President Trump after he made good on his threat to bar them from covering official events. Trump told White House reporters on Friday that he was fed up after what he called two years of unfair and negative coverage.
"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposefully negative things," Trump told reporters Friday. "Now, if they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my — into the people's house."
The news outlets accuse Trump of violating not only their right to freedom of speech under the First Amendment, but also to due process under the Fifth.
"The President has been explicit that this ban is intended to punish reporting he doesn't like and to intimidate journalists and news organizations covering him and his administration," the lead attorney for the news outlets, Theodore J. Boutrous of Gibson Dunn, said in a statement. "This ban on the free press harms the American people, who are entitled to rigorous, fact-based coverage of the President of the United States."
Boutrous represented NPR and three Colorado public radio stations on similar grounds: a federal judge found a Trump executive order that banned federal agencies from distributing federal funds to public media outlets because he didn't like NPR's coverage to be unconstitutional. (Trump still succeeded in convincing the Republican-led Congress to pull back nearly all federal funding for public media.)
White House debuts an alternative
Trump famously loves the spotlight and basks in the glow of TV cameras. After all, he's a former reality TV star.
But barring CNN in particular posed a dilemma for him Monday. CNN was set to be the pool TV network, meaning it would film the president as he went about his official duties and distribute that footage to other major television networks. None stepped in to fill CNN's place, in a show of solidarity. And many of CNN's competitors are not airing video of the president from other sources. (NPR, which is a member of the White House radio pool, has also declined to broadcast audio of Trump.)
That left Trump cutting a ribbon on a new White House helipad on Monday in a video released by the administration. There was just one problem: the whirling helicopter parked in the background drowned out whatever Trump was saying. The audio was inaudible.
The White House had tried to circumvent the press pool by debuting its own streamer on YouTube, called Trump TV. While Trump is having a busy week at the U.N. General Assembly in New York, Trump TV features a collection of past press conferences and official events (all with high-quality audio).
Reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico are following Trump as he travels through New York. On Tuesday at the United Nations, CNN's Kaitlin Collins stood with other journalists and shouted a question about the unpopularity of the war in Iran.
Trump ignored the question, instead telling her, "You should not be here covering me." She pointed out that the United Nations had given her press credentials. Not all locations are under his — or the federal government's — control. The court case will determine to what extent the president can dictate terms of reporting on him from the White House itself.
News outlets want access restored
Previous judicial rulings appear to offer ballast to CNN, MSNOW and Politico's legal argument.
As Trump noted, there is no constitutional or legal right that requires the president to let any particular journalist — or anyone at all — to report on federal matters from the White House grounds. The administration has argued in public statements that reporting from White House grounds is a privilege not a right.
But once a journalist is given credentials to report from the White House, they cannot be prevented from returning simply because the administration does not like their coverage. That would be "viewpoint discrimination" that the courts have held violate their free speech rights under the First Amendment.
Under a 1977 U.S. Court of Appeals ruling that still holds today, reporters cannot be barred from the White House or denied a permanent White House press pass without a clear explanation from the Secret Service that incorporates due process.
Trump barred the Associated Press from the White House last year, after he deemed the Gulf of Mexico should be called the Gulf of America, but the news wire declined to follow suit. The AP sued under similar grounds as the three news outlets' lawsuit. That case is ongoing.

In mid-August, along the Bengaluru-Mysuru expressway, an agricultural labourer in C.K. Tandya village in South Bengaluru district (formerly known as Ramanagara) noticed something unusual on a strip of farmland: a heap of medical waste.
This wasn’t the first time that the villagers in South Bengaluru had noticed suspicious objects or activity around the area which contained a farmhouse, say the police. They had seen men frequently moving in and out of it on a scooter without a number plate. They had also seen courier and e-commerce delivery vehicles making regular trips to the secluded location.
Spanning nearly eight acres and fenced by a compound wall, the farmland is situated on the outskirts of the village. According to the police, the owners, who live in Bengaluru, seldom visited the place.
The villagers would whisper among themselves about what they suspected — until the day the labourer decided to report the dumped medical waste to the local beat police.
The officers at Taverekere police station put the farmhouse and the movements around it under surveillance, while also making inquiries about the property and its occupants. The people they spoke to did not seem to know anything substantial.
According to an officer, the police learned that the farmhouse had been rented about a year earlier. But what was happening inside the compound remained unclear.
Days later, the police and Karnataka’s health department, in a joint operation, decided to enter the premises. What they saw there — labels, medicine boxes, drugs, and other items associated with the preparation and packaging of medicines — changed the nature of the investigation. They alerted senior officers, who joined hands with officers from the State Drugs Control Department and conducted a raid on August 18.
The police took four people into custody. They discovered that the secluded farmhouse was being used as a counterfeit drug repackaging and re-labelling facility. What began as a local’s suspicion had opened the door to a much larger pharmaceutical investigation.
According to investigators, the operation involved the procurement of low-cost, substandard, or expired pharmaceutical formulations from other States, which were then transferred into fresh vials and given counterfeit labels and packaging. “The aim was to make the medicines appear as genuine products of established pharmaceutical companies and introduce them into the pharmaceutical supply chain,” says a police official familiar with the investigation.
During the seizure, the police recovered more than 5,600 vials of counterfeit antibiotic injections used in treating serious bacterial infections. The total seizure was estimated at ₹4.91 crore.
They also seized ledgers, invoices, mobile phones, and other records, which provided them with details of the supply chain.
From a farmhouse to the big city
The police then moved their investigation beyond C.K. Tandya. A Special Investigation Team (SIT) was constituted.
The trail led to Bengaluru and to Krupa Healthcare, a wholesale pharmaceutical distributor located on a busy commercial street in the city. According to the police, the operators in the farmhouse supplied medicines to Krupa Healthcare, which distributed them.
The police found that the counterfeit medicines were not limited to antibiotics, but also included critical-care injections and cancer medicines. They say some of the medicines were offered to hospitals at “discounts of up to 50%”.
Krupa Healthcare owner Veeresh Kumar Jain, who was arrested by the SIT, allegedly employed more than 15 medical representatives to promote the medicines and offered commissions to push the discounted stocks to private hospitals and medical centres.
The police then found that the alleged racket was not confined to Karnataka. A joint force subsequently carried out simultaneous searches across Karnataka, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, and Telangana. The police are currently on the hunt for Bengaluru resident R. Prashant, who they believe is a key figure in the network. He is currently in Azerbaijan, and is Jain’s partner, say the police.
Unanswered questions
The families of patients are shocked and angry at these revelations. On his WhatsApp profile picture, Maheshprasad Upadhya, 30, poses with his mother. A cervical cancer patient, she passed away in 2024. After hearing the news, Upadhya, a native of Odisha, cannot help second-guessing the events before his mother’s death.
She was diagnosed with cancer in 2022, he says. For a year, she underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy in Mumbai. The doctors then suggested immunotherapy. As treatment in Mumbai was expensive and there were also logistical difficulties in travelling to the city, the family decided to shift treatment to Bhubaneswar.
“The doctor we consulted referred a Bengaluru-based pharmaceutical distributor to us. I bought a medicine from them. It cost ₹1,65,990 per vial. My mother needed two vials. The distributor said if we purchase one, we would get another free,” recalls Upadhya.
He searched online and found that the manufacturer did offer such a programme. He decided to go ahead with it.
Upadhya spent about ₹20 lakh on the overall treatment. “But we saw no improvement in her condition,” he says. “When she was diagnosed with cancer, the doctor had said she would live up to five years. My mother passed away in one and a half years.”
Upadhya sounds calm, but he admits within him a tumult of emotions — anger, suspicion, and helplessness. “One person who had got his father treated at the Bhubaneswar hospital had advised us against buying this medicine from this particular distributor,” he says. “But we didn’t listen since the doctor himself had advised it. After my mother passed away, I started suspecting something, perhaps a nexus, but I was in no state of mind to think about it. Now I’m questioning everything.”
He confesses that there are times when he considers migrating abroad “after seeing how the corrupt try to profit from the desperation of the most vulnerable.”
Parth Sharma, a resident of Gurugram, returned to India in 2017 to care for his ageing parents and mother-in-law, after spending 37 years abroad. “The people I came here for are no more,” he says.
In October 2020, Sharma’s mother was diagnosed with myelodysplastic syndrome, a condition where the bone marrow doesn’t make enough healthy blood cells. The doctors informed the family that the disease was not curable. Given the patient’s age — she was in her 70s — a bone marrow transplant was also not an option, they said. Nevertheless, treatment, including chemotherapy injections and blood transfusions, was started at a private hospital in December.
Sharma remembers that some of the expensive medicines were not available in India. “The doctor gave us the phone number of a person and said he would help get it imported. When you are desperate, you simply trust everyone. So, we contacted him,” he says.
Sharma’s mother’s condition never improved. With her body too weak to fight the disease, she passed away in May 2021.
“After the report on the counterfeit drug racket came out, I started wondering more deeply about something I had suspected all along: were the medicines even working? We had spent a lot of money and given her the prescribed medicines. At that point, we trusted the system and did not even suspect the possibility of fake medicines,” he says. He still has some of the tablets, which cost him around ₹80,000.
Living in uncertainty
The police say the suspect medicines have so far reached more than 90 hospitals and clinics in Karnataka and other States. While the State government has published a list of antibiotics seized during the Bidadi raid, it has not yet disclosed the names of oncology drugs or the hospitals and clinics that may have received the medicines, or the names and batch numbers of counterfeit medicines reportedly linked to serious illnesses such as cancer. There is pressure on the government to disclose this information.
According to the Karnataka Minister for Health and Family Welfare, U.T. Khader, the full list of spurious and counterfeit drugs has been communicated to the Union government and all State governments. “The SIT has taken charge of the investigation now. Once the report is finalised, we will reveal everything. We have got the list of hospitals. But when the SIT is there, it is not right on my part to disclose anything,” he says.
As the SIT continues with its investigation, Upadhya wonders what patients must be going through with the information they have. “Imagine their state of mind. Would they want to continue or discontinue treatment when they have no way of knowing whether the medicine they are taking is genuine or counterfeit,” he asks.
Dr. B.S Ajaikumar, radiation and medical oncologist and Founder and Chairman at HealthCare Global (HCG) Enterprises, says counterfeit drugs are a major problem in India today.
“I have been sounding the alarm on this for several years,” he says. “Whenever somebody — say insurance companies — wants to bring drugs from outside, I don’t allow it at HCG because I’m concerned it could be spurious. Any drug we purchase should come directly from the manufacturer. The authorities should also lay down stringent guidelines and ensure they are enforced. They should consult major users of oncology drugs like us, collaborate with us to develop a plan, and ensure spurious drugs don’t enter the system.”
Noting that cancer treatment often depends on the right drug, at the right dose, given at the right time, Dr. Nitish Ranjan Acharya, Surgical Oncologist at Manipal Hospital, Bhubaneswar, points out that any compromise in the authenticity or quality of a medicine can directly affect a patient’s treatment.
“If a patient receives a counterfeit, substandard, or expired medicine, the drug may not work as intended. This can delay disease control, allow the cancer to progress and, in some cases, affect the chances of achieving a good treatment response. The impact may be particularly difficult to identify because a lack of response can sometimes be mistaken for the cancer becoming resistant to treatment,” he explains.
Dr. Acharya adds that there are more risks when the contents of the counterfeit drugs are unknown. “A drug could contain an incorrect dose, inactive ingredients, contaminants, or substances that may cause unexpected side effects. These risks can be especially serious for patients already receiving multiple cancer medicines,” he notes. He also stresses the importance of appropriate storage and handling to maintain quality.
The question of accountability
The alleged racket also raises questions about what hospitals should do when patients may have already been exposed to counterfeit medicines. As S.V. Joga Rao, a lawyer who specialises in healthcare law and ethics, says, “Given the circumstances in India, a detailed investigation may take time. By that time, the spurious drugs may have found their way to patients.”
According to him, hospitals need to work with investigating agencies to identify the medicines in question and their batch numbers. “If there is some kind of leeway in terms of information, the hospital has an ethical duty to inform potentially affected patients,” he says.
Noting that regulatory authorities need to be mindful of Section 17B of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which defines a spurious drug, and Section 18, which prohibits their manufacture, sale, stocking, distribution and other related activities, Rao also points to the legal duty of hospitals to procure responsibly, verify authenticity, and detect sophisticated counterfeiting. “If there are warning signs, they need to respond to that. The duties of the hospitals and regulators operate concurrently, although they are different in nature. It is a shared responsibility,” he says.
Dr. Gopal Dabade, president of Drug Action Forum, Karnataka, says, “Drug inspectors are the first line of foot soldiers, but they are not adequately equipped. Punishment for wrongdoing is also not stringent enough.” He is a part of the All India Drug Action Network, a group of non-profits working to “increase access and improve the rational use of essential medicines”.
Another reality is the high cost of medicines, particularly cancer drugs, which can create a parallel market for cheaper counterfeit versions. “Better access to good quality and affordable treatment is the crux of the issue,” Dabade says.
Sylvia Karpagam, a public health doctor and researcher, says people must demand an accountable public health system as part of the election mandate. She also points to the responsibility of doctors, and questions the role they play in ensuring accountability within the healthcare system. “Doctors who harp about ‘evidence-based practice’ in allopathy go mum when such incidents occur. Other than for their own pay cheques and to oppose any form of regulation, one barely sees doctors protesting on behalf of patients,” she says.
She also stresses the importance of adequate budgets, trained and sufficient staff, and regular public scrutiny. “Unless the government has an ongoing system to prevent drug rackets, and makes it known to the public through ongoing reports, these kinds of incidents will continue — some get picked up, and many don’t.”
SIT head C. Vamshikrishna says he cannot comment on the case while the investigation is on. Repeated phone calls and messages to reach Srinivas K. Commissioner of the Food Safety and Drug Administration, Karnataka, have not elicited any response.
