Srinagar, Sep 23: Police on Wednesday attached a residential property in Jammu and Kashmir's Baramulla district under UAPA in a terror-related case.
The residential property was attached under Section 25 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, in connection with an FIR registered in the north Kashmir district, a police spokesman said.
The attached property comprises a double-storeyed residential house at Namblan village in Sheeri belonging to accused Aijaz Ahmad Ganie, he said.
During the course of the investigation, the property was found, prima facie, to have been used for providing shelter and logistical support to terrorists and facilitating terrorist activities, thereby attracting the relevant provisions of the UAPA concerning proceeds of terrorism, the spokesman said.
The attachment was carried out after obtaining requisite approval from the Director General of Police, he said.
A public notice was also displayed at the property, prohibiting its sale, transfer, lease, mortgage or creation of any third-party interest, the spokesman added.
He said the action forms part of Baramulla Police's sustained efforts to disrupt and dismantle the logistical and support infrastructure of terror networks and to proceed, in accordance with law, against persons and properties found involved in facilitating terrorist activities.

So far, AI in the inbox has so far meant assistance in drafting. Microsoft has pushed Copilot deeper into Outlook, Google has embedded Gemini across Workspace, to provide AI assistants designed to organise inbox, draft replies in your specific tone, and capture meeting notes directly. Almost all of them still wait for the final go-ahead. Sol, a proactive AI assistant, wants to flip that order. Founded in 2025 by three former Cred executives, Anish Karan, Prateek Srivastava and Ranjith Nair, the startup emerged from stealth today with $4 Mn (over ₹38 Cr) from General Catalyst, Nexus Venture Partners, DeVC, Peercheque and Kunal Shah. The offering: if a user has already written "I'll send the deck" or "I'll set up time", an AI automatically begins working without waiting for a prompt. The product scans a user's Gmail (Google Mail) for commitments and then produces the work those promises imply, from research and documents to slide decks, calendar coordination and reply drafts assembled from several threads. The user retains final approval. Sol runs in its own computer environment, can browse the web and draws on a library of more than 100 specialist skills, running on OpenAI’s model under-the-hood. Some of the use cases include: Creating or reviewing a document in Word or Notion, or building and reviewing slides Finding and shortlisting time slots across internal and external calendars Running research ahead of a reply or a decision Drafting replies that pull context from scattered email threads The idea surfaced during the cofounders stint at Cred. While Karan worked in the product of the fintech major, Nair was in the design and product team, and Srivastava was the engineering lead. After identifying the problem, Karan spoke to around 55 enterprise teams from the US, South Korea and Australia to check whether the problem was local for companies in India. It was not. "People whose work runs through email often have to repeat themselves: first in email, then again when they ask an AI tool to act," Karan told Inc42. "We shouldn't have to become experts in AI to benefit from it." Commercially, Sol is pre-revenue with no pricing tiers fixed yet. Karan says the pricing model will be usage or outcome-based with a fixed component to start, since the work varies in volume and complexity per user. Pricing will be in US dollars with no India currency pricing plan yet. He declined to commit to a gross margin target, arguing that model costs are falling and adoption matters more, for now. The go-to-market motion is “prosumer” first: anyone can sign up (waitlist at the moment), and an enterprise sales motion follows once enough people in one organisation use it. Integrations begin with Google Workspace, covering Gmail, Docs and Slides, while Outlook is open to a small group of testers. The stack is model-agnostic, using OpenAI models today with routers that switch between them, and runs on AWS in the US. Karan argues Sol has no direct competitor, only the workflow it replaces, and that reliability plus a simple interface are the moats a challenger must cross. That claim faces incumbents bundling agents into the inbox for free, and the trust problem every email agent inherits: an unapproved draft is harmless, but an approved one carries the user's name. Karan explains that the fresh capital is earmarked mainly for R&D, including talent, model costs and customer time. Sol plans to widen access beyond the waitlist soon. Whether proactive assistants become the default layer of work email, or get absorbed into Gmail and Outlook as features, only time will tell.

Bong Joon Ho will start detailed screenwriting on a slate of crime and horror projects next year once his animated feature “Ally” is complete, the Oscar-winning Korean filmmaker tells Variety ahead of receiving the Stella della Mole Award at Torino’s Museo Nazionale del Cinema on Wednesday.
Asked about the Seoul subway-set horror film he has previously discussed, Bong says: “Yeah, it’s still in my head. Now I have two or three stories. I’ve always been a huge fan of crime stories and dark horror action movies.” The ideas have been circling for years, and he intends to go back to those genres after “Ally.”
“Actually, I’m in the middle of post-production. Even last night I had a Zoom call with my crew members in Seoul and London,” Bong says of the animation, which has teams in Korea, the U.K., Montreal and Mumbai. He wrapped additional dubbing and voice recording last month, and expects the film to be fully finished around late January or February 2027.
Popular on Variety
The distributors have yet to set a date but are looking at June, July or August — a window Bong suggests fits a film set entirely against a deep blue ocean.
“Sundance or Berlin is possible, and also Cannes. But I don’t know, it all depends on the release strategy of the distributors,” Bong says of a possible festival premiere, adding that he hopes to present the film to a festival audience.
Pathé will release “Ally” in France, Benelux, Switzerland and West Africa, and Neon has North America. South Korea, Vietnam, Turkey and Indonesia go to CJ and Penture. Pathé is also handling international sales outside Japan, China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, which CJ and Penture are selling.
Looking back across his career, Bong compares the present moment to half-time in a soccer match and says he hopes to keep making films for another 25 years. “At that time I was a director who had made two films. Now I’m a director who has made eight films,” he says of his first visit to Torino.
That visit came in 2003, when “Memories of Murder” won the Torino Film Festival‘s audience prize and its screenplay award. Bong says he is particularly excited to meet Torino audiences again, given that the earlier prize was decided by public vote.
On the Korean industry’s post-pandemic box office recovery in the first half of 2026, Bong says he is firmly convinced that cinemas will never vanish, since watching a film with a packed house offers something that solo streaming at home cannot. He notes that this year’s local theatrical hits spanned very different genres and filmmakers. “It was a very good and optimistic sign. So, yeah, we are expecting something more next year,” he says.
He sees streaming and theatrical as partners that can grow together rather than rivals. “Actually, South Korea was the country that set up a whole high-speed internet system at a very early stage, around the late 1990s. So it was very helpful and a very good chance for Korea,” Bong says.
In the years since “Parasite,” Bong believes Korean creators have become more ambitious, citing the influence of that film and “Squid Game.” “But at the same time, the people in the industry, my fellow filmmakers, are also very grounded,” he says.
“Parasite” won the Palme d’Or and went on to take four Academy Awards, including best picture — the first non-English-language film to win the top prize. Bong’s most recent film is “Mickey 17” (2025), starring Robert Pattinson.
The Torino event, curated by Marco Fallanca, begins at Cinema Massimo with the award presentation and a masterclass in conversation with Museo Nazionale del Cinema director Carlo Chatrian. Later, Bong will introduce a screening of “Parasite.” The evening also launches a full retrospective of his features.

The 2013 sci-fi blockbuster film Gravity, starring Sandra Bullock and George Clooney, popularized the notion of the Kessler syndrome. In the movie, Russia shoots down a defunct satellite and creates a cloud of debris, leading to serious tension in orbit.
The movie is fantastic, a true thriller, and while some liberties were taken with the depiction of outer space, the basic premise of a cascading series of collisions rendering orbits too cluttered with debris to be usable is valid. The idea was first proposed by NASA scientists Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais nearly half a century ago.
Still, the movie was science fiction, right?
Well, a lot has changed since Gravity‘s release. At the time that theatergoers were sitting on the edges of their seats and watching Bullock dodge debris, there were only about 1,000 active satellites in orbit. Today, that number is closer to 17,000, according to CelesTrak.
The preponderance of this growth has been driven by SpaceX’s Starlink constellation, which now has approximately 11,000 satellites in orbit, with many thousands more on the way. And SpaceX is not alone in the race to provide Internet from space. Amazon has launched hundreds of satellites, with thousands more to follow. Multiple Chinese Internet constellations are likewise in progress.
We’ve written a lot about these constellations, and they have generated a bunch of questions. Most prominent among them: Just how sustainable is all of this? Will we see the Kessler syndrome play out in real time? Here are some answers.
How bad is the situation?
It depends on who you ask, so let’s start with the glass-half-empty and glass-half-full outlooks.
Starting with the pessimists: A few years ago, one of the world’s experts in orbital debris, University of Texas at Austin professor Moriba Jah, told Ars that he worries a lot about the consequences of satellites and debris in low-Earth orbit.
“I think we are going to lose the ability to use certain orbits because the carrying capacity is going to get saturated by objects and junk,” Jah said. ” I also predict that we will see a loss of human life by (1) school bus-sized objects reentering and surviving reentry and hitting a populated area, or (2) people riding on this wave of civil and commercial astronauts basically having their vehicle getting scwhacked by an unpredicted piece of junk. I predict that both those things are going to happen in the next decade.”
At the other end of the spectrum is the person almost solely responsible for the remarkable growth in satellites over the last decade, SpaceX founder Elon Musk. His attitude has largely been that space is big, and things will probably be just fine. For example, during a SpaceX-produced interview this summer at the company’s Starlink terminal factory in Bastrop, Texas, Musk said, “Space is really big. It’s not like space is gonna get crowded. Space is enormous. If you actually look at it relative to the Earth, the satellites are so tiny you can’t even see them.”
So in one way of thinking, very, very bad things are coming. In another, everything’s fine. Where does the truth actually lie?
What’s really happening?
One of the most credible sources for this kind of information is the European Space Agency, which has long studied space debris and its impacts on various orbits.
Fortunately, it just released its annual Space Environment Report a week ago. The European agency has produced such a report over the last decade to provide a transparent overview of global space activities and assess the quality of efforts to preserve the sustainability of spaceflight.
There are some striking—and concerning—changes this year. For example, the European report has dramatically increased its projections of future satellites in this year’s report after reassessing the current trajectory of large constellations.
“The notable increase in the index this year is primarily driven by the substantially larger future population resulting from the current extrapolation scenario,” the report states. “In particular, the growing influence of large constellations highlights the limitations of traditional mitigation approaches when applied to future traffic at unprecedented scales. At the same time, the results are affected by the limited availability of detailed and verifiable information on future deployment plans, operational practices, and end-of-life strategies of these systems.”
The projection for objects in orbit in this year’s report has gone up dramatically.
Credit:
European Space Agency
The projection for objects in orbit in this year’s report has gone up dramatically.
Credit:
European Space Agency
More satellites mean an increasing probability of collisions, which helps to push us toward a Kessler-like scenario.
As part of the report, the European scientists modeled a number of different scenarios. Assuming that satellite launches continue to increase—by far the most likely trend—even if operators continue to follow best practices in terms of disposing of older satellites and avoiding collisions, the orbital environment will still become significantly more cluttered.
“The extrapolation of our current behavior, which assumes the continuation of explosion in orbits at current rates, adherence by constellations to at least the minimum desirable post-mission disposal success rates, and continuation of the currently estimated post-mission disposal success rates for all other objects, leads to an unstable environment with collision rates increasing exponentially,” the report states.
In its technically precise language, the European Space Agency is essentially saying we’re on a road that could ultimately lead to something like the Kessler syndrome. Such a scenario, with a dramatic growth in constellations using best practices for satellite disposal, looks like this in terms of collisions in orbit.
Number of cumulative collisions in low-Earth orbit in simulations.
Credit:
European Space Agency
Number of cumulative collisions in low-Earth orbit in simulations.
Credit:
European Space Agency
It does indeed start to look pretty dicey by mid-century.
Also worth noting: The projections in ESA’s 2026 report do not include the new category of orbital data centers, as they exclude projects “still being prepared” for launch. It remains unclear whether these mega-megaconstellations of data centers in space will prove to be economically viable, but if they do, they could be the ultimate tipping point for orbital sustainability.
What is happening up there now?
The European Space Agency talks a lot about the need for responsible behavior, and in managing its massive Starlink constellation, SpaceX has been responsible. The company has been effective at deorbiting satellites that lose functionality and at managing a constellation of thousands of satellites. It’s an unprecedented task that the company has learned, on the fly, to carry out at a scale no government or company has attempted before.
We know from mandatory reporting to the Federal Communications Commission that SpaceX is frequently moving satellites around in orbit, making small but precise maneuvers to avoid collisions. Five years ago, its (much smaller) constellation made about 500 such maneuvers a month. During the most recent reporting period, through May 2026, that number had jumped to nearly 35,000 per month. That comes to one maneuver every 75 seconds.
It is important to characterize these properly. Each maneuver is not a “near miss.” Rather, SpaceX has significantly lowered the probability threshold to trigger a collision avoidance maneuver. The NASA standard for maneuver is 1-in-10,000. At the outset of Starlink, though, SpaceX used a 1-in-100,000 threshold and has since become even more conservative, with a threshold of 3-in-10 million, according to a 2025 letter to the FCC.
So it’s clear that SpaceX is not operating its Starlink constellation in a cavalier manner. But it’s also clear that the company’s constellation, and those like it, are cause for significant concern going forward.
What should we be worried about?
No credible experts are saying that the Kessler syndrome could happen imminently—a single collision won’t set off a Gravity-style cascade.
But space is getting more crowded, and some orbits, particularly from 520 km to 1,000 km above Earth. A 2025 paper by Hugh Lewis and Kessler (yes, that Kessler) found that some orbital bands in this region have already reached what is known as a “collisional-runaway threshold,” which is to say that any serious collisions there may create new debris faster over time than debris would be naturally removed by the pull of gravity, down into Earth’s atmosphere.
Another concern comes from spent “rocket bodies,” upper stages from rockets that were not properly disposed of after launch. This was more common in decades past, but some launches today still do not reserve enough propellant to properly deorbit a second or third stage. These school bus-sized stages are particularly problematic at altitudes of 840 and 975 km, said LeoLabs space debris expert Darren McKnight. They are winging around uncontrolled, of course. And the higher the altitude, the longer the debris hangs around, from decades to centuries.
Finally, because there is so much stuff flying around orbit, it would be relatively easy for bad actors to start shooting missiles at satellites in low-Earth orbit, creating debris fields that could potentially wipe out communications and cause massive financial damage. The probability of Kessler syndrome becomes much higher if humans start deliberately blowing things up in space. Did we mention that Iran recently became the ninth country to put a domestically built satellite into orbit?
What’s the bottom line?
In the near term, it seems unlikely that space will become unusable. But it will likely become more and more expensive to operate there when considering avoidance technology, people to manage all of this, and propellant for maneuvers. And finding launch windows that avoid known debris will become more difficult.
Longer term, perhaps as early as 15 years from now but more likely longer, a Kessler-syndrome type outcome may start to become increasingly plausible.
Eric Berger is the senior space editor at Ars Technica, covering everything from astronomy to private space to NASA policy, and author of two books: Liftoff, about the rise of SpaceX; and Reentry, on the development of the Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon. A certified meteorologist, Eric lives in Houston.

Harmanpreet Kaur has done what no one else can claim to have done, or may do for a while — be the captain of an Asian Games-winning cricket team twice in a row. And she has the medals to prove it.
Firm favourite to defend its title at the Korogi Athletics Park even before the team landed in Tokyo, and coming after the high of clinching the Asia Cup, the gulf between the Women in Blue and the rest was far too wide.
But even the Indians would not have expected the kind of domination they managed in the final, packing off Sri Lanka for a 147-run victory.
“As cricketers, we always wanted to be a part of the Asian Games or Commonwealth Games or Olympics, because otherwise we only play cricket tournaments or bilateral series. We did not know the value of what a medal actually means; we had no experience of that, but we are grateful to have the opportunity to experience this.
“We are lucky to have done it twice now because the cricketers before us did not have this. Now we can also frame two medals back home because when we win a trophy, it feels good but it goes to the BCCI office. This is something we will have with us forever... this is ours,” Harmanpreet said on Tuesday.
That the team’s gold was also the first for India at the ongoing Games only made it extra special.
“Since we came here, our aim was to win gold and see the national flag high... [we] talked about the national anthem playing. But we didn’t know we would be the first to experience it here. We are just lucky and grateful for this because there were other athletes over the past two days who could have done it and came close. But I am sure that we have opened the golden gates. There will be many more [gold medals] coming through for India from all the different sports. We will be rooting for them,” she declared.
Shreyanka Patil, returning from an ankle injury that kept her out of the Asia Cup, was elated to be back playing.
“It’s very hard when you have back-to-back injuries and then you’re out for a while and come back. If you stay positive and keep telling you can do it, anything is possible. When I was out there, I was full of happiness and I just couldn’t express it. I was all around jumping, roaming, talking, everyone was like, ‘O, Shrey is back,’”she laughed.
“It’s my first time holding a gold medal... so I’m really grateful and happy. The whole campaign was good for us. We’ve done really well with the ball and the bat. But most of all, I’m just happy to be back on the field,” she added.
Smriti Mandhana, whose 45-ball 79 laid the foundation for India’s success, was more measured in her reaction, her ambitions clearly much bigger than continental domination.
“I feel everyone played really good cricket. Having said that, we all have to look forward and work on ourselves and keep getting better. We have to keep playing good cricket against better opposition. We can’t dwell on this win a lot, we have to see what we can do for the next 1.5-2 years to get in the best place to win an Olympic medal,” she declared.

Trump is hailing his new deal with Greenland and Denmark — but a deal already existed. So what changed?
The United States signed a security arrangement with Denmark and Greenland in 1951
Recently, U.S. President Donald Trump said on his social media platform that for over 100 years, presidents have recognized the strategic importance of Greenland, "but NONE of them were able to do anything about it."
The president then wrote that he had "permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation." On Tuesday, a new security agreement between the U.S., Denmark and Greenland was officially signed at the UN General Assembly in New York.
However, the U.S. already had a security arrangement with Denmark and Greenland dating back 75 years. So what, if anything, has changed?
"If we try to look at the new defence agreement compared to the old defence agreement, I would characterize it as a moderate improvement for the U.S.," Mikkel Runge Olesen, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute of International Studies, told CBC News.
"But it's a moderate improvement that has come at an immense cost."
- NATO will share Arctic responsibility as Greenland security deal with U.S. moves forward, Denmark says
- AnalysisTrump flexes 'American power' on UN's biggest stage
That cost, some observers say, is the damage done to the relationships between the U.S. and some of its NATO allies including Denmark and Greenland, borne from Trump's repeated threats to seize the northern island and make it part of the U.S.
"Even though I don't think this deal has a lot of new stuff in it, I think everyone should be happy that it's finally getting signed," said Imran Bayoumi, a deputy director with the GeoStrategy Initiative in the Atlantic Council's Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security.
But he added that the "gains are minimal" considering the harm inflicted on the direct relationships between the U.S. and its NATO allies.
Comparing the agreements
In 1951, the U.S. and Denmark signed the Defense of Greenland Treaty that authorized U.S. military presence in agreed upon areas on the island.
During the Cold War, the U.S. maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel in Greenland. Today, only Pituffik Space Base remains, staffed by some 150 U.S. military personnel.
With this new deal, it was also announced that the U.S. plans to open two new military bases.
But under the previous arrangement, the U.S. already had the right to expand its bases. Instead, it decreased its presence in terms of numbers and size over the years, according to Marc Weller, the director of the Global Governance and Security Centre and the International Law Programme at Chatham House, a think-tank based in London, England.
"Now they have the right, in consultation with the Danes and the Greenlanders, to agree on additional bases," Weller said.
But he says both parties had already indicated they were happy to accept an expansion of U.S. bases.
"It was a non issue."
- Trump says deal struck to boost U.S. military presence in Greenland
- Greenland, Denmark say deal with U.S. will not cede sovereignty
The new agreement also prohibits foreign adversaries of the U.S., like Russia and China, from establishing bases on Greenland.
But even under the 1951 agreement, that kind of scenario would have been "unthinkable," said Olesen.
"How many Russian and Chinese bases do we really see in NATO countries these days? It is sort of a given that of course it was never going to happen. But now it's on paper."
The new agreement gives the U.S. the ability to veto investments in critical infrastructure and other mining sectors from geopolitical adversaries.
But Bayoumi notes that there are logistic obstacles already preventing that. He says it's very difficult to build in Greenland, and that the infrastructure to support the launch of a critical mineral extraction project just isn't there.
Not only would it be costly and time consuming to build that infrastructure, he says Greenlanders themselves have vetoed and voted against some other mineral extraction projects in the past over concerns about environmental degradation.
But if the U.S. is going to veto other countries from investing in Greenland, Bayoumi wondered if it's ready to potentially take on a broader role "in facilitating economic development in the island."
'Infinite Life' agreement
The deal also does not have an end date, something Trump described as an "Infinite Life" agreement.
Bayoumi says this is a new development, as the 1951 pact was tied to the existence of NATO. The new agreement also makes provisions for Greenland to exercise its right to determine its independence.
But Bayoumi also notes that NATO is unlikely to disappear in the near future, and Greenland independence is unlikely to come any time soon.

According to the new pact, if Greenland chooses to become independent, it will agree to remain in NATO and take on Denmark's rights and obligations under the deal.
"This would have been implied probably in the previous stages, but it is useful for the U.S. to clarify this," Weller said.

The 2026 US midterm elections, scheduled for November 3, are likely to determine control of Congress and could directly shape the final two years of Donald Trump's presidential term amid the ongoing war with Iran.
Held midway through a president's four-year term, the midterms are nationwide elections in which all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one-third of the 100 seats in the Senate are contested, along with numerous state and local offices.
The presidency itself is not on the ballot. However, the elections determine which party controls Congress, making them crucial to a president's ability to advance his legislative agenda during the remaining two years of his term.
Why are the US midterms important for Trump?
Historically, the president's party tends to lose congressional seats during midterm elections.
Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress.
A shift in either chamber can therefore change the balance of power in Washington.
If Republicans retain control of both chambers, Trump would have greater congressional backing to pursue his legislative priorities during the second half of his term.
However, if Democrats gain control of either chamber, Trump could face greater congressional scrutiny and more difficulty towards advancing his legislative agenda.
This comes as Trump faces challenges on several fronts. Recent US Supreme Court rulings have also affected aspects of his administration's policies.
Losing ground in Congress could deal a severe blow to his push on tariffs and other agenda items and will affect Trump's ability to pass legislation, approve appointments and pursue his policy priorities.
Polls overshadowed by the Iran war
The 2026 midterms come as Trump's administration faces questions over the US military campaign against Iran.
The US and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28, with Tehran saying thousands of people were killed. Iran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
Is Trump's approval rating under pressure?
The polls come at a time when Trump's approval rating has faced pressure.
A recent CNN/SSRS poll found that 64% of Americans said the US was not winning the war in Iran, while 36% said it was. Nearly two-thirds of respondents also said Trump was not doing enough to end the conflict.
“What the midterms usually are is a reflection of presidential popularity,” foreign policy scholar Trevor Thrall told DW.
Addressing world leaders at the United Nations on Tuesday, Trump highlighted US military action and argued that his administration had responded directly to threats rather than relying on diplomacy alone.
“While others have talked, I have acted. While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace,” Trump said.

A fungus that can cause severe pneumonia in people with weaker or weakened immune systems appears to have become resistant to a drug that never intended to kill it, according to the findings of a study by researchers from around the world published in Science Translational Medicine.
The study focused on mycophenolic acid (MPA), an immunosuppressive drug used with people who have received solid-organ transplants. MPA helps keep the immune system from rejecting the organ — but it was also found to affect Pneumocystis jirovecii fungi.
The team analysed 163 P. jirovecii samples from China, Denmark, Germany, Japan, Switzerland, and the U.S., of which 96 came from recipients of transplanted organs, most of whom were also involved in pneumocystis pneumonia outbreaks from 2005 to 2019. The remaining samples were controls.
MPA works by inhibiting an enzyme called IMPDH in human immune cells. The fungus possesses a similar enzyme, and the researchers believe this could be the link. The team found six relatively common mutations in the fungal gene that produces IMPDH. Some 86% of samples from transplant recipients contained a mutation in that gene, versus 13% in the non-transplant samples.
The researchers also produced normal and mutated versions of the fungal IMPDH enzyme in the lab and exposed them to MPA. Depending on the mutation, considerably more MPA was required to inhibit the mutated enzymes than the normal enzyme.
The mutations also appeared in at least 11 fungal strains and varied between countries and over time. That is, rather than resistance arising once and spreading from that source, P. jirovecii seem to have evolved similar adaptations as different populations encountered the same selective pressure.
The researchers have acknowledged that they have only established resistance at the enzyme level, rather than in infected patients, and that their cohort sizes and clinical data were limited.
Nonetheless, researchers understand antimicrobial resistance as microorganisms evolving to resist antibiotics, antifungals or other medicines. But in the study, a drug intended to act on the human body was found unintentionally exerting pressure on a pathogen as well. And mutant fungi that could better tolerate MPA may have enjoyed an advantage among transplant recipients taking the drug, allowing them to survive and spread.
The “results challenge the current status quo on P. jirovecii’s unknown resistance,” the study authors wrote, “calling for reevaluating immunosuppressive strategies and infection control measures and highlighting the broader potential for other pathogens to evolve under selective pressures imposed by human-targeted therapies.”

In September 2026, a rumor circulated online that the footwear company Converse had allegedly released an advertisement that some social media users believed evoked Ku Klux Klan and lynching imagery.
The advertisement that Converse purportedly published showed the bottom half of a person in white holding Converse shoes. The shadows and lighting in the ad create an optical illusion that looked, to some, like a Ku Klux Klan hood and the feet of a hanging person.
Much of the online discourse related to the ad took place on Threads, although posts on Reddit, X, Facebook (screenshotted) and Instagram (screenshotted) also expressed outrage or shared thoughts about the ad's imagery.
Snopes readers asked us if the ad was real and searched the website for "racist Converse ad" and if there was a "Nike Converse commercial" that "looked like a lynching." (Nike owns Converse.)
Converse did, in fact, publish the advertisement (archived) in question as part of its campaign with singer Karina, a member of the K-pop girl group Aespa, to promote the "Chuck 70 X," a newer version of the company's classic Chuck 70 shoes. As such, we have rated this claim as true.
The footwear company did not immediately return an inquiry for more information about its design and approval process, as well as whether Converse plans to pull the ad following online backlash.
A spokesperson for Converse sent the following statement over email when we asked about the ad:
We're sorry. We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened, and we will do better.
As of this writing, a link connected to Converse's official Threads account still shows the image in a Sept. 3 post. However, the post does not show up on Converse's main Threads page (archived), suggesting the company may have archived the post to hide it from viewers.
(Converse on Threads)
Per the Wayback Machine archive, an earlier, Aug. 22 version of Converse's U.S. page advertising the Karina and Chuck 70 X collaboration showed that the company had at one point used the image in question on its website. It has since been removed and replaced with a clip of Karina modeling the shoes while wearing a white skirt — presumably the same skirt shown in the controversial picture.
An Aug. 22 version of the Converse page promoting Chuck 70 X shoes in collaboration with Karina. (Converse/Wayback Machine)
Was the campaign created outside US?
Some of the claim posts also said the campaign was created in Malaysia, and thus the team behind it might not have had the cultural and historical context necessary to understand why
Social media users shared screenshots indicating that the image may have initially been posted on the Converse Malaysia Instagram page.
Without more information from Converse, it was not possible to verify whether any members of the creative team were based in or from the U.S. That image was not on Converse Malaysia's Instagram account. A search of the Converse Malaysia website for "Chuck 70 X" returned an error message.
Some posts also shared another advertisement showing a person on a ladder holding Converse shoes, which some social media users similarly thought evoked lynching imagery.
That image is a real Converse ad, too, as evidenced by the fact that was still on Converse Chile's account (screenshotted) as of this writing.
However, the image of the person on the ladder came from a separate campaign that was shot in Italy, according to a LinkedIn post from the founder of Palmes, a tennis and menswear company that collaborated with Converse on it.

US President Donald Trump returned to the United Nations podium Tuesday wearing two very different hats. One moment he was the global peacemaker who had "ended eight wars", the next he was threatening to wipe out Iran.
The gap between these two versions captures the uncertain order Trump has built, or perhaps enabled, during his second term in the White House.
Trump used much of his address to the General Debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly to list his achievements, much as he did a year ago when he cast himself as the standout contender for the Nobel Peace Prize. This year, though, the prize went unmentioned. Instead, his tone hardened, with attacks on the International Criminal Court (ICC), the UN's climate agenda and Unesco.
Trump also pointed to his effort to launch a "Board of Peace" in January, which appeared another swipe at the UN, with him at one point suggesting his new creation might end up replacing it.
Ironically, within a month of the board's creation, the US and Israel launched a joint military operation against Iran, one that has continued in some form since.
"Since I took office, it has been my great honour to settle eight wars, and in so doing, become friendly with the leaders of many of those countries. 
It was a great honour to do it. Numerous of these wars have gone on for many years and even decades," he told the assembled leaders.
He credited his success to what he called "very special relationships", along with the use and threat of tariffs.
Among the conflicts he claimed to have resolved were the disputes between Cambodia and Thailand, Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, Pakistan and India, and Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as the war in Gaza.
He repeated a claim India has long rejected, that he brokered peace between India and Pakistan last year.
"The Prime Minister of Pakistan, terrific man, said that Donald Trump was responsible for saving 30 million lives and probably many more than that," Trump said.
India has always maintained the ceasefire came from direct talks between the two countries' military operations chiefs, with Pakistani DGMO seeking the truce amid Operation Sindoor.
He also mentioned Russia and Ukraine, saying his team is "working very closely" with both sides. "We will get that one done. It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand," he said.
Peacemaker to annihilator
Having spent much of the speech basking in the image of a dealmaker, Trump turned to Iran, warning that Tehran must either negotiate with Washington or face destruction.
Iran would never be allowed to have nuclear weapons, he said, adding that he faces "a big decision to make."
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?"
He went further still, asking, "Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" He then predicted a deal was more likely once the midterm elections were over, since Iran was "waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," despite Trump not being on the ballot himself.
Lo and behold, Trump's speech offered a portrait of a President who saw no contradiction in claiming the mantle of peacemaker while reserving the language of annihilation for those who resist his terms.

Iranian officials held three hours of talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Donald Trump disclosed on Tuesday.
He said there would a further meeting in the very near future.
Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation to agree a memorandum of understanding in Switzerland in June.
Iranian officials confirmed the meeting with Witkoff involved its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and was mediated by diplomats from Qatar.
A senior Iranian official also indicated that the country was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week, as long as the US took reciprocal steps to ease the military and economic pressure it is applying on Iran.
Previously, Iran had set seven onerous preconditions for lifting its blockade on the strait, one of the world’s key oil shipping routes, including an end to the US war “on all fronts” and a commitment by the US to end all aggressive actions against Iran, including sanctions.
The new position, revealed amid frantic backstage negotiations at the UN general assembly in New York and set out by an Iranian official in Tehran to the Japanese news agency Kyodo and then to Reuters, would involve relaxing some of those preconditions.
The official claimed the position had been approved by Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, and the country’s supreme national security council, although some Iranian media close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) denied any new position had been adopted, reflecting disputes in Tehran.
Diplomats had been testing the ground for possible talks between the US and Iran, with Qatar’s diplomats in talks with Araghchi. A meeting between Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and Trump had largely been ruled out as too combustible, however.
Pezeshkian is due on Wednesday to address the UN general assembly, where most of the Iranian delegation left the hall during Trump’s speech on Tuesday after he described Iran as the bully of the Middle East and the number one terror organisation on Earth.
But earlier, the IRGC issued a statement that said there was no contradiction between staging negotiations and waging war at the same time, a position echoed by Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, in recent remarks delivered online to the Iranian parliament.
The official said Iran was seeking signs from Washington that it was prepared to return to negotiations and take steps toward ending its military blockade of Iranian ports and halting military operations related to the strait of Hormuz. In that case, Iran was prepared to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days and return to the negotiating table, according to the official.
Such preconditions are less stringent than those issued by other senior Iranian figures in the previous 48 hours.
Experience has shown that initially appealing Iranian offers can emerge to be more complex once the small print is revealed, and there is a barely disguised tussle being played out in Tehran between hardliners and figures like Pezeshkian over the value of any talks.
Resolving these disputes is not made easier by the low profile kept by the supreme leader, normally the arbiter in such internal ructions.
Trump, in his remarks to the general assembly, said he had a big decision to make: whether to annihilate Iran, or to help it become a great country.
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he asked, adding he expected Iran to make a deal immediately after the US midterm elections. “There are two options; one could be a very bad thing, and the other could lead to greatness and progress for this country. Therefore, I think they want to do this.”
Overall, his demeanour, and the mixed signals out of Tehran, suggest the two sides are still too far apart to reach a deal, which would have to start with agreement between Iran and Oman on a new route for commercial shipping in the strait of Hormuz that largely goes through Iranian waters. The Gulf states have not endorsed such a deal.
Saudi Arabia also wanted to be a signatory and authoriser of the route, but Iran insisted it had to be endorsed only by the two countries in which the strait’s waterways pass – Iran and Oman.
Tehran is also under growing pressure as the US blockade of its oil exports plays havoc with its currency reserves and domestic inflation. In his speech, Trump called on other countries to isolate Iran economically, including by demanding that all nations prevent any Iranian civilian planes from landing at their airports. US diplomats have warned Turkey and Iraq to comply or face sanctions.
Many of the Gulf states were also planning to urge Trump to do more to press Israel to meet its commitments under the six-month-old peace plan to withdraw from Gaza.
The Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, prompted a walkout by the Israeli delegation when he described Gaza as “the world’s largest graveyard and the most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time”.
He added: “Israel refuses to stop the occupation. We are faced with a genocidal mindset that can never get enough of killing. No one with a sense of humanity, mercy or compassion, no one guided by justice and conscience, can possibly remain indifferent to this picture.”
Jordan’s King Abdullah, in his address, claimed: “With Israel, resolutions end where they began on paper. This result is a state without restraint. This government’s sense of impunity has reached terrifying levels. It no longer feels compelled to ask: ‘Can we get away with this?’ It already knows the answer.”
He added that what was unfolding across the occupied West Bank was not a series of isolated acts but rather “elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land. And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime.”
A statement from eight Gulf foreign ministers also called on Israel to immediately fulfil its outstanding commitments under the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, including by ensuring the immediate, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance and early recovery supplies, and facilitating the rehabilitation of critical infrastructure.
The ministers reiterated their categorical rejection of any measures aimed at the expulsion or the forced displacement of the Palestinian people from their homeland or attempts to alter the territorial or demographic character of the occupied Palestinian territory.

In the world’s first clash of the drone boats, a Ukrainian naval drone destroyed a Russian explosive drone boat using a remote-controlled machine gun turret. This comes as the war in Ukraine has already seen widespread deployment of such uncrewed surface vessels in combat, along with swarms of flying attack drones and ground robots.
The lopsided battle took place on September 12 when members of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence detected the Russian uncrewed surface vessel (USV) in the Black Sea and directed a Ukrainian Navy drone boat to intercept. The Russian vessel was “positively identified” as an Orcan surface drone with a “jet ski type steerable water jet” designed to ram targets and explode, according to naval analyst HI Sutton in Naval News.
Such Orcan drones have already been used to attack Ukrainian ports and ships. These often work in coordination with flying drones such as Russian Geran drones that provide aerial reconnaissance and can boost communication between drone operators and drone boats, Sutton explained.
In this case, the Russian drone was hunted down by a Ukrainian Sargan-3000 drone boat armed with a 12.7 mm machine gun mounted on a remote weapon station made by the Norwegian company Kongsberg.
“It was inevitable that there would be USV-on-USV combat,” Sutton told New Scientist. “We have seen the same in the air and on the ground.”
The Ukrainian Navy released a video showing the Sargan-3000 firing upon the Russian drone from a distance of one kilometer, disabling the latter’s communications antenna before riddling the Russian drone until it sank, according to the Ukrainian government media platform United24.

Jammu, Sep 23: The 17-year-old son of BJP Hiranagar MLA Vijay Kumar was traced to Delhi early Wednesday, a day after he was reported missing from his hometown in Kathua district of Jammu and Kashmir, officials said.
Aditya Kumar, a Class 11 student, left for Delhi on Tuesday evening to meet his sister without informing his family, prompting them to file a missing person report at the local police station, the officials said.
After hectic efforts, police teams traced Kumar while he was travelling on a Delhi-bound bus.
Acting on leads gathered during the night-long search, the police located the bus and established contact with the teenager, who is now being brought back to Jammu, the officials said.
His father had also left for Delhi on getting information about his son's whereabouts

US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
- Published
The US has criticised Australia's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms, saying it amounts to "censorship of protected speech".
Under Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, tech firms risk hefty fines if they fail to give users the option to turn off algorithms in a bid to protect them from harmful content.
In a rare submission to the proposed laws, the US embassy in Canberra said it had "serious concerns" and allowing the government to "enforce vague definitions of 'harm'" would lead to "viewpoint-based censorship".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the legislation was not about giving governments control but giving it back to individuals.
"We ask that Australia clarify how exactly 'harm' and 'risks' shall be determined... ensuring these definitions do not encroach on protected speech," the US said in its submission.
The US also claimed that the proposed laws may risk "reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics" if tech firms had to "pre-emptively demote" them.
An opt-out option would "allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements" on tech firms and this could affect users outside of Australia, it said.
"Mandated platform design features, especially when applied to algorithms, may affect what users see, say, and hear not just in or from Australia, but globally."
The US also called on Australia to address industry concerns that the "biases and preferences" of government officials do not "disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech".
Another worry was that the proposed laws could affect Australia's "reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation," the submission said.
The criticism comes during Albanese's visit to the US to speak at the UN's General Assembly about his government's tech policies.
On Tuesday, local time in New York, Albanese responded to the criticism and claims of the proposed laws being government overreach.
"It's not about giving government control," he told the media in New York.
"It's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices."
US President Donald Trump meanwhile used his speech at the UN to play down fears about AI, rejecting proposals for guardrails on it and arguing it should be renamed "super intelligence" as "the use of the word artificial makes it sound fake".
This latest move by Australia to protect its online users from harm comes less than a year after the country introduced a social media ban for children under 16 last December.

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

The festive season has officially arrived, and Indian kitchens are once again coming alive with preparations of laddus, payasam, halwa, burfis, and other traditional sweets. With the rising awareness about the impact of sugar, however, some ingredients in popular sweets are being changed. Refined sugar is increasingly being replaced with jaggery, while some consumers are also experimenting with artificial sweeteners such as stevia, and of late, monk fruit sweetener.
The intention is understandable: enjoy festive food while reducing sugar use. The science behind these sweeteners however, is more nuanced. Not every alternative to sugar is nutritionally equivalent, and ‘natural’ does not automatically mean low-sugar. The important question is not simply what sweetener is being used, but how much sweetness and sugars a person consumes overall.
Jaggery counts as sugar
Jaggery has long been associated with traditional Indian cooking and is often perceived as a healthier alternative to refined sugar because it undergoes less refining and may retain small amounts of minerals. However, it remains a concentrated source of sugar.
This distinction becomes particularly important during festivals, when sweets are rarely eaten in isolation. A person may have a laddu, a serving of payasam/kheer, sweetened beverages and several savoury foods in the same day, or worse in a single meal.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that free sugars contribute less than 10% of total daily energy intake, with a further reduction to below 5% providing additional health benefits. For a person consuming around 2,000 calories a day, 5% is roughly 20 to 25 grams, or 4 to 5 teaspoons of sugar.
Therefore, replacing sugar with jaggery does not make a sweet sugar-free. From a doctor’s perspective, portion size and the total amount of free sugar consumed during the day remain far more important than whether the sweetener is brown or white.
Artificial sweeteners
Across the country, many people are now using low-calorie or no-calorie sweeteners. These include artificial sweeteners such as sucralose, saccharin and aspartame, as well as naturally derived sweeteners such as steviol glycosides and monk fruit extract.
Monk fruit extract, the newest addition to sweeteners in the mass market, is particularly interesting because its sweetness comes from compounds called mogrosides. Monk fruit extracts can be approximately 100 to 250 times sweeter than sugar, depending on their mogroside content. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has noted that the use of monk fruit extract is ‘generally recognised as safe’ under its intended conditions of use.
Artificial sweeteners work differently. They provide intense sweetness with little or no calories and are commonly used in products marketed as ‘sugar-free’, ‘light’ or ‘diet’. Approved high-intensity sweeteners are considered safe within their specified conditions of use, and several have established acceptable daily intake levels.
However, a ‘safe’ label does not necessarily mean beneficial. The World Health Organization currently advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners as a strategy for long-term weight control. Its recommendation is conditional and is based on evidence that replacing free sugars with non-sugar sweeteners does not provide a clear long-term benefit for reducing body fat.
This is an important distinction for consumers. A sweetener can be safe to consume and still not be a reason to increase the amount of sweet food in the diet.
A better approach
The biggest misconception is that changing the sweetener automatically changes the nutritional quality of the sweet.
A jaggery laddu is still sweet. A sugar-free dessert can be calorie-dense if it contains large amounts of ghee, nuts, cream or other ingredients. Similarly, replacing sugar with monk fruit does not make an otherwise highly processed dessert a health food.
The more useful approach is for us to look at our entire festive eating pattern. One traditional sweet enjoyed occasionally is very different from consuming several servings every day throughout the season. The goal is not to find a sweetener that allows unlimited sweetness; it should be to reduce excessive sweets while retaining the cultural and social pleasure associated with festivals.
So, if a festival sweet is made with sugar, moderation matters. If it is made with jaggery, moderation still matters. Monk fruit essence or other non-sugar sweeteners do not automatically bestow a license to eat more.
The aim should be not to move from sugar to jaggery or from jaggery to monk fruit. It should be to simply learn to enjoy our favourite sweets alittle less sweet, and a little less often. This also aligns with broader dietary recommendations from the WHO that advise building diets on minimally and unprocessed foods, and restricting free sugars.
There is no need to cut out every single sweet, but do practice portion control and choose wisely. Instead of five laddus, have one and enjoy it mindfully. Keep the overall diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains and fibre, and let sweets remain a small part of the meal.
(Suparna Mukherjee is a dietician with Narayana Health City, Bengaluru. suparna.mukherjee@narayanahealth.org)

For example, GoPro sent a Laowa 7.5-mm lens for me to test with. When HyperSmooth is on, that's the equivalent of shooting with a 23-mm lens on a full-frame camera. With HyperSmooth off, it becomes a 20-mm lens. I bring this up mainly because if you want to go really wide on the ILS, you'll need a very, very wide lens (fisheye lenses are probably your best bet).
Now for the downside to the ILS: There are no electrical contacts, which means lenses that rely on electronic focus or aperture control probably won't work. For example, my all-time favorite MFT lens, Panasonic's original 20-mm pancake, won't work on the ILS because there's no manual aperture ring.
Your best bet is to stick with fully manual lenses that have a mechanical aperture ring. There aren't many, but there are enough with quality glass to cover a good range of focal lengths. GoPro's Abe Kislevitz put together a nice collection of lenses that he has tested with the Mission 1 Pro ILS, along with his recommendations for various shooting scenarios. Be aware that the camera is sold body-only, and so far, we haven't seen any bundles from GoPro or resellers that include a lens.
And yes, you have to manually focus. I could drop some jokes here about kids today not knowing how to do it, but the truth is, I shoot vintage manual-focus lenses all the time on my Sony A7R II. While I've shot sports and wildlife with these lenses and had a pretty high success rate, I struggled to focus on the ILS.
The problem with focusing on the ILS is the small screen. It's hard to see, not just in bright daylight. It's just really small. There is focus peaking, which uses color banding to indicate what's in focus, but it can be hard to see exactly where it ends, and I've learned from my Sony not to fully rely on peaking.
You can zoom in to get very precise focus, which is what I do on the Sony, but again the small screen makes it hard to see. Worse, for filmmakers especially, you have to have the camera at eye level to focus it well, which limits your shooting ability (or you get to contort into all sorts of weird poses). I would love to see the next Mission 1 Pro ILS get a tilting screen; it's not waterproof anyway, so it doesn't seem like there would be a need to reengineer. GoPro no doubt would suggest using the app on my phone, as it does make it considerably easier to focus, but then you need a cage, and then a handle, and at that point most of the Mission 1 Pro ILS' size advantage is gone; you might as well get a Panasonic GH7, which has an even larger sensor.
Ultimately, while focusing on the small screen is challenging, using a phone or other external monitor sidesteps that issue (and is what pro filmmakers do anyway), but the inability to control the lens iris electronically feels like a bigger limitation since it eliminates a significant number of lenses. It would be nice to see a future Mission 1 Pro ILS support at least electronic connectors for aperture and manual focusing on lenses that require it.
Shooting With the Mission 1 Pro ILS
Once you get past the hurdle of manual focusing, there's a lot to love about the ILS footage. Testing it reminded me more than anything of the Blackmagic Pocket Cinema Camera from several years ago. I can't believe this tiny little thing can match the quality of those early Blackmagic cameras.

Silicon Valley has long celebrated the college dropout. Now some of its biggest names are backing an educational institution of their own.
The Horowitz Andreessen Academy has raised $42 million and recruited prominent tech figures as instructors, guest speakers, and mentors.
Venture-capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, better known as A16z, is backing the Horowitz Andreessen Academy, a new for-profit school for young people interested in building companies, products, and emerging technologies.
Its network includes executives and founders from OpenAI, Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, and Stripe.
The San Francisco academy will trade degrees, traditional grades, and lecture-heavy coursework for independent projects, short classes, and work placements at technology companies.
Its tuition-free founding class is due to arrive in 2027, but the school's longer-term plan is to charge fees comparable to an elite private university.
What is it and where is it?
The academy is a full-time, in-person, for-profit educational program in San Francisco aimed primarily at recent high-school graduates.
Its first offering, the Founding Class Fellowship, is a one-year program scheduled to begin in September 2027 with about 50 students. The academy won't initially award degrees or grant college credit and isn't accredited, making it a college alternative rather than a university.
The program is organized around courses, co-ops, or structured work placements at participating technology companies, and "pursuits," its term for self-directed projects. Students will spend September through April at the San Francisco campus, travel abroad in May, and complete co-ops from June through August, according to the academy's website.
The school has not disclosed the precise location of its campus. Its founders say San Francisco itself is part of the appeal, pointing to its concentration of technology companies, investors, research labs, and startup founders.
Gagan Biyani, a cofounder of the online learning platform Udemy, is the academy's CEO. Marc Andreessen and fellow A16z partner Erik Torenberg sit on its board.
How do I apply, and how much does it cost?
Applications are open online via a form on the website. The early deadline is November 5, 2026, with decisions due by late January 2027. The regular deadline is January 15, after which applications may be considered on a rolling basis if places remain.
Applicants must have completed high school or an equivalent qualification by August 2027. Current college students may apply, but they cannot have completed more than one year of full-time college after high school.
Applicants must submit a portfolio website showing what they have built, a short video, test scores, and a high-school transcript. The academy says admission will be weighted heavily toward "proof of work" rather than grades.
The inaugural fellowship has no tuition. Students must, however, arrange and pay for their housing, meals, and other living expenses in San Francisco. Some need-based assistance may be available.
Participants will receive more than $50,000 in computing credits and a $5,000 travel and research budget.
The academy intends to introduce a two-year paid program in 2028, subject to regulatory approval, with tuition comparable to that of an elite private university.
Who's teaching?
The academy's roster is a major part of its appeal, though anyone expecting to get Sam Altman or Jensen Huang as a full time professor may be disappointed.
While both are listed on the academy's website, they won't be teaching regular classes.
Andreessen is listed as an instructor for "The Next Platform Shift," while Ben Horowitz is on the roster for "Leading Through the Hard Things."
Altman, by contrast, is billed as a guest speaker, although he is 'featured' in the track named "AI Products & Platforms."
The wider network ranges from technology executives, including Nvidia CEO Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, to figures from other fields, such as actor and writer B.J. Novak.
Its subject tracks are similarly eclectic: an AI program features Fei-Fei Li and Meta chief AI scientist Yann LeCun, while other pathways involve neuroscientist Andrew Huberman, longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, former UK government advisor Dominic Cummings, and former US Treasury Secretary Larry Summers.
Those names sit alongside an extensive corporate network. Ten founding partners, including OpenAI, Google, Meta, Nvidia, Palantir, and Anduril, will help shape the curriculum and provide resources.
A broader group of hiring partners, including Databricks, Kraken, and Flock Safety, may consider students for internships and full-time roles.
An 'epic' opportunity or the latest college alternative doomed to fail?
Early reactions on X ranged from enthusiasm about new educational options to those who saw it as unnecessary, potentially overpriced, and even doomed to fail.
Supporters praised the opportunities available to young people. Entrepreneur Jesse Genet called them "epic."
